\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}sitting, and looking up at the shelf{]}} A
clock-case with no face on it. How is anybody meant to tell the time?

\textbf{Tortoise:} The Genie's things don't show you their faces. You
get one look, when they've finished, and that's all.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{first-challenge-the-fifteen-hour-dial}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{First Challenge --- \emph{The Fifteen-Hour
Dial}}{First Challenge --- The Fifteen-Hour Dial}}\label{first-challenge-the-fifteen-hour-dial}}

\textbf{Achilles:} How do you tell how long a thing takes to come round,
if you may look at it only once?

\textbf{Tortoise:} You don't count the ticks. You hear how far one tick
turns it.

\textbf{Achilles:} I should count them. I'd sit in front of it with a
pencil and make a stroke at every tick, till it was home.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Then let's give you something to count, on paper,
where counting costs nothing. \emph{{[}She takes a sheet of paper and a
pencil from the work-bag.{]}} This will be a dial of fifteen hours, with
a paper hand on a pin; the top mark is nought, and an hour is found by
counting marks round from it. One tick sends the hand from the hour it
stands at to seven times that hour, counted round and round the dial.
Ticking it is free.

\emph{{[}She draws a circle and pricks fifteen marks round it, evenly
spaced, the first at the very top, on the side of the sheet furthest
from Achilles, and writes nothing beside any of them; an hour is counted
from it clockwise as Achilles sees it. From the edge of the sheet she
cuts a narrow paper hand, pins it through the centre with a brass pin,
and turns it to the first mark past the top.{]}}

\begin{center}
\tickdial*{hand at one}{the paper dial}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} It starts at one.

\textbf{Achilles:} One tick, then. Seven ones are seven.

\emph{{[}The hand points at the first mark past the top: one. Achilles
takes its tip and carries it round clockwise, past the second mark and
the third and on, counting the marks under his breath, and stops it on
the seventh. The circle, its marks and the pin have not moved. The hand
is the same slip of paper, the same length, pinned at the same place;
only what it points at has changed. One has become seven.{]}}

\begin{center}
\tickdial{hand ticked once}{after a tick}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Two ticks. Seven sevens are forty-nine; less three
fifteens, four. \emph{{[}He carries the hand on round, past the top, to
the fourth mark.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Three ticks. Seven fours are twenty-eight; less one
fifteen, thirteen. \emph{{[}Round again, to the thirteenth mark, two
short of the top.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Four ticks. Seven thirteens are ninety-one; less six
fifteens, one. Home.

\emph{{[}The hand goes over the top once more and stops on the first
mark past it, where it began. It has pointed at seven, at four and at
thirteen on the way; now it points at one, as though it had never
left.{]}}

\begin{center}
\tickdial{hand ticked four times}{home again}
\end{center}

\emph{{[}Up the lane, after all their tumbling, the bells fall back into
the order they began in, the highest first and the deepest last, and
ring it through once and again; then they stop. Achilles lifts his head
at the quiet, and blows on his fingers, and looks back down at the
dial.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Four ticks to come round. That was easy. Any dial can
be ticked round like this; a bigger one only takes a few more ticks.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The dials the Office uses have more hours than there
are grains of frost on that pane. A hand on one of those may take nearly
as many ticks as there are hours before it comes home.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then I'd need a great deal of pencil. But somebody
must know a quicker way.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Nobody has found a quicker way, with paper and
ticking. Nobody has shown there isn't one.

\textbf{Achilles:} And is it worth the pencil? What does anyone want
with a dial's ticks home?

\textbf{Tortoise:} Know them, and they'll split the dial's hours into
two smaller dials. But that's for later.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}looking at the paper hand, back at one{]}}
It's been round and round, and here it is on the same mark, the same
hand, as if it had never left.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The ticking changes where it stands, never what it
is.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then how could anyone find the ticks home without
ticking them all?

\textbf{Tortoise:} By listening to something the ticking doesn't move,
only turns. Can you think of anything on this dial that a tick would
turn, and not move?

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{second-challenge-the-round-turned-whole}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Second Challenge --- \emph{The Round Turned
Whole}}{Second Challenge --- The Round Turned Whole}}\label{second-challenge-the-round-turned-whole}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Nothing. A tick moves the hand; that's all a tick
does. Unless you've something in that bag.

\textbf{Tortoise:} I have. \emph{{[}She brings out a loop of pale twine
threaded with small rings of plain wood, each with an ivory bead set in
it.{]}} This is a round: a loop of string with a ring for each hour the
hand visits, in the hand's order, and in each ring a bead set at some
part of a turn. Laid on the dial, each ring sits at its hour. To tick a
round, you carry every ring to the hour the hand would go to next, and
its bead rides with it, unchanged.

\emph{{[}She lays the round on the dial. A bead at rest stands at the
top of its ring as Achilles sees it; turned round, or forward, it goes
clockwise as he sees it, and turned back, the other way. At one sits a
ring whose bead stands at rest; at seven, a ring whose bead is turned a
quarter back; at four, a bead at a half; at thirteen, a bead three
quarters back. The loop runs straight from each ring to the next in the
order the hand went, and from the last back to the first, crossing
itself once.{]}}

\begin{center}
\tickdial*{first round}{the round as laid}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Tick it.

\emph{{[}The round lies on the dial: at rest at one, a quarter back at
seven, a half at four, three quarters back at thirteen. Achilles lifts
the ring from one and sets it down at seven. The ring from seven he
carries to four, the ring from four to thirteen, and the ring from
thirteen over the top to one. He does not touch a bead: each rides in
its ring, set exactly as it was. When he takes his hands away, every
hour the round covered is covered still, by the same loop in the same
order; but at each hour now sits a different ring. At one, where the
bead at rest stood, there is a bead three quarters back. At seven, where
a quarter back stood, a bead at rest. At four, where the half stood, a
quarter back. At thirteen, where three quarters back stood, a half.{]}}

\begin{center}
\tickdial{first round ticked once}{the round, ticked}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Every ring has gone to a new hour, and not one hour
is empty. And at each hour \emph{{[}going round with a finger{]}} the
bead there now stands a quarter on from the bead that stood there
before. One, a quarter on. Seven, a quarter on. Four, and thirteen, the
same.

\textbf{Achilles:} \ldots Oh. The round hasn't gone anywhere. Every ring
has moved, and the round lies where it lay, only turned, all of it at
once, a quarter round.

\emph{{[}The Tortoise draws the candlestick nearer the dial for him, and
it turns a little in her claw as she sets it down. The twist of its
brass stem goes round with it, and every coil of the twist seems to
climb a step up the stem, though nothing on it has risen.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Tick it four times, then, and it has turned a whole
round, and every bead is back as you set it.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The ticking changes where it stands, never what it
is.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then the round's turn is the thing a tick turns and
doesn't move. A quarter at every tick: four ticks and it's home. I
needn't tick at all; I need only read the quarter.

\textbf{Tortoise:} If you can read it. A bead's turn is not a thing a
window shows you. Let me draw how one would listen for it. \emph{{[}She
spreads her drawing-cloth beside the dial.{]}} My cloth again: what I
lay on it is a picture of a thing, not the thing.

\emph{{[}They both draw in to the cloth, and the Tortoise's chair clacks
over as she comes; Achilles pulls his chair in after her, his breath
showing in the candlelight. Up the lane the ringers have begun again, a
longer piece than the first: the order changes every time through, and
changes faster, and once two bells strike together, a clash that makes
Achilles lift his head, before they part and go on.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}setting her little box of rings and the
packet of tubes on the table beside the cloth, laying a cord across the
part of the cloth nearest Achilles, and threading a red end-ring on its
left end as he sees it{]}} First the round, drawn small: a cord that
begins at a red end-ring, which I'll call the wheel. Lit, with its bead
at a half, it stands for a round the tick turns by a quarter; dark, with
its bead at rest, for a round the tick doesn't turn at all.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}laying a second cord above it, further from
Achilles, and threading a green end-ring at rest on its left end{]}} And
this is a listener: a cord that begins at a green end-ring at rest,
which is a knob set crosswise and dark. It keeps whatever turn it hears.
To read it, I slide one of last night's yellow tubes onto its ring,
which turns the ring red: red at rest reads dark, and red at a half
reads lit.

\emph{{[}On the listener's cord she threads a green ring, and on the
wheel cord another, just below it, each from its cord's loose far end.
She ties both down to a red ring set to their right, midway between the
cords, each by its own short cord, a tie, and from that red ring she
hangs a short pendant running on to the right and ending in a small
green ring of its own, which hangs free.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} This is my shorthand for ``tick the round only if the
listener is lit'', and I'll call it a controlled turn: the red ring in
the middle is its hub, and the little one hanging from it is its bob.
For a turn of a quarter, each green ring gets its bead at an eighth,
half the turn, and the bob gets an eighth back.

\emph{{[}She sets the beads: an eighth on the listener's ring, an eighth
on the wheel's ring, an eighth back on the bob. The hub she leaves
bare.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} It doesn't look as if it cares which cord is which.

\textbf{Tortoise:} It doesn't. Light the wheel.

\emph{{[}She turns the bead in the wheel's end-ring to a half: lit. The
picture as it stands: above, the listener's green end-ring at rest, then
its green ring at an eighth; below, the wheel's red end-ring at a half,
then its green ring at an eighth; the two green rings tied to the bare
red hub, and the bob hanging from the hub at an eighth back.{]}}

\begin{center}
\tickcloth*{one listener; wheel lit}{a controlled turn, the wheel lit}
\end{center}

\emph{{[}First she slides the eighth off the wheel's green ring onto a
little green bob of its own, hung from that ring on a short length: the
ring is at rest now, its new bob at an eighth, and nothing else has
changed. Then she pushes the lit end-ring along the wheel cord into the
ring, the stretch of wheel cord it ran along swallowed with it. It goes
in, and the ring is gone; out come copies of the lit end, one on each
length that led into the ring: one on the wheel cord beyond, one at the
foot of the tie, one on the short length to the new bob. That last copy
meets the new bob, and the two close up into no ring at all, only a turn
of the whole picture, an eighth, which she sets aside, off the cloth.
The copy at the foot of the tie she slides along it into the red hub,
the tie swallowed behind it: red into red, and the hub, bare a moment
ago, stands at a half.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} An eighth set aside. Now the hub goes through the
bob.

\emph{{[}The hub, red at a half, has two cords left: the tie up to the
listener's ring, and the pendant down to the bob. She pushes it down the
pendant into the bob. Its half passes into the bob and, the bob having
no other cord, is gone; the bob's bead, which stood an eighth back,
turns the other way and stands an eighth forward, and its old turn, an
eighth back, she sets aside beside the first. The hub is left at rest
with two cords, and it slips off: tie and pendant are one cord now,
running from the listener's ring straight to the bob.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} An eighth set aside, and an eighth back. What we set
aside, we get back.

\emph{{[}She slides the bob along that cord up into the listener's ring,
the cord swallowed with it. Green into green: they run together, and
their beads add, an eighth and an eighth. The listener's ring and its
end-ring, green on one cord, slide together too, the ring back along the
cord into the end-ring, the stretch between swallowed, into one end-ring
at a quarter. What lies on the cloth now: no hub, no bob, no tie. The
wheel's end-ring lies just past where its green ring stood, lit, red at
a half, and the wheel cord runs on from it to its far end as before.
What has changed is the listener alone: it began at rest, and now it
holds a quarter. What has held is the wheel, lit going in and lit coming
out.{]}}

\begin{center}
\tickcloth[push the wheel]{one listener; wheel lit}{the turn landed}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} So what you're saying is that the wheel gave its
quarter to the listener.

\textbf{Tortoise:} It gave nothing away; it's lit as it was. The
listener asked to be ticked, and the turn came back to the cord that
asked. Now dark.

\emph{{[}She gathers the cloth clear, the rings into her little box of
rings and the string into her work-bag, and lays it all again: the
listener at rest, the two green rings at an eighth, the bob at an eighth
back, and this time the wheel's end-ring red with its bead at rest. She
pushes the dark end in the same way, the stretch of wheel cord it runs
along swallowed with it. Its copies carry nothing: the eighth she slid
off the wheel's ring onto its own bob closes up into nothing at all, and
there is nothing to set aside. The hub, red at rest, slips off. The bob,
an eighth back, runs up into the listener's ring, the cord swallowed
with it, an eighth forward, and they cancel; the ring, at rest with two
cords, slips off too. The listener lies as it was laid, a green end-ring
at rest, and the wheel is dark in and dark out. The whole controlled
turn has fallen away.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} From now on it's one move. Push a dark end through a
controlled turn, and the whole turn falls away; push a lit end through,
and the whole turn lands on the other cord's ring.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then I have it. One listener, one tube, and it tells
me the turn.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Does it? \emph{{[}She takes two green end-rings from
her little box of rings, sets one bead a quarter round and the other
three quarters round, and lays them side by side on the cloth.{]}} Here
are two listeners, one that heard a quarter and one that heard three
quarters.

\emph{{[}She holds the two rings up to the candle. The beads stand at
the same slant from upright, the one leaning to the right, the other to
the left, like a minute hand at a quarter past and at a quarter to.
Nothing about them differs but the side. She lays them back where they
lay.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} A tube asks only how near to rest a bead stands, and
these two stand equally near: even odds, both of them. A turn of none
reads dark every time, and a half lit every time; anything else, only
odds.

\emph{{[}The ringing up the lane has stopped, and in the quiet the
church clock gives a single stroke. It is the one stroke it gives at
every half hour, and the one it gives at one in the morning; heard by
itself, it is the same stroke at half past any hour. Achilles tucks his
hands under his arms and frowns at the candle.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Then one listener can never tell a quarter from three
quarters.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Not by itself. What would a listener hear, do you
think, if the wheel ticked twice for it?

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{third-challenge-twice-the-pace}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Third Challenge --- \emph{Twice the
Pace}}{Third Challenge --- Twice the Pace}}\label{third-challenge-twice-the-pace}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Twice a quarter is a half. And a half reads lit every
time.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Let's see it. \emph{{[}She gathers the cloth clear,
the rings into her little box of rings and the string into her work-bag,
and lays it out again: the wheel cord lowest, its end-ring lit; above it
the listener, with its controlled turn for a quarter laid as before,
close to the end-rings.{]}} A second listener above the first, and a
controlled turn that ticks the wheel twice for it: twice the turn, so a
quarter on each of its green rings and a quarter back on its bob.

\emph{{[}The second listener goes above the first, beginning at a green
end-ring at rest; it is the upper listener now, and the first the lower.
On it she threads a green ring at a quarter, further along than the
first turn's rings, and on the wheel cord a second green ring at a
quarter, below it, each from its cord's loose far end; she ties both to
a new red hub set to their right, between the lower listener's cord and
the wheel cord, the tie from above passing beneath the lower listener's
cord, joined to it nowhere, and hangs from the hub a bob a quarter back,
running on to the right.{]}}

\begin{center}
\tickcloth*{two listeners}{another listener above}
\end{center}

\emph{{[}She pushes the lit wheel end along its cord, the cord it runs
along swallowed behind it. It meets the first controlled turn, and the
whole turn lands on the lower listener's ring: a quarter. It runs on,
lit still, into the second, and the whole of that turn lands on the
upper listener's ring: a half. On each listener's cord the green ring
slides back along it into the end-ring, as before, the stretch between
swallowed. Then she runs the wheel's end-ring on to the wheel cord's far
end. No hub or bob is left on the cloth. The wheel cord ends as it
began, lit. The lower listener has gone from at rest to a quarter, and
the upper from at rest to a half.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}taking a tube from the packet and sliding it
onto the upper listener's end-ring, where it goes in and is gone; the
ring turns red, its bead still at a half{]}} Lit.

\textbf{Achilles:} And if the wheel turned three quarters? Twice three
quarters is one and a half, and a whole turn is no turn, so a half. Lit
again. For a half, twice a half is a whole: dark. For none, dark.

\textbf{Tortoise:} So the upper listener hears only whether the quarters
are odd. It can't tell you which odd.

\emph{{[}Achilles looks up from the cloth, past the candle, to the print
on the wall facing the window: Escher's
\textup{Regular Division of the Plane}.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} A sheet filled edge to edge with figures fitted
against one another, with no gap between them. If you slid it along,
would it land on itself, and how far would you have to slide it?

\emph{{[}As he looks, the candle flame leans in a breath of air from the
stairs, and its light slides across the sheet from one edge of the frame
to the other, and back, and is still. The Tortoise does not look up from
the cloth.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} The lower listener heard a quarter, or three
quarters. The upper one has told us which kind it was: odd. So take the
odd quarter away, and see what's left.

\emph{{[}Between the upper listener's cord, just past its end-ring, and
the lower listener's cord she lays one more controlled turn: a green
ring on each, threaded on from the cord's loose far end, both beads an
eighth back, tied to a red hub to their right, between the two
listeners' cords, whose bob hangs an eighth forward, running on to the
right.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} A controlled turn of a quarter back, and the upper
listener's own reading drives it.

\emph{{[}The upper listener's end-ring is red, at a half: lit. She
pushes it along its cord into the new controlled turn, the stretch it
runs along swallowed with it, and the whole turn lands on the lower
listener's ring: a quarter back, and that ring slides back along its
cord into the lower listener's end-ring, as before. The lower listener,
which held a quarter, now holds a quarter and a quarter back, which is
none. The upper listener's end-ring runs on, lit, as it was, and comes
to rest just past where its green ring stood. What has changed is the
lower listener only, from a quarter to at rest.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}taking another tube from the packet and
sliding it onto the lower listener's end-ring, where it goes in and is
gone; the ring turns red, at rest{]}} Dark.

\textbf{Achilles:} And for three quarters, three quarters and a quarter
back make a half. Lit.

\textbf{Tortoise:} And if the upper had read dark, the correction would
have fallen away, and the lower would keep what it heard, none or a
half. Now, which to read first.

\emph{{[}The two listeners' far ends lie one above the other, the
upper's above, the lower's below. She takes them and crosses them, the
lower's end passing over the other without touching it, and lays them
down again. Not a bead on either cord has changed, nor an end; only
which lies on top. The lower listener's reading now lies uppermost.{]}}

\begin{center}
\tickcloth[push the wheel, on to the far end, tube on the upper, lay the correction, push the upper, tube on the lower, cross]{two listeners}{read, and the far ends crossed}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} The half first, then the quarter.

\textbf{Achilles:} So the top one says whether the wheel turns a half,
and the one beneath says whether there's an odd quarter besides. None is
dark and dark. A quarter is dark, then lit. A half is lit, then dark.
Three quarters, lit and lit.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Every one of them certain. And a wheel that turned in
eighths would want a third listener, ticked four times, and another
correction; every listener ticked twice as fast hears one finer place.

\textbf{Achilles:} And the wheel? \emph{{[}He touches the wheel cord's
far end: red, at a half.{]}} It has been ticked once for one listener
and twice for the other, and it comes out lit, just as it went in.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The ticking changes where it stands, never what it
is.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}turning to the shelf{]}} Then a case built
to do all that could read its wheel in one passage.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}taking the candlestick up to the shelf{]}}
This is the Genie's clock-case, and the Office sent it for one wish. The
knob low on its left side is the only thing on it you may set: down for
dark, up for lit, and tonight it stands down. Down the right side are
its windows, the first and the second above and the wheel window lowest,
level with the knob; after the passage each shows dark, a plain pane, or
lit, a small gleam, and keeps what it shows.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}bending to the top of the case, where a
small oval of enamel is set{]}} And a plate on top. \emph{{[}reading{]}}
``The Terms. One wish, one passage. Inside is a wheel: lit, it turns by
the same whole number of quarter-turns at every tick; dark, it does not
turn. With the wheel knob down, every window shows dark. What the case
does with the wheel lit is the wisher's business.''

\textbf{Achilles:} The same whole number of quarters at every tick, and
it doesn't say how many. None, one, two or three: just what your
listeners read.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}setting the candlestick back on the
table{]}} The Terms are short, and they keep to them. The lamp is the
same as last night: rub it once, and the Genie comes.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}reaching up, and taking the lamp down from
the shelf{]}} Once, I remember.

\emph{{[}The lamp lies in Achilles's hands as it has lain on the shelf
since last night: brass, tarnished, cold, its wick dry, never lit. He
rubs its side once with his thumb. Nothing in it warms. From the spout a
pale thread leans out into the cold air, turns on itself like a ribbon
being wound, and fills; and there between the table and the window
stands the Genie, straightening his cuffs. The lamp in Achilles's hands
is just as it was, dull and cold and no lighter. What is new is a third
at the table. Achilles sets the lamp down beside the candlestick.{]}}

\emph{{[}While the pale thread stood, the candlelight drew in off the
walls toward the lamp, the corners of the room going dark one after
another as though the light were being gathered up; now it goes back out
to them, and every shadow settles where it was. Achilles's breath shows
white at every word, and the Tortoise's; the Genie's does not show at
all. Up the lane the tower is silent.{]}}

\textbf{Genie:} The Office of Wishes. \emph{{[}He glances along the
shelf to the case.{]}} Ah. You have the newer model. The Office is
rather proud of it.

\textbf{Genie:} One wish is one passage of the whole case, however often
its wheel turns inside. What the case does inside is the case's
business.

\textbf{Achilles:} And turning the knob?

\textbf{Genie:} Setting the knob is not a wish. Nor is any arithmetic
you do afterwards with what the windows show. There is one wish this
evening.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then I wish to be told how many quarters the wheel
turns.

\textbf{Genie:} Referred. \emph{{[}He tilts his head, as though
listening up a stairwell, and straightens at once.{]}} The Meta-Genie
regrets. The quarter-turns are the case's to tell, and the case tells
only by passage. Nothing has been spent.

\emph{{[}On the table a point of candlelight runs up the lamp's curved
handle to the top and down again, all in the one instant, though neither
the candle nor the lamp has moved. The lamp is as cold as it was.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Then I wish to have the wheel ticked a thousand
times, with the front open, while I watch.

\textbf{Genie:} Referred. \emph{{[}A blink.{]}} The reply has come down
from well above the Meta-Genie: a wish to watch is a wish to see inside,
and the front opens on a spent case and on no other. Your wish is
untouched.

\textbf{Achilles:} From well above, and back already?

\textbf{Genie:} No floor of the Office keeps a reply waiting. It goes
all the way up, and the answer comes all the way down, at once.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then one more. If the passage shows me nothing I can
use, I wish for a second.

\textbf{Genie:} Referred. \emph{{[}A blink.{]}} The reply is that there
is one wish this evening. A reading that fails to give what the wisher
wanted is still a spent wish; another reading would be another wish, and
the Office grants one.

\textbf{Tortoise:} You'll wear the Meta-Genie out.

\textbf{Genie:} Nobody has yet.

\emph{{[}Achilles laughs in spite of himself, and the Tortoise's chair
clacks as she sits back to enjoy it. He winds his scarf once more round
his neck and holds his hands to the candle.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} May I at least bring the case to the table?

\textbf{Genie:} Carrying is not a wish either. Keep it upright. The
Office labels its boxes for a reason.

\emph{{[}Achilles lifts the case from the shelf in both hands and sets
it on the table beside the cloth, its front towards him, its knob on the
left side, its windows down the right, evenly spaced, each a round pane
in a thin brass rim. Down the front's right-hand edge, where the front
closes against the side, a faded paper band is pasted down the join: the
seal. It stands as it has stood all evening: knob down, every pane
plain, the seal whole.{]}}

\emph{{[}He puts his fingers to the wheel knob. It stands down: dark. He
turns it up until it stops. The knob is the only thing on the case that
has moved; the panes are plain, the seal is whole, the front is shut, as
before. Down has become up: the wheel is lit.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} The wheel lit, and everything the case does inside,
ticking and all. Is that one wish?

\textbf{Genie:} One passage of the whole case, as it is now set. One
wish.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then I wish it.

\textbf{Genie:} Granted.

\emph{{[}The case as it stands: knob up, every pane plain, the seal
whole. At the word nothing on it moves, not the knob, not the front.
Behind the first window the pane stays plain. Behind the second a small
gleam comes up and stays. Behind the wheel window, another. Achilles
touches the knob, and it will not turn back; it is locked where he set
it. The seal down the front's right-hand edge has parted of itself, in
the middle. What has changed: two gleams, the lock, the seal. What has
held: the knob, up; the first pane, plain; the front, still shut.{]}}

\begin{center}
\clockcase*[windows]{knob up; granted}{after the passage}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} The first plain, the second lit, and the wheel lit.
No half, and an odd quarter: one quarter, no more.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}looking across at the paper dial, where the
hand stands at one{]}} \ldots Oh. A quarter round at every tick, so home
in four. And nobody ticked it where I could count.

\emph{{[}Achilles's hand goes to his waistcoat pocket, as it does
whenever he wants to count something, and comes out with his watch. He
looks at it once: the short hand most of the way to nine, and the long
hand, which goes round so much faster, at the eight. That one look gives
him the time to the minute, and he puts the watch away.{]}}

\textbf{Genie:} The case is spent. A secret read is no longer a secret,
and the front may be opened.

\emph{{[}The case as it stands: spent, the knob locked up, the second
pane and the wheel pane gleaming, the first plain, the seal parted.
Achilles takes the front by its edge and swings it open on its hinge at
the left. The knob does not move, nor the panes, nor their gleams; only
the front swings back, and the candle shines into the case.{]}}

\emph{{[}Inside, row by row from the top. The upper row begins at a
green ring whose bead stands a quarter round, with nothing to the left
of it. From that ring a cord runs along the row, through a fixed yellow
collar set crosswise on it, to a second green ring, whose bead stands an
eighth back; it is knotted at the one ring and at the other. From the
second ring another cord runs on, and down, to the second window,
knotted at the ring and at the window. Below, the lower row begins at a
green ring whose bead stands at rest; from it a cord runs through a
second fixed collar and then up to the first window, knotted at the ring
and at the window. On the way these two cords cross, the one going down
and the other going up, the one going up passing over the one going down
without touching it. Lowest lies the wheel row: a cord from the wheel
knob to a green wheel ring, whose bead stands three eighths round,
knotted at the knob and at the ring; and from the wheel ring a cord on
to the wheel window, knotted at both its ends. Among the rows hang red
hubs, with no beads in them, each between the rows it ties, one after
another from left to right. The first hub has a tie of its own up to the
upper row's first ring, another down to the wheel ring, and a pendant
hanging to a small green bob a quarter back. The second hub has a tie to
the lower ring, another to the wheel ring, and a pendant to a bob an
eighth back. The third hub has a tie to the upper row's second ring,
another to the lower ring, and a pendant to a bob an eighth forward.
Every length is knotted at both its ends, and no cord passes through a
ring. What has changed is only that the inside can be seen; every gleam
can now be followed back, cord by cord, to where it began.{]}}

\begin{center}
\clockcase*[inside]{knob up; granted; front open}{the front open}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} A quarter round on the upper row's first ring. The
quarter was in the case all along, and no window showed it until it was
asked the right way.

\textbf{Tortoise:} So the first window has the half, and the second the
quarter.

\textbf{Genie:} The wish has been spent in accordance with the Terms.
The Office does not collect spent boxes.

\emph{{[}The lamp stands where Achilles set it down beside the
candlestick, cold, as it has been since he rubbed it. The Genie folds in
on himself from the shoulders down, as a ribbon is wound back onto its
card, thins to the pale thread he came as, and the thread runs into the
spout and is gone. The lamp does not stir or warm. The case stays open
on the table, its panes still showing what they showed, and nothing else
in the room has moved. There are two at the table again.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}taking up the lamp and setting it back on
its shelf{]}} Back where it lives.

\emph{{[}Up on its shelf, out of the candle's reach, the lamp is only
brass again, beside the clean patch in the dust where the case stood all
evening. Up the lane the bells begin again: a plainer piece than before,
easy to follow, the highest bell working down through the others one
place at a time and then back up, while the rest give way to it in turn.
The Tortoise sits back down, and her chair clacks.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}looking from the open case to the paper
dial{]}} The Office's case had its wheel lit on a round of its own; the
Office saw to that. But the dial's hand, standing at one, isn't on any
one round at all.

\textbf{Tortoise:} No.~It's on all of them. What do you suppose one wish
would read from a hand that stands on every round at once?

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{fourth-challenge-every-round-at-once}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Fourth Challenge --- \emph{Every Round at
Once}}{Fourth Challenge --- Every Round at Once}}\label{fourth-challenge-every-round-at-once}}

\textbf{Achilles:} One round's turn, I suppose. But which?

\textbf{Tortoise:} Let's lay them all, and see. First put yours back as
I set it.

\emph{{[}The first round still lies on the dial as Achilles last left
it, ticked once: three quarters back at one, at rest at seven, a quarter
back at four, a half at thirteen. He ticks it three times more, each
time carrying every ring on to the hand's next hour, beads untouched; at
each tick every hour's bead stands a quarter on again. After the third,
the ring whose bead is at rest is back at one, a quarter back at seven,
a half at four, three quarters back at thirteen: every bead where she
first set it, and the loop lying where it always lay.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Four ticks in all, and it's as you laid it.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}bringing three more loops out of the
work-bag, each threaded with rings like the first{]}} These are the rest
of this dial's rounds. The one you ticked goes a quarter back at each
step along the hand's way; this one stands at rest all round; this one
goes a half at each step; and this one three quarters back.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Laid one over another, the beads at each hour are
read together, as pointers. Two beads pointing opposite ways cancel, and
I turn both face down; beads all at rest add, and stay face up.

\emph{{[}She lays the other three rounds over the first on the dial, so
that at each of the hand's hours four rings sit together in a little
square, side by side so that every bead shows: the ring of the round he
ticked at the far left as Achilles sees it, the ring of the round at
rest at the far right, the half's at the near left and the three
quarters back's at the near right. At one: four beads, every one at
rest. At seven: one at rest, one a quarter back, one at a half, one
three quarters back, pointing four ways. At four: two at rest, two at a
half. At thirteen: one at rest, one three quarters back, one at a half,
one a quarter back, four ways again.{]}}

\begin{center}
\tickdial{every round}{the rounds together}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}going round with a finger{]}} At one they
all agree. At seven, the one at rest faces the half, and the quarter
back faces the three quarters back. At four, rest faces half, twice
over. At thirteen, just as at seven.

\emph{{[}The Tortoise takes the rings at seven in pairs, each bead with
the one that points against it, and turns each pair face down on the
dial, bead to bead, so that neither shows and the pair lies as one plain
ring, the two pairs at an hour side by side; then the rings at four, and
then at thirteen. The loops still run from hour to hour, but at seven,
four and thirteen no bead shows at all. At one the four rings lie face
up in their little square, their beads all at rest. What has changed:
every hour the hand visits but one shows nothing. What has held: the
hour one, and the four beads on it, at rest, where the hand began.{]}}

\begin{center}
\tickdial{every round; pairs face down}{turned face down}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} So all the rounds laid together are the hand at one,
and nothing else.

\emph{{[}Achilles's eye goes past the dial to the floor under the shelf.
Where the candlelight passes through the tall glass jar, it comes out on
the floor beyond as a faint patch of colours, red at one edge and violet
at the other; everywhere else in the room it is only candlelight.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} So a passage with the hand at one can only read one
round's turn, and which round is chance, the same chance for each: none,
a quarter, a half or three quarters.

\textbf{Achilles:} And if we tick the whole pile, each round turns by
its own amount, and not one of them goes anywhere?

\textbf{Tortoise:} The ticking changes where it stands, never what it
is.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then let me rub the lamp and see which round we get.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The wish is spent, and the Genie with it. We'll
suppose instead. Suppose a case built on this dial, with the hand at one
inside it where the wheel was, had shown you a half.

\textbf{Achilles:} A half at every tick: two ticks home.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Tick it and see.

\emph{{[}The paper hand stands at one. Achilles carries it once round to
seven, and once more, seven sevens less three fifteens, to the fourth
mark; and there he lets go. It points at four, not at one. Two ticks
have moved it twice, and it has not come home.{]}}

\begin{center}
\tickdial{hand ticked twice; every round; pairs face down}{the hand gone on}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Four. Not home.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}frowning at the slack loops{]}} The half
came from the round that goes a half at each step, and that round comes
home in two. The hand doesn't.

\textbf{Tortoise:} And the other readings?

\textbf{Achilles:} A quarter says four ticks home, and so does three
quarters, and four ticks from one bring the hand home. None says nothing
at all. Two of the four readings give it, then. Half the time.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Half the time, from one wish. And a half or a none is
still a spent wish; another reading would be another wish.

\emph{{[}Up the lane the plain piece comes to its end, and the bells
fall into the order they began the evening with, highest to deepest, and
ring it over and over, every bell in its own place; at every deepest
stroke the jar under the shelf hums back. Achilles sits back, tucks his
hands under his arms, and listens.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} So the wish finds the ticks home half the time. But
you said the ticks home would split the dial.

\textbf{Tortoise:} They will. How would you measure one number by
another, with nothing but paper?

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{fifth-challenge-euclids-strips}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Fifth Challenge --- \emph{Euclid's
Strips}}{Fifth Challenge --- Euclid's Strips}}\label{fifth-challenge-euclids-strips}}

\textbf{Achilles:} With a ruler, I suppose. Only I haven't brought one.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}bringing a rule, a pair of scissors and a
fresh sheet out of the work-bag{]}} I have a rule, marked in thumbs, and
scissors. Lay a short strip along a long one as many times as it fits,
pencil how many times on the long strip, and cut off what's left; then
lay what you cut off along the short one, the same way. When a cut
leaves nothing, the last short strip measures both.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then what do I measure?

\textbf{Tortoise:} The dial, by the hand at half its ticks home. Four
ticks home: half of four is two, and after two ticks the hand stood at
four.

\emph{{[}Up the lane the ringers are ringing down: the strokes come
quicker and softer and closer together, the order lost among them, until
they run into one small jangle and stop. The tower is silent, and the
jar under the shelf gives a last faint hum and is still.{]}}

\emph{{[}Achilles cuts a strip fifteen thumbs long, for the dial, and
another four thumbs long, for the hand. The long strip lies along the
table's edge on his side; the short one lies beside it, further from
him, their left ends level. He lays the short strip at the long one's
left end, pencils a tick where it stops, and lays it again from the
tick, and again: three times it fits, and past the last tick there is a
piece of the long strip that the four cannot cover. He sets the short
strip back beside it.{]}}

\begin{center}
\tickstrips*{fifteen and four}{the short strip laid along}
\end{center}

\emph{{[}He pencils the count on the long strip and snips it at the last
tick; the measured part, with its count on it, he lays aside, and the
piece left past the last tick he slides along the edge to where the long
strip began. What has changed: the long strip is gone from the edge, and
in its place lies the piece it could not measure, three thumbs long.
What has held: the four-thumb strip, which has not been cut at all.{]}}

\begin{center}
\tickstrips[first cut]{fifteen and four}{after the snip}
\end{center}

\emph{{[}The three goes along the four once, and one thumb is left over;
he cuts it off. The one goes along the three three times, and nothing is
left.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} One thumb. That measures anything, and it tells me
nothing.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Not the hour itself. One either side of it.

\textbf{Achilles:} Three and five. Why those?

\textbf{Tortoise:} Multiply them and you get the hour times itself, less
one. The hour times itself is the hand ticked on as many ticks again,
which is home at one: one past a whole number of dials. Take the one
away, and three times five is whole dials exactly, so each of them may
take a share of the dial.

\emph{{[}A fresh strip of fifteen thumbs, and one of three. The three
goes along the fifteen five times, and at the fifth the ends meet
exactly; there is nothing to cut. He does the same with a strip of five:
it goes along three times, and nothing is left.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Fifteen is three fives.

\emph{{[}Down in the lane feet go by on the frozen ruts: two of the
ringers going home past the house, the one with a long stride and the
other with a short. Their steps fall together, and apart, and together
again, at every third step of the one and every fifth of the other,
until they are out of hearing.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Now a harder dial. \emph{{[}She draws a second circle
on the fresh sheet, pricks twenty-one marks round it, the first at the
top, on the side furthest from Achilles, as on the first, and pins a
second paper hand at its centre, turned to one.{]}} This one has
twenty-one hours, and its tick doubles the hour. Suppose a finer case
than the Office's had read its turn for you as five parts in thirty-two.

\textbf{Achilles:} Five parts in thirty-two isn't a quarter or a half of
anything.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Strips, then. Thirty-two and five.

\emph{{[}Achilles cuts a strip thirty-two thumbs long and one of five.
The five goes along the thirty-two six times, and two thumbs are left
over; he pencils six on the long strip and cuts the two off. The two
goes along the five twice, and one thumb is left; he pencils two and
cuts. The one goes along the two twice, and nothing is left at all. The
counts he has pencilled read, in order, six, two, two.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Five goes into thirty-two six times, with a little
over. So five parts in thirty-two is a little less than one part in six:
a sixth of a turn at every tick, and six ticks home.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The later counts only say how little the little over
is. A real case for a dial this size would be made finer still, so that
the strips can't mislead; five in thirty-two is only our supposing.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}ticking the new hand from one{]}} Two, four,
eight, sixteen. Thirty-two, less twenty-one: eleven. Twenty-two, less
twenty-one: one. Home in six.

\emph{{[}Ticked six times, the second hand has pointed at two, four,
eight, sixteen and eleven, and now stands again on the first mark past
the top, where it started. It is the same paper hand on the same pin;
the twenty-one marks have not moved.{]}}

\begin{center}
\tickdial{twenty-one hours; hand ticked six times}{the new hand, home}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Six ticks, and it's on the mark it left.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The ticking changes where it stands, never what it
is.

\textbf{Achilles:} Half of six is three, and after three ticks it stood
at eight. One either side: seven and nine.

\emph{{[}A strip of twenty-one thumbs and one of seven: the seven goes
along three times, and nothing is left. A fresh twenty-one and a nine:
the nine goes along twice, and three are left over; he cuts them off,
and the three goes along the nine three times, and nothing is left. The
last short strips lie side by side: seven thumbs, and three.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Seven, and three. Twenty-one is three sevens.

\textbf{Tortoise:} So what has the evening done?

\textbf{Achilles:} A tick moves the hand, but it only turns a round. One
listener hears the turn, but blurred. Listeners ticked twice, and four
times, each hear one finer place, and one wish reads the whole turn. The
hand at one is every round at once, so a wish reads a round at random,
and half the time that's enough. Then paper and strips do the rest.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The case only reads the turn. Turning a turn into
factors is done with strips, and how long it all takes was reckoned on
paper, not by drawing.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}looking at the candle{]}} The candle's
burned lower than I thought.

\textbf{Tortoise:} It always goes faster up here. The cold makes it
hurry.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}looking into the open case{]}} And its panes
are still showing. The second, and the wheel.

\textbf{Tortoise:} It'll keep them. It's spent; showing is all it has
left to do.

\textbf{Achilles:} Like the casket downstairs, with the jam.

\textbf{Tortoise:} They'll have a great deal to say to each other.

\emph{{[}Achilles laughs, and the Tortoise laughs under her breath with
him, and for a while neither says anything. The lane is quiet now the
ringers have gone. Somewhere below them, in the parlour, the stove's
iron ticks now and then as it cools, to no count at all.{]}}

\emph{{[}Achilles unwinds his scarf and puts it round the Tortoise's
shoulders.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Keep it up here tonight. It seems to belong to this
room.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}settling it{]}} Thank you. I'll bring it
down in the morning, and the stair can groan at me for a change.

\emph{{[}Up the lane, the church clock begins to strike.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}a finger lifting at each stroke, under his
breath{]}} \ldots seven, eight, nine. Nine o'clock. I counted every
stroke.

\textbf{Tortoise:} You always will.

\textbf{Achilles:} How do you tell how long a thing takes to come round,
if you may look at it only once?

\textbf{Tortoise:} You don't count the ticks. You hear how far one tick
turns it.

\emph{{[}She takes up the candlestick, and the case stays open on the
table, its panes still showing.{]}}

\emph{{[}The candle stands low in its stick, guttered down to a small
flame, and as she lifts it every shadow in the room swings round and
shortens. With her free claw she takes the scarf from her shoulders,
folds it, and lays it folded on the seat of her chair, where it will be
in the morning. On the wall facing the window, past her shoulder, the
print is at the edge of the light again, half in her shadow: a sheet in
a plain dark frame on a cold wall. Then the candle goes to the door, and
Achilles after it, and the stair takes them down its one turn; halfway,
a tread groans under Achilles's foot, as it will for him every time.
Behind them the top room is dark and still: the case open on the table
where Achilles set it, the lamp on its shelf, the paper and the strips
where they were left, the print that nobody can see now, and over the
whole of the pane the frost going on with its work, the old initials
white in it. From the foot of the stairs comes the sound of the stove
door opening, and the kettle going on. Up the lane the tower is dark,
and the clock in it goes on round towards ten, and at ten it will strike
again, whether anyone counts or not.{]}}

\hypertarget{chapter-14-shors-hidden-periods}{%
\chapter{Chapter 14: Shor's Hidden
Periods}\label{chapter-14-shors-hidden-periods}}

\emph{--- Aria with Periodic Variations ---}

\emph{Part IV: Algorithms}

\emph{Escher: ``Regular Division of the Plane'' --- a sheet filled edge
to edge with figures fitted against one another, with no gap between
them}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

How do you tell how long a thing takes to come round, if you may look at
it only once?

With a clock the answer is easy, because you may keep looking. You watch
the hand until it is back where it began and count the ticks on the way.
The tides, the phases of the moon and a child on a swing are all timed
the same way: you wait for the return. The method is honest and certain,
and it costs exactly as many ticks as the thing takes to come round. For
anything that comes round slowly, that is a great many.

Now suppose you may not watch. The thing is sealed in a case, it ticks
inside, and you are allowed one glance. One glance at a hand tells you
where it stands. It does not tell you how fast it is going. A hand that
has come round once in twelve ticks and a hand that has come round five
times look exactly alike if they happen to stand at the same place.
Where a thing stands is a fact about one moment. How long it takes to
come round is a fact about all the moments together, and a glance is
only one of them.

It turns out that one of the oldest problems in arithmetic is a problem
of exactly this kind. Take a large number, multiply by a fixed smaller
number over and over, and keep only the remainders on dividing by a
third. The remainders come round in a cycle, and the length of that
cycle holds the key to splitting the third number into its factors.
Nobody knows a quick way to find the length by ticking. The cycle can be
longer than the age of the universe measured in ticks of the fastest
machine anyone could build.

This chapter finds it with one glance, or close to it. The trick is that
a quantum glance need not be at the hand. It can be at something the
ticking does not move, only turns, and a turn can be read, digit by
digit, by listeners that tick at doubled pace. The pictures of the last
six chapters will show how the listening works, down to where each digit
is heard. They will not show everything. The step from the length of a
cycle to a factor is number theory, and it has no picture. We will say
where the pictures stop, and why.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-fifteen-hour-dial}{%
\section{§14.1 The Fifteen-Hour Dial}\label{the-fifteen-hour-dial}}

Chapter 13 closed with a promise: ``Chapter 14 keeps the pattern and
changes the layers. Simon's round, with the second layer of Hadamards
replaced by a Fourier transform over a larger group, is where Shor began
\ldots{} The box will hide not a string but a period, the query will be
a controlled multiplication, and the pictures will again be kickback
diagrams, the marks copied back along their ties. What will change is
how much of the work the pictures can do. The number theory that turns a
period into a factor stays on the blackboard, and we will say so.'' We
begin with the period.

\textbf{On the blackboard.} Fix a whole number \(N>1\), the number we
would like to factor, and a \textbf{base} \(a\) with \(1<a<N\) that
shares no factor with \(N\), \(\gcd(a,N)=1\). We work with remainders on
dividing by \(N\): write \(u\equiv v\pmod N\) when \(N\) divides
\(u-v\), and \(u\bmod N\) for the remainder, a number between \(0\) and
\(N-1\). Shor writes \(n\) for the number and \(x\) for the base; we
write \(N\) and \(a\) throughout.

Picture the \(N\) remainders as the hours of a dial, with \(0\) at the
top. One \textbf{tick} moves the hand from the hour \(x\) to the hour
\(ax\bmod N\). Start the hand at \(1\). Take \(N=15\) and \(a=7\). The
first tick gives \(7\). The second gives \(49=3\cdot15+4\), so \(4\).
The third gives \(28=15+13\), so \(13\). The fourth gives
\(91=6\cdot15+1\), so \(1\): the hand is home after four ticks. The
least number of ticks that brings the hand home from \(1\) is the
\textbf{order} of \(a\) mod \(N\), written \(r\): the least \(r\ge1\)
with \(a^r\equiv1\pmod N\) (Shor §5). For \(7\) mod \(15\), \(r=4\). It
is a period hidden in the multiplication table.

The quantum version of the tick is a box. Take enough wires to hold the
numbers \(0,\dots,N-1\) in binary, top wire most significant (four wires
for \(N=15\)), and define the \textbf{tick box}

\[U_a\,\ket x\;=\;\ket{ax\bmod N}\qquad(0\le x<N),\]

letting \(U_a\) leave alone any basis state \(\ket x\) with \(x\ge N\)
that the wires can also hold.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 14.1 (the order, and the tick box).} If \(\gcd(a,N)=1\),
then \(x\mapsto ax\bmod N\) is a permutation of \(\{0,\dots,N-1\}\), so
\(U_a\) is unitary; the order \(r\) exists; and \(U_a^r=I\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} If \(ax\equiv ax'\) then \(N\) divides \(a(x-x')\), and
since \(a\) shares no factor with \(N\), \(N\) divides \(x-x'\), so
\(x=x'\). A one-to-one map of a finite set to itself is a permutation,
so \(U_a\) permutes basis states and its matrix has one \(1\) in each
row and column: it is unitary. The powers \(a,a^2,a^3,\dots\) take at
most \(N\) values mod \(N\), so two agree, \(a^i\equiv a^{i+d}\) with
\(d\ge1\); multiplying by the inverse of \(a^i\) (which exists, since
\(x\mapsto a^ix\) is a permutation) gives \(a^d\equiv1\). The least such
\(d\) is \(r\). Finally \(U_a^r\ket x=\ket{a^rx\bmod N}=\ket x\).
\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch14/HandsRound.py}, which also
checks the order by ticking against the least \(r\) with \(a^r\equiv1\)
for random pairs \((N,a)\).

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} The tick box is Chapter 5's tall box (§5.3),
laid across the register's wires and labelled \(U_a\). It hides
everything inside it, as an oracle's box did in Chapter 13. For one
small dial we can open it. Since \(16=15+1\), doubling a number below
\(15\) just rotates its four bits: the top bit, worth \(8\), becomes
worth \(16\equiv1\) and comes round to the bottom. So multiplying by
\(8\) is three such rotations, and three rotations one way are one
rotation the other way. And \(7\equiv-8\), while \(15-x\) is the four
bits of \(x\) flipped. So multiplying by \(7\) is: rotate the bits three
places, then flip every bit. In pictures, a rotation is crossings and a
flip is a red \(\pi\) dot (§8.2, the NOT). The bottom wire climbs to the
top, crossing the other three, which each step down one row; then a red
\(\pi\) sits on every wire:

\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=3.26em, x=1.3em, y=1.3em]
  \path (0,-1.2) (0,6.6);
  \foreach \y in {5.4,3.6,1.8,0} { \draw[wire] (0,\y) -- (3,\y); }
  \node[sdbox, minimum height=8.6em] at (1.5,2.7) {$U_7$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;\overset{1\le x<N}{=}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=3.26em, x=1.3em, y=1.3em,
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1.2) (0,6.6);
  \draw[wire] (0,5.4) -- (0.8,5.4) -- (3.2,3.6) -- (5.2,3.6);
  \draw[wire] (0,3.6) -- (0.8,3.6) -- (3.2,1.8) -- (5.2,1.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.8) -- (0.8,1.8) -- (3.2,0) -- (5.2,0);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (0.8,0) -- (3.2,5.4) -- (5.2,5.4);
  \foreach \y in {5.4,3.6,1.8,0} { \node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (4.2,\y) {}; }
\end{tikzpicture}\]

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 14.2 (the fifteen-hour dial as a picture).} Call the
right-hand picture \(C_7\). Exactly, as matrices on the four wires:
\(C_7\ket x=\ket{7x\bmod15}\) for \(1\le x<N\), and
\(C_7\ket0=\ket{15}\). Moreover \(C_7^2\) is the pure crossing that
exchanges wires \(1\leftrightarrow3\) and \(2\leftrightarrow4\), which
multiplies by \(4\) on \(1\le x<N\); and \(C_7^4=I\) on all sixteen
basis states.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} On the blackboard: for \(0\le x<15\) with top bit \(b\),
\(2x=16b+2(x-8b)\equiv b+2(x-8b)\), which is the left rotation of the
bits; so three rotations send \(x\) to \(8x\bmod15\). For \(1\le x<N\)
that remainder \(y\) is again an hour between \(1\) and \(N-1\), and
flipping all four bits sends it to \(15-y\equiv-8x\equiv7x\), again
between \(1\) and \(N-1\). So \(C_7\ket x=\ket{7x\bmod15}\) there. At
\(x=0\) the rotation gives \(0\) and the flips give \(15\), which is not
an hour of the dial; the orbit of \(1\) never goes there. In the
sketchbook: in \(C_7^4\), slide every red \(\pi\) along its wire,
through the crossings, to the right end (only the connectivity matters,
row 63). Each wire collects four red \(\pi\) dots, and fusion (Theorem
8.1, row 57) gives a red dot of phase \(4\pi\), which is no turn: a
two-legged red dot with no phase is a plain wire (§8.2). The crossings
compose to twelve rotations of four wires, which is none. With two
copies, two red \(\pi\)s fuse to nothing on each wire and six rotations
are two: wires \(1\leftrightarrow3\), \(2\leftrightarrow4\). Two
rotations multiply by \(4\). No scalar appears anywhere: a red \(\pi\)
dot with one leg in and one out is \(X\) exactly. \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch14/HandsRound.py}, which derives \(C_7^4\) by the rules
and checks that \(C_7\) sends \(0001\) to \(0111\).

The picture is special to this dial. It works because \(15\) is one less
than a power of two and \(7\) is minus a power of two. A general
multiplication mod \(N\) is a reversible arithmetic circuit (Shor §3)
with no such picture, and from here on the tick box stays closed.

\textbf{How long does ticking take?} It takes \(r\) ticks, and \(r\) can
be large. It can be nearly as large as \(N\): when \(N\) is an odd
prime, some \(a\) has order \(N-1\), because the multiplication of
nonzero remainders mod an odd prime is cyclic, one base running through
them all (a classical fact we state and do not prove; Shor §5 uses it
for every odd prime power). For numbers of the size used in
cryptography, \(N\) has hundreds of digits and so can \(r\). Cleve,
Ekert, Macchiavello and Mosca put the state of knowledge plainly:
``There is no known classical procedure for doing this in time
polynomial in \(n\), where \(n\) is the number of bits of \(N\).''
Shor's abstract calls factoring and discrete logarithms ``generally
thought to be hard on a classical computer''. Both statements are
careful. No fast classical method is known; none has been proved
impossible.

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why chase the order, when what we
want is a factor? Because the order is a \emph{period}, and periods are
what waves are good at finding; §14.5 shows that a period gives a factor
with a few lines of arithmetic. And why a box that multiplies by \(a\),
rather than one that computes \(a^x\) from \(x\)? Because multiplying by
\(a\) can be undone (Result 14.1), so it is a single unitary that can be
applied again and again, and ``applied again and again'' is exactly what
a period is about. Shor's own circuit computes \(a^x\) into a second
register; Cleve et al.~show that the two views give the same network
(§14.3 and §14.5).

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Feynman's Notebook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{A thesis with two escape clauses.} Peter W. Shor, of AT\&T
Research, published a preliminary version of the factoring algorithm in
the proceedings of the 35th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer
Science, held in Santa Fe, New Mexico, on 20--22 November 1994; the full
paper, ``Polynomial-time algorithms for prime factorization and discrete
logarithms on a quantum computer'', was posted in its revised form on 25
January 1996. It opens with Church's thesis in a quantitative form: any
physical computing device can be simulated by a Turing machine in a
number of steps polynomial in the resources it uses. Shor points to two
escape clauses, in the words ``physical'' and ``resources'', and reminds
the reader that ``the universe is in reality quantum mechanical''. He
names his inspiration directly: ``Simon's algorithm inspired the work
presented in this paper.'' He is equally direct about the hardware:
``Currently, nobody knows how to build a quantum computer''. And he adds
that even if none is ever built, the result says something about the
world: any general method for simulating quantum mechanics with at most
a polynomial slowdown would lead to a polynomial-time algorithm for
factoring.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-round-turned-whole}{%
\section{§14.2 The Round Turned Whole}\label{the-round-turned-whole}}

Ticking moves the hand. Is there anything on the dial that a tick does
not move, but only turns?

\textbf{On the blackboard.} Try a sum over the orbit of \(1\) with a
turning phase. For \(7\) mod \(15\) the orbit is \(1,7,4,13\). Put a
quarter-turn back at each step:

\[\ket{\psi_1}\;=\;\tfrac12\bigl(\ket1-i\ket7-\ket4+i\ket{13}\bigr).\]

The phases are \(1\), \(e^{-i\pi/2}=-i\), \(e^{-i\pi}=-1\) and
\(e^{-3i\pi/2}=i\). Apply the tick box: each hour moves to the next,
\(1\to7\to4\to13\to1\), and keeps its phase,

\[U_7\ket{\psi_1}\;=\;\tfrac12\bigl(\ket7-i\ket4-\ket{13}+i\ket1\bigr)\;=\;i\cdot\tfrac12\bigl(\ket1-i\ket7-\ket4+i\ket{13}\bigr)\;=\;i\,\ket{\psi_1}.\]

The state has not moved. It has turned, whole, by a quarter:
\(i=e^{2\pi i/4}\). We call such a state a \textbf{round}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 14.3 (eigenrounds).} For \(k=0,1,\dots,r-1\) let
\[\ket{\psi_k}\;=\;\frac1{\sqrt r}\sum_{s=0}^{r-1}e^{-2\pi iks/r}\,\ket{a^s\bmod N}.\]
Then \(U_a\ket{\psi_k}=e^{2\pi ik/r}\ket{\psi_k}\), and the \(r\) rounds
are orthonormal.
\end{quote}

This is Cleve et al.'s Eqs. (6.1) and (6.2), with their exponent \(j\)
written \(s\) and the factor \(r^{-1/2}\), which they leave out, written
in.

\emph{Proof.} \(U_a\) sends \(\ket{a^s\bmod N}\) to
\(\ket{a^{s+1}\bmod N}\), so
\[U_a\ket{\psi_k}=\frac1{\sqrt r}\sum_{s=0}^{r-1}e^{-2\pi iks/r}\ket{a^{s+1}}=e^{2\pi ik/r}\,\frac1{\sqrt r}\sum_{s=1}^{r}e^{-2\pi iks/r}\ket{a^{s}}=e^{2\pi ik/r}\ket{\psi_k},\]
where the last step uses \(a^r\equiv1=a^0\) and \(e^{-2\pi ikr/r}=1\),
so the term \(s=r\) is the old term \(s=0\). The hours
\(a^0,\dots,a^{r-1}\) are distinct (else \(a\) would come home sooner),
so \(\braket{\psi_{k'}|\psi_k}=\frac1r\sum_s\omega^s\) with
\(\omega=e^{2\pi i(k'-k)/r}\). If \(k=k'\) this is \(1\). Otherwise
\(\omega\neq1\) and \(\omega^r=1\), so the geometric sum
\(\frac{\omega^r-1}{\omega-1}\) is \(0\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch14/KickedTurn.py}.

The eigenvalue carries the period. If we could read the turn \(k/r\) of
a round, we would have \(r\) in the denominator. The rest of the chapter
is about reading a turn.

\hypertarget{a-listener-on-a-controlled-box}{%
\subsection{A listener on a controlled
box}\label{a-listener-on-a-controlled-box}}

A turn by itself is invisible: \(\ket{\psi_k}\) and
\(e^{2\pi ik/r}\ket{\psi_k}\) are the same state up to an overall phase
(Chapter 3), and no reading tells them apart. What makes a turn visible
is doing it \emph{on one branch only}. Let \(U\) be any unitary with an
eigenvector \(\ket u\) (normalized),
\(U\ket u=e^{2\pi i\varphi}\ket u\), and call \(\varphi\) its
\textbf{phase}, measured as a fraction of a whole turn;
\(\theta=2\pi\varphi\) is the same angle in radians. Kitaev's
\textbf{controlled-\(U\)} acts on one extra control wire and the
register:

\[\Lambda(U)\;=\;\ket0\bra0\otimes I\;+\;\ket1\bra1\otimes U .\]

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 14.4 (kickback of an eigenphase).} For \(c\in\{0,1\}\),
\(\Lambda(U)\bigl(\ket c\ket u\bigr)=e^{2\pi ic\varphi}\ket c\ket u\).
Hence for every control state \(\ket\chi\),
\(\Lambda(U)\bigl(\ket\chi\ket u\bigr)=\bigl(Z(\theta)\ket\chi\bigr)\ket u\),
where
\(Z(\theta)=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\theta}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\).
And \(\Lambda(U^{2^m})\) leaves \(e^{2\pi ic2^m\varphi}\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} On \(\ket0\ket u\) nothing happens; on \(\ket1\ket u\),
\(U\) acts and gives \(e^{2\pi i\varphi}\ket1\ket u\). Linearity in the
control gives the second statement, and
\(U^{2^m}\ket u=e^{2\pi i2^m\varphi}\ket u\) the third.
\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch14/KickedTurn.py}, which tests it
with a random complex non-diagonal \(U\), so that a slip between
\(\varphi\) and \(-\varphi\) would show.

This is Chapter 5's kickback (row 37) in general form. There the
eigenvalue was \(-1\), a half-turn; here it is any turn. The register
does not change. The control wire does: its \(\ket1\) branch has been
turned by \(\theta\).

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} The tall box \(\Lambda(U)\) spans the
control wire and the register, and \(\ket u\) is a state box on the
register. The kickback says the tall box can be removed, leaving a green
dot with phase \(\theta\) on the control wire, which is exactly
\(Z(\theta)\) (Chapter 8's \(Z(1,1,\theta)\)):

\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.985em, x=1.3em, y=1.3em]
  \path (0,-1.0) (0,2.9);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.9) -- (4.2,1.9);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (4.2,0);
  \node[sdstate] at (0,0) {$u$};
  \node[sdbox, minimum height=4.2em] at (2.8,0.95) {$\Lambda(U)$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.985em, x=1.3em, y=1.3em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1.0) (0,2.9);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.9) -- (3.2,1.9);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (3.2,0);
  \node[sdstate] at (0,0) {$u$};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$2\pi\varphi$}}] at (1.9,1.9) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\]

exactly. For a general \(U\) this picture is \textbf{borrowed from the
blackboard}. The tall box hides everything, and no rule of Chapter 8 can
open it; the equation is Result 14.4, drawn. Chapter 6 borrowed the
transpose in the same way. But when \(U\) is itself a phase box, the
whole thing can be drawn with dots, and then the rules can prove it.

\hypertarget{the-controlled-turn}{%
\subsection{The controlled turn}\label{the-controlled-turn}}

Take the smallest case: the register is one wire and \(U=Z(\alpha)\), a
phase box that turns \(\ket1\) by \(\alpha\). Then
\(\Lambda(Z(\alpha))\) turns \(\ket{11}\) by \(\alpha\) and leaves the
other three basis states alone:

\[\mathrm{CP}(\alpha)\;=\;\mathrm{diag}\bigl(1,1,1,e^{i\alpha}\bigr).\]

This is the \textbf{controlled phase}. Its matrix does not care which
wire is the control: \(\ket{11}\) is the only state touched, and it is
symmetric. So we will call it the \textbf{controlled turn} and draw it
without an arrow of control.

Here is the drawing. It is the one new picture element of this chapter,
and it is built entirely from Chapter 8's dots. On each of the two wires
sits a green dot with phase \(\alpha/2\), with a third leg, a
\textbf{tie}, running off the wire. The two ties meet at one phase-free
red dot, the \textbf{hub}. From the hub hangs a third short leg, the
\textbf{pendant}, ending in a green point with phase \(-\alpha/2\). This
shape is the \textbf{phase gadget} of van de Wetering's survey (his Eq.
(86), and Eq. (162) for exactly this decomposition of a controlled
phase):

\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.44em, x=1.3em, y=1.3em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \draw[wire] (0,2.6) -- (4.4,2.6);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (4.4,0);
  \draw[wire] (1.6,2.6) -- (1.6,1.3);
  \draw[wire] (1.6,1.3) -- (1.6,0);
  \draw[wire] (1.6,1.3) -- (2.9,1.3);
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\alpha/2$}}] at (1.6,2.6) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\alpha/2$}}] at (1.6,0) {};
  \node[xsp] at (1.6,1.3) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]right:{$-\alpha/2$}}] at (2.9,1.3) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.44em, x=1.3em, y=1.3em]
  \draw[wire] (0,2.6) -- (3.6,2.6);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (3.6,0);
  \node[sdbox, minimum height=4.9em] at (1.8,1.3) {$\mathrm{CP}(\alpha)$};
\end{tikzpicture}\]

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 14.5 (the controlled turn).} Exactly, for every angle
\(\alpha\), the bare gadget above is
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\,\mathrm{CP}(\alpha)\). It is unchanged when the two
wires are exchanged.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} Follow a basis state \(\ket x\ket y\). A green dot with
phase \(\alpha/2\), one leg in, and two out (the wire and the tie) is
\(Z(1,2,\tfrac\alpha2)\): it sends \(\ket x\) to
\(e^{i\alpha x/2}\ket x\ket x\), keeping the bit on the wire and sending
a copy up the tie. So the two ties carry \(x\) and \(y\), with the
factor \(e^{i\alpha(x+y)/2}\). The hub, a phase-free red dot with the
two ties in and the pendant out, is
\(X(2,1,0)=\ket+\bra{++}+\ket-\bra{--}\), and on \(\ket x\ket y\) it
gives
\(\tfrac12\bigl(\ket++(-1)^{x+y}\ket-\bigr)=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\ket{x\oplus y}\):
it reads the parity. The pendant's green point, met by \(\ket z\), gives
\(e^{-i\alpha z/2}\). Altogether
\[\ket x\ket y\;\mapsto\;\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\,e^{i\alpha(x+y-x\oplus y)/2}\,\ket x\ket y\;=\;\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\,e^{i\alpha xy}\ket x\ket y,\]
since \(x+y-x\oplus y=2xy\) for bits. That is
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\mathrm{CP}(\alpha)\). The picture has the same shape
with its wires exchanged. \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch14/KickedTurn.py}, which checks it at \(\alpha=\pi/2\)
and \(\alpha=3\pi/7\).

The \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) is the price of the hub, as a bare tie in
Chapter 13 cost \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\). As in Chapters 9 to 13, every
picture equation in this chapter is exact, and its scalar is drawn.

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why draw a controlled phase as a
gadget of four dots, when a tall box would do? Because the tall box
hides its insides and the gadget does not: every piece of it is a dot,
so every rule of Chapter 8 can reach it. The gadget also shows at a
glance what the circuit hides, that control and target are
interchangeable. Van de Wetering makes the same remark: the symmetry of
a phase gadget ``is clear in the representation of a phase gadget as a
ZX-diagram'', but not in a circuit.

\hypertarget{a-basis-point-passes-through}{%
\subsection{A basis point passes
through}\label{a-basis-point-passes-through}}

What does a controlled turn do when one of its wires carries a definite
bit? On the blackboard it is immediate. Write \(\ket c\) with
\(c\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\ket\psi\) for any state of the other wire. Then
\(\mathrm{CP}(\alpha)\bigl(\ket c\otimes\ket\psi\bigr)=\ket c\otimes Z(c\alpha)\ket\psi\):
if \(c=0\) nothing happens, and if \(c=1\) the other wire is turned by
\(\alpha\).

In the sketchbook, recall the points of Chapters 11 to 13: a red point
is \(\sqrt2\ket0\) and a red \(\pi\) point is \(\sqrt2\ket1\). We call
them \textbf{dark} and \textbf{lit}, and with Chapter 10's
bit-times-\(\pi\) spider (row 75) we draw both at once as a red point
with phase \(c\pi\).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 14.6 (the basis-point lemma).} Exactly, for every
\(\alpha\) and \(c\in\{0,1\}\):
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.44em, x=1.3em, y=1.3em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\draw[wire] (0,2.6) -- (4.4,2.6);
\draw[wire] (-0.6,0) -- (4.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.6,2.6) -- (1.6,1.3);
\draw[wire] (1.6,1.3) -- (1.6,0);
\draw[wire] (1.6,1.3) -- (2.9,1.3);
\node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$c\pi$}}] at (0,2.6) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\alpha/2$}}] at (1.6,2.6) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\alpha/2$}}] at (1.6,0) {};
\node[xsp] at (1.6,1.3) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]right:{$-\alpha/2$}}] at (2.9,1.3) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.44em, x=1.3em, y=1.3em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\draw[wire] (0,2.6) -- (2.6,2.6);
\draw[wire] (-0.6,0) -- (2.6,0);
\node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$c\pi$}}] at (0,2.6) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$c\alpha$}}] at (1.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] A basis point passes straight through a controlled
turn and leaves its turn on the other wire: a dark point leaves nothing,
a lit point leaves a green \(\alpha\). On the blackboard,
\(\mathrm{CP}(\alpha)\bigl(\ket c\otimes\ket\psi\bigr)=\ket c\otimes Z(c\alpha)\ket\psi\).
\end{quote}

The scalars agree: by Result 14.5 the left side is
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\mathrm{CP}(\alpha)\) applied to \(\sqrt2\ket c\),
which is \(\ket c\otimes Z(c\alpha)\); the right side is
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\cdot\sqrt2\ket c\otimes Z(c\alpha)\), the same.

\emph{Proof, in pictures.} Take the lit point, \(c=1\). Copy (Theorem
8.3) needs a phase-free dot, so first run fusion (Theorem 8.1)
backwards: the top ring's \(\alpha/2\) slides off onto a green point
hanging from a new leg, and the ring is left phase-free. Now the lit
point enters the ring and is copied onto its three other legs: the wire,
the tie and the new leg. The copy on the new leg meets the green
\(\alpha/2\) point there and the two close into a number. Next, the copy
on the tie fuses into the hub, which becomes a red \(\pi\) dot with two
legs. Then \(\pi\)-commutation (Theorem 8.4) pushes that \(\pi\) through
the pendant's point, whose turn flips from \(-\alpha/2\) to
\(+\alpha/2\), and the hub, now phase-free with two legs, is a plain
wire. Last, the pendant's point fuses into the bottom ring:
\(\alpha/2+\alpha/2=\alpha\).

  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
