\end{tikzpicture}
\;\overset{\pi\text{-comm., fusion}}{=}\;\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\,e^{i\alpha/2}\,e^{-i\alpha/2}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.44em, x=1.3em, y=1.3em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \draw[wire] (0,2.6) -- (2.6,2.6);
  \draw[wire] (-0.6,0) -- (2.6,0);
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (0,2.6) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\alpha$}}] at (1.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\]

The two turns cancel and the scalar is \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\), as claimed.
For the dark point, \(c=0\), the same moves run with nothing to carry:
the copy on the new leg closes against the \(\alpha/2\) point into the
number \(\sqrt2\) with no turn; the hub, fed a dark point, stays
phase-free and has two legs, so it is a plain wire; and the pendant's
\(-\alpha/2\) fuses into the bottom ring's \(+\alpha/2\) to give \(0\),
a plain wire again. The scalar is
\(\tfrac12\cdot\sqrt2=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) once more. \(\;\blacksquare\)
See \texttt{Code/Ch14/KickedTurn.py}, which checks the lemma for both
points at \(\alpha=\pi/2\) and \(3\pi/7\), and each scalar of the
derivation separately.

So for a phase box the kickback picture is no longer borrowed. A lit
point fed into the wheel's side of a controlled turn is the eigenstate
\(\ket1\) of \(Z(\alpha)\), and the lemma proves that its turn lands on
the other wire.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Coecke's Sketchbook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{The ledger of the lemma.} Every scalar in that derivation can be
named. The copy sends one point into a phase-free dot with three other
legs, and a point in, three points out, costs \(\tfrac12\):
\(\sqrt2\ket c\) becomes \(\sqrt2\ket{ccc}\), which is \(\tfrac12\)
times three points of \(\sqrt2\) each. The copy that meets the
\(\alpha/2\) point closes into
\(\sqrt2\bra c\,(\ket0+e^{i\alpha/2}\ket1)=\sqrt2\,e^{ic\alpha/2}\): the
ring's turn goes into the scalar only if the point is lit. Chapter 8
left the scalar of \(\pi\)-commutation unstated, and here it matters, so
here it is:
\(X\bigl(\ket0+e^{-i\alpha/2}\ket1\bigr)=\ket1+e^{-i\alpha/2}\ket0=e^{-i\alpha/2}\bigl(\ket0+e^{i\alpha/2}\ket1\bigr)\).
The pendant's old turn comes out as \(e^{-i\alpha/2}\), exactly
cancelling the \(e^{i\alpha/2}\) from the closing. Fusion and the
removal of a plain two-legged dot cost nothing. So the whole bill is
\(\tfrac12\cdot\sqrt2=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\), for the dark point and the lit
point alike. The cancellation is not luck: the gadget splits \(\alpha\)
into two halves and a correction, and the correction is exactly what the
lit point pays back.
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{one-listener-and-its-blur}{%
\subsection{One listener, and its
blur}\label{one-listener-and-its-blur}}

Now read the turn. Put one control wire at \(H\ket0\), apply
\(\Lambda(U)\) with \(\ket u\) on the register, apply a Hadamard to the
control, and read it. This is Kitaev's measuring operator, his Eq. (16):
a Hadamard gate on each side of \(\Lambda(U)\). Try two phases. With
\(\varphi=\tfrac{1}{4}\) the kickback leaves the control at
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket0+i\ket1)\), and the Hadamard gives
\(\tfrac12\bigl((1+i)\ket0+(1-i)\ket1\bigr)\): the reading is \(0\) or
\(1\) with probability \(\tfrac12\) each. With \(\varphi=\tfrac34\) the
control is \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket0-i\ket1)\), and the odds are again
\(\tfrac12\) each. A quarter turn and three quarters cannot be told
apart.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 14.7 (one listener; Kitaev's Eq. (17)).} The reading is
\(0\) with probability \(\tfrac12\bigl(1+\cos2\pi\varphi\bigr)\) and
\(1\) with probability \(\tfrac12\bigl(1-\cos2\pi\varphi\bigr)\). It
depends on \(\varphi\) only through \(\cos2\pi\varphi\), so \(\varphi\)
and \(1-\varphi\) give the same odds.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} By Result 14.4 the control ends at
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket0+e^{i\theta}\ket1)\) before the last Hadamard,
which turns it into
\(\tfrac12\bigl((1+e^{i\theta})\ket0+(1-e^{i\theta})\ket1\bigr)\). And
\(\lvert1\pm e^{i\theta}\rvert^2=2\pm2\cos\theta\). \(\;\blacksquare\)
See \texttt{Code/Ch14/KickedTurn.py}.

The picture says the same thing in one line. The control is a green
point turned by \(\theta\); read it through a yellow box against the
dark point. Colour change (Theorem 8.2, row 58) makes the green point
red, fusion joins it to the dark point, and a red dot with no legs at
all is the number \(1+e^{i\theta}\) (its two branches, with nothing left
to agree on, are the numbers \(1\) and \(e^{i\theta}\)):

\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.3em, y=1.3em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (3,0);
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\theta$}}] at (0,0) {};
  \node[hbox] at (1.5,0) {};
  \node[xsp] at (3,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;\overset{\text{colour}}{=}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.3em, y=1.3em,
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2,0);
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$\theta$}}] at (0,0) {};
  \node[xsp] at (2,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;\overset{\text{fusion}}{=}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.3em, y=1.3em,
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$\theta$}}] at (0,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;1+e^{i\theta}.\]

The two points carry \(\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2=2\), so the amplitude of the
dark reading is \(\tfrac12(1+e^{i\theta})\). For a quarter this is
\(\tfrac12(1+i)\) and for three quarters \(\tfrac12(1-i)\): different
numbers, the same size. The picture shows why. A lone red dot turned by
\(\theta\) is worth \(1+e^{i\theta}\), and turning it the other way only
takes the mirror image of that number.

Kitaev's own way out, in his §3, is to repeat and to vary. Many
repetitions estimate \(\cos2\pi\varphi\); substituting \(iU\) for \(U\)
changes the cosine into minus the sine; and the two together fix
\(\varphi\) to a constant precision (his Lemma 9). The controlled powers
\(\Lambda(U^{2^j})\) then sharpen the estimate to precision \(2^{-l-2}\)
(his Lemma 10). And when \(U\) is a permutation, as the tick box is, he
measures \(\varphi\) exactly, by applying Euclid's algorithm to the
measured value (his Theorem 1). We will take a different road to the
same place, the one in the dialogue: instead of repeating one listener,
add a second that ticks twice as fast.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Feynman's Notebook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{Measuring an eigenvalue.} A. Yu. Kitaev, of the L. D. Landau
Institute for Theoretical Physics in Moscow, posted ``Quantum
measurements and the Abelian Stabilizer Problem'' on 20 November 1995.
Its abstract states its aim plainly: ``Thus we extend famous Shor's
results''. The problem of the title includes both factoring and discrete
logarithms, and the method, as the abstract says, ``is based on a
procedure for measuring an eigenvalue of a unitary operator''. That
procedure is this section's listener: one control bit, a Hadamard gate
on each side of \(\Lambda(U)\), read many times. Kitaev's paper is also,
as he puts it, ``a rather detailed introduction to the theory of quantum
computation'', with its own models of circuits, reversible computation
and precision. Cleve et al.~later drew the moral: Shor's algorithm, ``in
effect, estimates the eigenvalue'' of the multiplication box. That box
is a permutation, a permutation has eigenvalues that are roots of unity,
and the denominator of the root is the length of the cycle. Find the
eigenvalue, and the period comes with it.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{twice-the-pace}{%
\section{§14.3 Twice the Pace}\label{twice-the-pace}}

One listener hears \(\cos2\pi\varphi\) and cannot tell a quarter from
three quarters. Here is the way out.

\textbf{On the blackboard.} Give the listener \(\Lambda(U^2)\) instead
of \(\Lambda(U)\). By Result 14.4 it hears the turn \(2\varphi\). For
\(\varphi=\tfrac{1}{4}\) that is \(\tfrac12\). For \(\varphi=\tfrac34\)
it is \(\tfrac32\), which is \(\tfrac12\) plus a whole turn, and a whole
turn is no turn at all. Both give a half-turn, and by Result 14.7 a
half-turn reads \(1\) with probability \(\tfrac12(1-\cos\pi)=1\):
certainly. A turn of \(0\) or \(\tfrac12\), on the other hand, would
read \(0\) with certainty. So the doubled listener says, with certainty,
whether the number of quarters is odd, and it cannot say which odd.

Now correct the single listener. It carries \(\tfrac{1}{4}\) or
\(\tfrac34\). If the doubled listener read \(1\), turn the single
listener back a quarter: \(\tfrac{1}{4}\) becomes \(0\) and \(\tfrac34\)
becomes \(\tfrac12\), and a Hadamard now reads the half with certainty.
Two readings, both certain, and together they are the turn: \emph{a half
or not}, then \emph{a quarter or not}.

In binary this is shifting a point. Write the phase as a binary
fraction,
\(\varphi=0.j_1j_2\cdots j_t=\tfrac{j_1}2+\tfrac{j_2}4+\cdots+\tfrac{j_t}{2^t}\),
so that \(\varphi=j/2^t\) for the integer \(j=j_1j_2\cdots j_t\). A
quarter is \(0.01\) and three quarters \(0.11\). Doubling moves the
point one place right, \(2\varphi=j_1.j_2\cdots j_t\), and the digit
that crosses the point is a whole turn, which vanishes.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 14.8 (doubling shifts the point).} If
\(\varphi=0.j_1j_2\cdots j_t\), then \(\Lambda(U^{2^{t-m}})\) kicks the
turn \(e^{2\pi i\,0.j_{t-m+1}\cdots j_t}\) onto its control. The
listener at the fastest pace, \(2^{t-1}\), hears only the last digit
\(j_t\), as a half-turn or none.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} \(2^{t-m}\varphi=j_1\cdots j_{t-m}.j_{t-m+1}\cdots j_t\),
and the part before the point is a whole number of turns. Result 14.4
does the rest. \(\;\blacksquare\)

Each listener hears one digit more than the listener at twice its pace,
and the new digit is the one it must be corrected for. The correction
for \(t\) listeners is a known transform, run backwards.

\hypertarget{the-quantum-fourier-transform}{%
\subsection{The quantum Fourier
transform}\label{the-quantum-fourier-transform}}

Let \(q=2^t\) and number the basis states of \(t\) wires
\(\ket0,\dots,\ket{q-1}\), reading the bits top wire first. The
\textbf{quantum Fourier transform} is

\[F_q\,\ket x\;=\;\frac1{\sqrt q}\sum_{y=0}^{q-1}e^{2\pi ixy/q}\,\ket y .\]

This is Shor's Eq. (4.1), his matrix \(A_q\), with his labels \(a\) and
\(c\) written \(x\) and \(y\). For \(t=1\) it is the Hadamard:
\(F_2=H\). For \(t=2\),

\[F_4\;=\;\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1&1\\1&i&-1&-i\\1&-1&1&-1\\1&-i&-1&i\end{pmatrix},\qquad F_4\ket1=\tfrac12\bigl(\ket0+i\ket1-\ket2-i\ket3\bigr).\]

Look at that last column as a state on two wires. It is
\(\tfrac12\bigl(\ket{00}+i\ket{01}-\ket{10}-i\ket{11}\bigr)=\tfrac12(\ket0-\ket1)(\ket0+i\ket1)\):
a product, the top wire turned by a half and the lower wire by a
quarter. That is exactly what two listeners hold after the controlled
powers for \(\varphi=\tfrac{1}{4}\). The top listener, at double pace,
heard \(2\cdot\tfrac{1}{4}=\tfrac12\); the lower heard \(\tfrac{1}{4}\).
The listeners' state is \(F_4\ket1\), and \(\varphi=\tfrac{1}{4}\) is
\(j/4\) with \(j=1\). It is not a coincidence.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 14.9 (the product form; Cleve et al., Eq. (4.2)).} For
\(x=x_1x_2\cdots x_t\) in binary, top wire first,
\[\begin{aligned}F_q\ket x\;=\;\frac1{\sqrt q}\,&\bigl(\ket0+e^{2\pi i\,0.x_t}\ket1\bigr)\bigl(\ket0+e^{2\pi i\,0.x_{t-1}x_t}\ket1\bigr)\\&\cdots\bigl(\ket0+e^{2\pi i\,0.x_1x_2\cdots x_t}\ket1\bigr).\end{aligned}\]
The top wire carries only the last digit; each wire below carries one
more.
\end{quote}

Cleve et al.~note that the state ``is unentangled, and can in fact be
factorised''. The proof is the Dirac's Blackboard below. See
\texttt{Code/Ch14/QuarterClock.py}, which checks the product form for
\(t=3\) on every basis state.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Dirac's Blackboard.}\nopagebreak

\emph{Factoring the Fourier sum.} Write \(y=y_1y_2\cdots y_t\) in
binary, top wire first, so \(y=\sum_{m=1}^{t}y_m2^{t-m}\) and
\(y/q=\sum_m y_m2^{-m}\). The phase then splits into one factor per
wire: \[e^{2\pi ixy/q}=\prod_{m=1}^{t}e^{2\pi i\,x\,2^{-m}\,y_m}.\] Now
\(x\,2^{-m}=x_1\cdots x_{t-m}.x_{t-m+1}\cdots x_t\), and the whole part
is whole turns, so
\(e^{2\pi ix2^{-m}y_m}=e^{2\pi i\,0.x_{t-m+1}\cdots x_t\,y_m}\). A sum
over all \(y\) of a product of one-wire factors is the product of the
one-wire sums:
\[\sum_{y}e^{2\pi ixy/q}\ket{y_1\cdots y_t}=\prod_{m=1}^{t}\Bigl(\sum_{y_m\in\{0,1\}}e^{2\pi i\,0.x_{t-m+1}\cdots x_t\,y_m}\ket{y_m}\Bigr),\]
and the factor for wire \(m\) is
\(\ket0+e^{2\pi i\,0.x_{t-m+1}\cdots x_t}\ket1\). Wire \(1\) gets
\(0.x_t\), wire \(t\) gets \(0.x_1\cdots x_t\). Check \(t=2\), \(x=01\):
wire \(1\) gets \(0.1\), a half; wire \(2\) gets \(0.01\), a quarter.
This is Chapter 13's sign sum again, with the signs \(\pm1\) replaced by
turns.
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{the-transform-as-a-network}{%
\subsection{The transform as a
network}\label{the-transform-as-a-network}}

The product form says how to build \(F_q\). Wire \(m\) must end up
turned by \(0.x_m\cdots x_t\) (before the wires are put in reverse
order). A Hadamard on a wire holding \(\ket{x_m}\) gives
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket0+e^{2\pi i\,0.x_m}\ket1\bigr)\), since
\((-1)^{x_m}=e^{2\pi i\,0.x_m}\): the first digit. Each further digit
\(x_{m'}\), from a lower wire \(m'>m\) still holding its bit, is added
by a controlled turn of angle \(\pi/2^{m'-m}\) between wires \(m\) and
\(m'\): it turns the \(\ket1\) branch by \(2\pi\,x_{m'}/2^{m'-m+1}\),
which puts \(x_{m'}\) in place \(m'-m+1\) after the point.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 14.10 (the transform's network).} For \(m=1,\dots,t\) in
turn, apply a Hadamard to wire \(m\), then a controlled turn
\(\mathrm{CP}(\pi/2^{m'-m})\) between wire \(m\) and each lower wire
\(m'\); finally put the wires in reverse order. The result is exactly
\(F_q\). Its inverse is the same network run backwards, with every turn
negated.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} On \(\ket{x_1\cdots x_t}\), wire \(1\) after its Hadamard
and its controlled turns holds
\(\ket0+e^{2\pi i\,0.x_1x_2\cdots x_t}\ket1\) (normalized by
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\)), because each lower wire is still in its basis
state and a controlled turn fed a basis bit acts on the other wire as
\(Z(x_{m'}\alpha)\) (the blackboard half of Result 14.6). Wire \(1\) is
never touched again. Wire \(2\) then gets \(0.x_2\cdots x_t\) the same
way, and so on down to wire \(t\), which gets \(0.x_t\) from its
Hadamard alone. Reversing the order puts \(0.x_t\) on top, and that is
Result 14.9. The inverse of a product of unitaries is the product of
their inverses in reverse order; \(H^{-1}=H\), a crossing undoes itself,
and \(\mathrm{CP}(\alpha)^{-1}=\mathrm{CP}(-\alpha)\).
\(\;\blacksquare\) This is the walk Cleve et al.~take through their Fig.
5. See \texttt{Code/Ch14/QuarterClock.py}, which checks the network
against \(F_q\) for \(t=2,3,4\), and Shor's own gate order as well.

Shor gives the same network in his Eq. (4.4): Hadamards, which he calls
\(R_j\), alternating with controlled phases \(S_{j,k}\) of angle
\(\theta_{k-j}=\pi/2^{k-j}\), his Eqs. (4.2) and (4.3). His order
interleaves them slightly differently, which changes nothing, since
gates on different wires commute. And he deals with the reversal as we
have: the network's output has its bits in reverse order, and ``to
obtain the actual quantum Fourier transform, we need either to do
further computation to reverse the bits \ldots{} or to leave these bits
in place and read them in reverse order''. He credits the construction
to Coppersmith and, independently, to David Deutsch, and calls it
``essentially the standard fast Fourier transform (FFT) algorithm
\ldots{} adapted for a quantum computer''.

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} Draw every controlled turn as a gadget and
every Hadamard as a yellow box (row 56). The network is a triangle: one
yellow box per wire, and between each wire and every wire below it a
controlled turn whose angle halves with each step down; then the
crossings that reverse the wires. Here it is for \(t=3\), with its three
bare gadgets paid for by the scalar in front:

\[F_8\;=\;2^{3/2}\;

  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=0.95em,inner sep=0pt},

has one controlled turn. Its inverse is what phase estimation will need:
a yellow box on the top wire, the controlled turn
\(\mathrm{CP}(-\pi/2)\), a yellow box on the lower wire, and the
crossing,

\[F_4^{-1}\;=\;\sqrt2\;

  \draw[wire] (0,2.6) -- (5.8,2.6) -- (7.8,0) -- (8.4,0);

  \draw[wire] (2.4,2.6) -- (2.4,1.3); \draw[wire] (2.4,1.3) -- (2.4,0); \draw[wire] (2.4,1.3) -- (3.5,1.3);

  \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$-\pi/4$}}] at (2.4,0) {};
  \node[xsp] at (2.4,1.3) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]right:{$\pi/4$}}] at (3.5,1.3) {};

exactly. Run backwards, the forward network would start with the
crossing and put its yellow box on the lower wire first. But a crossing
only exchanges rows, and the yellow boxes and the symmetric controlled
turn can slide through it and change rows as they go. So the inverse is
the transform's mirror image with every turn negated, redrawn with the
crossing moved back to the end: the same shape as the transform.

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why this transform and not some
other correction? Because it is the one whose output is a product of
single-wire turns, each holding a tail of the binary expansion (Result
14.9), and a product of single-wire states is what the controlled powers
produce. Any unitary that undoes the product would do; the inverse
Fourier transform is the one that does it for every \(x\) at once, with
a network of about \(t^2/2\) gates.

\textbf{Approximately is enough.} The controlled turns between distant
wires have tiny angles, \(\pi/2^{m'-m}\). Shor remarks that multiplying
by ``a very small phase factor \ldots{} would be very difficult to do
accurately physically'', and that Coppersmith showed they may be left
out. Coppersmith's report defines the transform with every controlled
turn between wires \(h\) or more apart deleted, that is, every angle
\(\pi/2^h\) or smaller. Each entry of the matrix then differs from the
true transform's by a factor \(e^{i\epsilon}\) with
\(\lvert\epsilon\rvert\le2\pi t\,2^{-h}\), and the network needs about
\(th\) two-wire operations instead of about \(t^2/2\). (In the report's
letters, \(L\) for our \(t\) and \(m\) for our \(h\).) For \(t=500\) and
\(h=20\) he estimates the phase error at about \(3/1000\): in Shor's
factoring it gives ``a fraction of a degree in each phase angle'', and a
decrease of less than one percent in the probability of each desirable
final state. We state this and do not prove it.

\hypertarget{phase-estimation}{%
\subsection{Phase estimation}\label{phase-estimation}}

Now put the pieces together: \(t\) listeners, the controlled powers at
doubling paces, and the inverse transform.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 14.11 (phase estimation on an eigenstate, exact for a
dyadic phase).} Let \(U\) be unitary,
\(U\ket u=e^{2\pi i\varphi}\ket u\) with \(\ket u\) normalized, and
\(\varphi=j/2^t\) for an integer \(0\le j<2^t\). Write
\(j=j_1j_2\cdots j_t\) in binary, so \(\varphi=0.j_1j_2\cdots j_t\), and
write \(\ket j\) top wire first, \(j_1\) on top. Let \(q=2^t\), and let
\(\Lambda_m(V)\) apply \(V\) to the register when counting wire \(m\)
(from the top) is \(\ket1\). Then, exactly, scalar included,
\[\bigl(F_q^{-1}\otimes I\bigr)\;\prod_{m=1}^{t}\Lambda_m\bigl(U^{2^{t-m}}\bigr)\;\bigl(H^{\otimes t}\ket0^{\otimes t}\otimes\ket u\bigr)\;=\;\ket j\ket u .\]
Reading the \(t\) counting wires returns \(j\) with certainty. The
\(\Lambda_m\) commute, so the order of the product does not matter.
\end{quote}

The attribution needs care. The idea of measuring an eigenvalue of a
unitary with controlled powers \(\Lambda(U^{2^j})\) is A. Yu. Kitaev's,
from 1995 (his §§3--4). His procedure uses one control bit at a time and
repeats it, with classical post-processing (Lemma 10). The one-network
form stated here, the controlled powers followed by an inverse Fourier
transform, is the presentation of Cleve, Ekert, Macchiavello and Mosca
(1997, §5, with their product state (5.1)), which they say was
``motivated by the method proposed by Kitaev (1995)''. They also show
(their §6) that for the tick box it is the same network as Shor's
algorithm. Both proofs of Result 14.11 are in §14.7. See
\texttt{Code/Ch14/QuarterClock.py}, which checks it exactly for
\(t=1,2,3\), every \(j\), with a random complex unitary \(U\).

The theorem is ``exact for a dyadic phase'', one of the form \(j/2^t\).
The phases of the tick box are \(k/r\), which are rarely of that form;
§14.4 deals with them. The rounds of the tick box also have a second
difficulty: we have no way to prepare them. That is §14.4's business
too.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Feynman's Notebook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{Electrons with spins.} Don Coppersmith's ``An approximate Fourier
transform useful in quantum factoring'' is an IBM Research Report from
the T. J. Watson Research Center in Yorktown Heights, dated June 1994 on
its title page. It was posted to the arXiv only in January 2002. Its
abstract says the transform ``may find application to the problem of
factoring integers with a quantum computer as is currently under
investigation by Peter Shor''. Coppersmith starts from the textbook fast
Fourier transform and pictures its passes physically: the amplitudes
belong to ``\(L\) electrons'' with spins up or down, and the transform
``is performed by a sequence of two-electron interactions''. He then
makes a pleasant observation. His approximate transform with the
smallest threshold, which keeps no controlled turns at all, is the
Hadamard transform, suitably indexed; with the largest, it is the full
Fourier transform. Chapter 13's layers of Hadamards and this chapter's
Fourier transform are the two ends of one family.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{every-round-at-once}{%
\section{§14.4 Every Round at Once}\label{every-round-at-once}}

Phase estimation reads the turn of a round. But we do not have a round.
Cleve et al.~say it bluntly: such a state ``is not at all trivial to
fabricate''. What we can easily make is \(\ket1\), the hand standing at
one.

\textbf{On the blackboard.} Add the four rounds of \(7\) mod \(15\). At
the hour \(1\) every round has the phase \(1\), so the four amplitudes
add. At each other hour the four phases are the four powers of a root of
unity, and they cancel: at \(7\) they are \(1,-i,-1,i\); at \(4\) they
are \(1,-1,1,-1\); at \(13\) they are \(1,i,-1,-i\). So
\(\ket{\psi_0}+\ket{\psi_1}+\ket{\psi_2}+\ket{\psi_3}=\tfrac12\cdot4\ket1=2\ket1\).
The hand at one is all four rounds laid together.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 14.12 (every round at once).}
\(\ket1=\dfrac1{\sqrt r}\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{r-1}\ket{\psi_k}\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.}
\(\sum_k\ket{\psi_k}=\frac1{\sqrt r}\sum_s\bigl(\sum_ke^{-2\pi iks/r}\bigr)\ket{a^s}\).
The inner sum is \(r\) when \(s=0\) and \(0\) otherwise, by the
geometric sum in the proof of Result 14.3. So the total is
\(\frac r{\sqrt r}\ket{a^0}=\sqrt r\ket1\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch14/EveryRound.py}.

This is Cleve et al.'s Eq. (6.4), which they write as
\(\ket1=\sum_k\ket{\psi_k}\). Their rounds carry no factor \(r^{-1/2}\)
and run over \(k=1,\dots,r\); with rounds normalized, as ours are, their
sum is \(\sqrt r\ket1\), and taken literally in their own normalization
it is \(r\ket1\). The statement above is the normalized one.

Now start phase estimation with \(\ket1\) in the register. The network
is linear, so it acts on each round separately, and each round is an
eigenstate.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 14.13 (a random round is read).} Suppose \(r\) divides
\(q=2^t\). Phase estimation with \(U=U_a\), started on \(\ket1\), ends
in \[\frac1{\sqrt r}\sum_{k=0}^{r-1}\ket{kq/r}\ket{\psi_k}.\] The
reading is \(c=kq/r\) for a uniformly random \(k\), each with
probability \(1/r\), and \(c/q=k/r\). For \(N=15\), \(a=7\), \(t=2\):
the readings \(0,1,2,3\) each occur with probability \(\tfrac{1}{4}\),
and exactly two of them, \(1\) and \(3\), give \(r=4\). One run finds
the period with probability exactly \(\tfrac12\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} By Result 14.12 and linearity, the output is
\(r^{-1/2}\sum_k(\text{output on }\ket{\psi_k})\). The phase of
\(\ket{\psi_k}\) is \(k/r=(kq/r)/q\), a dyadic fraction with numerator
\(kq/r<q\), so Result 14.11 gives \(\ket{kq/r}\ket{\psi_k}\). The rounds
are orthonormal (Result 14.3), so the probability of reading \(c\) is
the sum over \(k\) of \(\tfrac1r\,\lvert\braket{c|kq/r}\rvert^2\), which
is \(\tfrac1r\) when \(c=kq/r\). For the dial: \(q=4=r\), so \(c=k\). A
reading \(c\) suggests the period as the denominator of \(c/4\) in
lowest terms, and the suggestion is checked by one multiplication.
Reading \(1\) or \(3\) gives \(\tfrac{1}{4}\) or \(\tfrac34\) and the
period \(4\), and \(7^4\equiv1\). Reading \(2\) gives \(\tfrac12\) and
the candidate \(2\), but \(7^2=49\equiv4\), not \(1\): the round that
turns a half at each tick comes home in two, but the hand does not.
Reading \(0\) gives nothing. \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch14/EveryRound.py}, which runs phase estimation with
\(U_7\) on the four-wire register for \(t=2\) and \(t=3\).

The half reading fails for an honest reason. It came from the round
\(k=2\), whose turn \(\tfrac24\) is not in lowest terms: \(k\) and \(r\)
share a factor. A reading gives \(r\) exactly when the random \(k\) has
no factor in common with \(r\).

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} Our small wheel of §14.3 has a picture
version of the same fact. Take the one-wire phase box \(S=Z(\pi/2)\),
the smallest phase box that comes round in four ticks. Its rounds are
the basis states: \(\ket0\) with phase \(0\) (the dark wheel) and
\(\ket1\) with phase \(\tfrac{1}{4}\) (the lit wheel). A phase-free
green point is \(\ket0+\ket1\), which is the two red points added and
divided by \(\sqrt2\):

\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.3em, y=1.3em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
  \path (0,-1) (0,1);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.6,0);
  \node[zsp] at (0,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\Bigl(\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.3em, y=1.3em,
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
  \path (0,-1) (0,1);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.6,0);
  \node[xsp] at (0,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;+\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.3em, y=1.3em,
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1) (0,1);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.6,0);
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (0,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\;\Bigr).\]

A green point on the wheel is the equal mix of the wheel's two rounds,
and the whole picture splits into two: one with the wheel dark and one
with it lit. §14.8 evaluates both halves.

\hypertarget{when-the-phase-is-not-dyadic}{%
\subsection{When the phase is not
dyadic}\label{when-the-phase-is-not-dyadic}}

For a general dial, \(r\) does not divide any power of \(2\), and
\(k/r\) is not a binary fraction of finite length. Phase estimation then
reads a good approximation with good probability.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 14.14 (the general phase; Cleve et al., Eq. (5.4);
stated, not proved).} If \(\varphi\) is not of the form \(j/2^t\), the
network of Result 14.11 returns the \(t\)-bit fraction nearest to
\(\varphi\) with probability at least \(4/\pi^2=0.405\ldots\)
\end{quote}

Cleve et al.~derive it from a geometric series, their Eqs. (5.2) and
(5.3). They add that the success probability can be pushed to
\(1-\epsilon\) by adding \(O(\log(1/\epsilon))\) wires and discarding
the extra digits. \texttt{Code/Ch14/QuarterClock.py} checks the bound on
random phases for \(t=2,\dots,6\) as documentation; it is not a proof.

Shor's own analysis, in his §5, is for his version of the circuit, which
also reads the second register. In our letters, his outcome is a pair
\((c,\,a^s\bmod N)\): his exponent \(k\) is our \(s\). He takes \(q\) to
be the power of \(2\) with \(N^2\le q<2N^2\). For an integer \(z\),
write \(\{z\}_q\) for the remainder of \(z\) mod \(q\) taken in the
range \(-q/2<\{z\}_q\le q/2\).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 14.15 (Shor's analysis, §5; stated, not proved).} Each
outcome \((c,\,a^s\bmod N)\) with \(\lvert\{rc\}_q\rvert\le r/2\) (his
Eq. (5.11)) has probability at least \(1/(3r^2)\), for sufficiently
large \(N\); asymptotically the bound is \(4/(\pi^2r^2)\). For such
\(c\) there is an integer \(d\) with
\[\Bigl\lvert\frac cq-\frac dr\Bigr\rvert\;\le\;\frac1{2q}\qquad\text{(his Eq. (5.13))}.\]
Counting the good outcomes, one run yields \(r\) with probability at
least (the number of \(d<r\) with \(\gcd(d,r)=1\))\(/(3r)\), and
\(O(\log\log r)\) repetitions suffice for a high probability of success.
\end{quote}

Here \(d\) plays the part of the round index \(k\). The factor that
loses to \(\log\log r\) is the chance that the random \(d\) shares a
factor with \(r\), the failure we met at the half reading above.
\texttt{Code/Ch14/EveryRound.py} checks the per-outcome bound and the
success rate on three small instances, \((N,a,q)=(15,7,256)\),
\((21,2,512)\) and \((33,5,2048)\), as documentation. Shor proves the
bounds only for sufficiently large \(N\); they happen to hold on these
three.

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why start from \(\ket1\), when it
is not an eigenstate at all? Because it is the simplest state we can
prepare that has an equal share of every round and needs no knowledge of
\(r\). A superposition of eigenstates, fed to a process that reads
eigenvalues, gets one of them read at random, with the weight it
carries. Equal weights mean a uniform choice of \(k\), and a uniform
\(k\) is what makes the good fractions common.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{euclids-strips}{%
\section{§14.5 Euclid's Strips}\label{euclids-strips}}

The quantum part is over. It hands us a reading \(c\) out of \(q\),
close to \(d/r\) for an unknown \(d\). Two steps of ordinary arithmetic
remain: from the reading to the period, and from the period to a factor.
Both are Euclid.

\hypertarget{from-a-reading-to-a-period}{%
\subsection{From a reading to a
period}\label{from-a-reading-to-a-period}}

Take \(N=21\) and \(a=2\). Ticking gives \(1,2,4,8,16,11,1\), so the
order is \(6\); but suppose we did not know that. Shor's rule gives
\(q=512\), since \(21^2=441\le512<882\). The fraction \(1/6\) of \(512\)
is \(85.33\ldots\), so a likely reading is \(c=85\). How do we get from
\(85/512\) back to a fraction with a small denominator?

Run Euclid's algorithm on \(512\) and \(85\): \(512=6\cdot85+2\), then
\(85=42\cdot2+1\), then \(2=2\cdot1+0\). The quotients \(6,42,2\) are
the \textbf{continued fraction} of \(85/512\):

\[\frac{85}{512}\;=\;\cfrac{1}{6+\cfrac{1}{42+\cfrac12}} .\]

Cutting it off after each quotient gives the \textbf{convergents}
\(\tfrac16\), \(\tfrac{42}{253}\) and \(\tfrac{85}{512}\). The only one
with a denominator below \(N=21\) is \(\tfrac16\), and
\(\lvert\tfrac{85}{512}-\tfrac16\rvert=\tfrac1{1536}\le\tfrac1{1024}=\tfrac1{2q}\).
So the reading says \(d/r=1/6\), and \(r=6\). One multiplication checks
it: \(2^6=64=3\cdot21+1\).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 14.16 (from a reading to a period).} (i) If \(q\ge N^2\)
and \(\lvert c/q-d/r\rvert\le1/(2q)\) with \(r<N\), then \(d/r\) is the
only fraction with denominator less than \(N\) that is this close to
\(c/q\). (ii) \emph{(Stated, not proved; Shor §5.)} That fraction is one
of the convergents of \(c/q\), which Euclid's algorithm produces in
polynomial time.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof of (i).} Suppose \(d'/r'\neq d/r\) also has \(r'<N\) and is
within \(1/(2q)\) of \(c/q\). Then the two are within \(1/q\) of each
other. But
\(\lvert d/r-d'/r'\rvert=\lvert dr'-d'r\rvert/(rr')\ge1/(rr')>1/N^2\ge1/q\),
since the numerator is a nonzero whole number. The two cannot both be
that close. \(\;\blacksquare\)

Shor cites the classical theory of continued fractions for (ii): the
expansion ``finds all the best approximations of \(c/q\) by fractions''.
Kitaev's Theorem 1 does the same job with Euclid's algorithm applied to
his measured value. If \(d\) and \(r\) share a factor, the fraction in
lowest terms gives only a divisor of \(r\); the check \(a^r\equiv1\)
catches it, as the half reading was caught in §14.4. In the dialogue the
Tortoise supposes a coarser reading, \(5/32\) for the same dial, with
\(q\) smaller than Shor's rule asks; there Euclid gives the quotients
\(6,2,2\), whose first convergent is again \(\tfrac16\). Shor's \(q\) is
what makes such a reading safe in general. See
\texttt{Code/Ch14/SharedFactor.py}.

\hypertarget{from-a-period-to-a-factor}{%
\subsection{From a period to a factor}\label{from-a-period-to-a-factor}}

The period of \(7\) mod \(15\) is \(4\). Half of it is \(2\), and
\(7^2=49\equiv4\). One less than \(4\) is \(3\), one more is \(5\), and
\(\gcd(3,15)=3\), \(\gcd(5,15)=5\): \(15=3\cdot5\). For \(2\) mod \(21\)
the period is \(6\), \(2^3=8\), and \(\gcd(7,21)=7\), \(\gcd(9,21)=3\):
\(21=3\cdot7\). Here is why this works.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 14.17 (the reduction from factoring).} Let \(N\) be odd
and not a prime power, and let \(a\) have order \(r\) mod \(N\). If
\(r\) is even and \(a^{r/2}\not\equiv-1\pmod N\), then
\(\gcd(a^{r/2}-1,\,N)\) is a factor of \(N\) other than \(1\) and \(N\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} \((a^{r/2}-1)(a^{r/2}+1)=a^r-1\equiv0\), so \(N\) divides
the product. \(N\) does not divide \(a^{r/2}-1\), or \(a\) would come
home after \(r/2\) ticks, before \(r\). \(N\) does not divide
\(a^{r/2}+1\), by hypothesis. If \(\gcd(a^{r/2}-1,N)\) were \(1\), then
\(N\) would have to divide \(a^{r/2}+1\); so the gcd is more than \(1\).
And it is less than \(N\), since \(N\) does not divide \(a^{r/2}-1\).
\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch14/SharedFactor.py}.

The reduction fails only when \(r\) is odd or \(a^{r/2}\equiv-1\). Shor
shows (his §5, which we state and do not prove) that for \(a\) chosen at
random among the numbers that share no factor with \(N\), it succeeds
with probability at least \(1-1/2^{\ell-1}\), where \(\ell\) is the
number of distinct odd prime factors of \(N\) (his \(k\)). For \(N=15\),
\(\ell=2\) and the bound is \(\tfrac12\); in fact, of the eight numbers
below \(15\) that share no factor with it, six split it, and the two
failures are \(a=1\) (order \(1\), odd) and \(a=N-1\) (order \(2\), and
\(a^{1}\equiv-1\)). Shor credits the reduction to earlier work (1976),
and says that prime powers, the case excluded above, can be factored
efficiently by classical methods.

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} The gcd has no picture, and neither has the
continued fraction. The one step of this section that the pictures reach
is the squaring. By Result 14.2, \(C_7^2\) is a pure crossing, and it
multiplies by \(4=7^2\bmod15\):

\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=2.72em, x=1.1em, y=1.1em,
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=0.9em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \draw[wire] (0,5.4) -- (0.6,5.4) -- (2.8,3.6) -- (5.8,3.6) -- (8,1.8) -- (9.6,1.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,3.6) -- (0.6,3.6) -- (2.8,1.8) -- (5.8,1.8) -- (8,0) -- (9.6,0);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.8) -- (0.6,1.8) -- (2.8,0) -- (5.8,0) -- (8,5.4) -- (9.6,5.4);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (0.6,0) -- (2.8,5.4) -- (5.8,5.4) -- (8,3.6) -- (9.6,3.6);
  \foreach \y in {5.4,3.6,1.8,0} { \node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (4,\y) {}; \node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (8.9,\y) {}; }
\end{tikzpicture}
\;\overset{\text{fusion}}{=}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=2.72em, x=1.1em, y=1.1em]
  \draw[wire] (0,5.4) -- (0.5,5.4) -- (3,1.8) -- (3.5,1.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,3.6) -- (0.5,3.6) -- (3,0) -- (3.5,0);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.8) -- (0.5,1.8) -- (3,5.4) -- (3.5,5.4);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (0.5,0) -- (3,3.6) -- (3.5,3.6);
\end{tikzpicture}\]

exactly, after sliding the four pairs of red \(\pi\)s together along
their wires. That is \(a^{r/2}\) as a picture, and it is as far as the
pictures go. The subtraction of \(1\) and the greatest common divisor
are arithmetic on numbers, not processes on wires.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Dirac's Blackboard.}\nopagebreak

\emph{The same algorithm twice.} Euclid's algorithm divides the larger
number by the smaller, keeps the remainder, and repeats until nothing is
left. Here it is on the two jobs of this section, side by side.
\[\begin{array}{r@{\;}c@{\;}l@{\qquad\qquad}r@{\;}c@{\;}l}
512 &=& 6\cdot85+2 & 15 &=& 5\cdot3+0\\
85 &=& 42\cdot2+1 & & & \\
2 &=& 2\cdot1+0 & & &
\end{array}\] On the left, the quotients \(6,42,2\) are the continued
fraction of \(85/512\), and the first of them already says ``about one
in six''. On the right, the last nonzero remainder is the greatest
common divisor: \(3\) measures \(15\) exactly, so \(\gcd(3,15)=3\). The
first job reads the quotients, the second reads the last remainder, and
neither needs anything but division with remainder. Both run in a number
of steps proportional to the number of digits, since two steps always at
least halve the remainder: if the next remainder is at most half the
current one, it has halved already; if it is more than half, it goes
into the current one once, and what is left, the difference, is less
than half. That is why the classical half of Shor's algorithm is cheap.
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{the-whole-algorithm}{%
\subsection{The whole algorithm}\label{the-whole-algorithm}}

Here is Shor's algorithm assembled, with each step's owner named.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  If \(N\) is even, or a prime power, split it classically (Shor §5).
\item
  Choose \(a\) at random with \(1<a<N\). If \(\gcd(a,N)>1\), that is
  already a factor.
\item
  Choose \(t\) with \(q=2^t\) and \(N^2\le q<2N^2\). Run phase
  estimation (Result 14.11) with the tick box \(U_a\), the register
  started at \(\ket1\) (Result 14.12), and read \(c\).
\item
  Expand \(c/q\) in a continued fraction and take the convergent \(d/r\)
  with \(r<N\) nearest to \(c/q\) (Result 14.16). Check \(a^r\equiv1\).
\item
  If \(r\) is even and \(a^{r/2}\not\equiv-1\), output
  \(\gcd(a^{r/2}-1,N)\) (Result 14.17). Otherwise go back to step 2.
\end{enumerate}

Step 3 is the only quantum step. Its controlled powers
\(\Lambda(U_a^{2^{t-m}})\) are not made by applying the tick box
\(2^{t-m}\) times. As Cleve et al.~note, the sequence of controlled
powers is equivalent to the implementation, ``via repeated squarings'',
of modular exponentiation in Shor's algorithm (Shor §3):
\(a^2,a^4,a^8,\dots\) mod \(N\) are computed classically in advance, and
each controlled power is one reversible multiplication.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

105 & kickback:
\(\Lambda(U)(\ket c\ket u)=e^{2\pi ic\varphi}\ket c\ket u\) for
\(U\ket u=e^{2\pi i\varphi}\ket u\) (row 37, general form) & the tall
box \(\Lambda(U)\) over \(\ket u\) \(=\) a green \(2\pi\varphi\) on the
control wire beside \(\ket u\) (for general \(U\), borrowed from the
blackboard; for a phase box, row 104) \\
106 & \(F_q\ket x=q^{-1/2}\sum_ye^{2\pi ixy/q}\ket y\); product form;
network of \(H\) and \(\mathrm{CP}(\pi/2^{d})\), output reversed &
\textbf{the transform's triangle}: yellow boxes and controlled turns,
then the wires crossed into reverse order; the inverse is its mirror
image, every turn negated \\
107 & \textbf{phase estimation}: the network returns \(\ket j\ket u\)
exactly for \(\varphi=j/2^t\) & \textbf{\emph{The Quarter Clock}}
(\(t=2\)): each counting wire hears one digit, at twice the pace of the
wire below; the inverse transform's turns peel off the finer digit; the
yellow boxes read what is left \\
108 & \(U_a\ket x=\ket{ax\bmod N}\); \(\ket{\psi_k}\), eigenvalue
\(e^{2\pi ik/r}\); \(\ket1=r^{-1/2}\sum_k\ket{\psi_k}\) & the tall box
\(U_a\); for \(N=15\), \(a=7\): red \(\pi\)s and crossings (on the
residues \(1\le x<N\)); a green wheel point is the equal mix of the
wheel's rounds \\
109 & continued fractions; \(\gcd(a^{r/2}\pm1,N)\); Shor's bounds &
\textbf{no picture}: the number theory stays on the blackboard \\
\end{longtable}

\endgroup

Every row is exact, scalar included. In row 106, \(d\) is the distance
between the two wires of a controlled turn. None of these rows is a
statement about running time or success probability: rows 103 to 108 are
equalities of processes, and the bounds of this chapter are cited
(Results 14.14 and 14.15).

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-theorem-twice-14}{%
\section{§14.7 The Theorem, Twice}\label{the-theorem-twice-14}}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 14.11 (phase estimation on an eigenstate), restated.} For
\(U\ket u=e^{2\pi i\varphi}\ket u\) with
\(\varphi=j/2^t=0.j_1\cdots j_t\), exactly,
\(\bigl(F_q^{-1}\otimes I\bigr)\prod_{m=1}^{t}\Lambda_m\bigl(U^{2^{t-m}}\bigr)\bigl(H^{\otimes t}\ket0^{\otimes t}\otimes\ket u\bigr)=\ket j\ket u\),
with \(j_1\) on the top wire.
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{diracs-blackboard-14}{%
\subsection{Dirac's Blackboard}\label{diracs-blackboard-14}}

\textbf{Step 1: the Hadamards.} Each counting wire goes to
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket0+\ket1)\):
\[H^{\otimes t}\ket0^{\otimes t}\otimes\ket u\;=\;2^{-t/2}\bigotimes_{m=1}^{t}\bigl(\ket0+\ket1\bigr)\otimes\ket u .\]

\textbf{Step 2: the controlled powers.} The register stays in \(\ket u\)
throughout, so each \(\Lambda_m(U^{2^{t-m}})\) acts only by kickback
(Result 14.4), turning the \(\ket1\) branch of wire \(m\) by
\(2^{t-m}\varphi\). The \(\Lambda_m\) commute: on a basis state of the
counting wires, \(\ket{c_1\cdots c_t}\), the product applies
\(U^{\sum_mc_m2^{t-m}}\) to the register whatever the order, since
powers of one \(U\) commute. So
\[\prod_{m}\Lambda_m\bigl(U^{2^{t-m}}\bigr)\;2^{-t/2}\bigotimes_m(\ket0+\ket1)\otimes\ket u\;=\;2^{-t/2}\bigotimes_{m=1}^{t}\bigl(\ket0+e^{2\pi i\,2^{t-m}\varphi}\ket1\bigr)\otimes\ket u .\]
This is Cleve et al.'s product state, their Eq. (5.1).

\textbf{Step 3: shift the point.} By Result 14.8,
\(e^{2\pi i\,2^{t-m}\varphi}=e^{2\pi i\,0.j_{t-m+1}\cdots j_t}\). So
wire \(1\) carries \(0.j_t\), wire \(2\) carries \(0.j_{t-1}j_t\), and
wire \(t\) carries \(0.j_1\cdots j_t\). By the product form (Result
14.9) with \(x=j\), the counting wires are in the state \(F_q\ket j\):
\[2^{-t/2}\bigotimes_{m=1}^{t}\bigl(\ket0+e^{2\pi i\,0.j_{t-m+1}\cdots j_t}\ket1\bigr)\otimes\ket u\;=\;F_q\ket j\otimes\ket u .\]

\textbf{Step 4: undo the transform.}
\(\bigl(F_q^{-1}\otimes I\bigr)\bigl(F_q\ket j\otimes\ket u\bigr)=\ket j\ket u\).
The top wire holds \(j_1\), because \(\ket j\) is written top wire
first. \(\;\blacksquare\)

\hypertarget{coeckes-sketchbook-8}{%
\subsection{Coecke's Sketchbook}\label{coeckes-sketchbook-8}}

Take \(t=2\), a one-wire register, and the phase box \(U=Z(\theta)\)
with \(\theta=2\pi\varphi\), whose eigenstate \(\ket1\) is drawn as a
lit point: \(\sqrt2\ket1\). Then \(\varphi=0.j_1j_2\) and
\(\theta=\pi j_1+\tfrac\pi2j_2\), with the two digits left general. The
counting wires start at \(H\ket0\), which is a green point
(\(H\sqrt2\ket0=\ket0+\ket1\) by colour change) with \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\)
in front; the two counting points and the lit point together carry
\(2^{3/2}\). The controlled powers are controlled turns:
\(\Lambda(Z(\theta)^2)=\mathrm{CP}(2\theta)\) between the top wire and
the wheel, and \(\Lambda(Z(\theta))=\mathrm{CP}(\theta)\) between the
lower wire and the wheel. The inverse transform is the picture of §14.3.
Three bare gadgets carry \(2^{-3/2}\), so the drawn picture below is
exactly the left side of Result 14.11, with no scalar to add.

The crossing only exchanges rows, so the points slide through it:
\(j_1\) on top, \(j_2\) below, the lit wheel at the bottom. That is

\[2^{-3/2}\bigl(\sqrt2\ket{j_1}\bigr)\bigl(\sqrt2\ket{j_2}\bigr)\bigl(\sqrt2\ket1\bigr)\;=\;\ket{j_1j_2}\ket1 .\qquad\blacksquare\]

Every step was exact, and the scalar ledger is short: three points give
\(2^{3/2}\), three passages through controlled turns give \(2^{-3/2}\).
See \texttt{Code/Ch14/QuarterClock.py}.

Two debts must be stated. First, for a general \(U\), the step ``the lit
point passes through and leaves its turn'' is kickback (row 105), and
for a tall box that is \textbf{borrowed from the blackboard}: the
picture proves it only for a phase box. Second, for general \(t\) the
chain is the same, said in words rather than drawn: the fastest listener
hears one digit as a half-turn or none, its yellow box makes it a basis
point, and that point passes through every controlled turn of the
inverse transform that it meets (one application of Result 14.6 each),
peeling its digit off every slower listener; the next listener is then
left with one digit, and so on up the triangle.

\hypertarget{the-verdict-14}{%
\subsection{The verdict}\label{the-verdict-14}}

The blackboard wins, and not narrowly. Its four steps prove the theorem
for every \(t\) and every unitary \(U\), and once the product form is
known they are almost bookkeeping. The sketchbook needs five pictures to
prove one instance, \(t=2\) and a phase box, general in the two digits;
for a general \(U\) it borrows kickback from the blackboard, and for
general \(t\) it describes a chain it does not draw.

What the pictures show is the mechanism, which the blackboard's product
form compresses into one line. Each counting wire hears one digit, at
twice the pace of the wire below it. The fastest listener's yellow box
turns its half-turn into a bit. That bit passes through the inverse
transform's controlled turn and peels the finer digit off the slower
listener, and the slower listener's yellow box reads what is left. The
picture is an equality of processes. It says nothing about how often the
whole algorithm must be run, nor how long it takes.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-quarter-clock}{%
\section{§14.8 The Quarter Clock}\label{the-quarter-clock}}

Here is the chapter's master diagram, one instance of the headline drawn
whole. Take the circuit of §14.7 with \(t=2\), the phase box
\(S=Z(\pi/2)\) on the wheel, and the wheel's point lit:
\(\theta=\pi/2\), so \(\varphi=\tfrac{1}{4}=0.01\), with \(j_1=0\) and
\(j_2=1\). Put \(\theta=\pi/2\) into the first picture of §14.7, and
apply \textbf{fusion} (Theorem 8.1) everywhere it applies: every pair of
green dots joined by a plain wire slides together into one. On the top
row, the counting point fuses with its gadget's ring. On the lower row,
the counting point fuses with both rings. On the wheel, the two rings
fuse. Fusion is exact, so the result is the same process, drawn more
compactly. That drawing is the master.

From left to right: on the top row, a green ring with phase \(\pi/2\)
(the counting point and its half of the controlled \(U^2\)), a yellow
box, a green ring with phase \(-\pi/4\) (its half of the inverse
transform's controlled turn), and then the line crosses down to the
second output. On the lower row, a phase-free green ring (the counting
point, \(+\pi/4\) from the controlled \(U\) and \(-\pi/4\) from the
inverse transform, which cancel), a yellow box, and then the line
crosses up to the first output. On the wheel, the lit point, a green
ring with phase \(3\pi/4\) (the wheel's halves of both controlled
powers), and the third output. Below and between them, three phase-free
red hubs, each with its pendant: the first is tied to the top row's
first ring and the wheel ring, with a pendant at \(-\pi/2\) (the
controlled \(U^2\)); the second to the lower ring and the wheel ring,
pendant \(-\pi/4\) (the controlled \(U\)); the third to the top row's
second ring and the lower ring, pendant \(+\pi/4\) (the inverse
transform's \(\mathrm{CP}(-\pi/2)\)). The picture is called \textbf{The
Quarter Clock}.

The tie from the top row's first ring runs down past the place where the
lower row has not yet begun, and the two counting rows cross once,
without touching, before the outputs.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 14.18 (The Quarter Clock).} Exactly, with no scalar,
\[\text{The Quarter Clock}\;=\;\ket0\ket1\ket1 .\] The reading \(01\)
says \(\varphi=0.01=\tfrac{1}{4}\), and the wheel comes back lit. With
the wheel's point dark instead, the value is \(\ket0\ket0\ket0\); with
it green, the value is
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket0\ket0\ket0+\ket0\ket1\ket1\bigr)\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} Fusion is exact, so The Quarter Clock equals the
gate-by-gate circuit of §14.7 at \(\theta=\pi/2\), and the chain of
§14.7 with \(j_1=0\), \(j_2=1\) gives \(\ket0\ket1\ket1\): three points
worth \(2^{3/2}\) against three bare controlled turns worth
\(2^{-3/2}\), so no scalar is left. On the blackboard it is Result 14.11
with \(U=S\), \(\ket u=\ket1\) and \(j=01\). With the point dark, the
wheel is the eigenstate \(\ket0\) of \(S\), whose phase is \(0\); the
dark point passes every controlled turn leaving nothing (Result 14.6
with \(c=0\)), and the chain ends at \(\ket0\ket0\ket0\). With the point
green, it is \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) times the dark point plus the lit point
(§14.4), and the value is \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) times the sum of the two
values. \(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch14/QuarterClock.py}, which
builds this picture, evaluates it with its scalar, derives it from the
gate-by-gate circuit by fusion, and reduces it by the rules to one point
per output, with phase \(\pi\) on exactly the second and third; and
\texttt{Code/Ch14/EveryRound.py} for the green point.

The phase was chosen so that its reading does not read the same in both
directions. Read from the bottom counting wire up, the outputs would say
\(10\), a half; the book's convention, top wire first, gives \(01\), a
quarter, and the code checks that it is this one. The crossing is what
makes the convention come out right: it is the reversal of the
transform, and it is why the first output shows \(j_1\), the digit that
counts halves.

Look at the picture once more with the value in mind. The quarter was in
it all along, as the phase \(\pi/2\) on the top row's first ring. That
ring is the double-pace listener, and its turn is the controlled
\(U^2\)'s half-turn split into halves. The wheel's ring, at \(3\pi/4\),
holds the wheel's halves of both controlled powers, a quarter-turn's
worth from the double-pace gadget and an eighth from the single-pace
one. Nothing in the picture ticks four times, and nothing is repeated.
The period of four ticks comes out of one passage, as two binary digits.

With the wheel's point green, the reading is \(00\) or \(01\), each with
probability \(\tfrac12\), and the wheel comes out in the matching round:
the reading and the round are correlated. That is Result 14.13 for the
smallest wheel with a period of four, with only two of its four rounds
present, because one wire holds only two.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{what-the-picture-leaves-to-the-blackboard}{%
\section{§14.9 What the Picture Leaves to the
Blackboard}\label{what-the-picture-leaves-to-the-blackboard}}

Take stock. The order \(r\) of \(a\) mod \(N\) is a hidden period
(Result 14.1), and for one small dial it can even be drawn (Result
14.2). The tick box has rounds that it only turns (Result 14.3), and a
controlled box kicks the turn back onto its control (Result 14.4). For a
phase box the controlled box is a gadget of dots (Result 14.5), and a
basis point passes through it leaving its turn behind (Result 14.6). One
listener hears the turn only as a cosine (Result 14.7); listeners at
doubled paces each hear one binary digit more (Result 14.8); and the
inverse Fourier transform, a triangle of yellow boxes and controlled
turns (Results 14.9 and 14.10), peels the digits apart. Phase estimation
reads a dyadic phase exactly (Result 14.11), and The Quarter Clock is
one instance of it, drawn whole (Result 14.18). The hand at one is every
round at once (Result 14.12), so the reading is the turn of a random
round (Result 14.13), and continued fractions and a gcd finish the job
(Results 14.16 and 14.17).

Now the honest part. \textbf{The diagram shows the architecture; the
number theory stays on the blackboard.} The following have no picture in
this chapter: the continued fraction, the gcd, the reduction from
factoring to order finding, Shor's probability bounds (Result 14.15),
the general-phase bound (Result 14.14), and the running time. In Shor's
own letters, where \(n\) is our \(N\), his quantum factoring algorithm
``takes asymptotically
\(O\bigl((\log n)^2(\log\log n)(\log\log\log n)\bigr)\) steps on a
quantum computer, along with a polynomial (in \(\log n\)) amount of
post-processing time on a classical computer''. The best classical
method he cites, the number field sieve, takes time
\(\exp\bigl(c(\log n)^{1/3}(\log\log n)^{2/3}\bigr)\) for some constant
\(c\). Every one of those statements was proved by counting, or is cited
here and proved by counting elsewhere.

A rewrite proves that two processes are equal. The Quarter Clock proves
that one passage of that network returns \(01\). It proves no running
time. It proves nothing about how often the algorithm must be repeated,
and nothing at all about whether factoring is hard for a classical
computer. Shor calls it ``generally thought to be hard'', and Cleve et
al.~say only that no classical polynomial-time procedure is known. As
far as this chapter goes, a fast classical factoring method is not known
and not ruled out.

There is one more thing the chapter has quietly given up. In Chapters 5
and 13 the oracle was a sealed box, and the whole game was to count its
uses. In Shor's algorithm there is no sealed box. The controlled powers
\(\Lambda(U_a^{2^{t-m}})\) are, as Cleve et al.~show, modular
exponentiation by repeated squaring, a classical circuit made reversible
(Shor §3). Anyone who knows \(N\) and \(a\) can build it. The quantum
speed-up is not a count of queries; it is a claim about circuits, and it
rests on the number theory as much as on the pictures.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Coecke's Sketchbook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{What the picture does not count.} It is tempting to look at The
Quarter Clock and say that the picture shows why the period costs one
passage instead of four ticks. It shows something smaller. It shows that
this network, set this way, returns this state. Nothing in the rules of
Chapter 8 knows how many gates a picture has, or how hard a gadget is to
build, or how small an angle a laboratory can turn. The triangle of the
Fourier transform looks cheap, and it is, but that was proved by
counting its gates, and Coppersmith's approximate version by bounding
its errors. A second temptation is subtler. The picture for \(N=15\) and
\(a=7\) was a handful of crossings, and one might think that the tick
box is always so simple inside. It is not: that picture used the
accident that \(15\) is one less than a power of two. A general
multiplication mod \(N\) is a long arithmetic circuit, and the pictures
of this chapter never open it.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

The chapter's question has an answer. To tell how long a thing takes to
come round with one look, do not look at where it stands. Look at
something the ticking only turns, and listen to the turn with listeners
that tick at doubled paces, each hearing one binary digit more than the
last. Correct each by the digits already heard, and read them all at
once: that is phase estimation, and the correction is the inverse
Fourier transform. Start from the hand at one, which is every round at
once, and the reading is the turn of a random round; half the time or
so, Euclid's algorithm turns it into the period, and the period into a
factor. The pictures drew the listening, digit by digit, down to where
each digit is heard. The arithmetic around it they left to the
blackboard, and so did we.

Chapter 15 asks a different question of a different box. The box marks
one item among many, and the task is to find it. The quantum answer is
faster than searching the items one by one, but only by a square root,
and Chapter 13 has already told us, from BBBV's bound, that for a box of
this kind no quantum method does better. The picture that explains the
search is not a string diagram at all. It is a picture of a plane, with
two lines through it and a state that turns between them, a different
kind of diagram for a different kind of speed-up.

\hypertarget{toccata-in-square-root-time}{%
\chapter{Toccata in Square-Root
Time}\label{toccata-in-square-root-time}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\emph{凍星や}\\
\emph{折りてひらけば}\\
\emph{また高く}

\emph{iteboshi ya}\\
\emph{orite hirakeba}\\
\emph{mata takaku}

\emph{Stars in the hard frost ---}\\
\emph{each time I fold and unfold,}\\
\emph{higher once again.}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\emph{{[}The Tortoise's parlour, the next evening, after supper. The
plates are cleared. Achilles's scarf lies folded on the seat of the
Tortoise's chair.{]}}

\emph{{[}The stove has been fed after supper and burns bright behind its
mica, its iron ticking now and then as it heats. On the lower pane the
frost ferns have grown back since the morning, and past the black glass
above them the lane lies pale under the rime. At its far end the
smithy's doors stand open on a square of red, and the glow spills out
across the frozen ruts: the smith is working late, as smithies do in a
hard frost, when every horse in the parish wants its shoes sharpened for
the ice. Through the glass comes his iron, a clink, and a flurry of
clinks, and nothing, and a clink again, in no pattern anybody could
follow. Achilles sits with his feet to the fender and his hands round
his teacup, and the Tortoise's cup keeps warm on the hob beside the
pot.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} That was a supper for a hard frost. I shan't need to
eat again till spring.

\textbf{Tortoise:} You say that every winter, and every winter spring
comes round by breakfast.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}picking up the folded scarf{]}} And here's
my scarf, waiting on your chair like a guest who won't sit down.

\textbf{Tortoise:} I brought it down this morning, as I promised, and
the stair groaned at me, as you promised.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}winding it on{]}} Only once?

\textbf{Tortoise:} Twice. The second time I was carrying my seed-cabinet
up.

\textbf{Achilles:} Up? The whole cabinet?

\textbf{Tortoise:} On my back. It's the only way I carry anything. It
lived in the cupboard under the stairs, and this morning the cupboard
needed the room.

\textbf{Achilles:} For what?

\textbf{Tortoise:} For the clock-case. I went up first thing, and there
it was on the table, still standing open, still showing its panes, very
pleased with itself. I shut its front and carried it down, and now it
stands in the cupboard beside the casket and the jam.

\textbf{Achilles:} Two spent boxes and a jar of jam, in the dark
together.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The jam has heard all they have to say by now. And
when I went back up with the seed-cabinet, I found the Office had been
in the night. On the shelf, where the clock-case used to stand, there's
a new case with the Office's label on it.

\textbf{Achilles:} Up your stairs, over the loose tread, and not a
groan?

\textbf{Tortoise:} The Office never treads on anything.

\textbf{Achilles:} What does the label say this time?

\textbf{Tortoise:} ``For the wisher, top room. With the Office's
compliments. Keep in a cool place.''

\textbf{Achilles:} Then it's come to the right house.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}taking the candlestick from the mantel and
lighting it at the stove{]}} Bring my bag, and mind the tread. It's had
a busy day.

\emph{{[}She tops up both cups from the pot and sets them on the flat of
her shell, where they ride as level as on a tray. Achilles shoulders the
work-bag and grins at them.{]}}

\emph{{[}They go up, the candle first. Halfway, the tread groans under
Achilles's foot, and he pats the banister by way of apology.{]}}

\emph{{[}The stair is narrow and makes its one turn at the landing, and
their shadows climb the wall beside them, stretching and shrinking with
the candle. Under the candle the treads are all alike, each worn to the
same hollow in the middle, and nothing about any of them tells which is
the loose one; only a foot finds it. The cups on the Tortoise's shell go
up the whole flight without a ripple. On the stair the smithy's clink
comes fainter than in the parlour, and no more regular.{]}}

\emph{{[}The top room, as it was last night: the small table and two
chairs, the one window over the lane, the shelf beside it. Against the
wall beside the door stands the Tortoise's seed-cabinet, eight rows of
eight small drawers, each with its brass pull. On the shelf stands the
old brass lamp, and beside it a low, broad case of dark wood, about as
wide as a loaf, with the Office's label on its side. Along its front
runs a row of four small drawers with brass pulls; at its right end are
two small windows, one above the other; on its top is a little enamel
plate. The case is sealed.{]}}

\emph{{[}The top room is as small as it was last night, and colder,
tucked under the slope of the roof, and it has one of everything but
drawers. One door, standing open on the dark of the stairs. One window
over the lane, frosted over again since the morning from edge to edge,
white ferns lying close against the glass; low on the pane the pair of
initials that somebody scratched there long ago with a diamond comes up
white among them, as it does on every night of hard frost. One shelf
beside the window, where the old brass lamp stands tarnished nearly
brown, and beside it the new case, low and dark, in the place where the
clock-case stood. Under the shelf the empty butter-crocks keep their
row, and among them the tall glass jar. Against the wall by the door the
candle finds the seed-cabinet as it comes in and lies evenly across its
front, every drawer the same as its neighbour and every pull the same,
so that nothing in the light could tell one from another. On the wall
facing the window hangs a print in a plain dark frame: Escher's
\textup{Cubic Space Division}, a space divided into cubes by straight
beams. The candle, still in the Tortoise's claw, reaches only the lower
part of the frame. It was hanging there before the candle came up the
stairs, and it will be hanging there when the candle goes down. Through
the frosted pane the smithy goes on at the end of the lane, heard and
not seen: a clink, a pause, a clink and another, and nothing that could
be called a tune.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}setting the work-bag down by the table{]}}
So that's the seed-cabinet. It looks like a wall of drawers that
somebody has shrunk to fit a room.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Every drawer the same, and a packet of seed in each.
I know where the beans are, and the beans know it.

\textbf{Achilles:} It's colder up here than in the lane.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}setting the candlestick on the table{]}}
Then keep your scarf on and sit. The chair without the wobble is still
yours.

\emph{{[}She lowers herself into the chair with the wobble, and it rocks
under her with a small clack. Achilles lifts the cups down from her
shell, sets hers at her elbow, and keeps his own in both hands; his
breath shows white over it.{]}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{first-challenge-four-drawers-one-wish}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{First Challenge --- \emph{Four Drawers, One
Wish}}{First Challenge --- Four Drawers, One Wish}}\label{first-challenge-four-drawers-one-wish}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}taking the candlestick up to the shelf, so
that its light falls on the new case{]}} This is the Genie's
drawer-case, and the Office sent it for one wish. Along its front are
four little drawers, locked, and at its right end two windows, the upper
and the lower. There is nothing on it anyone can set; it hasn't so much
as a knob.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}rising, and bending at the shelf to the
plate on the top of the case, its drawers towards him and its windows at
his right{]}} And the Terms. \emph{{[}reading{]}} ``One wish, one touch
of the marker. Touched, the marked drawer is turned over, and the others
are left as they are. A passage of the case touches the marker once.''

\textbf{Achilles:} One of the drawers is marked, then. But turned over
how? A drawer turned over would spill.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The Terms don't say. Read on.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}reading{]}} ``The windows name a drawer:
both dark, the first; upper dark and lower lit, the second; upper lit
and lower dark, the third; both lit, the fourth. A spent case unlocks
its drawers. The marked drawer holds the key to its back.''

\begin{center}
\drawercase*{}{the Genie's drawer-case}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} So one drawer has the key in it, and I get one wish
to find out which.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}bringing the candlestick back to the table
and setting it at Achilles's right, a little beyond his place, as he
takes his chair again{]}} That's all the Terms promise. How would you go
about it?

\textbf{Achilles:} The plain way. I'd ask about one drawer, the first,
say: is it this one? If it is, I'm done, and if it isn't, I guess among
the rest.

\textbf{Tortoise:} And how often does that find it?

\textbf{Achilles:} A quarter of the time the first is the one, and I
have it at once. The other three quarters, I guess among three and I'm
right one time in three, which is another quarter. Half the time, all
told.

\textbf{Tortoise:} And to be sure?

\textbf{Achilles:} Ask the first, then the second, then the third; if
all three say no, it's the fourth. Three wishes, to be sure. And the
Terms give me one.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Then the plain way, on one wish, is half the time.
Now the Office's way. \emph{{[}She takes from the work-bag a strip of
cream card, with a wooden peg in each of its slits, and a pencil, and
lays the card on the table in front of him, the right way round for him:
its first slit at his left, and every slit running away from him, so
that a peg slides up its slit away from him and down towards him. The
pencil she lays beside it.{]}} This is my peg-card: four slits in a row,
one for each drawer, first to fourth from the left, with a middle line
pencilled across them and notches marked above it and below. The peg in
each slit slides up or down, and its height, in notches, is how strongly
its drawer is being asked about; a peg below the line stands less than
nothing. A drawer's odds are its peg's height squared, out of all four
squares together.

\emph{{[}She slides each of the four pegs up its slit to the first notch
above the middle line.{]}}

\begin{center}
\pegcard*{even row}{level across the card}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} The even row: every peg one notch up. That is every
drawer asked at once, evenly, and that is how the Office's marker is
touched, on all four drawers at once. It is still one touch.

\textbf{Achilles:} One notch each. One, one, one and one, squared, and a
quarter of the odds apiece. Fair.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Now you are the marker, and the second drawer is
marked. Do to its peg what the Terms say.

\textbf{Achilles:} Turned over. \emph{{[}considering the peg{]}} Then it
goes under the line, as far below as it stood above.

\emph{{[}The four pegs stand in a level row, each one notch above the
middle line, and each drawer holds a quarter of the odds. Achilles puts
a finger on the second peg alone and slides it down its slit, to the
middle line and through it, and on, until it stands one notch below. The
first, the third and the fourth have not moved, nor has the line. The
second peg is exactly as far from the line as it was, only on the other
side: under. Its square is what it was.{]}}

\begin{center}
\pegcard[touch the second]{even row}{the marked peg under}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} One, one, one, one. The squares haven't changed.

\emph{{[}Down the lane, faint through the frost, a hammer gives the
anvil a single light tap. Achilles lifts his head, but no blow follows
it, and the smithy goes quiet.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} A quarter of the odds on every drawer, just as
before. Then a touch on all four drawers at once is wasted. It leaves a
mark nobody can see.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Nobody can see it in the odds. But look at the pegs:
the second is under, and the others aren't. The touch has left its mark;
it's only upside down.

\emph{{[}Achilles's eyes go to the window. The frost ferns lie white and
close against the glass from edge to edge, and from the chair, by
candlelight, there is no telling whether they have grown on this side of
the pane or on the far side. The Tortoise waits for him to look
back.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} What would you have to do to the pegs, without
looking to see which is under, to make that one stand taller than the
rest?

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{second-challenge-the-turn-about}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Second Challenge --- \emph{The
Turn-About}}{Second Challenge --- The Turn-About}}\label{second-challenge-the-turn-about}}

\textbf{Achilles:} If I could look, I'd pull the one that's under
straight up. Without looking, I'd have to do the same thing to every
peg.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The same thing to every peg, yes, but not the same
distance. I call it the turn-about. Add the four heights and take a
quarter of the sum, which is their average; then move every peg to the
other side of that average, just as far as it stood from it.

\textbf{Achilles:} A peg standing at the average stays where it is,
then, and a peg far from it goes far.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Let's play it from the beginning, two hands in turn:
you touch, and I turn about.

\emph{{[}She slides the second peg up again, through the middle line to
the first notch above, level with its neighbours: the even row once
more, a quarter of the odds on every drawer.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}sliding the second peg down through the
middle line to one notch under, the others left standing{]}} The marker
turns it over.

\textbf{Tortoise:} And we turn it about.

\emph{{[}Down the lane the smith's hammer taps the anvil, light, and the
striker's sledge comes down after it, heavy, just where the tap fell.
Then the smithy is quiet again.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} First the average.

\textbf{Achilles:} One, less one, one and one: two notches in all. A
quarter of two is half a notch.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Then every peg goes to the other side of half a
notch.

\textbf{Achilles:} The level ones stand half a notch above it, so they
go to half a notch below it, which is the line itself.

\textbf{Achilles:} And the one that's under stands a notch and a half
below it, so it goes a notch and a half above. Two notches up.

\emph{{[}The row as it stands: the first, third and fourth pegs one
notch up, the second one notch under, and the average, half a notch up,
lying between them. Achilles pencils a small tick at half a notch in the
card's left margin, beside the first slit, and there it stays. He slides
the three level pegs down, one notch each, until each rests on the
middle line. Then he takes the second peg from below the line and slides
it up, past the line, past his pencilled tick, past the first notch, to
the second notch above. The line, the tick and the slits are where they
were. What has changed: three pegs that stood a notch up now stand at
nothing, and the peg that was under stands higher than any peg has stood
tonight. What has held: the average, still half a notch; and the four
squares together, still four.{]}}

\begin{center}
\pegcard[touch the second, mark the average, turn about]{even row}{turned about, a tall peg}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Now the odds.

\textbf{Achilles:} Nothing, four, nothing, nothing, out of four.

\textbf{Achilles:} \ldots Oh. All the odds are on the second drawer.

\textbf{Achilles:} The mark nobody could see, and the turn-about has
stood it up where anybody could.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The turn-about never looked to see which peg was
under. It only took the average of all four, and the average knew.

\emph{{[}Achilles takes up his cup, finds the tea only warm, drinks, and
sets it down harder than he meant. The tea rocks over in the cup: the
side that dipped comes up as far above the level as it went below, the
side that rose goes down as far, and all the while the middle of it does
not move.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} So what you're saying is that the turn-about does the
finding, and the touch is only a formality.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Then let it find something without one. \emph{{[}She
slides the three pegs on the line up a notch each, and the tall one down
from two notches to one: level again, every peg a notch up, and a
quarter of the odds on each.{]}} The even row, and no touch. Turn it
about.

\textbf{Achilles:} One and one and one and one: four, and a quarter of
four is one. Every peg stands at the average already. \emph{{[}He puts a
finger to each peg in turn and moves none of them.{]}} Nothing moves. It
found nothing.

\textbf{Tortoise:} It turns an even row into itself. It needs the
touch's mark to find anything: two hands.

\emph{{[}Her own cup stands at her elbow where she set it down, gently,
and the tea in it lies level and does not stir. She warms her claws
round it a moment before she reaches for the work-bag.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Now the same turn-about another way. \emph{{[}She
spreads her drawing-cloth beside the peg-card, on its right as Achilles
sees it, between the card and the candlestick, and brings out string,
rings, beads and yellow tubes.{]}} My drawing-cloth again, with last
night's rings and tubes and last night's rules: what I lay on it is a
picture of a thing, not the thing. Two cords, one for the upper pane and
one for the lower, and on them a turn-about built of pieces you know: a
tube on each cord, a ring at a half on each, the controlled turn for a
half between them, and a tube on each again.

\emph{{[}She lays two cords across the cloth from Achilles's left to his
right, one above the other, the upper further from him. Near the left
end of each she slides on a yellow tube. Beyond the tubes she threads a
green ring on each cord, each from its cord's loose right-hand end, and
sets both beads at a half; a bead at rest stands at the top of its ring
as Achilles sees it; turned round, it goes clockwise as he sees it, and
turned back, the other way. Beyond those she threads another green ring
on each cord the same way, its bead a quarter round, and ties each by a
tie of its own to a bare red hub set to their right, midway between the
cords; from the hub a short pendant runs on to the right to a small
green bob, a quarter back. Beyond, a yellow tube on each cord again,
threaded on from the loose right-hand end, which runs on a little way
past it.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} The controlled turn for a half, as last night: push a
dark end-ring through it and the whole of it falls away; push a lit one
through and a half lands on the other cord, as a ring at a half. And a
ring at a half lets a dark end pass with nothing set aside, but a lit
end sets the half aside, off the cloth.

\textbf{Tortoise:} First the even setting. \emph{{[}She threads a green
end-ring, its bead at rest, on the left end of each cord.{]}} Green at
rest on both cords: every drawer, evenly.

\begin{center}
\aboutcloth*{even setting}{the build, set even}
\end{center}

\emph{{[}The picture as it stands: the two green end-rings at rest at
the left; then the tubes, the rings at a half, the controlled turn, and
the far tubes. She pushes the upper end-ring along its cord into its
tube, the stretch of cord it runs along swallowed with it, as every end
she pushes tonight swallows the cord it travels; it comes out red at
rest: dark. Its bead has not moved; only its colour has. The lower does
the same. She pushes the dark upper end on through its ring at a half:
the ring is gone, and nothing is set aside. The lower dark end passes
its own ring the same way. The upper dark end runs into the controlled
turn, and the whole of it falls away, both its rings, the hub, the
pendant and the bob; the lower dark end runs on along a cord with
nothing left on it. At the far tubes both ends turn green again, at
rest, and each comes to rest just past where its far tube stood. What
lies on the cloth now: on each cord, just past where its far tube stood,
a green end-ring at rest, with only the short loose end of its cord
beyond it, bare; and nothing set aside. Everything between has gone, and
the setting has come out just as it went in.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} It comes out as it went in. Like the even row on the
pegs.

\emph{{[}Down the lane the smithy has gone to work in earnest: taps and
blows so close upon one another that nobody at this distance could say
which answers which. Achilles blows on his fingers and draws his chair
in to the cloth.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Now tilt it. \emph{{[}She gathers the cloth clear,
the end-rings and what is left of the cords into her work-bag, and lays
the whole build again from the work-bag, piece for piece as before, and
this time sets the bead of the upper green end-ring at a half; the lower
she leaves at rest.{]}} Green at a half on the upper cord: that is the
tilted setting on that cord.

\emph{{[}As it stands: the upper green end-ring at a half, the lower at
rest, and the build between them. Through the tubes, the upper comes out
red at a half, lit; the lower red at rest, dark. The lit upper end goes
through its ring at a half: the ring is gone, and a half is set aside:
she lays a small green bob from her work-bag, its bead at a half, off
the cloth just beyond its near edge at the right-hand end, by the
candlestick. The dark lower end passes its own ring with nothing set
aside. The lit upper end runs on into the controlled turn: the whole
turn vanishes from between the cords, and on the lower cord, where its
ring was, lies a single green ring at a half. The dark lower end reaches
that ring and passes it, with nothing set aside. At the far tubes the
upper end turns green at a half again, and the lower green at rest, each
coming to rest just past where its far tube stood. What has held: each
cord's setting, exactly as it went in. What has changed: one half lies
set aside by the candlestick, and a half set aside turns the whole
picture over.{]}}

\begin{center}
\aboutcloth[push through]{tilted setting}{the tilted setting, pushed through}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} The same setting, with a half set aside: turned over.

\textbf{Achilles:} The even setting comes out as it was, and the tilted
one comes out turned over. But what has a tilted setting to do with my
pegs?
