\textbf{Tortoise:} The upper cord at a half puts under the line every
drawer whose upper pane would be lit. That's the third and the fourth.
Set them so.

\emph{{[}Achilles slides the first and second pegs to one notch up, and
the third and fourth to one notch under.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} One, one, under, under. The average: one and one,
less one, less one. Nothing. So every peg goes to the other side of the
line itself.

\emph{{[}As it stands: the first and second pegs a notch up, the third
and fourth a notch under, and the average lying on the middle line,
below his pencilled tick, which still stands at half a notch. Achilles
slides each peg straight across the line to the notch opposite: the
first and second down to a notch under, the third and fourth up to a
notch above. No peg has come nearer the line or gone farther from it,
and every square is what it was. Only the sides have changed, every one
of them.{]}}

\begin{center}
\pegcard[turn about]{one, one, under, under; tick at half a notch}{tilted, then turned about}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Under, under, one, one. The whole row turned over,
and not one peg taller.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Your arithmetic and my cords do the same thing: an
even row they leave alone, and a row that averages to nothing they turn
over.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then the Office's case needs only one touch.

\textbf{Tortoise:} For four drawers. Shall we see whether the Office
agrees?

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{third-challenge-one-touch}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Third Challenge --- \emph{One
Touch}}{Third Challenge --- One Touch}}\label{third-challenge-one-touch}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}looking up at the shelf{]}} The lamp?

\textbf{Tortoise:} The Genie's lamp, the same as last night. Rub it
once, and he comes.

\emph{{[}Achilles reaches up and takes the lamp down from the shelf. It
is as it has stood all evening: brass, tarnished, cold, its wick dry,
never lit. He rubs its side once with his palm. The lamp does not warm.
From the spout comes a breath of pale mist, like a breath on a frosty
morning, and instead of fading it gathers, rises and thickens; and
there, between the table and the window, stands the Genie, brushing a
little frost from his sleeves. The lamp in Achilles's hands is as cold
and dull as before. What is new is a third at the table. Achilles sets
the lamp down beside the candlestick.{]}}

\emph{{[}While the mist gathered, the candle flame bowed toward the lamp
and every shadow in the room leaned after it, as though the light were
being drawn in at the spout; now the flame stands up again, and the
shadows go back to their places. Achilles's breath shows white at every
word, and the Tortoise's; the Genie's does not show at all. Down the
lane the smithy is quiet: the iron is back in the fire.{]}}

\textbf{Genie:} The Office of Wishes. \emph{{[}He glances along the
shelf to the drawer-case.{]}} Ah. The Office's newest. They are very
pleased with it upstairs.

\textbf{Genie:} One wish is one touch of the marker. A passage of this
case touches it once, so a passage is one wish. What the case does in a
passage besides that touch is the case's business, and costs you
nothing.

\textbf{Achilles:} So the case may do as much as it likes inside, and I
pay only for the touch. And if I simply asked you about a drawer?

\textbf{Genie:} A plain question is also one touch: ask me whether a
drawer you name is the marked one, and I shall put it to the marker
myself and bring you yes or no. That, too, is one wish. Reading windows
is not a wish, nor opening a spent case's drawers, nor anything you do
on paper, card or cloth. There is one wish this evening.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then I wish to be told which drawer is marked.

\textbf{Genie:} Referred. \emph{{[}He tilts his head, as though
listening up a stairwell, and straightens at once.{]}}

\emph{{[}Under the shelf the tall glass jar gives one faint note that
climbs and falls back in the same instant, over before anyone could turn
to it. Down the lane the smithy stays quiet.{]}}

\textbf{Genie:} The Office marks drawers; it does not name them. Nothing
has been spent.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then I wish the case to touch its marker as often as
I like, and all of it to count as this one wish.

\textbf{Genie:} Referred. \emph{{[}A blink.{]}}

\textbf{Genie:} The reply has come down from well above the Meta-Genie:
every touch is a wish. Your wish is untouched.

\textbf{Achilles:} Untouched! Is that the Office's idea of a joke?

\textbf{Genie:} The Office does not joke. It is exact.

\emph{{[}Achilles laughs under his breath, and the Tortoise hides her
smile in her cup; the Genie waits, exactly. Achilles winds his scarf
once more round his neck and holds his hands to the candle.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Then let me see inside the case first, to know how
it's built.

\textbf{Genie:} Referred.

\emph{{[}Down in the lane, outside the smithy, a waiting horse strikes
the ice once with its hoof, and the smithy's own wall gives the sound
back before the sound itself has finished. Then the lane is still.{]}}

\textbf{Genie:} The back opens with the key, and the key is in the
marked drawer. The drawers open on a spent case and on no other.

\textbf{Achilles:} Up all those floors and back already.

\textbf{Genie:} It goes up as far as it must, and the answer comes down
at once. It always has.

\textbf{Tortoise:} You'll wear the Meta-Genie out.

\textbf{Genie:} Not yet, madam. Not in all the Office's history.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}to the Tortoise{]}} Then the plain question.
We've been marking the second drawer all evening; I could simply ask
whether it's the second.

\textbf{Genie:} That is one touch, and so one wish.

\textbf{Achilles:} And if the answer's no, I'm left guessing among the
other three. Half the time, all told. \emph{{[}He shakes his head.{]}}
No.~Not the plain question.

\textbf{Achilles:} May I at least bring the case to the table?

\textbf{Genie:} Carrying is not a wish. Keep it level.

\emph{{[}Achilles lifts the drawer-case from the shelf in both hands and
sets it on the table beside the peg-card, just beyond it, its drawers
towards him and its windows at his right. It is just as it was on the
shelf: the drawers locked, both panes plain, the back sealed.{]}}

\emph{{[}Behind him the shelf stands bare, with the clean places in its
dust where the lamp and the case stood all day. The Tortoise moves the
candlestick a little to make room, and settles back with a clack.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} One passage of the case, then, with everything it
does inside. Is that one wish?

\textbf{Genie:} One passage touches the marker once. One touch, one
wish.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then I wish it.

\textbf{Genie:} Granted.

\emph{{[}The case as it stands: the drawers shut and locked, both panes
plain, the back sealed, and nothing on it set, for nothing on it can be.
At the word nothing on the case moves. Behind the upper window the pane
stays plain. Behind the lower a small gleam comes up and stays. Along
the front runs a little row of clicks as the drawer locks let go. What
has changed: one gleam, and the locks. What has held: the upper pane,
plain; the back, still sealed; every drawer still shut.{]}}

\begin{center}
\drawercase{granted}{upper plain, lower gleaming}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Upper dark, lower lit. The second drawer.

\textbf{Achilles:} The second! I'd have had it from the plain question
too.

\textbf{Tortoise:} This time. The case would have had it whichever
drawer the Office marked.

\emph{{[}Down the lane the smithy, quiet since the lamp was rubbed,
gives one light tap of the hammer and one heavy blow of the sledge after
it, and then the long hiss of hot iron going into water. One heat, and
the work is done.{]}}

\emph{{[}The drawers stand in their row, shut, their locks let go.
Achilles draws out the first towards him by its brass pull: it slides
open on a bare wooden floor, with nothing in it, and he pushes it shut
again. He draws out the second towards him. On its floor lies a small
brass key.{]}}

\begin{center}
\drawercase{granted; first drawer open; first drawer shut; second drawer open}{the key, found}
\end{center}

\emph{{[}He takes the key up. Nothing else on the case has stirred: the
upper pane is plain and the lower pane gleams, as before; only the
second drawer stands open, and its key is in his hand.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}holding up the key{]}} The key to its back.

\textbf{Genie:} The case is spent. A drawer found is no longer a secret,
and the back may be opened.

\emph{{[}Achilles swings the case round on the table so that its back
faces him and the candle at his right, fits the key to the small lock in
the back panel, and turns it. The panel comes away in his hands, and he
lays it on the table beside the case, the key still in its lock. The
panes do not change, nor the drawers; only the back is open now, and the
candle shines into the case.{]}}

\emph{{[}Inside, two rows of cord run the length of the case, one above
the other, from its left end, where they begin, to its right end, where
the windows are; seen from behind, as Achilles now sees them, they begin
at his right and run to the windows at his left, and every bead in the
case reads as he sees it from behind, at rest at the top of its ring and
turned round clockwise. They run straight, and neither crosses the
other. The upper row begins at a red end-ring whose bead is at rest:
dark. From it a cord runs through a fixed yellow collar to a green ring
with its bead a quarter round, the marker's upper ring, knotted at the
end-ring and at the ring. From the marker's upper ring another cord runs
through a collar to a green ring at a half, the turn-about's upper
half-ring, knotted at both. From that half-ring a short cord, with no
collar on it, runs to the turn-about's upper ring, a quarter round. And
from that ring a cord runs through a collar to the upper window, knotted
at the ring and at the window.{]}}

\emph{{[}The lower row begins the same way, at a red end-ring at rest,
and a cord runs from it through a collar to the marker's lower ring, a
quarter round. But from there a short cord, with no collar, runs to a
green ring at a half that has no partner on the upper row: the marker's
half-ring. From the marker's half-ring a cord runs through a collar to
the turn-about's lower half-ring, at a half; from that, a short cord to
the turn-about's lower ring, a quarter round; and from that ring a cord
through a collar to the lower window. Each length is knotted at both its
ends.{]}}

\emph{{[}In the gap between the rows, nearer the start, sits the
marker's hub, a bare red ring. A tie runs up from it to the marker's
upper ring, and another tie down to the marker's lower ring; and from
the hub a pendant lies out along the gap, towards the end-rings, to a
small green bob, a quarter back. Nearer the windows sits the
turn-about's hub, bare too, with a tie up to the turn-about's upper
ring, a tie down to the turn-about's lower ring, and a pendant along the
gap, towards the windows, to its own bob, a quarter back. No tie crosses
a row, and no pendant crosses either. Every length in the case is
knotted at both its ends, and no cord passes through a ring. What has
changed is only that the inside can be seen: the lower pane's gleam can
be followed back, cord by cord, to where it began.{]}}

\begin{center}
\drawercase*[back]{granted; first drawer open; first drawer shut; second drawer open; key taken; back open}{the inside, from behind}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} The marker's pieces aren't the same on the two rows.
The lower row has a ring at a half there, and the upper row hasn't.

\textbf{Tortoise:} And the far end of it is my build from the cloth:
collars for my tubes, a half on each cord, the controlled turn for a
half, and collars again.

\textbf{Achilles:} The marker near the start and the turn-about near the
windows, and one passage runs through both.

\textbf{Genie:} The wish has been spent in accordance with the Terms.
The Office does not collect spent boxes.

\emph{{[}The lamp lies where Achilles set it beside the candlestick,
cold. The Genie draws in from his edges, as the mist on a pane draws in
when the warmth leaves it, thins to the pale breath he came as, and the
breath runs back into the spout and is gone. The lamp does not stir or
warm. The case stays on the table with its back open, its upper pane
plain and its lower pane gleaming, and nothing else in the room has
moved. There are two at the table again.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}taking up the lamp and setting it back on
its shelf{]}} Home again.

\emph{{[}Up on its shelf, out of the candle's reach, the lamp is only
brass again, beside the clean place in the dust where the case stood all
day. The Tortoise sits back down, and her chair clacks. Down in the lane
the new-shod horse stamps on the frozen ruts, and somebody speaks to it
low.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}looking from the open case to the
seed-cabinet by the door{]}} Four drawers, one touch. But the Genie said
every touch is a wish. What would a case with as many drawers as your
seed-cabinet need?

\textbf{Tortoise:} More than one, and not as many as you'd think. How
many would you guess?

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{fourth-challenge-the-turning-plane}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Fourth Challenge --- \emph{The Turning
Plane}}{Fourth Challenge --- The Turning Plane}}\label{fourth-challenge-the-turning-plane}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Four drawers took one touch, and your cabinet has
sixteen times as many drawers. Sixteen touches, drawer for drawer.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Let's see, on paper, where touching costs nothing.
\emph{{[}From the work-bag she brings a sheet of paper, her rule marked
in thumbs, a needle, and the paper hand from last night's first dial,
still on its pin.{]}} This sheet is a picture of the whole case at once.
A line across it will stand for every unmarked drawer together, a line
up it for the marked drawer, and last night's paper hand, on its pin
where they cross, for where the case stands. The higher its tip above
the line across, as a part of the hand's length, the taller the marked
drawer's peg.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Here the touch and the turn-about are both folds. For
a fold I pencil a dot at the tip, lift the hand off with its pin, fold
the sheet along a line, prick through the dot with the needle, and
unfold; then the pin goes back where it was and the hand is laid out to
the new hole.

\emph{{[}She slides the peg-card along to Achilles's left and lays the
sheet on the table before him, where the card lay, between him and the
case, square to his edge of the table, its long sides running away from
him. She draws a line straight up it, away from him, nearer its left
edge than its right, and a line across it, half way up, crossing at
right angles, and pushes the pin through the crossing. The hand, eight
thumbs long, turns on the pin. She lays it out to the right of the pin
as Achilles sees it, so that its tip stands four thumbs above the line
across, measuring with her rule, pencils a mark at the tip, and rules a
third line from the pin through the mark, tilted up from the line across
by a third of a right angle, rising to the right.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} For four drawers. The line across is the unmarked
line, the line up is the marked line, and this tilted one is the even
line. The tip stands four thumbs up, half the hand's length.

\begin{center}
\handsheet*{four drawers}{the sheet ruled, the hand laid}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Half the hand, and half squared is a quarter. A
quarter of the odds on the marked drawer, as the even row gave it.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The marker's fold is along the unmarked line: it
turns the marked part of the hand over and leaves the rest alone. The
turn-about's fold is along the even line. Watch both.

\emph{{[}The hand as it stands: on its pin at the crossing, lying along
the even line, its tip four thumbs above the unmarked line. The Tortoise
pencils a dot at the tip and lifts the hand off the sheet, pin and all.
She folds the sheet along the unmarked line, creasing it with a
thumbnail, and pushes the needle through the dot and through the paper
beneath. She unfolds the sheet flat: a second hole shows below the
unmarked line, just as far below it as the dot is above. She puts the
pin back through its hole at the crossing and lays the hand out from it
to the new hole. The hand is the same length and turns on the same pin,
and it reaches just as far along the unmarked line as it did. Only its
height has gone to the other side: the tip stands four thumbs under.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Four thumbs under. The second peg, under the line.

\emph{{[}The tip stands four thumbs under the unmarked line. The
Tortoise dots it and lifts the hand, pin and all. This time she folds
along the even line, which runs up from the crossing at its tilt; the
dot below the unmarked line comes over onto the paper high above, and
she pricks through. Unfolded, the new hole stands on the marked line
itself, near the top of the sheet. The pin goes back through the
crossing, and she lays the hand out to the new hole: straight up the
marked line. Its length has not changed, nor its pin. But the tip, that
stood four thumbs under, now stands eight thumbs up, the hand's whole
length.{]}}

\begin{center}
\handsheet[a step]{four drawers}{after the folds, upright}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}laying her rule from the unmarked line to
the tip{]}} Eight thumbs of eight. All the odds on the marked drawer.

\textbf{Tortoise:} That is what the pegs did.

\textbf{Achilles:} \ldots Oh. Two folds, and the hand isn't folded at
all; it has turned round the pin. It lay a third of a right angle up
from the unmarked line, and now it stands at a right angle to it.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Two folds make a turn: twice the tilt between the
lines you fold along, towards the marked line.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Now your sixteen times as many. \emph{{[}She lifts
the hand off the first sheet, pin and all, and sets that sheet aside on
the table. She takes a fresh sheet and lays it where the first lay,
square to Achilles's edge of the table, draws the unmarked line across
it and the marked line up it at the same places as on the first, and
pins the hand at the crossing. She lays the hand out to the right of the
pin, so that its tip stands one thumb above the unmarked line, marks the
tip, and rules the even line from the pin through the mark: a tilt so
slight that the two lines hardly part.{]}} A case with as many drawers
as my seed-cabinet. Asked evenly, the marked drawer's peg is one eighth
of the whole: one thumb of eight.

\textbf{Achilles:} One thumb up, and one in sixty-four of the odds. The
even line hardly leaves the unmarked line at all.

\emph{{[}Achilles looks up from the sheet, past the candle, to the print
on the wall facing the window: Escher's
\textup{Cubic Space Division}.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} A space divided into cubes by straight beams. How
many drawers would a case need, to give each of those cubes a drawer of
its own?

\emph{{[}As he looks, the candle flame draws up tall and perfectly
still, and for that moment its light reaches the print from the bottom
of the frame to the top, as it has not all evening. Then the flame
settles, and the upper part of the frame goes back into shadow.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} More than my cabinet, whatever it is. Let's learn
what mine needs first. Two hands in turn: you take the marker's fold,
and I'll take the turn-about's.

\emph{{[}Down the lane the smithy takes up its work again, steady now:
the smith's light tap, and the striker's heavy blow after it, and a
little pause while the iron is turned on the anvil, and tap and blow
again. Achilles draws his chair in to the sheet.{]}}

\emph{{[}The hand as it stands: along the even line, its tip one thumb
up. Achilles pencils a dot at the tip, lifts the hand with its pin,
folds the sheet along the unmarked line, pricks through the dot, and
unfolds. The new hole lies one thumb under; he pins the hand back and
lays it out to it. The same hand, the same pin, the same slight angle to
the unmarked line; only the side has changed.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} The marker turns it over.

\emph{{[}The Tortoise dots the tip, one thumb under, lifts the hand, and
folds along the even line. Pricked and unfolded, the new hole stands
well above the even line, and the hand laid out to it has swung up round
the pin, farther from the unmarked line than it has been yet.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} And we turn it about.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}laying the rule from the unmarked line up to
the tip{]}} Just under three thumbs.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}folding along the unmarked line, so that the
tip that stood just under three thumbs up now stands as far under{]}}
The marker turns it over.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}folding along the even line; the hand swings
up past the hole where it stood before{]}} And we turn it about.

\textbf{Achilles:} Four and three quarters.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}folding the tip's height under the unmarked
line, four and three quarters below it now{]}} The marker turns it over.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}folding along the even line; up the hand
comes again, steeper than before{]}} And we turn it about.

\textbf{Achilles:} Six and an eighth. \emph{{[}He looks at the holes
marching round the sheet.{]}} It turns the same each time, but the tip
climbs less.

\textbf{Tortoise:} It's nearing the top, and near the top a turn carries
it more across than up.

\emph{{[}Down the lane the tap and the blow keep their turn, the same
each time, but under them the ring of the iron grows thinner and
brighter as the work comes near its shape. The Tortoise holds the sheet
flat with one claw and warms the other at the candle.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}folding; the tip goes down to six and an
eighth under, the hand now pointing steeply below the line{]}} The
marker turns it over.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}folding; the hand comes back up, higher than
it has stood yet{]}} And we turn it about.

\textbf{Achilles:} Seven and a quarter.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}folding; the long hand swings down steeply
below the line, seven and a quarter under{]}} The marker turns it over.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}folding; the hand rises to stand a little
short of the marked line{]}} And we turn it about.

\textbf{Achilles:} Seven and seven eighths.

\emph{{[}The hand as it stands: a little short of the marked line, its
tip seven and seven eighths up. Achilles dots the tip, lifts the hand
with its pin, folds along the unmarked line and pricks. Unfolded, the
new hole lies seven and seven eighths below, and the hand, pinned back
and laid out to it, points nearly straight down.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} The marker turns it over.

\emph{{[}The Tortoise dots the tip and lifts the hand, folds along the
even line, and pricks. Unfolded, the new hole stands at the top of the
sheet, just on the far side of the marked line from the even line, to
its left as Achilles sees it. She pins the hand and lays it out: it
stands upright, leaning by a whisker past the marked line. The same
hand, the same pin, the same turn as at every step before; and the tip
has climbed its last little way, to within a hair of the hand's whole
length.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} And we turn it about.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}measuring{]}} All but a hair of eight. Just
past upright.

\begin{center}
\handsheet[six steps]{sixty-four drawers}{climbed to the top}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Stop there. Six touches.

\emph{{[}Down the lane the smith lets his hammer ring on the bare face
of the anvil, bright and empty, and the sledge does not fall again. Then
comes the long hiss of the finished iron going into the water, and the
smithy is quiet.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} It's still a hair short of eight. One more, and it'll
be surer.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}with perfect courtesy{]}} By all means.

\emph{{[}The hand as it stands: upright, leaning a whisker past the
marked line, its tip all but a hair of eight. Achilles dots the tip,
lifts the hand, folds along the unmarked line and pricks. Unfolded, the
new hole lies far down, just past straight below the pin, and the hand
laid out to it points almost at his knees. The Tortoise takes her turn
along the even line, and the new hole comes up high again, but on the
far side of the marked line, to its left, and farther from it than
before; laid out to it, the hand leans over the marked line towards the
far edge of the sheet. Its length is the same, the pin is the same, and
the turn has been just as large as every other. But the tip, that had
all but reached eight, has come down.{]}}

\begin{center}
\handsheet[seven steps]{sixty-four drawers}{turned too far}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}measuring{]}} Seven and five eighths. It's
come down!

\textbf{Tortoise:} It goes round. Too many, and it turns away.

\emph{{[}Achilles sits back and regards the sheet as though it had been
rude to him, and the Tortoise's chair clacks as she sits back too. Down
the lane the smithy has not struck again.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Seven and five eighths: about nine in ten of the
odds. And what did six give?

\textbf{Tortoise:} All but about three in a thousand. Nearly certain,
not certain. Of all our cases, only the four drawers came out certain,
because there the two folds land exactly on the marked line. Four
drawers were a lucky fit.

\textbf{Achilles:} Six touches, where the plain way wants up to
sixty-three asks. And I guessed sixteen.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Once the case is big, four times the drawers takes
about twice the touches. It goes by the square root of the drawers, not
by the drawers.

\textbf{Achilles:} And a million drawers?

\textbf{Tortoise:} About eight hundred touches, this way of searching.
Asking plainly, up to a million less one.

\textbf{Achilles:} Six wishes, then, for your cabinet. Every touch is a
wish, and the Office grants one an evening.

\textbf{Tortoise:} So we suppose on paper, and wish nothing.

\emph{{[}Achilles's eye goes to the lamp on its shelf, out of the
candle's reach, and stays there a moment: only brass. He tucks his hands
under his arms.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}frowning at the sheet{]}} But six is only
how we folded. A cleverer way of touching might need fewer.

\textbf{Tortoise:} How far could any touch move the hand, do you think,
if the drawer it touches is one you've hardly asked?

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{fifth-challenge-no-faster-hand}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Fifth Challenge --- \emph{No Faster
Hand}}{Fifth Challenge --- No Faster Hand}}\label{fifth-challenge-no-faster-hand}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Not far, I suppose. But how far is not far?

\textbf{Tortoise:} First, where the hand would be with nothing to find.
\emph{{[}She lifts the hand from where the seventh step left it and pins
it back as it began, its tip at the first dot, one thumb up on the even
line.{]}} Suppose no drawer is marked at all.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then my fold has nothing to turn over. I make none.

\emph{{[}The hand as it stands: along the even line, its tip one thumb
up. The Tortoise dots the tip, lifts the hand with its pin, and folds
along the even line. The dot lies on the crease itself, and the needle
goes through it and through nothing else. Unfolded, there is no new
hole: the prick is the dot. She pins the hand back at the crossing and
lays it out to that same hole. Nothing has changed: not its length, not
its tilt, not its tip.{]}}

\begin{center}
\handsheet[seven steps, back to the first dot, no drawer marked, the turn-about's fold]{sixty-four drawers}{unmarked, the hand stays}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} It hasn't moved. It can't; it lies along the very
line you fold on.

\textbf{Tortoise:} With nothing marked, the hand never leaves the even
line, however often we fold, and every peg stays at an eighth of the
whole.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Now the rule. A touch can pull the hand away from
where it would stand with nothing marked by at most twice the height of
the marked drawer's peg, as that peg stands in the unmarked case when
the touch comes.

\textbf{Achilles:} Every peg there stands an eighth. So each touch pulls
it at most a quarter of a hand.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}laying her rule from the tip on the even
line to the top of the marked line{]}} And from where it stands unmarked
to the top of the marked line is ten and a half thumbs, and a little
over. A little under one and a third hands.

\textbf{Tortoise:} So how many touches, at the very least?

\textbf{Achilles:} Four touches, one hand: not enough. Five, one and a
quarter hands: still short. Six, one and a half: enough. That's the six
we found.

\textbf{Tortoise:} That's for touching evenly, as the Office's case
does. Now touch any way you please: whatever you do between touches, the
pegs' squares always make one whole, so each touch shares out one whole
portion of asking among the drawers. After two touches, two portions
among sixty-four drawers, and some drawer has had no more than two
sixty-fourths.

\textbf{Achilles:} Split evenly, that's a sixty-fourth at each touch: an
eighth of height, and a quarter of a pull, twice over. Half a hand at
most.

\textbf{Tortoise:} And split unevenly it's less. So that drawer's
touches can have pulled the hand at most half its length from where it
would stand unmarked: a drawer asked so little can hardly be told from
no drawer at all. The people who counted touches proved it properly.
I've only shown you why it's believable.

\emph{{[}Across the room the one candle's light lies spread over the
whole front of the seed-cabinet, and each drawer has so small a share of
it that its face can hardly be told from the dark. No drawer has more of
it than its neighbour; there is only the one flame to go round.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Then with a million drawers, even the Office's
cleverest case needs hundreds of touches, not a handful. And every cord
added to a case doubles its drawers, and the search still grows.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Yes. A great saving, and not a miracle.

\textbf{Tortoise:} So what has the evening done?

\textbf{Achilles:} A touch puts the marked drawer under the line, where
no look can see it. The turn-about stands every peg on the other side of
the average, and that makes the one that's under tall. Together they
turn the hand by twice the tilt.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Four drawers take one touch, and it's certain.

\textbf{Achilles:} Sixty-four take six, nearly certain, and a seventh
spoils it. And no way of touching does much better.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The cords showed how the case was built, and that one
touch finds one drawer in four. How many touches a bigger case needs,
and that nobody can do better, was reckoned on paper, not by drawing.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}looking at the candle{]}} The candle's
burned lower than I thought.

\textbf{Tortoise:} It always does when there's arithmetic. It likes to
listen.

\emph{{[}Achilles laughs, and the Tortoise laughs under her breath with
him. Down the lane the smithy's doors bang shut for the night, and a
horse goes home past the house, its new-sharpened shoes biting the ice
at every step, sure-footed, until it is out of hearing.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}looking into the open case{]}} And the lower
pane is still gleaming.

\textbf{Tortoise:} It'll go on showing the second drawer until somebody
asks it something else, and nobody will.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}at the window{]}} There's frost on the
inside of the pane.

\textbf{Tortoise:} A hard one. Keep your scarf on for the lane, and
don't give it to me tonight; I have a cabinet full of seeds to keep
warm, and they keep me.

\emph{{[}Achilles comes back from the window, winding his scarf tighter,
and holds his hands to the candle one last time. The Tortoise drains her
cup, cold as it is, and neither of them is in any hurry.{]}}

\emph{{[}Up the lane, the church clock begins to strike, and strikes
ten.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Ten already. And the tread will be waiting for me on
the way down.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Step over it if you like. It groans at people who
step over it; it thinks they're being clever.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}looking from the sheet, with its holes
marching round the pin, to the seed-cabinet's rows of brass pulls{]}}
So, for any wall of drawers, however big: how many times must you ask to
find the one that's marked, and why can nobody ask fewer?

\textbf{Tortoise:} That's the question for any wall. Tonight we only
tried it on mine.

\emph{{[}She takes up the candlestick. The case stays open on the table,
its lower pane still gleaming.{]}}

\emph{{[}The candle stands low in its stick, guttered down to a small
flame, and as she lifts it every shadow in the room swings round and
shortens. Achilles sets the two empty cups on the flat of her shell,
where they ride as level as they came. As she passes the table the
candle reaches just inside the open case, and moves on; the lamp stands
on its shelf, only brass; the peg-card, the cloth and the sheets lie
where they were left. On the wall facing the window, past her shoulder,
the print is at the edge of the light again, a plain dark frame on a
cold wall, and then behind it. The light goes once more across the front
of the seed-cabinet, every drawer alike, and leaves it. Then the candle
goes to the door, and Achilles after it, and the stair takes them down
its one turn; halfway, Achilles steps carefully over the loose tread,
and it groans at him anyway. Behind them the top room is dark and still,
and on the inside of the pane the frost goes on with its work, the old
initials white in it. Down the lane the smithy is dark, its fire banked
for the morning, and up the lane the church clock goes on round towards
eleven.{]}}

\hypertarget{chapter-15-searching-in-square-root-time}{%
\chapter{Chapter 15: Searching in Square-Root
Time}\label{chapter-15-searching-in-square-root-time}}

\emph{--- Toccata in Square-Root Time ---}

\emph{Part IV: Algorithms}

\emph{Escher: ``Cubic Space Division'' --- a space divided into cubes by
straight beams}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

If one drawer in a wall of identical drawers holds what you are looking
for, how many drawers must you open to find it, and could any trick at
all open fewer?

Picture the wall. Every drawer has the same brass pull, and nothing is
written on any of them. One of them holds a key, and the rest are empty.
There is no order to go by: the key was not put in alphabetically, or by
size, or by date. So you open drawers. Each one tells you only ``yes,
here it is'' or ``no, not here'', and a ``no'' tells you nothing about
any other drawer. With luck you find the key in the first drawer you
open. Without luck you open every drawer but the last, and then you
know. On average you open about half of them.

Nothing cleverer seems possible, and for an ordinary searcher nothing
cleverer is. The drawers share no structure that a clever order could
exploit. Any plan, however ingenious, comes down to opening drawers one
at a time, and a plan that opens few drawers usually misses.

A quantum searcher is allowed a stranger kind of touch. It can touch
every drawer at once. But the touch does not open anything. It leaves
behind a mark that no look can see: every drawer is still exactly as
likely to be the one as any other. And yet something has changed, and a
second operation, which knows nothing about the key, can turn that
invisible mark into a visible lean towards the right drawer. Repeat the
pair of operations and the lean grows. For a million drawers, about
eight hundred such touches find the key almost certainly, where opening
drawers one by one takes half a million on average.

Two facts make this chapter worth reading, and they pull in opposite
directions. The first is that the speed-up is real: the square root of
the number of drawers, not the number itself. The second is that it is
not larger. A square root is all any quantum method can gain at this
task, and there is a proof. We will see how the touches work, why they
must be counted and stopped at the right moment, and why nobody can do
better.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{four-drawers-one-wish}{%
\section{§15.1 Four Drawers, One Wish}\label{four-drawers-one-wish}}

Chapter 14 ended by pointing here. ``The box marks one item among many,
and the task is to find it. The quantum answer is faster than searching
the items one by one, but only by a square root, and Chapter 13 has
already told us, from BBBV's bound, that for a box of this kind no
quantum method does better. The picture that explains the search is not
a string diagram at all. It is a picture of a plane, with two lines
through it and a state that turns between them, a different kind of
diagram for a different kind of speed-up.''

That is true, and it could mislead. The book's two strands still run in
this chapter, as in every chapter. The algebra and the string diagrams
prove the chapter's headline theorem, and the string diagrams derive a
whole four-drawer search, dot by dot, with every scalar. What they do
not do is count steps. The picture of a plane is a third picture, which
we will call the \emph{Turning Plane}. It explains how many steps a
larger search needs, and it is a drawing of algebra, not a diagram of
processes. We will keep the three apart.

The chapter's question, in the form we can answer: \textbf{how many
times must you ask to find one marked item among \(N\), and why can no
method ask fewer than about \(\sqrt N\) times?}

\textbf{On the blackboard.} Take \(n\) wires, which this chapter calls
\textbf{cords} as the dialogues do, and let \(N=2^n\). Each
\textbf{drawer} is an \(n\)-bit string \(x\), written top cord first.
Exactly one drawer \(w\) is \textbf{marked}. We write
\(w_1w_2\cdots w_n\) for its bits and \(\bar w_i=1-w_i\) for the
opposite bit. The only way to learn anything about \(w\) is to
\textbf{ask}, and an ask is one evaluation of the test
\[f(x)\;=\;[\,x=w\,],\] using the bracket of Chapter 12: \([\,x=w\,]\)
is \(1\) if \(x=w\) and \(0\) otherwise. A classical method asks about
drawers one at a time, possibly choosing each drawer from the answers so
far and possibly tossing coins, and at the end \textbf{names} a drawer.
It succeeds if the drawer it names is \(w\).

Take four drawers, \(00,01,10,11\), and ask in that order. If \(w=00\),
one ask finds it. If \(w=01\), two asks. If \(w=10\), three. If
\(w=11\), three asks also suffice, because three answers ``no'' leave
only one drawer. Averaged over the four choices of \(w\), that is
\((1+2+3+3)/4=2.25\) asks.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 15.1 (asking one by one).} Ask about the drawers in a
fixed order, stopping at the first ``yes'', and name the last drawer
without asking if every earlier answer was ``no''. Then the worst case
takes \(N-1\) asks, and for a uniformly random marked drawer the
expected number of asks is \[\frac{N-1}{2}+\frac{N-1}{N}.\] For four
drawers this is \(2.25\), and for sixty-four it is \(32.48\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} If \(w\) is the \(j\)-th drawer in the order and
\(j\le N-1\), the method asks \(j\) times. If \(w\) is the last drawer,
it asks \(N-1\) times and names the last one. Each position has
probability \(1/N\), so the expected number is
\(\tfrac1N\bigl(1+2+\cdots+(N-1)+(N-1)\bigr)=\tfrac{N-1}{2}+\tfrac{N-1}{N}\).
\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch15/FourDrawers.py}.

Could a cleverer plan do better? Here is the most modest alternative:
ask once, about a fixed drawer, and if the answer is ``no'', guess
uniformly among the others. It succeeds if the drawer asked about is
\(w\) (probability \(1/N\)), or if it is not and the guess is right
(probability \(\tfrac{N-1}{N}\cdot\tfrac{1}{N-1}\)). That is \(2/N\) in
all: one half for four drawers, one in thirty-two for sixty-four. Each
ask, it seems, buys one drawer's worth of chance, and the final guess
buys one more. That is true of every classical plan.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 15.2 (no classical shortcut).} For a uniformly random
marked drawer, every classical method that asks at most \(k\) times and
then names a drawer succeeds with probability at most \((k+1)/N\). In
particular, one ask and a guess can reach exactly \(2/N\); success with
probability \(\tfrac12\) needs at least \(\tfrac N2-1\) asks; and
certainty needs \(N-1\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} First fix the method's coin tosses, so that it is
deterministic. Consider the run in which every answer is ``no''. In that
run the method asks about some drawers \(x_1,\dots,x_k\) (each chosen
from the answers so far, which are all ``no'') and names some drawer
\(z\). Now take any marked drawer \(w\) outside the set
\(\{x_1,\dots,x_k,z\}\). With that \(w\), the first ask is about
\(x_1\ne w\) and gets ``no'', so the second ask is about \(x_2\), which
also gets ``no'', and so on: the method follows the all-``no'' run
exactly and names \(z\ne w\). So it can succeed only for the at most
\(k+1\) drawers in the set, out of \(N\) equally likely ones. With coin
tosses, the success probability is an average of such numbers, each at
most \((k+1)/N\). The special cases follow by setting \((k+1)/N\) equal
to \(\tfrac12\) and to \(1\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch15/FourDrawers.py}.

Grover opens his paper with the same count: to find a name in a
directory of \(N\) names ``arranged in completely random order'' with
probability \(\tfrac12\), any classical algorithm ``will need to look at
a minimum of \(N/2\) names''. Result 15.2 is that sentence proved, with
the named drawer counted as one of the looks.

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why count asks and nothing else?
Because the drawers are sealed and share no structure, the ask is the
only part of the work that touches the secret, and everything else a
method does is its own private business. Chapter 13 made the same choice
for the same reason, and the quantum count below uses the same unit.

\hypertarget{the-marker}{%
\subsection{The marker}\label{the-marker}}

The quantum ask is Chapter 13's \textbf{query box} (Result 13.1, row
97): the tall box \[U_f\,\ket x\ket y\;=\;\ket x\ket{y\oplus f(x)}\]
laid across the \(n\) cords (Chapter 13's \textbf{rods}) and one extra
cord (the \textbf{flag}). One use of it is one query, even when the rods
carry a superposition of drawers. With the flag in the difference state
\(\ket-=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket0-\ket1)\), the box does not change the flag
at all. It turns the rods' sign instead: that is phase kickback (Chapter
5, row 37), which Chapter 13 drew as a copy (Result 13.4, row 100).

For the search this gives the operation the chapter is built on. The
\textbf{marker} is
\[O_w\;=\;I-2\ket w\bra w,\qquad O_w\ket x=(-1)^{[x=w]}\ket x .\] It
turns the marked drawer over and leaves every other drawer as it is.
This is step (ii)(a) of Grover's algorithm: in case the condition holds,
``rotate the phase by \(\pi\) radians'', and otherwise ``leave the
system unaltered''.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 15.3 (the marker is one query).} For every \(w\) and
every state \(\ket\psi\) of the rods,
\[U_f\bigl(\ket\psi\otimes\ket-\bigr)\;=\;\bigl(O_w\ket\psi\bigr)\otimes\ket- .\]
The marker is unitary, \(O_w^2=I\), and it changes no odds:
\(\lvert\bra x O_w\ket\psi\rvert^2=\lvert\braket{x|\psi}\rvert^2\) for
every drawer \(x\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} On a drawer,
\(U_f\ket x\ket-=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket x\ket{f(x)}-\ket x\ket{1\oplus f(x)}\bigr)=(-1)^{f(x)}\ket x\ket-\),
and \((-1)^{f(x)}\ket x=O_w\ket x\). Both sides are linear in
\(\ket\psi\) and agree on every drawer, so they agree everywhere.
\(O_w\) is diagonal with entries \(\pm1\), so \(O_w^2=I\), and each
amplitude only changes sign. \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch15/FourDrawers.py}.

Grover makes the same remark about every operation of this kind: ``the
probability in each state stays the same since the square of the
absolute value of the amplitude in each state stays the same.'' Bennett,
Bernstein, Brassard and Vazirani (BBBV, whom we met in Chapter 13)
describe the same trick for their query tape: with the target bit in
\((\ket0-\ket1)/\sqrt2\), an oracle call ``leaves the entire state
unchanged while introducing a phase factor \(-1\)'' when the answer is
\(1\).

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} Draw three rods and the flag, as Chapter 13
did. The flag's difference state is a green \(\pi\) point, which is
\(\sqrt2\ket-\) (Chapter 13). Result 15.3, multiplied through by
\(\sqrt2\), says that the query box with a green \(\pi\) point on its
flag equals a tall box \(O_w\) across the rods alone, with the green
\(\pi\) point passing by untouched:

\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=2.0em, x=1em, y=1em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1.3) (0,5.2);
  \foreach \y in {4.5,3,1.5} { \draw[wire] (0,\y) -- (4.4,\y); }
  \draw[wire] (0.6,0) -- (4.4,0);
  \node[sdbox, minimum height=6.2em] at (2.5,2.25) {$U_f$};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi$}}] at (0.6,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=2.0em, x=1em, y=1em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1.3) (0,5.2);
  \foreach \y in {4.5,3,1.5} { \draw[wire] (0,\y) -- (4.4,\y); }
  \draw[wire] (0.6,0) -- (4.4,0);
  \node[sdbox, minimum height=4.7em] at (2.5,3) {$O_w$};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi$}}] at (0.6,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\]

The equation is exact, and neither side carries a number, because the
same point stands on both. From here on the flag is left out of the
pictures and the marker is drawn as its own box. Section §15.2 opens
that box into dots.

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why a sign and not a flag? A flag
saying ``here'' would be read, and reading a superposition of drawers
picks one drawer at random, which returns us to asking one by one. A
sign cannot be seen by any reading (Result 15.3), but it lives in the
amplitudes, where a later operation can turn it into odds. The whole
search is a way of making that later operation happen.

\hypertarget{the-even-state}{%
\subsection{The even state}\label{the-even-state}}

Grover's step (i) prepares ``the same amplitude to be in each of the
\(N\) states''. Write \(W=H^{\otimes n}\) for a Hadamard on every cord,
the Walsh--Hadamard transform, with entries
\(W_{xy}=2^{-n/2}(-1)^{x\cdot y}\), where \(x\cdot y\) is the bitwise
dot product taken mod \(2\) (Chapter 13). The \textbf{even state} is
\[\ket s\;=\;W\ket{0\cdots0}\;=\;\frac1{\sqrt N}\sum_x\ket x .\]

Before stating it in general, take two cords:
\(H\ket0\otimes H\ket0=\tfrac12(\ket0+\ket1)(\ket0+\ket1)=\tfrac12(\ket{00}+\ket{01}+\ket{10}+\ket{11})\),
every drawer with amplitude \(\tfrac12\) and odds \(\tfrac14\).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 15.4 (the even state).} For every \(n\),
\(W\ket{0\cdots0}=\ket s\), \(W\) is real and symmetric, and \(W^2=I\).
In pictures, \(n\) red points each followed by a yellow box are \(n\)
green points, and those are \(2^{n/2}\ket s\):
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.19em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-0.8) (0,3.2);
\draw[wire] (0,2.4) -- (2.6,2.4);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2.6,0);
\node[xsp] at (0,2.4) {};
\node[xsp] at (0,0) {};
\node[hbox] at (1.3,2.4) {};
\node[hbox] at (1.3,0) {};
\node at (1.3,1.35) {$\vdots$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.19em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
\path (0,-0.8) (0,3.2);
\draw[wire] (0,2.4) -- (1.6,2.4);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.6,0);
\node[zsp] at (0,2.4) {};
\node[zsp] at (0,0) {};
\node at (0.8,1.35) {$\vdots$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;2^{n/2}\,\ket s .\]
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} \(H\ket0=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket0+\ket1)\) on each cord, and
the product over \(n\) cords is \(2^{-n/2}\sum_x\ket x\). The entries
\(2^{-n/2}(-1)^{x\cdot y}\) are real and symmetric in \(x\) and \(y\),
and \(W^2=I\) because \(H^2=I\) on each cord. In the picture, a red
point is \(\sqrt2\ket0\), and a yellow box on the only leg of a red
point turns it into a green point of the same phase (colour change,
Theorem 8.2, row 58). A green point is \(\ket0+\ket1\), and \(n\) of
them are \(\sum_x\ket x=2^{n/2}\ket s\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch15/FourDrawers.py}.

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why start from the even state?
Because nothing is known about \(w\), and a start that favoured some
drawers would be a guess made before any touch. The even state favours
none. It is also the state that the turn-about of §15.2 leaves exactly
where it is, so the search starts on the one line it can pivot about.

Now touch the even state once.
\(O_w\ket s=\ket s-\tfrac{2}{\sqrt N}\ket w\): every amplitude is still
\(\pm1/\sqrt N\), and every drawer still has odds \(1/N\). For four
drawers with \(w=01\) the amplitudes are \(\tfrac12(1,-1,1,1)\) in the
order \(00,01,10,11\). The mark is there, as a minus sign on the second
entry, and a reading cannot see it. It is a wish spent on a secret that
no look reveals. Something must turn the sign into a height.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Feynman's Notebook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{A directory in random order.} Lov K. Grover wrote ``A fast quantum
mechanical algorithm for database search'' at Bell Labs in Murray Hill,
New Jersey. The version we read is, in its own words, ``an updated
version of a paper that originally appeared in Proceedings, STOC 1996,
Philadelphia PA USA, pages 212-219''. It begins with a telephone
directory whose \(N\) names are in completely random order and a number
to be found, and it promises that the number ``can be obtained in only
\(O(\sqrt N)\) steps''. Grover is precise about what the marking step
means physically. One part of the system senses the state and decides
whether to turn the phase, and it must do so ``so that no trace of the
state of the system be left'', so that the paths can still interfere.
``The implementation does not involve a classical measurement.'' His
acknowledgments give the paper's company: Peter Shor introduced him to
quantum computing, Ethan Bernstein provided the lower-bound argument of
his §6, and Gilles Brassard's comments helped him update the STOC paper.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-turn-about}{%
\section{§15.2 The Turn-About}\label{the-turn-about}}

Take the four amplitudes left by the touch, \(\tfrac12(1,-1,1,1)\).
Their average is \(\tfrac14\). Now move every entry to the other side of
the average, as far below it as it was above, or as far above as it was
below: an entry \(v\) becomes \(2\cdot\tfrac14-v\). The three entries
\(\tfrac12\) become \(0\). The entry \(-\tfrac12\) becomes \(1\). The
result is \((0,1,0,0)\): the second drawer, with certainty. One touch
and one turn about the average have found one drawer in four.

\textbf{On the blackboard.} Grover calls this operation
\textbf{inversion about average} and gives its matrix, the
\textbf{diffusion transform} \(D\) (his (4.0)): the entries are \(2/N\)
off the diagonal and \(-1+2/N\) on it. Writing \(J\) for the
\(N\times N\) matrix of all ones, \[D\;=\;\frac2N\,J-I .\] On any vector
\(v\) with entries \(v_x\) and average \(\bar v=\tfrac1N\sum_xv_x\), the
vector \(Jv\) has every entry \(N\bar v\), so
\[(Dv)_x\;=\;2\bar v-v_x .\] That is the move we just made by hand.
Grover writes it as \(D=-I+2P\), where \(P=\tfrac1NJ\) and ``\(P\)
acting on any vector \(v\) gives a vector each of whose components is
equal to the average of all components''. We will call \(D\) the
\textbf{turn-about}.

Grover also shows (his Theorem 1) that \(D\) factors as \(D=WRW\), where
\(R\) is diagonal with \(R_{00}=1\) and \(R_{xx}=-1\) for every other
\(x\): \[R\;=\;2\ket{0\cdots0}\bra{0\cdots0}-I .\] Grover calls \(R\)
``the rotation matrix'', in the sense of his selective rotation of
phases: it turns the phase of every drawer but one by \(\pi\). As a map
of the space, though, it is a reflection. It fixes the line through
\(\ket{0\cdots0}\), reverses every direction at right angles to that
line, and satisfies \(R^2=I\). We will call it a reflection, because
§15.4 is about reflections.

Finally, write \(C^{n-1}Z=I-2\ket{1\cdots1}\bra{1\cdots1}\) for the
\textbf{multi-controlled \(Z\)}, which turns over the all-ones drawer
and nothing else. For \(n=2\) it is \(\mathrm{CZ}\), and for \(n=1\) it
is \(Z\) itself. Here is the headline theorem.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 15.5 (the turn-about is a reflection about the even
state).} For every \(n\ge1\) and \(N=2^n\), exactly,
\[D\;=\;W\,R\,W\;=\;-\,W\,X^{\otimes n}\,C^{n-1}Z\,X^{\otimes n}\,W\;=\;2\ket s\bra s-I .\]
Hence \((Dv)_x=2\bar v-v_x\) for every vector \(v\) (inversion about
average); \(D\ket s=\ket s\); \(Du=-u\) for every vector \(u\) whose
entries sum to \(0\); and \(D^2=I\).
\end{quote}

It is proved twice in §15.7, once on each strand. The companion file
checks it exactly for \(n=1,\dots,6\) and tests inversion about average
on a random complex vector: see \texttt{Code/Ch15/TurnAbout.py}.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Dirac's Blackboard.}\nopagebreak

\emph{Grover's matrix, entry by entry.} Grover proves \(D=WRW\) by
multiplying out. Write \(R=2\ket{0\cdots0}\bra{0\cdots0}-I\) and use
\(W_{xz}=2^{-n/2}(-1)^{x\cdot z}\):
\[(WRW)_{xy}\;=\;\sum_z W_{xz}R_{zz}W_{zy}\;=\;2^{-n}\Bigl(2-\sum_z(-1)^{x\cdot z\,\oplus\, z\cdot y}\Bigr).\]
The \(2\) is the \(z=0\) term counted with \(R_{00}=1\) instead of
\(-1\). Since \(x\cdot z\oplus z\cdot y=(x\oplus y)\cdot z\), the sum is
\(\sum_z(-1)^{u\cdot z}\) with \(u=x\oplus y\), which is \(2^n\) if
\(u=0\) and \(0\) otherwise (each bit of \(u\) equal to \(1\) splits the
\(z\)'s into equal halves of opposite sign). So
\((WRW)_{xy}=2/N-[\,x=y\,]\): \(2/N\) off the diagonal, \(-1+2/N\) on
it. That is Grover's \(D\), entry for entry.
\end{quote}

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} The turn-about is built from a box that
turns over one drawer. Start with the smallest one,
\(\mathrm{CZ}=I-2\ket{11}\bra{11}\). Chapter 5 taught us to write a box
as a sum of pictures (rows 34--36), and Chapter 10 gave us the effects
we need: a red effect with phase \(c\pi\) is \(\sqrt2\bra c\), the
mirror of the red point \(\sqrt2\ket c\). We keep Chapter 14's names: a
phase-free red point is \textbf{dark} (\(\sqrt2\ket0\)), a red \(\pi\)
point is \textbf{lit} (\(\sqrt2\ket1\)), and likewise for effects. So a
lit effect over a lit point, on each of two cords, is
\(\sqrt2\bra1\cdot\sqrt2\bra1\) followed by
\(\sqrt2\ket1\cdot\sqrt2\ket1\), which is \(4\ket{11}\bra{11}\). Half of
that is \(2\ket{11}\bra{11}\), and so \(\mathrm{CZ}\) is the two bare
cords minus half of the picture with lit effects and lit points. The
same bookkeeping works for any drawer \(c\) on any number of cords.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 15.6 (one thing turned over).} For every \(n\) and every
\(n\)-bit string \(c\), exactly, \[I-2\ket c\bra c\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.19em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em]

\draw[wire] (0,2.4) -- (2.8,2.4);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2.8,0);
\node at (1.4,1.35) {$\vdots$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;-\;2^{1-n}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.19em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-1.1) (0,3.5);
\draw[wire] (0,2.4) -- (1.0,2.4);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.0,0);
\draw[wire] (2.8,2.4) -- (3.8,2.4);
\draw[wire] (2.8,0) -- (3.8,0);
\node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$c_1\pi$}}] at (1.0,2.4) {};
\node[xsp,label={[ph]below:{$c_n\pi$}}] at (1.0,0) {};
\node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$c_1\pi$}}] at (2.8,2.4) {};
\node[xsp,label={[ph]below:{$c_n\pi$}}] at (2.8,0) {};
\node at (1.9,1.35) {$\vdots$};
\end{tikzpicture}\] on the right, \(n\) bare cords, minus \(2^{1-n}\)
times \(n\) red effects with phases \(c_i\pi\) beside \(n\) red points
with the same phases. Three cases name the chapter's boxes:
\(c=1\cdots1\) gives \(C^{n-1}Z\) (row 111); \(c=w\) gives the marker
\(O_w\) (row 110); and \(c=0\cdots0\) gives
\(I-2\ket{0\cdots0}\bra{0\cdots0}=-R\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} Cord \(i\) contributes
\(\sqrt2\ket{c_i}\cdot\sqrt2\bra{c_i}=2\ket{c_i}\bra{c_i}\), so the
right-hand picture is \(2^n\ket c\bra c\), and \(2^{1-n}\) times it is
\(2\ket c\bra c\). The difference of two pictures is a sum of pictures
with signed weights (Chapter 5). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch15/TurnAbout.py}.

The shape is worth saying in words: \textbf{all the cords, minus twice
the one thing}. The marker has this shape with the marked drawer as the
one thing. Section §15.7 shows that the turn-about has it too, with the
even state as the one thing and an overall sign.

\hypertarget{two-cords-with-no-sign}{%
\subsection{Two cords, with no sign}\label{two-cords-with-no-sign}}

For two cords the tall boxes can be opened into dots with Chapter 14's
\textbf{controlled turn} (Result 14.5, row 103) at \(\alpha=\pi\): a
green ring with phase \(\pi/2\) on each cord, the two rings tied to one
phase-free red hub, and from the hub a pendant green point with phase
\(-\pi/2\). Bare, it is \(\mathrm{CP}(\pi)/\sqrt2=\mathrm{CZ}/\sqrt2\).
A green dot with phase \(\pi\), one leg in and one out, is \(Z\) exactly
(row 53); on a cord we call it a \textbf{half-ring}. Before stating the
result, compute one product by hand. On \(\ket{01}\), \(\mathrm{CZ}\)
does nothing and \(Z\otimes Z\) gives \((+1)(-1)\), so
\((Z\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CZ}\ket{01}=-\ket{01}\). On \(\ket{11}\),
\(\mathrm{CZ}\) gives \(-1\) and \(Z\otimes Z\) gives \((-1)(-1)\), so
the product is \(-\ket{11}\). On \(\ket{00}\) nothing happens. That is
Grover's \(R\) for two cords, and no overall sign is needed.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 15.7 (two cords, no sign).} Exactly: (i)
\(R=(Z\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CZ}=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)\); (ii) for
every \(w\),
\(O_w=(-1)^{\bar w_1\bar w_2}\,\bigl(Z^{\bar w_2}\otimes Z^{\bar w_1}\bigr)\,\mathrm{CZ}\);
in particular \(O_{01}=(I\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CZ}\). In pictures, with
the half-ring on the lower cord for the marker of the second drawer and
on both cords for \(R\),
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.44em, x=1.3em, y=1.3em,

\draw[wire] (1.8,1.3) -- (1.8,0);
\draw[wire] (1.8,1.3) -- (0.5,1.3);

\node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi/2$}}] at (1.8,0) {};

\;=\;\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.44em, x=1.3em, y=1.3em]

\draw[wire] (0,2.6) -- (3.0,2.6);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (3.0,0);
\node[sdbox, minimum height=4.9em] at (1.5,1.3) {$O_{01}$};
\end{tikzpicture}\]
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.44em, x=1.3em, y=1.3em,

\;=\;\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.44em, x=1.3em, y=1.3em]
\path (0,-1.0) (0,3.6);
\draw[wire] (0,2.6) -- (3.0,2.6);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (3.0,0);
\node[sdbox, minimum height=4.9em] at (1.5,1.3) {$R$};
\end{tikzpicture}\] For a general \(w\) the half-ring goes on the lower
cord if \(w_1=0\) and on the upper cord if \(w_2=0\), and for \(w=00\)
the number \(-1\) is written beside the picture.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} On the blackboard, every factor is diagonal, so it is
enough to compare signs on the four drawers \(c_1c_2\). \(\mathrm{CZ}\)
gives \((-1)^{c_1c_2}\), and a \(Z\) on the upper cord gives
\((-1)^{c_1}\), on the lower \((-1)^{c_2}\). With half-rings \(h_1\) on
top and \(h_2\) below (\(h_i\in\{0,1\}\)), the sign on \(c_1c_2\) is
\((-1)^{c_1c_2+h_1c_1+h_2c_2}\). For \(R\), \(h_1=h_2=1\), and
\(c_1c_2+c_1+c_2\) is odd unless \(c_1=c_2=0\): that is
\(\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)\). For the marker, \(h_1=\bar w_2\) and
\(h_2=\bar w_1\), and
\[c_1c_2+\bar w_2c_1+\bar w_1c_2+\bar w_1\bar w_2\;=\;(c_1+\bar w_1)(c_2+\bar w_2),\]
which is odd exactly when \(c_1=w_1\) and \(c_2=w_2\). So the sign is
\((-1)^{[c=w]}\) times \((-1)^{\bar w_1\bar w_2}\), which is (ii).

In the sketchbook, feed the two cords a dark or lit point each, red with
phases \(c_1\pi\) and \(c_2\pi\). By the basis-point lemma (Result 14.6,
row 104) at \(\alpha=\pi\), the upper point passes the controlled turn
and leaves a green \(c_1\pi\) on the lower cord, for the price
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\). On the lower cord that green dot fuses with the
half-ring, if there is one (fusion, Theorem 8.1). A green dot with phase
\(\varphi\), one leg in and one out, multiplies a point \(\sqrt2\ket c\)
by \(e^{ic\varphi}\), so each cord's green phase becomes a sign:
\((-1)^{c_2(c_1+h_2)}\) below and \((-1)^{c_1h_1}\) above. The product
is the sign found on the blackboard. \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch15/TurnAbout.py}, which also derives both pictures by the
rules.

So for two cords the reflection \(R\), and with it the turn-about
\(D=WRW\), can be drawn with no number beside it: collars (yellow boxes)
on both cords, a half-ring on each, the controlled half-turn, and
collars again. Bare, that picture is exactly \(D/\sqrt2\).

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why reflect about the average,
rather than simply lift the marked drawer? Because the turn-about must
not know which drawer is marked: only the marker knows that, and every
use of the marker is a query. So the turn-about treats all drawers alike
and may look only at what they share. Turning every entry over, \(-I\),
also treats them alike, but it changes no odds. A reflection about the
average treats every drawer alike and still makes a sign visible as a
height.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{one-touch}{%
\section{§15.3 One Touch}\label{one-touch}}

We can now put Grover's algorithm together. On \(n\) cords, with
\(N=2^n\) drawers:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Step (i).} Prepare the even state \(\ket s=W\ket{0\cdots0}\)
  (Result 15.4).
\item
  \textbf{Step (ii).} Repeat a \textbf{step}, the marker followed by the
  turn-about, \[G\;=\;D\,O_w,\] some number of times. Grover's own text
  says ``\(O(\sqrt N)\) times (the precise number of repetitions is
  important as discussed in {[}BBHT96{]})''.
\item
  \textbf{Step (iii).} Read the cords. Grover asks for the marked drawer
  ``with a probability of at least \(\tfrac12\)''.
\end{enumerate}

The reference {[}BBHT96{]} is the paper by Michel Boyer, Gilles
Brassard, Peter Høyer and Alain Tapp (we write BBHT) that §15.4 follows.
They write the step as \(G=-TS_0TS_{i_0}\), where \(S_{i_0}\) is our
marker \(O_w\), \(S_0=I-2\ket{0\cdots0}\bra{0\cdots0}=-R\), and \(T\) is
their letter for the Walsh--Hadamard transform. We keep Grover's \(W\)
for that transform and save \(T\) for counting touches, so their step
reads \(G=-WS_0WO_w=WRWO_w=DO_w\). BBHT write \(i_0\) for the marked
drawer, and in their §7, like BBBV, \(y\). We write \(w\) throughout and
keep \(y\) for the flag bit.

\textbf{What counts.} Each step uses the marker once, and so, by Result
15.3, one query. The turn-about uses none: it is the same for every
\(w\). BBBV say so exactly. After the first query they call Grover's
``inversion about the average'' ``an oracle-independent unitary
transformation'', one that turns the phase difference into an amplitude
difference, ``leaving the \(y\) term with the same sign as all the other
terms but a magnitude approximately threefold larger''. So we count
\textbf{one touch per step}. BBHT count differently, and we say it once
to avoid confusion. In their table model the entry must first be
fetched, to decide on the phase shift, and then erased, to allow
interference, so they charge ``two table look-ups'' per step. In Chapter
13's query model, one use of the box with the flag at \(\ket-\) does the
whole marker (Result 15.3).

Here is the complete search for four drawers with \(w=01\). The even
state is \(\tfrac12(1,1,1,1)\). The marker gives \(\tfrac12(1,-1,1,1)\).
The turn-about, by inversion about the average \(\tfrac14\), gives
\((0,1,0,0)=\ket{01}\). The reading shows the second drawer. The same
happens for every \(w\).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 15.8 (one step finds one drawer in four).} For \(N=4\)
and every marked drawer \(w\), exactly, \[D\,O_w\ket s\;=\;\ket w ,\] so
one step and one reading find \(w\) with certainty.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} \textbf{On the blackboard.} Since
\(\braket{w|s}=\tfrac12\), the marker gives
\(O_w\ket s=\ket s-2\cdot\tfrac12\ket w=\ket s-\ket w\). By Result 15.5,
\(D(\ket s-\ket w)=2\ket s\bigl(\braket{s|s}-\braket{s|w}\bigr)-\ket s+\ket w=2\ket s\cdot\tfrac12-\ket s+\ket w=\ket w\).

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} Take \(w=01\). The two green points are
\(2\ket s\) (Result 15.4). Row 110 opens the marker into two pictures:
the bare cords, minus \(\tfrac12\) times a dark and a lit effect beside
a dark and a lit point (Result 15.6 with \(c=01\)). Feed it the green
points. On the bare cords they pass untouched. On the second picture
each red effect meets a green point and closes to
\(\sqrt2\bra{c}(\ket0+\ket1)=\sqrt2\) (Chapter 10), so the two cords
give \(2\) and cancel the \(\tfrac12\):

\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.74em, x=1.1em, y=1.1em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
  \path (0,-1.2) (0,2.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.8) -- (3.4,1.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (3.4,0);
  \node[zsp] at (0,1.8) {};
  \node[zsp] at (0,0) {};
  \node[sdbox, minimum height=3.2em] at (1.9,0.9) {$O_{01}$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.74em, x=1.1em, y=1.1em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
  \path (0,-1.2) (0,2.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.8) -- (1.4,1.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.4,0);
  \node[zsp] at (0,1.8) {};
  \node[zsp] at (0,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;-\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.74em, x=1.1em, y=1.1em,
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1.2) (0,2.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.8) -- (1.4,1.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.4,0);
  \node[xsp] at (0,1.8) {};
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi$}}] at (0,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\]

On the blackboard this reads \(O_{01}\,2\ket s=2\ket s-2\ket{01}\): the
green points minus a dark point above a lit point. Now the turn-about.
By Result 15.5, \(D=2\ket s\bra s-I\). The two green points are
\(2\ket s\) and the two green effects, their mirror image, are
\(2\bra s\), so \(D\) is \(\tfrac12\) times green effects beside green
points, minus the bare cords. A green effect closes to \(2\) on a green
point and to \(\sqrt2\) on a red point, dark or lit. So the turn-about
takes the green points to \(\tfrac12\cdot4-1=1\) copy of themselves, and
the dark-and-lit pair to \(\tfrac12\cdot2=1\) copy of the green points
minus the pair itself. Subtract: the green points cancel exactly, and
the dark point above the lit point is left. That is
\(\sqrt2\ket0\cdot\sqrt2\ket1=2\ket{01}\), so
\(D\,O_{01}(2\ket s)=2\ket{01}\). Every equality here is exact. The
other three drawers go the same way, with the dark and lit points
exchanged to spell \(w\). §15.8 draws this search gate by gate, with the
marker and the turn-about opened into dots. \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch15/SecondDrawer.py}, which checks all four drawers.

BBHT make the same observation in a more general form: when a quarter of
all drawers are marked, ``a solution is found with certainty after a
single iteration'' (their §3.1). Four drawers with one marked is the
smallest such case.

For more drawers one step is not enough. Starting from \(\ket s\) and
repeating the computation in the proof of Result 15.8 with
\(\braket{w|s}=1/\sqrt N\) gives
\[D\,O_w\ket s\;=\;\Bigl(1-\frac4N\Bigr)\ket s+\frac{2}{\sqrt N}\ket w,\]
so the marked amplitude rises from \(1/\sqrt N\) to \((3-4/N)/\sqrt N\),
just under three times as large, which is BBBV's ``approximately
threefold''. For sixty-four drawers that is \(0.367\), with odds about
\(0.135\): better than \(1/64\), but far from certain. So we repeat the
step. How often, and why ``precise''? The next section answers both
questions.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-turning-plane}{%
\section{§15.4 The Turning Plane}\label{the-turning-plane}}

Take four drawers again and do a second step, although the first already
found \(w\). The state is \(\ket w\). The marker turns it over, giving
\(-\ket w\). The turn-about gives
\(-(2\ket s\braket{s|w}-\ket w)=\ket w-\ket s\), whose entries are
\(\tfrac12\) at \(w\) and \(-\tfrac12\) everywhere else. Every drawer
now has odds \(\tfrac14\), just as before the search began. The second
step has undone the first.

So more steps are not always better, and adding up improvements step by
step cannot tell us when to stop. We need to see the whole path of the
state at once. Two facts make that possible.

\textbf{The plane.} Write
\[\ket{w^{\perp}}\;=\;\frac1{\sqrt{N-1}}\sum_{x\ne w}\ket x\] for the
even state of the unmarked drawers, and let \(\theta\) be the angle with
\(\sin\theta=1/\sqrt N\), between \(0\) and \(\pi/2\). Then
\[\ket s\;=\;\sin\theta\,\ket w+\cos\theta\,\ket{w^{\perp}},\] because
the amplitude of \(\ket s\) at \(w\) is \(1/\sqrt N=\sin\theta\) and the
remaining \(N-1\) amplitudes \(1/\sqrt N\) make up
\(\sqrt{(N-1)/N}\,\ket{w^{\perp}}=\cos\theta\,\ket{w^{\perp}}\). The two
vectors \(\ket{w^{\perp}}\) and \(\ket w\) are real, orthogonal and of
length one, so the real combinations \(a\ket w+b\ket{w^{\perp}}\) form a
\textbf{plane}, and we can draw it on paper with \(\ket{w^{\perp}}\)
pointing right and \(\ket w\) pointing up. The marker maps this plane to
itself: it fixes \(\ket{w^{\perp}}\) and sends \(\ket w\) to
\(-\ket w\). It is the \textbf{reflection across the \(\ket{w^{\perp}}\)
line}. The turn-about maps it to itself too, since \(D=2\ket s\bra s-I\)
and \(\ket s\) lies in the plane. It fixes \(\ket s\) and turns over the
vector \(\ket{s^{\perp}}=\cos\theta\ket w-\sin\theta\ket{w^{\perp}}\),
whose entries sum to \(0\) (Result 15.5). So it is the
\textbf{reflection across the \(\ket s\) line}. A step is two
reflections in a row.

What do two reflections make? Hold a sheet of paper and fold it along
one line through a pin, then along another line through the pin at angle
\(\beta-\alpha\) to the first. The sheet has not been turned over, since
two turnings-over cancel. It has been turned round the pin, and by twice
the angle between the folds.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 15.9 (two folds make a turn).} In the real plane, let
\(F_{\alpha}\) be the reflection across the line at angle \(\alpha\) to
the first axis:
\[F_{\alpha}\;=\;\begin{pmatrix}\cos2\alpha&\sin2\alpha\\ \sin2\alpha&-\cos2\alpha\end{pmatrix}.\]
Then for every \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), \(F_{\beta} F_{\alpha}\) is the
rotation by \(2(\beta-\alpha)\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} \(F_{\alpha}\) fixes \((\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)\) and
reverses \((-\sin\alpha,\cos\alpha)\), as a direct multiplication shows,
so it is the reflection named. Write \(c_{\alpha}=\cos2\alpha\) and
\(s_{\alpha}=\sin2\alpha\), and likewise for \(\beta\). Multiplying,
\[F_{\beta} F_{\alpha}=\begin{pmatrix}c_{\beta} c_{\alpha}+s_{\beta} s_{\alpha}&c_{\beta} s_{\alpha}-s_{\beta} c_{\alpha}\\ s_{\beta} c_{\alpha}-c_{\beta} s_{\alpha}&s_{\beta} s_{\alpha}+c_{\beta} c_{\alpha}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos2(\beta-\alpha)&-\sin2(\beta-\alpha)\\ \sin2(\beta-\alpha)&\cos2(\beta-\alpha)\end{pmatrix}\]
by the difference formulas for cosine and sine. \(\;\blacksquare\) The
companion file for this result and the next two is
\texttt{Code/Ch15/TurningPlane.py}.

In the plane with \(\ket{w^{\perp}}\) as the first axis and \(\ket w\)
as the second, the marker is \(F_0\): its matrix is
\(\mathrm{diag}(1,-1)\). The turn-about is \(F_{\theta}\): in the same
coordinates, \(2\ket s\bra s-I\) has entries
\(2\cos^2\theta-1=\cos2\theta\), \(2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\sin2\theta\)
and \(2\sin^2\theta-1=-\cos2\theta\). So a step, \(F_{\theta} F_0\), is
a rotation by \(2\theta\).

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why a plane, when the state lives
in \(N\) dimensions? Because the marker changes only the direction of
\(\ket w\) and the turn-about changes only the direction of
\(\ket{s^{\perp}}\), and both of those directions lie in the plane.
Everything at right angles to the plane is left alone by both, and the
search starts in the plane. So the whole search, however many drawers,
happens on one sheet of paper.

\textbf{A different kind of picture.} This is where the chapter's one
new picture comes in. We draw the plane itself: the unmarked line
\(\ket{w^{\perp}}\) across the page and the marked line \(\ket w\) up
it, meeting at a pin; the \textbf{even line} through the pin at the
small angle \(\theta\) above the unmarked line; and the state as an
arrow from the pin, a \textbf{hand}. The marker folds the paper along
the unmarked line, and the turn-about folds it along the even line. We
call this the \textbf{Turning Plane}. It is not a string diagram. Its
lines are directions in a real plane, not wires. Its hand is a vector,
not a process. None of the rules of Chapter 8 apply to it. Grover's
paper does not draw it, and we attribute it to no one: it is BBHT's
formula, which follows, drawn.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=1cm, y=1cm, >=stealth]
  \draw[->, line width=0.6pt] (-0.5,0) -- (4.3,0) node[right] {$\ket{w^{\perp}}$};
  \draw[->, line width=0.6pt] (0,-1.3) -- (0,4.2) node[above] {$\ket w$};
  \draw[dashed, gray, line width=0.6pt] ({-0.8*cos(14.48)},{-0.8*sin(14.48)}) -- ({4.2*cos(14.48)},{4.2*sin(14.48)}) node[right, black] {\small even line};
  \draw[->, line width=1.2pt] (0,0) -- ({3.4*cos(14.48)},{3.4*sin(14.48)}) node[pos=0.72, below] {$\ket s$};
  \draw[->, line width=1.2pt] (0,0) -- ({3.4*cos(43.43)},{3.4*sin(43.43)}) node[right] {$G\ket s$};
  \draw[->, line width=1.2pt] (0,0) -- ({3.4*cos(72.39)},{3.4*sin(72.39)}) node[above right] {$G^2\ket s$};
  \draw[->, dashed, line width=0.8pt] (0,0) -- ({3.4*cos(-14.48)},{3.4*sin(-14.48)}) node[right] {$O_w\ket s$};
  \draw[line width=0.5pt] (1.1,0) arc (0:14.48:1.1);
  \node at (1.45,0.18) {\small $\theta$};
  \draw[line width=0.5pt] ({2.3*cos(14.48)},{2.3*sin(14.48)}) arc (14.48:43.43:2.3);
  \node at ({2.6*cos(29)},{2.6*sin(29)}) {\small $2\theta$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

\emph{The Turning Plane.} A picture of the real plane spanned by
\(\ket w\) and \(\ket{w^{\perp}}\), drawn for sixteen drawers
(\(\sin\theta=\tfrac14\), \(\theta\approx14.5^{\circ}\)). It is not a
string diagram. It draws one side of the equation
\[D\,O_w\Big|_{\mathrm{span}\{\ket w,\ket{w^{\perp}}\}}\;=\;\text{rotation by }2\theta ,\]
and the three solid hands are the states
\[G^k\ket s\;=\;\sin\bigl((2k+1)\theta\bigr)\ket w+\cos\bigl((2k+1)\theta\bigr)\ket{w^{\perp}}\qquad(k=0,1,2),\]
at \(14.5^{\circ}\), \(43.4^{\circ}\) and \(72.4^{\circ}\). The dashed
hand is the even state after the marker alone, folded to \(-\theta\);
the turn-about folds it across the even line to \(3\theta\). The height
of each hand's tip is the marked amplitude.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 15.10 (the search turns).} For every \(N=2^n\) and every
\(k\ge0\), exactly,
\[G^k\ket s\;=\;\sin\bigl((2k+1)\theta\bigr)\ket w+\cos\bigl((2k+1)\theta\bigr)\ket{w^{\perp}},\]
where \(\sin\theta=1/\sqrt N\). So after \(k\) steps the marked drawer
has amplitude \(a_k=\sin((2k+1)\theta)\), each unmarked drawer has
amplitude \(b_k=\cos((2k+1)\theta)/\sqrt{N-1}\), and the probability
that reading the cords gives \(w\) is \(\sin^2((2k+1)\theta)\).
\end{quote}

This is BBHT's Eq. (2). Their step count \(j\) is our \(k\), and their
amplitudes \(k_j\) and \(\ell_j\) are our \(a_k\) and \(b_k\).

\emph{Proof.} \(\ket s\) is the unit vector at angle \(\theta\) in the
plane. By Result 15.9 with \(\alpha=0\) and \(\beta=\theta\), each step
turns it by \(2\theta\), so after \(k\) steps it is at angle
\((2k+1)\theta\). Its coordinates are the cosine and sine of that angle.
The amplitude of any single unmarked drawer is \(\cos((2k+1)\theta)\)
times the amplitude \(1/\sqrt{N-1}\) of that drawer in
\(\ket{w^{\perp}}\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch15/TurningPlane.py}, which checks Eq. (2) against direct
simulation for \(N=4,8,16,64,4096\), and against an eight-drawer search
built from spiders.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Dirac's Blackboard.}\nopagebreak

\emph{From the recurrence to the sine.} BBHT start from what one step
does to a state with amplitude \(k\) at the marked drawer and \(\ell\)
at each other drawer (their Eq. (1)). In our letters,
\[a_{k+1}=\tfrac{N-2}{N}\,a_k+\tfrac{2(N-1)}{N}\,b_k,\qquad b_{k+1}=\tfrac{N-2}{N}\,b_k-\tfrac2N\,a_k .\]
They reach the sine ``by standard techniques---and a little sweat''. The
plane removes the sweat. Put \(c_k=\sqrt{N-1}\,b_k\), the component
along \(\ket{w^{\perp}}\). Since \(\sin\theta=1/\sqrt N\), we have
\(\cos2\theta=1-2/N=\tfrac{N-2}{N}\) and
\(\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\tfrac{2\sqrt{N-1}}{N}\), so
\[a_{k+1}=\cos2\theta\,a_k+\sin2\theta\,c_k,\qquad c_{k+1}=\cos2\theta\,c_k-\sin2\theta\,a_k .\]
That is the rotation of \((c_k,a_k)\) by \(2\theta\). It starts at
\((c_0,a_0)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\), so induction gives
\(a_k=\sin((2k+1)\theta)\) and \(c_k=\cos((2k+1)\theta)\).
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{when-to-stop}{%
\subsection{When to stop}\label{when-to-stop}}

The hand starts just above the unmarked line and climbs by \(2\theta\)
per step. Success is certain when it stands upright, at \(\pi/2\), which
would take \(\tilde m=(\pi-2\theta)/4\theta\) steps. That is rarely a
whole number, so BBHT take the nearest safe whole number below.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 15.11 (when to stop, and the square root).} Let
\(m=\lfloor\pi/4\theta\rfloor\). After \(m\) steps the probability of
failure is
\[\cos^2\bigl((2m+1)\theta\bigr)\;\le\;\sin^2\theta\;=\;\frac1N ,\] and
\(m\le\tfrac\pi4\sqrt N\). For large \(N\), \(m\) is close to
\(\tfrac\pi4\sqrt N\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} Since \(\tilde m=\pi/4\theta-\tfrac12\) and
\(\pi/4\theta-1<m\le\pi/4\theta\), we have
\(\lvert m-\tilde m\rvert\le\tfrac12\), so \((2m+1)\theta\) lies within
\(\theta\) of \((2\tilde m+1)\theta=\pi/2\). Writing
\((2m+1)\theta=\pi/2+\delta\) with \(\lvert\delta\rvert\le\theta\), we
get
\(\lvert\cos((2m+1)\theta)\rvert=\lvert\sin\delta\rvert\le\sin\theta\).
Finally \(\theta\ge\sin\theta=1/\sqrt N\), so
\(m\le\pi/4\theta\le\tfrac\pi4\sqrt N\). For large \(N\), \(\theta\) and
\(\sin\theta\) are nearly equal. \(\;\blacksquare\) This is BBHT's §3
argument. See \texttt{Code/Ch15/TurningPlane.py}.

Here is the square root in numbers, with the worst case of asking one by
one (Result 15.2) beside it:
