\end{longtable}

For eight drawers \(m=2\), and for sixteen \(m=3\). The last row is
BBHT's own example: for \(2^{20}\) possibilities they ``achieve almost
certainty of success after 804 iterations''. Every step is one touch.
Multiply the drawers by four and the steps roughly double.

Now the warning in Grover's step (ii). For sixty-four drawers,
\(\theta\approx7.18^{\circ}\) and the success probabilities after
\(0,1,2,\dots,8\) steps are
\[0.0156,\;\; 0.135,\;\; 0.344,\;\; 0.591,\;\; 0.816,\;\; 0.964,\;\; 0.9966,\;\; 0.907,\;\; 0.718 .\]
After six steps the hand stands at \(13\theta\approx93.4^{\circ}\), just
past upright. A seventh step carries it to
\((2\cdot7+1)\theta\approx107.7^{\circ}\), and the odds fall back to
about nine in ten. The hand does not stop at the top, and neither do the
odds. BBHT say it plainly: Grover proved that some number of iterations
below \(\sqrt{2N}\) gives success at least \(\tfrac12\), and ``this is
correct, but one must be careful in using his algorithm because the
probability of success does not increase monotonically with the number
of iterations.'' By \(\sqrt{2N}\) iterations, they compute, the
probability has ``dropped down to less than \(9.5\%\)'', and about
\(\tfrac\pi2\sqrt N\) iterations, twice the right number, give ``a
negligible probability of success''. They also note that half the
number, about \(\tfrac\pi8\sqrt N\), suffices for a \(50\%\) chance,
``as Grover considered in his original paper''. The explicit count, and
not only its order, is what makes the search usable.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Coecke's Sketchbook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{Two mirrors of one shape.} Set the marker and the turn-about side
by side as sums of pictures. The marker is the bare cords minus
\(2^{1-n}\) times red \(w\)-effects over red \(w\)-points (Result 15.6).
The turn-about is \(2^{1-n}\) times green effects over green points,
minus the bare cords (§15.7). The two have the same shape in the two
colours: all the cords, minus twice the one thing. The overall sign
differs, and it swaps which line is kept: the marker turns its one thing
over, while the turn-about keeps its one thing and turns over everything
at right angles to it. On a whole step the sign is global and changes no
odds. The picture even measures the angle between the two mirrors. Close
a red \(w\)-effect against a green point on every cord: each cord gives
\(\sqrt2\bra{w_i}(\ket0+\ket1)=\sqrt2\), so \(n\) cords give
\(2^{n/2}\). Divide by the \(2^{n/2}\cdot2^{n/2}\) that the effects and
points carry, and \(\braket{w|s}=2^{-n/2}=\sin\theta\). What the picture
cannot do is iterate. A string diagram of \(k\) steps is just \(k\)
copies laid end to end, and no rule of Chapter 8 reads a sine off it.
The count lives in the plane.
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{many-marked-drawers}{%
\subsection{Many marked drawers}\label{many-marked-drawers}}

BBHT treat the case of \(t\) marked drawers in their §3. The same plane
appears, with \(\ket w\) replaced by the even state of the marked
drawers, and the same two folds.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 15.12 (many marked drawers; Boyer, Brassard, Høyer and
Tapp, §3 and §3.1; stated, not proved).} If exactly \(t\) drawers are
marked, and \(\theta\) is chosen with \(\sin^2\theta=t/N\), then after
\(k\) steps each marked drawer has amplitude
\(\sin((2k+1)\theta)/\sqrt t\) and each unmarked one
\(\cos((2k+1)\theta)/\sqrt{N-t}\) (BBHT's Eq. (3)). With
\(m=\lfloor\pi/4\theta\rfloor\) the probability of failure is at most
\(t/N\), and \(m\le\tfrac\pi4\sqrt{N/t}\). When \(t=N/4\), one step
succeeds with certainty.
\end{quote}

We state it and do not prove it here. Their proof is the one above, with
\(\sin\theta=\sqrt{t/N}\), the marked even state in place of \(\ket w\),
and the marker turning over every marked drawer. The companion code
checks the amplitudes for several \(t\) and \(N\). See
\texttt{Code/Ch15/TurningPlane.py}.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Feynman's Notebook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{A little sweat.} ``Tight bounds on quantum searching'' is by
Michel Boyer, Gilles Brassard and Alain Tapp of the Université de
Montréal and Peter Høyer of Odense University. Its title page calls it a
full paper for PhysComp96, in a draft dated 10 May 1996; the arXiv stamp
on the copy we read is 23 May 1996. It reads Grover's step (ii) closely,
turns the repeated step into a recurrence solved in closed form ``by
standard techniques---and a little sweat'', and draws the practical
consequences. Their largest example is the most striking. For \(2^{20}\)
possibilities and one solution, 804 iterations make success almost
certain. The same 804 iterations, they point out, ``would yield a
solution with probability less than one in a million should there be 4
solutions!'' In the plane of §15.4 the reason is plain to see: with four
marked drawers the hand turns twice as fast, and after 804 steps it has
swung round to lie almost along the unmarked line again. They go on to
handle an unknown number of solutions, to sketch a quantum way of
counting them, and, in their §7, to prove the lower bound we meet next.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{no-faster-hand}{%
\section{§15.5 No Faster Hand}\label{no-faster-hand}}

Chapter 13 stated BBBV's bound as Result 13.14: for a random oracle, no
quantum machine running in time \(o(2^{n/2})\) decides every problem in
NP. It also recorded their remark that Grover's search meets the bound.
In this chapter's terms: a search on \(N=2^n\) drawers takes about
\(\sqrt N=2^{n/2}\) touches, and nothing takes fewer. This section shows
where the \(\sqrt N\) comes from.

Start with an example. Run Grover's search on sixty-four drawers with
\textbf{no drawer marked}, so that the marker is the identity. Each step
is then the turn-about alone, and \(D\ket s=\ket s\): the hand never
moves. With drawer \(w\) marked, the hand moves by \(2\theta\) per step,
and after \(T\) steps the distance between the two final states is the
chord \(2\sin(T\theta)\). That is \(0.496\) after two steps and
\(1.366\) after six. The distance from \(\ket s\) to \(\ket w\) is
\(\sqrt{2-2\sin\theta}=\sqrt{1.75}\approx1.323\). So the question ``how
many touches?'' becomes ``how far can \(T\) touches pull the marked run
away from the unmarked run?'' The answer depends on how much of the
state each touch spends on the marked drawer.

\textbf{On the blackboard.} Consider any method with \(T\) touches. It
may use extra cords as workspace. It starts from a fixed state and
applies unitaries \(V_0,V_1,\dots,V_T\) that do not depend on \(w\),
with a touch between each pair: the marker \(O_w\) on the \(n\) drawer
cords and nothing on the workspace. Its final state is
\[\ket{\varphi^{w}}\;=\;V_T\,O_w\,V_{T-1}\cdots V_1\,O_w\,V_0\ket{\text{start}} .\]
The \textbf{unmarked run} is the same with every \(O_w\) replaced by
\(I\); call its final state \(\ket{\varphi^{\varnothing}}\). Let
\(\ket{\psi_i}\) be the unmarked run's state just before its \(i\)-th
touch, and for each drawer \(x\) let \(\alpha_{i,x}\) be the length of
the part of \(\ket{\psi_i}\) in which the drawer cords hold \(x\). BBBV
call the square \(q_x=\alpha_{i,x}^2\) the \textbf{query magnitude} of
\(x\) at that touch (their Definition 3.2).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 15.13 (a touch moves the hand only by its share).} For
every such method and every drawer \(w\),
\[\bigl\lVert\,\ket{\varphi^{w}}-\ket{\varphi^{\varnothing}}\,\bigr\rVert\;\le\;2\sum_{i=1}^{T}\alpha_{i,w}.\]
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} For \(j=0,\dots,T\) let \(\ket{h_j}\) be the final state
of the run that uses \(I\) at the first \(j\) touches and \(O_w\) at the
rest, so \(\ket{h_0}=\ket{\varphi^{w}}\) and
\(\ket{h_T}=\ket{\varphi^{\varnothing}}\). The runs \(h_{j-1}\) and
\(h_j\) agree up to touch \(j\), where both are in the state
\(\ket{\psi_j}\). At touch \(j\) one applies \(O_w\) and the other
\(I\), and afterwards both apply the same unitaries, which preserve
distances. So
\[\bigl\lVert\ket{h_{j-1}}-\ket{h_j}\bigr\rVert=\bigl\lVert(O_w-I)\ket{\psi_j}\bigr\rVert=2\,\bigl\lVert(\ket w\bra w\otimes I)\ket{\psi_j}\bigr\rVert=2\alpha_{j,w}.\]
The triangle inequality over \(j=1,\dots,T\) gives the result.
\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch15/NoFasterHand.py}, which tests
it on random methods.

This is BBHT's Lemma 6(1), with their \(y\) renamed \(w\), and its proof
is the telescoping argument of BBBV's Theorem 3.3. It holds just as well
if a touch is the query box \(U_f\) with the flag in any state, since
\(U_f-I=\ket w\bra w\otimes(X-I)\) and \(X-I\) at most doubles a length.

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} The smallest case can be drawn and weighed.
The Second Drawer of §15.8 is a method with one touch on four drawers.
Its unmarked run is the same picture with the marker taken out. The
yellow boxes that stood either side of the marker then meet and cancel
(row 58). What is left is the two dark points, the turn-about's
half-rings, rings and hub, and the last pair of yellow boxes. The
turn-about's middle is \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}R\) (Result 15.7), and \(R\) is
\(\tfrac12\) times dark effects beside dark points, minus the bare cords
(row 112). A dark effect closes on a dark point to \(2\), so the dark
points come through as \(\tfrac12\cdot4-1=1\) copy of themselves. The
last yellow boxes turn them green (colour change), and the unmarked run
is exactly \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) times two green points, which is
\(\sqrt2\ket s\). The picture is \(\sqrt2\) times the run itself: its
two dark points carry \(2\), and its one remaining hub only
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\). Divide by that \(\sqrt2\): the unmarked run ends at
\(\ket s\), and the marked run ends at \(\ket{01}\) (Result 15.8). Their
difference, \(\tfrac12(-1,1,-1,-1)\), has length exactly \(1\). At its
one touch the unmarked run is in \(\ket s\), whose part on drawer \(01\)
has length \(\tfrac12\), so Result 15.13 allows at most
\(2\cdot\tfrac12=1\). The bound is met with equality. Both values are
exact equalities of pictures. The inequality, for every method, stays on
the blackboard: a rewrite proves an equality of processes, never a bound
(row 117). See \texttt{Code/Ch15/NoFasterHand.py}.

Each touch has only one unit of squared amplitude to spread over \(N\)
drawers, since \(\sum_x\alpha_{i,x}^2=1\). So over \(T\) touches the
squares add up to \(T\), and on average a drawer gets \(T/N\) of them.
If the searcher cannot find a drawer except by pulling its run far from
the unmarked run, then the drawers that get only their fair share are
out of reach. Here is the whole argument, with a modest constant.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 15.14 (no faster hand, in a weak form).} Suppose a method
with \(T\) touches names the marked drawer with probability at least
\(\tfrac12\) for every choice of \(w\). Then
\[T\;\ge\;\frac{\sqrt N}{4\sqrt2}-\frac12 .\]
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} Write \(S_x=\sum_i\alpha_{i,x}^2\), so that
\(\sum_xS_x=T\). At most \(N/4\) drawers can have \(S_x>4T/N\), since
otherwise those alone would add up to more than \(T\). This is the
counting of BBBV's Corollary 3.4. The method's final reading names a
drawer; write \(P_x\) for the projection onto the outcomes that name
\(x\), so the \(P_x\) are orthogonal and add up to at most \(I\). The
probabilities \(\lVert P_x\ket{\varphi^{\varnothing}}\rVert^2\) add up
to at most \(1\), so at most \(N/4\) drawers have
\(\lVert P_x\ket{\varphi^{\varnothing}}\rVert^2\ge4/N\). That leaves at
least \(N/2\) drawers \(x\) with \(S_x\le4T/N\) and
\(\lVert P_x\ket{\varphi^{\varnothing}}\rVert<2/\sqrt N\). Take one of
them as \(w\). On one side,
\(\lVert P_w\ket{\varphi^{w}}\rVert\ge1/\sqrt2\), so
\[\bigl\lVert\ket{\varphi^{w}}-\ket{\varphi^{\varnothing}}\bigr\rVert\;\ge\;\bigl\lVert P_w\ket{\varphi^{w}}\bigr\rVert-\bigl\lVert P_w\ket{\varphi^{\varnothing}}\bigr\rVert\;>\;\frac1{\sqrt2}-\frac2{\sqrt N}.\]
On the other side, by Result 15.13 and the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality,
\(\sum_i\alpha_{i,w}\le\sqrt T\sqrt{S_w}\le2T/\sqrt N\), so the distance
is at most \(4T/\sqrt N\). Together, \(4T/\sqrt N>1/\sqrt2-2/\sqrt N\),
which rearranges to the bound. \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch15/NoFasterHand.py}.

The constant is poor. For \(2^{20}\) drawers the bound says at least
\(181\) touches, while Grover's search needs about \(402\) for even odds
and \(804\) for near-certainty. But the shape is right: the touches must
grow like \(\sqrt N\). The example shows the same count at work in
Grover's own run. There every touch spends exactly \(1/\sqrt N\) of
amplitude on each drawer, so Result 15.13 bounds the distance after
\(T\) touches by \(2T/\sqrt N\), which is \(T/4\) for sixty-four
drawers. The bound is \(0.5\) after two touches, against the actual
\(0.496\), so Grover's touches waste almost nothing. After five touches
the bound is \(1.25\), which is short of the \(1.323\) from \(\ket s\)
to \(\ket w\), so five touches of this kind cannot bring the hand to the
marked line. Six give \(1.5\), and six are what the stopping rule
prescribes.

The sharp constant is BBHT's, and we state it without proof.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 15.15 (Boyer, Brassard, Høyer and Tapp, Theorem 7;
stated, not proved).} Let the marked drawer \(w\) be chosen uniformly at
random among \(N\), and let \(M\) be any oracle quantum machine with
bounded error probability. Then the expected number of times \(M\) must
query the oracle ``in order to determine \(y\) with probability at least
\(1/2\) is at least \(\lfloor(\sin(\pi/8))\sqrt N\rfloor\)'', where
their \(y\) is our \(w\).
\end{quote}

Grover's search reaches probability \(\tfrac12\) after about
\(\tfrac\pi8\sqrt N\) steps, and \((\pi/8)/\sin(\pi/8)\approx1.026\).
So, counting one query per step, the search spends about \(2.6\%\) more
than the bound. BBHT call their bound ``only a few percent smaller than
the number of iterations required by Grover's algorithm''. Because they
charge two table look-ups per step (§15.3), their own conclusion reads
that Grover's algorithm is ``roughly within a factor 2 of being optimal
in terms of the number of table lookups''. Grover's §6 summarizes BBBV's
result in words: ``any quantum mechanical algorithm running for \(T\)
steps is only sensitive to \(O(T^2)\) queries'', and ``{[}BBHT96{]}
gives a direct proof of this result along with tight bounds showing the
algorithm of this paper is within a few percent of the fastest possible
quantum mechanical algorithm.'' Result 15.14 is a weak form of that
sensitivity, with its proof written out.

\textbf{What the bound does not say.} It speaks of drawers with no
structure, a box that can only be asked. It does not say that quantum
computers cannot solve problems in NP. Grover makes the point from the
other side in his §1.1: if the number of steps could be reduced ``to a
finite power of \(O(\log N)\) (instead of \(O(\sqrt N)\) as in this
paper), it would yield a polynomial time algorithm for NP-complete
problems''. BBBV's reading, quoted in Chapter 13, is that ``there is no
black-box approach to solving NP--complete problems by using some
uniquely quantum-mechanical features''. A problem with structure is not
a sealed wall of drawers, and Shor's algorithm in Chapter 14 used
structure.

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why measure a touch by the squared
amplitude it spends on a drawer, rather than by which drawers it ``looks
at''? Because a quantum touch looks at every drawer a little, and the
only honest measure of how much is how much of the state is on that
drawer when the touch happens. The query magnitude is that measure, and
its total over all drawers is fixed at one per touch. That fixed total
is the whole reason the answer is a square root.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-theorem-twice-15}{%
\section{§15.7 The Theorem, Twice}\label{the-theorem-twice-15}}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 15.5 (the turn-about is a reflection about the even
state), restated.} For every \(n\ge1\) and \(N=2^n\), exactly,
\[D\;=\;W\,R\,W\;=\;-\,W\,X^{\otimes n}\,C^{n-1}Z\,X^{\otimes n}\,W\;=\;2\ket s\bra s-I ,\]
and hence \((Dv)_x=2\bar v-v_x\), \(D\ket s=\ket s\), \(Du=-u\) whenever
the entries of \(u\) sum to \(0\), and \(D^2=I\).
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{diracs-blackboard-15}{%
\subsection{Dirac's Blackboard}\label{diracs-blackboard-15}}

\textbf{Step 1: \(R\) through the \(X\)s.} \(X^{\otimes n}\) flips every
bit, \(X^{\otimes n}\ket x=\ket{\bar x}\). \(C^{n-1}Z\) turns over
\(\ket{\bar x}\) exactly when \(\bar x=1\cdots1\), that is, when
\(x=0\cdots0\). So
\[X^{\otimes n}\,C^{n-1}Z\,X^{\otimes n}\;=\;I-2\ket{0\cdots0}\bra{0\cdots0}\;=\;-R .\]

\textbf{Step 2: \(WRW\).} By Result 15.4, \(W\ket{0\cdots0}=\ket s\),
and since \(W\) is real and symmetric, \(\bra{0\cdots0}W=\bra s\). With
\(W^2=I\),
\[WRW\;=\;2\,W\ket{0\cdots0}\bra{0\cdots0}W-W^2\;=\;2\ket s\bra s-I .\]
Together with Step 1, \(-WX^{\otimes n}C^{n-1}ZX^{\otimes n}W=WRW\).

\textbf{Step 3: Grover's entries.} \(\ket s\bra s\) has every entry
\(1/N\), so \((2\ket s\bra s-I)_{xy}=2/N-[\,x=y\,]\), which is Grover's
\(D\) (his (4.0)).

\textbf{Step 4: the consequences.} For any \(v\),
\(\braket{s|v}=\tfrac1{\sqrt N}\sum_xv_x=\sqrt N\,\bar v\), so
\((2\ket s\braket{s|v})_x=2\bar v\) and \((Dv)_x=2\bar v-v_x\). Next,
\(D\ket s=2\ket s-\ket s=\ket s\). If the entries of \(u\) sum to \(0\),
then \(\braket{s|u}=0\) and \(Du=-u\). Finally
\(D^2=4\ket s\braket{s|s}\bra s-4\ket s\bra s+I=I\). \(\;\blacksquare\)

step below names its rule.

\textbf{Step 4: read off the value.} The \(n\) green points are
\(2^{n/2}\ket s\) (Result 15.4), and the \(n\) green effects are their
mirror image, \(2^{n/2}\bra s\). So the first term is
\(2^{1-n}\cdot2^{n}\ket s\bra s=2\ket s\bra s\), and the bare cords are
\(I\). The scalar \(2^{1-n}\) is carried unchanged through Steps 1 to 3:
fusion, the removal of a plain dot, \(H^2=I\) and colour change cost
nothing.

The entries come back as closed pictures too. Close the last picture
with red effects \(x\) on the right and red points \(y\) on the left,
each worth \(\sqrt2\) times the corresponding bra or ket. A green effect
meeting a red point gives \((\bra0+\bra1)\sqrt2\ket{y_i}=\sqrt2\) on
each cord, and so does a red effect meeting a green point. The first
term closes to \(2^{1-n}\cdot2^{n/2}\cdot2^{n/2}=2\). The bare cords
close to \(\prod_i\sqrt2\bra{x_i}\sqrt2\ket{y_i}=2^n[\,x=y\,]\). So
\(2^n\bra xD\ket y=2-2^n[\,x=y\,]\), which is Grover's \(2/N\) off the
diagonal and \(-1+2/N\) on it. \(\;\blacksquare\)

The picture chain is general in \(n\) and exact. What it does not do is
open \(C^{n-1}Z\) into dots: it uses the tall box and its sum of
pictures (row 111). For two cords the tall box is the controlled turn at
a half (Result 15.7), derived by the rules. For three cords it needs
eighth-turns (§15.9), and that drawing is checked by matrix, not derived
here.

\hypertarget{the-verdict-15}{%
\subsection{The verdict}\label{the-verdict-15}}

The blackboard wins, and by a wide margin. Step 2 is two lines, it holds
for every \(n\), and Step 1 is a remark about flipping bits. The
sketchbook needs four pictures and a paragraph of scalars to reach the
same equation. Shor and Grover are won by the algebra, and this
chapter's headline is no exception.

What the pictures show is the shape the algebra compresses: \textbf{all
the cords, minus twice the one thing, seen crosswise}. The marker turns
over a dark-and-lit thing. The turn-about, apart from its overall sign,
turns over the even thing, and the collars are what turn ``dark'' into
``even''. The same shape in two colours is the reason the two operations
are reflections of the same kind, and it is the reason §15.4's plane
exists. But the picture is an equality of processes, and it counts
nothing. It does not say how many steps a search needs, or that
\(\sqrt N\) is the right number, or that no method does better. Those
came from the blackboard and from the Turning Plane.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-second-drawer}{%
\section{§15.8 The Second Drawer}\label{the-second-drawer}}

Here is the chapter's master diagram: a whole search on four drawers,
Grover's steps (i), (ii)(a) and (ii)(b) done once, with the second
drawer marked. On the blackboard it is \[W\,R\,W\;O_{01}\;W\ket{00}.\]
It is drawn \textbf{gate by gate, unfused}, so that the marker and the
turn-about stay separate pieces, as Grover's two operations are. Fusing
the green dots on each cord would be a valid rewrite (Theorem 8.1) and
would give the same process drawn more compactly, but it would merge the
marker's half-ring into the marker's ring and the turn-about's
half-rings into its rings, and the two operations would no longer be
told apart.

From left to right. The \textbf{upper row}: a dark point; a yellow box;
a green ring \(\pi/2\), the marker's upper ring; a yellow box; a green
\(\pi\), the turn-about's upper half-ring; a green ring \(\pi/2\), the
turn-about's upper ring; a yellow box; the first output. The
\textbf{lower row}: a dark point; a yellow box; a green ring \(\pi/2\),
the marker's lower ring; a green \(\pi\), the marker's half-ring; a
yellow box; a green \(\pi\), the turn-about's lower half-ring; a green
ring \(\pi/2\), the turn-about's lower ring; a yellow box; the second
output. \textbf{The marker's hub} is a phase-free red dot between the
rows, tied to both marker rings, with a pendant green point \(-\pi/2\)
hanging to the left: this is the controlled half-turn, and with the
half-ring on the lower row it is \(O_{01}=(I\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CZ}\)
(Result 15.7). \textbf{The turn-about's hub} is the same, tied to both
turn-about rings, with its pendant hanging to the right; with the two
half-rings it is \(R=(Z\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CZ}\), and with the yellow
boxes on either side it is \(WRW=D\). We call the picture \textbf{The
Second Drawer}.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, x=1.4em, y=1.4em,

The rows run straight, and no tie crosses a row: each hub sits between

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 15.16 (The Second Drawer).} Exactly, with no scalar,
\[\text{The Second Drawer}\;=\;\ket0\ket1 .\] The upper output is dark
and the lower is lit: read top cord first, the second drawer, \(01\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} \textbf{On the blackboard.} The two dark points are
\(\sqrt2\ket0\) each, together \(2\ket{00}\). The two bare controlled
half-turns are \(\mathrm{CZ}/\sqrt2\) each (Result 14.5), together
\(\tfrac12\) times the matrices. With Result 15.7, the picture is
\(2\cdot\tfrac12\cdot W(Z\otimes Z)\mathrm{CZ}\,W\;(I\otimes Z)\mathrm{CZ}\;W\ket{00}=WRW\,O_{01}\,W\ket{00}=D\,O_{01}\ket s\),
and by Result 15.8 this is \(\ket{01}\).

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} Colour change (Theorem 8.2) turns each dark
point with its yellow box into a green point. By Result 15.7, the
marker's piece is \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}O_{01}\), and by Result 15.6 with
\(c=01\) it is \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) times the difference of two pictures:
the bare cords, minus \(\tfrac12\) times a dark and a lit effect beside
a dark and a lit point. Feed it the two green points. On the first term
they pass untouched. On the second, each red effect meets a green point
and closes to \(\sqrt2\bra{c}(\ket0+\ket1)=\sqrt2\), so the two cords
give \(2\) and cancel the \(\tfrac12\). What remains is

\[\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\Biggl(\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.74em, x=1.1em, y=1.1em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
  \path (0,-1.2) (0,2.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.8) -- (1.4,1.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.4,0);
  \node[zsp] at (0,1.8) {};
  \node[zsp] at (0,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;-\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.74em, x=1.1em, y=1.1em,
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1.2) (0,2.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.8) -- (1.4,1.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.4,0);
  \node[xsp] at (0,1.8) {};
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi$}}] at (0,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;\Biggr),\]

two green points minus a dark point above a lit point: on the
blackboard,
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(2\ket s-2\ket{01}\bigr)=\sqrt2\,O_{01}\ket s\).
Now the turn-about's piece. By Result 15.7 it is \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}D\),
and by the chain of §15.7 with \(n=2\) it is
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\tfrac12\,\text{(green effects beside green points)}-\text{bare cords}\bigr)\).
Apply it to each of the two pictures above. A green effect meeting a
green point closes to \((\bra0+\bra1)(\ket0+\ket1)=2\), and meeting a
red point it closes to \(\sqrt2\). So the two green points give
\(\tfrac12\cdot4\) green points minus the green points themselves, which
is the green points once more. The dark-and-lit pair gives
\(\tfrac12\cdot2\) green points minus the dark-and-lit pair.
Subtracting, the green points cancel exactly, and with the two factors
of \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) what is left is

\[\tfrac12\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.74em, x=1.1em, y=1.1em,
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1.2) (0,2.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.8) -- (1.4,1.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.4,0);
  \node[xsp] at (0,1.8) {};
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi$}}] at (0,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;\tfrac12\cdot\sqrt2\ket0\cdot\sqrt2\ket1\;=\;\ket0\ket1 .\]

\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch15/SecondDrawer.py}, which builds
this picture, evaluates it with its scalar, and reduces it by the rules
to one point per output, phase-free above and \(\pi\) below.

The drawer was chosen so that its reading is not the same both ways up.
Read from the bottom cord up, the outputs would say \(10\), the third
drawer, and the code checks that the amplitude there is exactly \(0\).
The drawer is also written into the picture itself: the marker's
half-ring sits on the lower row, and the lower row is the one that comes
out lit. Mark the third drawer instead and the half-ring moves to the
upper row. Mark the fourth and it disappears. Mark the first and the
marker has a half-ring on each row and the number \(-1\) beside it
(Result 15.7). In each case the search finds its drawer, with the first
drawer's value carrying the marker's sign, \(-\ket{00}\).

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Coecke's Sketchbook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{The ledger of the Second Drawer.} Every number in the proof can be
named, and they balance. The picture carries two points worth \(\sqrt2\)
each, which is \(2\), and two bare controlled half-turns worth
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) each, which is \(\tfrac12\). So nothing needs to be
written beside it. Inside the proof, three closings do the work. A red
effect meets a green point: \(\sqrt2\). A green effect meets a green
point: \(2\). A green effect meets a red point: \(\sqrt2\). The marker's
\(2^{1-n}=\tfrac12\) is paid back by two of the first kind. In the
turn-about, the green points are fed back into themselves, which gives
\(\tfrac12\cdot4-1=1\) copy, while the dark-and-lit pair returns
\(\tfrac12\cdot2=1\) copy of the green points. The two copies cancel,
and only the dark-and-lit pair survives, at \(\tfrac12\) from the two
hubs. The cancellation is the search. After the touch the state is half
the even state plus a part whose entries sum to zero. The turn-about
keeps the first and turns the second over, and what is left is the
marked drawer alone.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{what-the-pictures-leave-to-the-blackboard}{%
\section{§15.9 What the Pictures Leave to the
Blackboard}\label{what-the-pictures-leave-to-the-blackboard}}

Take stock. Asking one by one costs \(N-1\) asks in the worst case
(Result 15.1), and no classical plan does better than \((k+1)/N\) with
\(k\) asks (Result 15.2). The marker is one query, a sign that no
reading sees (Result 15.3), laid on the even state (Result 15.4). The
turn-about is a reflection about the even state (Result 15.5), built
from one-thing-turned-over boxes (Result 15.6), and for two cords both
reflections are drawn with no sign (Result 15.7). One step finds one
drawer in four (Result 15.8), and The Second Drawer derives that search
in dots (Result 15.16). Two folds make a turn (Result 15.9), so the
search turns by \(2\theta\) a step (Result 15.10), stops after about
\(\tfrac\pi4\sqrt N\) steps (Result 15.11), and does the same with many
marked drawers (Result 15.12). A touch moves the answer only by its
share (Result 15.13), so no method has a faster hand than about
\(\sqrt N\) (Results 15.14 and 15.15).

Now the honest part. \textbf{Shor and Grover are won by the algebra, and
the book says so.} The following have no string-diagram proof in this
chapter: the step count, the closed form \(\sin((2k+1)\theta)\), the
stopping rule, the square root, and the bound that no method does
better. The first four came from the blackboard and from the Turning
Plane, which is a drawing of the blackboard's plane and not a diagram of
processes. The last is proved by counting (Results 15.13 and 15.14) or
cited (Results 13.14 and 15.15). A rewrite proves that two processes are
equal. It proves that this network, with this box, returns this state.
It proves no bound on queries, and nothing about optimality. The Second
Drawer shows that one step on four drawers is certain. It says nothing
about sixty-four.

There is also a limit to what the pictures in this chapter have been
built from. The Second Drawer uses only quarter-turns and half-turns:
rings at \(\pi/2\), half-rings at \(\pi\), pendants at \(-\pi/2\). For
eight drawers the turn-about needs \(\mathrm{CCZ}\), the three-cord
\(C^{n-1}Z\), and its dots need eighth-turns. Here is the drawing. On
each of three cords sits a green dot with phase \(\pi/4\). Three hubs of
two ties each join the pairs of cords, through phase-free green rings,
with pendants at \(-\pi/4\). One hub of three ties joins all three
cords, with a pendant at \(+\pi/4\). The ties from the top cord to the
lowest hubs pass the middle cord without touching it: where a tie
crosses a cord and no dot is drawn, the two do not meet.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 15.17 (the eight-drawer turn-about needs eighths;
checked, not derived).} Exactly, the bare picture above is
\(2^{-5/2}\,\mathrm{CCZ}\). Each hub with \(k\) ties, with its pendant,
contributes \(2^{-(k-1)/2}\): three hubs of two ties and one of three
give \(2^{-3/2}\cdot2^{-1}\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Why it holds, on the blackboard.} On a drawer \(x_1x_2x_3\), each
phase-free green ring copies its cord's bit up its tie, each hub reads
the parity of the bits it receives (Result 14.5's mechanism), and each
pendant turns by its phase times that parity. For bits,
\[x_1x_2x_3\;=\;\tfrac14\bigl[(x_1+x_2+x_3)-(x_1\oplus x_2)-(x_2\oplus x_3)-(x_1\oplus x_3)+(x_1\oplus x_2\oplus x_3)\bigr],\]
as the eight cases confirm. Multiplied by \(\pi\), the right side is
exactly the sum of the turns in the picture, and the left side is the
turn of \(\mathrm{CCZ}\). A hub of \(k\) ties reading bits gives
\(2^{-(k-1)/2}\) times the parity point, which accounts for the scalar.
\(\;\blacksquare\) We have not derived this picture from the tall box by
the rules of Chapter 8, and we do not claim to. See
\texttt{Code/Ch15/TurnAbout.py}, which checks it by matrix and runs an
eight-drawer search built from it.

With collars and red \(\pi\)s on either side and \(-2^{5/2}\) beside it,
the picture is the eight-drawer turn-about. Its finest turn is an
eighth, and nothing in The Second Drawer is finer than a quarter.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

The chapter's question has an answer. To find one marked drawer among
\(N\), an ordinary searcher must open drawers one at a time, and no plan
does better than one drawer's worth of chance per ask. A quantum
searcher touches all the drawers at once, and each touch turns the
marked one over where no reading can see it. The turn-about then
reflects the whole state about its average. Together the two reflections
turn the state by a fixed small angle, twice the tilt between the even
line and the unmarked line. After about \(\tfrac\pi4\sqrt N\) touches
the state stands almost upright on the marked drawer, and one more touch
would carry it past. And no method can ask fewer than about \(\sqrt N\)
times, because each touch has only one unit of amplitude to spread over
all the drawers, and a drawer that gets only its fair share cannot be
told apart from an empty wall. The pictures drew the touch and the
turn-about, and the whole four-drawer search, dot by dot. The count they
left to the blackboard, and so did we.

Chapter 16 looks inside the pictures instead of at what they compute.
Everything in The Second Drawer is a quarter-turn or a half-turn, and
the eight-drawer turn-about needed an eighth. That looks like a small
difference, one angle halved. Chapter 16, \emph{Inside the Clifford
World}, asks what separates the circuits built from quarters and halves
from the ones that need eighths, and why that difference matters so much
more than its size suggests.

\hypertarget{twenty-four-preludes-and-a-t}{%
\chapter{Twenty-Four Preludes and a
T}\label{twenty-four-preludes-and-a-t}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\emph{春待つや}\\
\emph{二十四落ちて}\\
\emph{揺るる粒}

\emph{haru matsu ya}\\
\emph{nijūshi ochite}\\
\emph{yururu tsubu}

\emph{Waiting for the spring ---}\\
\emph{twenty-four drops have fallen,}\\
\emph{and one hangs, trembling.}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\emph{{[}The Crab's parlour, the afternoon of the next day. On the
table, on a folded woollen cloth, stands something low and square under
a cover of green baize; beside it stands a small stand of darker turned
wood with a pale wooden solid seated in it. The Tortoise is in the chair
nearest the fire, her work-bag at her feet. The door opens, and Achilles
comes in with his boots in one hand.{]}}

\emph{{[}The parlour he comes into is warm from end to end. The frost
went in the night, and all afternoon the eaves have been giving it up, a
drop past the glass and another and then a run of them together, into
the slush on the sill. The one tall window at the near end, each of its
small panes blown by hand, looks up the lane, all ruts and water now, to
the church at the top of it, where the ringers have come in for their
afternoon practice and are raising the tower's bells: a stray note, a
pause, two together, the tumble of them quickening and climbing as each
bell swings higher, in no order anybody could follow. On the long wall
the fire burns in a grate framed with blue-and-white Delft tiles, a
little ship or a flower painted on each. The tiler set every tile
whichever way up it came to his hand, and every one sits square against
its neighbours, and wherever four corners meet their painted sprigs make
a small flower between them. The kettle sits at the side of the hob; the
dresser holds the Crab's cups, bought one at a time, no two of a
pattern, and the cupboard beside it is shut. At the far end of the room,
on the end wall beyond the table, hangs a print in a plain black frame:
Escher's \textup{Stars}, many-sided solids hanging in a dark space. The
window's light reaches it only at second hand, off the ceiling, and the
dark inside the frame is darker than the wall round it. It was hanging
there before the postman came up the lane this morning, and it will be
hanging there when he next comes up it.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} The frost's broken! The lane's gone to soup from your
door to the church, and every eave in the village is dripping on
somebody.

\textbf{Crab:} It went in the night. I heard the first drip at three
o'clock and lay awake till it was light, waiting for the second. Boots
by the fender, if you please, and you by the fire.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}setting his boots by the fender and
unwinding his scarf{]}} The stair at Madam Tortoise's groaned at me on
the way down last night, exactly as she promised. I stepped over it, and
it groaned anyway.

\textbf{Tortoise:} It groans at people who step over it. And this
morning it said nothing at all when I came down. I think the thaw has
got into its temper.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}folding the scarf over the back of his
chair{]}} Then everything is softening today. Even stairs.

\textbf{Crab:} Except my patience. Tea first. \emph{{[}He pours for all
three, and sets the pot down on the side of the table away from the
fire, at the right of Achilles's place.{]}} And before you ask what is
on my table, because you were about to ask\ldots{}

\textbf{Achilles:} I was about to ask.

\textbf{Crab:} A parcel from Delft, this morning, from the little
workshop where the old man and his daughter made my music boxes. The
postman carried it up the lane as though it might hatch.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}nodding at the wooden stand{]}} Is that what
hatched?

\textbf{Crab:} That is the half I have unpacked. \emph{{[}He sets the
stand nearer the edge of the table on Achilles's side, at the left of
the tray as seen from Achilles's place, where they can all see it.{]}}
This is a model, turned from a single piece of pale wood, with six tips,
and every tip painted: a dark green and a pale green opposite each
other, a dark red and a pale red, a dark gold and a pale gold. And this
is its cradle: a socket in the middle to take the bottom tip, and four
notched lugs round it at the height of the model's waist, one at the
front, one at the right, one at the back and one at the left, each to
take a tip. The daughter's letter says it is for learning how a thing
may be turned and still sit.

\emph{{[}The model sits in its cradle as it came out of the straw, the
cradle's front lug towards Achilles's place and its right-hand lug at
his right: the dark green tip straight up, the pale green down in the
socket, the dark red in the front lug, the dark gold in the right-hand
lug, the pale red in the back lug and the pale gold in the left.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} It looks like a spinning top that has decided not to.

\textbf{Crab:} It is far too well brought up to spin. \emph{{[}He lays a
claw on the baize.{]}} And the other half of the parcel came last week,
and I have been keeping it covered for company.

\emph{{[}He lifts the baize away and folds it over the end of the
dresser. Beneath it, on the woollen cloth, stands a tray of unpolished
dark wood with a raised rim, its front towards Achilles's place, so that
its left and right are his. On the tray stand five small silver bells,
each mouth-down on its own green felt pad, each with a little crown loop
on top. One bell stands in the middle of the tray. The others stand one
near each corner: at the left, a left-back bell and a left-front bell;
at the right, a right-back bell and a right-front bell.{]}}

\emph{{[}Cream silk ties run between the crown loops, each knotted at
both its ends, each wearing a short yellow sleeve halfway along its
length. One tie runs from the middle bell to the left-back bell; one
from the middle bell to the left-front bell; one from the middle bell to
the right-back bell; one from the middle bell to the right-front bell.
At the left, one tie runs from the left-back bell to the left-front
bell; at the right, one from the right-back bell to the right-front
bell. The front and the back of the tray are open: no tie runs along
them.{]}}

\emph{{[}Every bell has its pull. From the left-back bell's crown loop
an inner length of cord runs to a small brass ring, knotted at the loop
and at the ring; from the same brass ring an outer length runs on,
knotted at the ring and at a silk tassel that hangs over the left side
of the rim, just by the left-back corner. The left-front bell's pull is
made the same way, an inner length to its brass ring and an outer length
to its tassel, and hangs over the left side of the rim by the left-front
corner. The right-back bell's hangs over the right side of the rim by
the right-back corner, and the right-front bell's over the right side by
the right-front corner, each made the same way. The middle bell's pull
runs straight forward to the front rim, between the two front bells,
crossing no tie: its inner length to its brass ring, its outer length to
its tassel. No cord passes through a ring; each length is knotted at
both its ends.{]}}

\emph{{[}As the baize comes away, the five bells shiver on their pads,
all together, a tremble with no sound in it, and are still again as soon
as the Crab's claw has gone. The window's pale light falls across the
left of the tray and the fire's across the right, so that the left
wing's silk lies grey and cool, the right wing's takes a warmer colour,
and the middle bell's own ties, and its pull running forward to the
front rim, catch a little of both. Each yellow sleeve is a short bright
collar on its tie, and the tassels hang over the rim without a stir.
Burnt small into the back of the rim are the workshop's little anchor
and the old man's initials.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} It's a bow tie. Two wings and a knot in the middle.

\textbf{Crab:} And the middle bell is the knot; the old man called it so
himself. This is a bell-tray, the newest thing from the same bench. The
five bells are hung together by their ties, so that no one of them is
quite a bell on its own any more.

\textbf{Tortoise:} He has been polishing the rules of it all week. Tell
him the rule.

\textbf{Crab:} There is only one. Nobody rings it. Pull a tassel sharply
and that bell tips on its pad and rings; you would hear that one bell,
and the others would go dull, and the tray is spent for the day.

\textbf{Achilles:} Not even a very small ring?

\textbf{Crab:} There is no such thing as a very small ring. Drink your
tea.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}taking the cup in both hands{]}} It's the
first thing today that's been warmer than I am.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}setting her work-bag against the leg of the
table{]}} Then sit, and let it do its work. The afternoon's long, now;
it gets a little longer every day.

\emph{{[}Achilles sits down by the fire with his cup and puts his
stockinged feet to the fender, beside his boots, which have begun to
dry. Up the lane the tumble from the tower has stopped: the bells are
up, and for a while the tower keeps quiet, and there is only the drip
from the eaves and the small talk of the fire. When his toes are warm he
draws his chair up to the table.{]}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{first-challenge-the-twenty-four}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{First Challenge --- \emph{The
Twenty-Four}}{First Challenge --- The Twenty-Four}}\label{first-challenge-the-twenty-four}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}looking at the model over his cup{]}} How
many ways will it sit in that cradle? Properly sat, I mean, with a tip
in the socket and a tip in every lug.

\textbf{Crab:} Try it and see. Turn it every way you like.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Count before you try. Six tips could be up, and any
of the others in front?

\textbf{Achilles:} Any of the other five. Six times five: thirty.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Then seat me one with the dark green still on top and
the pale green in the front lug.

\emph{{[}Achilles lifts the model clear of the cradle, keeping the dark
green tip upright between his fingers, and looks for the pale green. It
is straight underneath, pointing down at the socket. He turns the model
about its upright line, slowly, all the way round: the dark red comes to
the front, then the pale gold, then the pale red, then the dark gold,
and the dark red again. The pale green does not come round with them.
Whichever way he turns it, the pale green stays pointing at the socket,
opposite the dark green, and to bring it to the front he would have to
tip the dark green off the top.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \ldots Oh. Only the four round the top. The one
opposite the top is always in the socket.

\textbf{Tortoise:} So?

\textbf{Achilles:} Six tips to put up, and then only four of the rest
for the front. Six times four, twenty-four.

\emph{{[}He sets the model back as it came: the dark green up, the dark
red in the front lug, the pale green in the socket.{]}}

\begin{center}
\cradlemodel*{home}{Seated as it came}
\end{center}

\textbf{Crab:} Twenty-four, and I mean to see every one of them this
afternoon, each of them once, and the model home again at the end. You
turn, and I shall call. I have three calls.

\textbf{Achilles:} Only three?

\textbf{Crab:} The daughter says three are plenty. ``Quarter'': lift it
a hair, and turn it a quarter about the up-and-down line, so that the
front tip goes to the right-hand lug and the left tip comes round to the
front. ``Back'': the same the other way, so that the front tip goes to
the left lug and the right tip comes to the front.

\textbf{Tortoise:} And the third?

\textbf{Crab:} ``Over'', which is the one the letter is proudest of.
Take the model by the top tip and the front tip, and give it a half turn
about the middle of the edge between them: those two change places, the
left and right tips change places, and the back and bottom tips change
places.

\textbf{Crab:} And each time you set it down, name the seating: the tip
that is up, and the tip in the front lug. The other four follow from
those two.

\emph{{[}Up the lane the ringers begin again, and now in order: the
tower's bells one after another from the highest to the lowest, a plain
falling scale, and then the same scale, and the same, every stroke in
its place. Achilles sets his cup down on the table, well away from the
tray, and rubs his cold fingers together.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Then here's where it starts.

\textbf{Achilles:} Dark green up, dark red front.

\textbf{Crab:} Quarter.

\emph{{[}The model as it stands: the dark green up, the dark red in the
front lug, the dark gold at the right, the pale red at the back, the
pale gold at the left, the pale green in the socket. Achilles lifts it a
hair clear of the lugs and turns it a quarter about its upright line,
the way a key turns in a lock. The dark green stays on top and the pale
green stays beneath; only the waist goes round. The dark red swings from
the front lug to the right, the dark gold from the right to the back,
the pale red from the back to the left, and the pale gold comes round
from the left into the front. He lowers it, and four tips knock softly
into four lugs. What has changed: which tip sits in which lug round the
waist. What has held: the top, the bottom, and the order of the four
colours round the middle.{]}}

\begin{center}
\cradlemodel[quarter]{home}{Turned about the upright}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Dark green up, pale gold front.

\textbf{Crab:} Quarter again.

\emph{{[}Again the waist goes round a quarter under the unmoving dark
green: the pale gold leaves the front for the right-hand lug, and the
pale red comes round from the left into the front. Knock.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Dark green up, pale red front.

\textbf{Achilles:} And the dark red's gone round to the back, where the
pale red was. Two quarters, and every tip round the middle is where its
opposite stood.

\textbf{Crab:} Quarter.

\emph{{[}The pale red goes to the right; from the left the dark gold
comes into the front. The dark green has not stirred from the top.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Dark green up, dark gold front.

\textbf{Crab:} That is the dark green's four. Now: over.

\emph{{[}The model as it stands: the dark green up, the dark gold in the
front lug, the pale red at the right, the pale gold at the back, the
dark red at the left, the pale green in the socket. Achilles takes it by
the top tip and the front tip, one between the fingers of each hand,
lifts it clear, and turns it a half turn about the middle of the edge
that runs between those two tips, as one turns a pillow over by its
corner. The dark green comes down and forward into the front lug, and
the dark gold goes up to the top. The pale red and the dark red change
sides, right for left. The pale gold at the back swings down into the
socket, and the pale green comes up out of the socket into the back lug.
He sets it down, and it drops into its lugs with one knock. What has
changed: every tip's place, and, for the first time, the top. What has
held: every tip still has its opposite straight across from it, and
every lug has a tip in it.{]}}

\begin{center}
\cradlemodel[over]{Dark green up, dark gold front}{Turned over}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Dark gold up, dark green front.

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}leaning in{]}} By the tips, if you please, not
by the faces. The paint is three weeks old.

\textbf{Achilles:} My hands are still cold from the lane. I'm holding it
like an egg.

\textbf{Crab:} Then it is warming them, and you are warming it, and
everybody is served. Back.

\emph{{[}The model as it stands: the dark gold up, the dark green in the
front lug, the dark red at the right, the pale green at the back, the
pale red at the left, the pale gold in the socket. Achilles lifts it a
hair and turns it a quarter the other way about its upright line: the
dark green goes from the front to the left-hand lug, the pale red from
the left to the back, the pale green from the back to the right, and the
dark red comes from the right into the front. The dark gold on top and
the pale gold beneath do not move. He lowers it; the knock. What has
changed: the waist has gone round the other way. What has held: the top,
the bottom, and the order round the middle, read the other way.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Dark gold up, dark red front.

\textbf{Crab:} Back.

\emph{{[}The dark red goes from the front to the left; from the right
the pale green comes into the front.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Dark gold up, pale green front.

\textbf{Crab:} Back.

\emph{{[}The pale green goes to the left lug, and the pale red comes
round from the right into the front.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Dark gold up, pale red front.

\textbf{Crab:} Over.

\emph{{[}He takes it by the dark gold on top and the pale red in front,
and turns it over by the edge between them: the pale red rises to the
top and the dark gold comes down into the front lug; the dark green and
the pale green change sides; the dark red at the back drops into the
socket, and the pale gold comes up out of the socket into the back lug.
Knock.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Pale red up, dark gold front.

\emph{{[}The Tortoise nudges the sugar bowl across the table to him.
Achilles takes a lump in his fingers; it slips, tumbles across the
saucer, and comes to rest the way a lump always does, square on one of
its faces, though which face, and which way about, nobody could have
said before it fell. He drops it into his tea and licks the sweetness
off his thumb.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Whatever I do to it, it comes down with a tip in
every lug. Never an edge, never a face. The six places are always the
same six places; the only thing that changes is which tip is in each.

\textbf{Crab:} That is what it is to sit. A seating puts a tip where a
tip was. Quarter.

\emph{{[}The waist goes round a quarter under the pale red: the dark
gold goes to the right-hand lug, and the dark green comes round from the
left into the front.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Pale red up, dark green front.

\textbf{Crab:} Quarter.

\emph{{[}The dark green goes to the right, and the pale gold comes round
into the front.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Pale red up, pale gold front.

\textbf{Crab:} Quarter.

\emph{{[}The pale gold goes to the right, and the pale green comes round
from the left into the front. The pale red still points at the
ceiling.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Pale red up, pale green front.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}refilling her cup{]}} Half-way. You're
turning it more gently than you drink tea.

\textbf{Achilles:} It deserves it more. Over?

\textbf{Crab:} Over.

\emph{{[}Top and front change places: the pale red comes down into the
front lug and the pale green goes up. The gold tips change sides, right
for left; the dark green at the back goes down into the socket, and the
dark red comes up out of it to the back. Knock.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Pale green up, pale red front.

\textbf{Crab:} Back.

\emph{{[}The waist goes round the other way under the pale green: the
pale red goes to the left, and the dark gold comes from the right into
the front.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Pale green up, dark gold front.

\textbf{Crab:} Back.

\emph{{[}The dark gold goes to the left, and the dark red comes round
from the right into the front.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Pale green up, dark red front.

\textbf{Crab:} Back.

\emph{{[}The dark red goes to the left, and the pale gold comes from the
right into the front.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Pale green up, pale gold front.

\textbf{Crab:} Over.

\emph{{[}Achilles takes it by the pale green on top and the pale gold in
front and turns it over by their edge: the pale gold goes up and the
pale green comes down into the front; the reds change sides; the dark
gold at the back goes down into the socket, and the dark green comes up
out of it to the back. Knock.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Pale gold up, pale green front.

\textbf{Achilles:} Every tip has had its turn on top except the dark
red. It's been waiting all this while.

\textbf{Crab:} It will have its four. Quarter.

\emph{{[}The pale green goes from the front to the right, and from the
left the pale red comes round into the front.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Pale gold up, pale red front.

\textbf{Crab:} Quarter.

\emph{{[}The pale red goes to the right, and the dark green comes round
into the front.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Pale gold up, dark green front.

\textbf{Crab:} Quarter.

\emph{{[}The dark green goes to the right, and the dark red comes round
from the left into the front.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Pale gold up, dark red front.

\textbf{Crab:} Over.

\emph{{[}Top and front change places once more: the dark red rises to
the top at last and the pale gold comes down into the front lug; the
greens change sides; the pale red at the back goes down into the socket,
and the dark gold comes up out of it into the back lug. Knock.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Dark red up, pale gold front.

\textbf{Crab:} Back.

\emph{{[}The pale gold goes to the left, and from the right the pale
green comes into the front.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Dark red up, pale green front.

\textbf{Crab:} Back.

\emph{{[}The pale green goes to the left, and the dark gold comes into
the front.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Dark red up, dark gold front.

\textbf{Crab:} Back.

\emph{{[}The dark gold goes to the left, and the dark green comes round
from the right into the front.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Dark red up, dark green front.

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}softly{]}} And over.

\emph{{[}The model as it stands: the dark red up, the dark green in the
front lug, the pale gold at the right, the pale green at the back, the
dark gold at the left, the pale red in the socket. Achilles takes it by
the dark red and the dark green and turns it over by the edge between
them: the dark green rises to the top and the dark red comes down into
the front; the dark gold comes across to the right and the pale gold to
the left; the pale green at the back drops into the socket, and the pale
red comes up out of it into the back lug. It knocks into its lugs. Every
tip is where it was when it came out of the straw.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Home again.

\emph{{[}Up the lane the tower is still at its plain falling scale,
stroke after stroke in the same order, just as it was when the Crab made
his first call. The Crab lets out a breath he seems to have been holding
all the while.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} Every seating once, and not one twice. \emph{{[}He puts
his claws together.{]}} The daughter will be pleased with you.

\textbf{Crab:} And the three calls were all it needed. There is no
seating the model has that they cannot reach.

\textbf{Achilles:} But I'd have thought the plainest turns would be
half-turns, straight about one of its own lines. You never called one.

\textbf{Crab:} They are in the twenty-four already. Let me show you.
\emph{{[}He takes the model from the cradle himself, between two careful
claws.{]}}

\emph{{[}The model as it stands, at home: the dark green up, the dark
red in the front lug, the pale red at the back, the dark gold at the
right, the pale gold at the left, the pale green in the socket. The Crab
holds it by the dark red and the pale red, one claw at each, and turns
it a half turn about the line between them, like a spit. The dark red
and the pale red stay where they are, front and back. The dark green
goes down and under into the socket, and the pale green comes up to the
top; the dark gold goes over from the right to the left, and the pale
gold from the left to the right. He sets it down: it sits, a tip in
every lug. What has changed: four tips have gone to the places of their
opposites. What has held: the front and the back, and every line from a
tip to its opposite, which still runs up and down, or front to back, or
side to side.{]}}

\begin{center}
\cradlemodel[a half about the red line]{home}{Turned like a spit}
\end{center}

\textbf{Crab:} A half about the red line.

\textbf{Achilles:} Every tip is either in its own place or in its
opposite's.

\emph{{[}The Crab turns it the same half again about the same line, and
every tip goes back: the dark green to the top, the golds to their own
sides. Home. Then he holds it by the dark green and the pale green and
turns it a half about the up-and-down line: the top and the bottom hold;
the dark red goes to the back and the pale red comes to the front; the
golds change sides. It sits. He turns it the same half again, and it is
home.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} A half about the green line.

\emph{{[}Last, he holds it by the dark gold and the pale gold and turns
it a half about the side-to-side line: the golds hold, right and left;
the dark green goes down into the socket and the pale green comes up;
the dark red goes to the back and the pale red to the front. It sits.
The same half again, and it is home, the dark green up and the dark red
in the front lug.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} And a half about the gold line. Each of them seats it,
and each of them sends every tip to its own place or its opposite's.
Remember the red half and the green half. We shall want them presently.

\emph{{[}Achilles finishes his tea, sweet at the bottom, and the Crab
fills the cup again without being asked. The fire settles in the grate
with a soft collapse, and in the new light from it the tiles round it
show their little ships and flowers, every one of them sitting
square.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}glancing from the model to the bell-tray
beside it{]}} On the bells? Can you turn one of those without the others
knowing?

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{second-challenge-safe-touches}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Second Challenge --- \emph{Safe
Touches}}{Second Challenge --- Safe Touches}}\label{second-challenge-safe-touches}}

\textbf{Crab:} Not freely. The old man hung the five bells even, and
then knotted on the ties one by one; each tie gives the bell at one end
a green half whenever the bell at the other end is lit. So no bell on
that tray is a bell by itself any more. Turn one, and the ties tell the
others.

\emph{{[}From the church the falling scale breaks into changes: at every
stroke two of the bells, side by side in the order, trade places, so
that no order comes twice running. Achilles glances up at the window. On
the table, a yard from the glass, the tray's bells do not so much as
stir.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} And ringing it spoils the lot.

\textbf{Crab:} Ringing spoils the lot. But there are touches it does not
notice. \emph{{[}From his waistcoat pocket he takes a small painted tin,
opens it, and sets it on the table beside him.{]}} These are my clips.
Each snaps onto one of the brass rings on the pulls, and each is red or
green, with a little bead set at a half, a quarter round or a quarter
back; a clipped ring takes its clip's colour and its turn, and not a
cord is changed. Two clips of one colour on a ring add their turns, and
two colours on one ring I never allow.

\textbf{Achilles:} So a red clip at a half does to its bell what your
half about the red line did to the model.

\textbf{Crab:} Just so. Now watch. Here is a touch the tray will not
notice.

\emph{{[}The tray as it stands: five bells on their pads, the ties in
their sleeves, every pull hanging in its two lengths from bell to brass
ring to tassel, and every brass ring bare. The Crab takes a red clip at
a half from the tin, its bead at the bottom as Achilles sees it,
half-way round from the top, where a bead at rest would stand, and snaps
it onto the knot's brass ring, where the knot's pull crosses the front
of the tray. Then a green clip at a half onto the left-back bell's ring;
a green half onto the left-front's; a green half onto the right-back's;
a green half onto the right-front's. Each snaps on with a tiny click,
and each time the ring it grips takes its colour. Not a cord has moved:
every tie lies where it lay, every inner and outer length hangs as it
hung, every bell sits still on its pad. What has changed: every brass
ring on the tray now wears a clip, red at the knot and green on all four
wings.{]}}

\begin{center}
\belltray*{the knot's touch}{Every ring clipped}
\end{center}

\emph{{[}At every click the bells have shivered on their pads, without a
sound, and settled again as his claw moved on to the next. The Crab does
not so much as glance at them.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} The safe touch at the knot: a red half on the knot's own
ring, and a green half on the ring of every bell tied to it. Nothing
else.

\textbf{Achilles:} Nothing else! You've changed every ring on the tray.
It must have noticed.

\textbf{Achilles:} Let me ask it. One little pull on the knot's
tassel\ldots{}

\emph{{[}He reaches for the tassel of the knot's pull, where it hangs
over the front rim.{]}}

\emph{{[}As his fingers come near it, the five bells shiver on their
pads, all of them at once, the way a cup shivers in its saucer when a
cart goes by in the lane. There is no sound in it at all.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}catching his wrist, gently{]}} Not the tassel.
That is not a question, it is a ring; you would hear the knot, and the
others would go dull, and the tray would be spent till tomorrow.
\emph{{[}He lets go.{]}} I have wanted to pull that tassel myself every
day since it came. I have not. Ask it any other way you like.

\emph{{[}Achilles, a little pink about the ears, puts both hands back
round his cup, where they can do no harm. On the tray the bells settle
on their pads and are still, and not one of them has made a sound.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Then we'll ask a picture instead. \emph{{[}She lifts
her drawing-cloth out of the work-bag and spreads it on the table beside
the tray, at its right as Achilles sees it, the cloth's near edge on his
side and the teapot just off that edge at its right-hand end, then
brings out string, a little box of rings with their beads, and her
yellow tubes.{]}} My drawing-cloth, and my rings and tubes, as ever:
what I lay on it is a picture of a thing, not the thing.

\emph{{[}She lays five green rings on the drawing-cloth, each bead at
rest, at the top of its ring as Achilles sees it, where a turn starts
and goes round clockwise, in the tray's pattern: one in the middle, one
near each corner. She ties the middle ring to each of the four corner
rings with string, and the two left rings to each other, and the two
right rings to each other, threading a yellow tube onto each length of
string before she knots its second end, and sliding it to the middle of
its tie. From each ring she runs a short loose cord out towards the edge
of the cloth: from the two left rings out to the left, from the two
right rings out to the right, and from the middle ring straight towards
the near edge.{]}}

\begin{center}
\bowcloth*{bare}{The net laid out}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Your tray, drawn. Now the same touch. \emph{{[}On the
knot ring's loose cord she threads a red ring from its free end and sets
its bead at a half; on each of the four corner rings' loose cords she
threads a green ring at a half.{]}}

\begin{center}
\bowcloth{the knot's touch}{Threaded for the knot}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Three rules you know. Two rings of one colour joined
by a cord slide together into one, and their beads add; a half and a
half make a whole turn, which is no turn at all, and leave the ring at
rest. A ring at rest with only two cords is just cord. And a ring with
two cords, pushed through a yellow tube, comes out the other colour with
its bead unchanged.

\textbf{Achilles:} Those I know. And one I don't?

\textbf{Tortoise:} A red ring at a half, pushed into a green ring at
rest, is gone from its cord and comes out as a red ring at a half on
every other cord of that ring. The green ring stays at rest, and nothing
is set aside. Only into a ring at rest.

\textbf{Achilles:} Why all of them at once?

\textbf{Tortoise:} A ring at rest keeps all its cords alike, all dark or
all lit. Turn one over, and you have turned them all.

\emph{{[}The picture as it stands: the knot ring green at rest in the
middle, tied to every corner ring, with a red ring at a half on its
loose cord; each corner ring green at rest, with a green ring at a half
on its own loose cord. The Tortoise puts one claw behind the red ring
and pushes it up its loose cord into the knot ring. It is gone from the
loose cord, which lies bare. On each of the knot ring's ties, just
beside it, a red ring at a half now sits; the knot ring itself is still
at rest. She pushes each of them out along its tie. Each reaches its
tube and passes through it, and comes out on the far side green, its
bead still at a half. Each slides on into the corner ring at the end of
its tie, and that ring is at a half now; and the green half waiting on
the corner ring's own loose cord slides in after it: a half and a half,
a whole turn. The bead comes round to rest. At all four corners the
same. What lies on the cloth now: five green rings at rest, the same
ties with the same tubes, every loose cord bare, and nothing set aside.
What has changed: every piece of the touch is gone. What has held:
everything else, exactly as she laid it.{]}}

\begin{center}
\bowcloth[push]{the knot's touch}{Every piece gone}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} It's the net you laid. Not a thing set aside.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Your tray, touched at the knot, is the one I drew.
And it has come out your tray untouched.

\textbf{Achilles:} Let me follow it my way, without a cloth. The knot
was hung even, and turning an even bell over leaves it even; all the red
half does is swap the knot's dark settings for its lit ones. But each
tie gives its far bell a green half whenever the knot is lit, so after
the swap each far bell gets that half exactly where it didn't before and
misses it where it did: one extra green half, everywhere. Your green
halves on the wing rings take those back.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The same answer, and not a cord of mine in it.

\textbf{Achilles:} So what you're saying is the touch did nothing at
all.

\textbf{Tortoise:} It did something to every ring. It did nothing to the
tray.

\emph{{[}Outside the window, at the corner of the house, the water-butt
stands full to the brim. The spout from the gutter pours the thaw into
it at one side, and at the other side it spills out over the top as fast
as it comes in, and the water in the butt has not risen or fallen by a
hair all afternoon.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} And a corner bell? The left-back's touch?

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}threading a red ring at a half on the
left-back ring's loose cord, and a green ring at a half on the loose
cords of the left-front ring and the knot{]}} A red half on its own
cord, and a green half on the cord of every ring tied to it: the
left-front and the knot. Nothing on the right.

\emph{{[}She pushes the red half up into the left-back ring. It comes
out on that ring's ties, one towards the left-front ring and one towards
the knot; each passes its tube and turns green at a half; each slides
into the ring at the end of its tie and meets the green half on that
ring's own loose cord, and the two make a whole turn. The right wing has
not been touched at all. The cloth is as she laid it.{]}}

\emph{{[}The Crab has found the paper of spiced biscuits that came
packed in the straw, and passes it round. Achilles takes one and eats it
in two bites without taking his eyes off the cloth; the Tortoise takes
two, and sets one by her saucer for later.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Fewer ties this time, and the right wing left alone.
And gone again.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then two at once. The left-back's touch and the
right-back's, on your tray, Mr Crab.

\textbf{Crab:} On my tray, then.

\emph{{[}The Crab unclips the knot's touch, ring by ring, and drops each
clip back in the tin; the brass rings are bare again, and nothing else
on the tray has stirred. Then he clips on the left-back's touch: a red
half on the left-back's ring, a green half on the left-front's, a green
half on the knot's. And the right-back's: a red half on the right-back's
ring, a green half on the right-front's, and a second green half on the
knot's ring, beside the first. The knot's ring now wears two green
halves: a half and a half, a whole turn, no turn. He takes them both off
again, and the knot's ring hangs bare. What is left: a red half on each
back bell's ring, a green half on each front bell's ring, and the knot
at rest.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} So the knot's left out of it altogether.

\textbf{Crab:} A touch and a touch is a touch.

\textbf{Crab:} And here is the thing the old man told me, the first day.
If you know every touch a tray will not notice, you know the tray. Only
one tray sits still for all of them.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then the tray is its touches.

\textbf{Crab:} It is known by them. \emph{{[}He unclips the four clips
and drops them in the tin, and the brass rings hang bare.{]}}

\emph{{[}The Tortoise takes the tin from beside him, opens it, and holds
up two small clips, one red and one green, their beads set at a
quarter.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} And half of a touch?

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{third-challenge-half-a-touch}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Third Challenge --- \emph{Half a
Touch}}{Third Challenge --- Half a Touch}}\label{third-challenge-half-a-touch}}

\textbf{Crab:} Half a touch. \emph{{[}He takes the quarter clips from
her, and a second green one from the tin.{]}} The left-back again, but
in quarters.

\emph{{[}The tray as it stands: every brass ring bare. The Crab snaps a
red clip, its bead a quarter round, at the right as Achilles sees it,
onto the left-back bell's ring, and a green clip, a quarter back, its
bead at the left, onto the left-front bell's ring, and another green
quarter back onto the knot's. Three small clicks. The right wing's rings
stay bare. No cord moves; no bell stirs on its pad. What has changed:
three rings wear quarter clips. What has held: every tie, every length,
every bell.{]}}

\begin{center}
\belltray{half the left-back's touch}{Red round, green back}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}bending close to the tray{]}} The cords are
all where they were. Every tie in its sleeve, every pull hanging just as
it hung. It's the same tray with three clips on.

\textbf{Tortoise:} It has noticed, this time. It isn't the same tray.
The left-front bell and the knot are no longer tied.

\textbf{Achilles:} The tie is right there, sleeve and all!

\textbf{Tortoise:} On the tray. Not in the net. Here is a rule I'll give
you without the working: a red ring a quarter round on a bell's loose
cord, and a green ring a quarter back on the loose cord of each bell
tied to it, or all of them the other way round, may be taken off, if the
bells tied to it are re-tied among themselves. Every two of them that
were tied are untied, and every two that were not are tied.

\textbf{Achilles:} And nothing else changes?

\textbf{Tortoise:} A tie gained or lost moves the picture's number, and
I keep that to one side, as ever.

\emph{{[}The cloth net as it stands: five green rings at rest in the bow
tie, the ties in their tubes, the loose cords bare. On the left-back
ring's loose cord the Tortoise threads a red ring a quarter round; on
the left-front ring's and the knot's, a green ring a quarter back each.
The left-back ring is tied to two rings, the left-front and the knot,
and those two are tied to each other. She unknots that tie, the one
between the left-front ring and the knot, draws its tube off, and lays
the tie at the near edge of the drawing-cloth, at its left, and the tube
just beyond the tie's right-hand end. Then she takes the three quarter
rings off their loose cords by their free ends, back into her box of
rings, and sets a small bone counter from her work-bag to one side, off
the cloth just beyond its near edge at the right-hand end, by the
teapot. What lies on the cloth now: the left-back ring tied to the
left-front ring and to the knot, but the left-front ring and the knot no
longer tied to each other; the left wing opened from a triangle into a
vee. The right wing as it was. Every ring at rest, every loose cord
bare; and at the near edge, the tie and its tube.{]}}

\begin{center}
\bowcloth[re-tie at the left-back]{half the left-back's touch}{A vee on the left}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} So the tray has every one of its cords, and the net
you've drawn for it has lost one. \emph{{[}He looks from the cloth to
the tray, and back.{]}} The cords don't tell you which tray you have.

\textbf{Tortoise:} They tell you what was knotted. The clips tell you
the rest.

\emph{{[}In the lane below the window, a puddle that froze in the night
still wears its lid of ice, white and whole, the same to look at as it
was at breakfast. A blackbird drops onto it, and the lid tips under him
like a loose tile: the water it was frozen fast to has drained away
underneath in the thaw, and it is fastened to nothing. The bird is off
again in a flurry, and the lid settles, white and whole.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} Then let me give it the other half. \emph{{[}He takes
three more quarter clips from the tin.{]}}

\emph{{[}The Crab snaps a second red quarter round onto the left-back's
ring, beside the first, at its left as Achilles sees it: two quarters
round, a half. A second green quarter back onto the left-front's ring:
two quarters back, which is a half back, and a half back is the same as
a half. The same on the knot's ring. The rings now carry a red half on
the left-back and a green half on the left-front and the knot: the
left-back bell's whole touch.{]}}

\begin{center}
\belltray{half the left-back's touch; half the left-back's touch}{Made whole}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} The left-back's safe touch. The one the tray doesn't
notice.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Then my net had better not notice either. \emph{{[}On
the left-back ring's loose cord she threads a red ring a quarter round
again, and on the left-front ring's and the knot's a green ring a
quarter back.{]}} Half a touch again, on the net as it stands now.

\emph{{[}The cloth as it stands: the left wing a vee, the left-front
ring and the knot not tied, and the three quarter rings on their loose
cords; at the near edge, the tie and its tube. The rings tied to the
left-back are still the left-front and the knot, and now they are not
tied to each other; so they must be. The Tortoise takes up the tie and
the tube from the near edge of the cloth, slides the tube back on over a
free end of the tie, and knots the tie between the left-front ring and
the knot, just where it was. She takes the three quarter rings off by
the free ends, back into her box, and takes the counter back from beside
the teapot into her work-bag. What lies on the cloth now: the bow tie,
every tie in its tube, every ring at rest, every loose cord bare. What
has changed since the first half: one tie, back. What has held, from the
start of the afternoon to now: the net.{]}}

\begin{center}
\bowcloth[re-tie at the left-back, half the left-back's touch, re-tie at the left-back]{half the left-back's touch}{Back to the bow}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} A tie lost moved the number one way, and a tie gained
moves it back. Two halves of a touch make a touch, and two re-tyings
make no change.

\textbf{Achilles:} And at the knot? Half the knot's touch?

\textbf{Crab:} Ah, at the knot the quarters would do a great deal more.
\emph{{[}He does not reach for the tin.{]}} Each wing's two bells would
come untied from each other, and each wing bell would be tied across to
both the bells of the other wing.

\textbf{Achilles:} A different shape altogether. And not a cord on the
tray moved.

\emph{{[}The changes from the tower go on, the same bells and the same
notes, in a new order at every stroke. Achilles, listening idly, tries
to keep one bell in his head from one stroke to the next, loses it by
the third, and gives it up with a laugh under his breath.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}drawing himself up a little{]}} I will tell you
what I have found, in all the years I have been buying from that bench.
Anything the workshop could make me out of quarters and halves turns out
to be a tray of bells: each bell seated one of the twenty-four ways, and
the bells tied, or re-tied.

\textbf{Tortoise:} And re-tie at one bell, then at a bell tied to it,
then at the first again, and the two change places in the net. Three
re-tyings in a row.

\emph{{[}The Crab unclips the six quarter clips from the three rings and
drops them back in the tin. The brass rings hang bare.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Then how do you keep track of which tray you have, if
the cords won't tell you?

\emph{{[}The Crab is already reaching into the dresser drawer.{]}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{fourth-challenge-the-crabs-ledger}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Fourth Challenge --- \emph{The Crab's
Ledger}}{Fourth Challenge --- The Crab's Ledger}}\label{fourth-challenge-the-crabs-ledger}}

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}laying a narrow bound book on the table at his
own place, at Achilles's left on the same side of the table, between the
model's stand and the window end, and opening it flat{]}} With this. My
ledger for the tray: one row for each bell, and in every row one cell
for each bell and one more for the sign. A cell holds nothing, or red,
or green, or gold, which is red and green together; the sign is plain,
or turned over. I keep a ledger for everything, but this is the one I am
proudest of, because it is so small.

\emph{{[}The page as it stands, upright to the Crab and to Achilles
beside him: five ruled rows, empty, headed at the side with the five
bells' names, and across the top the same five names and a narrow column
for the sign. The Crab dips his pen, red ink or green as each cell
needs, and fills each cell he marks with a wash of its colour. In the
left-back's row he writes red in the left-back's own cell and green
under the left-front and the knot, and leaves the right-back and the
right-front empty; the sign cell he leaves blank, which is plain; a sign
turned over would get a small inked square. In the left-front's row,
green under the left-back, red in its own cell, green under the knot. In
the knot's row, green under the left-back and the left-front, red in its
own cell, green under the right-back and the right-front. In the
right-back's row, green under the knot, red in its own cell, green under
the right-front; in the right-front's row, green under the knot and the
right-back, and red in its own cell; the left wing's cells empty in
