both. Every sign is plain. What has changed: the page has five full
rows. What has held: the tray; he has not touched it.{]}}

\begin{center}
\trayledger*{the tray's rows}{The tray's rows}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Red in its own cell, and green for every bell tied to
it. \emph{{[}He looks at the tin.{]}} Those are the touches! Every row
is a safe touch.

\textbf{Crab:} Of course they are. A tray is known by the touches it
does not notice, so I write those down, and nothing else.

\textbf{Achilles:} And when you turn a bell? Do you have to write it all
out again?

\textbf{Crab:} One column. Suppose I gave the knot an over, on paper
only. An over swaps red and green in that bell's column, leaves gold as
gold, and turns over the sign of every row that has gold there.

\emph{{[}The knot's column as it stands, reading down the five rows:
green, green, red, green, green. The Crab rules a line under the page
and writes the rows again below it, copying every other column exactly
as it was, and in the knot's column writing each mark swapped: red, red,
green, red, red. There is no gold in that column, so no sign turns over.
What has changed: one column, red for green and green for red. What has
held: every other cell, and every sign.{]}}

\begin{center}
\trayledger[an over on the knot]{the tray's rows}{The knot's column swapped}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Now let me count. Each cell is red or not, and green
or not: two marks a cell. Five cells and a sign: eleven marks a row,
fifty-five for the tray.

\textbf{Achilles:} And the tray's own numbers, one for every way the
five bells could read dark or lit, are thirty-two. You aren't saving
much.

\textbf{Crab:} Not with five. With a hundred bells, twenty thousand one
hundred marks, against a count thirty-one digits long.

\textbf{Achilles:} \ldots Oh.

\textbf{Achilles:} Not a count of numbers. A count thirty-one digits
long, just to say how many.

\textbf{Crab:} And twenty thousand one hundred marks fit in a ledger I
could carry to church.

\emph{{[}Up at the church the changes have been going long enough now to
have a shape one can hear: one bell working its way steadily down
through the others to the first place, and up through them again to the
last, and the rest stepping aside for it one after another. Not a ringer
in the tower has the whole of it written out. Each of them has a few
words by heart, and follows them, stroke by stroke. The Crab sits back
from his ledger and looks as though he could listen all day.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} The ledger follows the tray on paper. My cloth can
follow it another way. \emph{{[}From her little box of rings she takes
five green end-rings, each bead set a quarter round.{]}} End-rings: they
close a loose cord. Close every loose cord of a picture and it has no
ends left, and a picture with no ends is a single number: here, the
tray's answer to these five caps.

\textbf{Achilles:} And you find the number without writing one of the
thirty-two?

\textbf{Tortoise:} With one more rule. A ring in the middle, with no
loose cord and its bead a quarter round, can be pulled out: the rings
tied to it are re-tied among themselves, as before, and each of them is
turned a quarter back. And a lone ring, with no cord at all, is a
number: at rest, two; a quarter round, one and one turned a quarter; a
quarter back, one and one turned a quarter back; a half, nothing at all.

\emph{{[}The cloth net as it stands: the bow tie, every ring at rest,
every loose cord bare. The Tortoise caps each loose cord with a green
end-ring a quarter round, and each end-ring, joined to its ring by the
loose cord, slides along it into the ring, the loose cord swallowed with
it: a quarter round and at rest make a quarter round. Now every ring is
a quarter round, and not one has a loose cord.{]}}

\begin{center}
\bowcloth[cap every loose cord]{bare}{No loose end left}
\end{center}

\emph{{[}She takes hold of the left-back ring. It is tied to the
left-front ring and to the knot, and those two are tied to each other.
She unknots the left-back ring's ties at the left-front ring and at the
knot, lifts the left-back ring out with them and their tubes, and drops
the lot into her work-bag; unknots the tie between the left-front ring
and the knot and drops that, with its tube, into the bag too; turns the
left-front ring's bead a quarter back, from a quarter round to rest, and
the knot's the same, from a quarter round to rest; and sets a counter by
the teapot. The left-front ring lies at rest, tied to nothing now: a
lone ring. The knot, at rest, is still tied to the right wing.{]}}

\emph{{[}Then the right-back ring, a quarter round, tied to the knot and
to the right-front ring, which are tied to each other. She unknots its
ties at the knot and at the right-front ring and lifts it out with them
and their tubes into her work-bag; unknots the tie between the knot and
the right-front ring and drops that, with its tube, in after it; turns
each of those two a quarter back, the knot from rest to a quarter back,
the right-front from a quarter round to rest; and sets a second counter
by the teapot, on the first. What lies on the cloth now: three lone
rings, far apart, not a cord between them: the left-front ring at rest,
the knot a quarter back, the right-front ring at rest. What has changed:
the net is gone, and the picture is smaller than it has ever been. What
has held: the number it stands for, with what lies by the teapot.{]}}

\begin{center}
\bowcloth[cap every loose cord, pull out the left-back, pull out the right-back]{bare}{Pulled out to the last}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Nothing left but lone rings, and each of them is a
number. Put them together with what I set aside, and that's the tray's
answer.

\emph{{[}Across the lane, the snowman the children built on the first
morning of the frost has been going all afternoon. He is a single low
heap now, sunk into the slush, and round him on the wet ground lie the
things that made him, two coals and his buttons, each by itself. The
Tortoise sits back and reaches for the biscuit she saved.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Three lone rings and a little heap by the teapot. And
not one of the thirty-two numbers written down.

\textbf{Achilles:} So what you're saying is that anything built this way
can be followed on paper, and the machine is no better than paper.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Anything built of quarters and halves.

\textbf{Achilles:} And a turn that is neither a quarter nor a half?

\emph{{[}The Crab looks at the model, sitting at home in its cradle.{]}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{fifth-challenge-an-eighth}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Fifth Challenge --- \emph{An
Eighth}}{Fifth Challenge --- An Eighth}}\label{fifth-challenge-an-eighth}}

\emph{{[}The Tortoise sweeps the three lone rings into her work-bag, and
the two counters from beside the teapot after them, and lays two fresh
cords on the drawing-cloth, one above the other, the upper further from
Achilles, each running from his left to his right.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}nodding at the model{]}} An eighth.

\emph{{[}The model as it stands, at home: the dark green up, the dark
red in the front lug, the dark gold at the right, the pale red at the
back, the pale gold at the left, the pale green in the socket. Achilles
lifts it a hair and turns it about its upright line the way of a
quarter, but stops half-way. The dark red has gone only half-way from
the front lug to the right; the pale gold has come only half-way from
the left to the front. He lowers it. The pale green finds the socket.
But at the waist no lug meets a tip: each lug meets the edge between two
tips, and the model settles crooked on its notches. When he takes his
fingers away it rocks, and rocks again. What has changed: every lug has
lost its tip. What has held: the top, the bottom, and the order of the
colours round the middle; nothing else.{]}}

\begin{center}
\cradlemodel[an eighth]{home}{Rocking, crooked}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} It won't sit. The front lug has an edge in it,
between the dark red and the pale gold.

\textbf{Achilles:} I can't name it. It isn't one seating or another;
it's in between two of them.

\emph{{[}Achilles looks up from the rocking model to the print on the
wall: Escher's \textup{Stars}.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Many-sided solids hanging in a dark space. That is
how it sits now: hanging, held by no lug.

\emph{{[}A rook goes over the lane, low, and its shadow runs in at the
window, down the length of the room and across the glass of the print,
and for that moment the dark inside the frame is the darkest thing in
the parlour. Then the shadow is off the end wall, and it is a print
again.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}sliding the ledger along the table to Achilles,
its page upright to him as before{]}} And my ledger has no mark for
between. Nothing, red, green, gold: that is all a cell can say.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Nor has my cloth. Put a ring turned an eighth in the
middle of a net, and no rule I have will pull it out; the pulling needs
a quarter.

\emph{{[}The passage door has stood a little open since Achilles came
in. A draught finds it now and swings it to, and its latch comes to rest
on the lip of the keep, not in it, so that the door stands neither open
nor shut, stirring a little in its frame. Nobody gets up to see to
it.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Then give it another. \emph{{[}He takes hold of the
model again.{]}}

\emph{{[}The model as it stands: rocking, every lug on an edge. Achilles
turns it on, the same way, by the same small amount. The dark red comes
the rest of the way into the right-hand lug, and the pale gold the rest
of the way into the front; the tips at the back and the left follow. The
model drops into its lugs with a knock, and stops rocking. What has
changed: it is seated. What has held: the dark green on top, the pale
green beneath. It sits a quarter round from where it started, exactly as
if the Crab had called one quarter.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Seated. Two eighths make a quarter.

\emph{{[}Another breath of the draught, no stronger than the first, and
the door's latch goes over the lip and drops into its keep with a small
click. The door is shut, and the warmth of the fire gathers in the
room.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Then clip an eighth on a bell. Is there one in your
tin?

\textbf{Crab:} There is not. The tin has halves and quarters, and
nothing finer; the tray was built for them. \emph{{[}He goes to the
dresser, and comes back with a small lidded box, and sets it down by the
Tortoise.{]}} But the bench can do what the cradle can't. These are
eighth-ends, made ahead of time in the workshop, slowly: green end-rings
with the bead set at an eighth. Each one is used up the moment it is
tied on.

\emph{{[}He lifts the lid. Inside, on cotton wool, lie a few small green
end-rings, each bead set at an eighth.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Used up how?

\textbf{Tortoise:} Let me show you on the cloth. \emph{{[}She takes one
eighth-end from the box.{]}} The upper cord is any cord you like, set
however you like; the lower cord begins at this eighth-end. And between
them my joiner, as before: a green ring on the upper cord, tied by a
short length to a red ring on the lower. Then I read the lower cord at
its far end, and it reads dark or lit, half the time each; I don't
choose which.

\emph{{[}She threads a green ring on the upper cord and a red ring on
the lower, just across from it, and ties them together with a short
length. On the left end of the lower cord she ties the eighth-end.{]}}

\begin{center}
\eighthcloth*{the eighth-end}{The joiner, ready}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} If it reads dark, I close the far end with a red
end-ring at rest.

\emph{{[}The cloth as it stands: the upper cord with its green joiner
ring; the lower cord running from the eighth-end, through the red joiner
ring, to a red end-ring at rest. The Tortoise slides the red end-ring
along into the red joiner ring, the stretch of lower cord it runs along
swallowed with it: both red, both at rest, and they are one red ring at
rest, with only two cords left to it, the one back to the eighth-end and
the short length up to the green ring. A ring at rest with two cords is
just cord; she lifts the red ring away into her box of rings, knotting
the two cords it held end to end, and the eighth-end is tied straight to
the green ring on the upper cord. It slides along its cord and the short
length into that ring, both swallowed with it. What lies on the cloth
now: the upper cord alone, and on it one green ring with its bead at an
eighth. What has changed: the lower cord is gone, and the upper cord
carries the eighth. What has held: everything else on the upper
cord.{]}}

\begin{center}
\eighthcloth[the dark reading]{the eighth-end}{Carried up}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Dark: the eighth is on, the right way round.

\textbf{Achilles:} And lit?

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}clearing the drawing-cloth into her
work-bag, all but the green ring that took the eighth, which she slips
off the end of the upper cord and sets by the box; then laying the two
cords and the joiner out again as they were, with a second eighth-end
from the box at the head of the lower cord{]}} A fresh eighth-end first;
that one is spent. Lit, I close the far end with a red end-ring at a
half. And one old rule: a red half pushed into a green ring turns its
bead the other way round, and sets a little something aside.

\emph{{[}The cloth as it stands: the same, but with a red end-ring at a
half at the far end of the lower cord. It slides along the lower cord
into the red joiner ring, the stretch it runs along swallowed with it,
and the joiner ring is red at a half, with two cords, between the
eighth-end and the green ring above. The Tortoise slides the eighth-end
along the lower cord up to the red half, the stretch between swallowed,
and pushes the red half into it: the red half is gone, and the
eighth-end's bead is turned the other way round, an eighth back; a
counter goes by the teapot. The eighth-end, an eighth back now, slides
up the short length into the green ring on the upper cord, the short
length swallowed with it. Then she threads a green ring a quarter round
on the upper cord from its right-hand end, to lie beside it at its
right, and slides it in: a quarter round and an eighth back make an
eighth. What has changed: the lower cord gone again, and the upper cord
carrying an eighth. What has held: the rest of the upper cord. And the
eighth on it faces the same way as in the dark reading, once the quarter
is in.{]}}

\begin{center}
\eighthcloth[the lit reading]{the eighth-end}{Carried up again}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Lit: it went on the wrong way round, and a quarter
set it right. We have quarters in plenty. Either way, the eighth-end is
spent.

\emph{{[}The Crab rises and takes the two spent eighth-ends, the green
ring that took the eighth from the end of the upper cord and the first
from beside the box, turns them once in his claws, and drops them into
his waistcoat pocket.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} Keepsakes.

\emph{{[}He pats the pocket once, as a man pats a pocket with a letter
in it. The fire has burnt low while nobody was looking; the Crab takes a
block of applewood from the basket, split and dried last summer, and
lays it on the coals, and it catches at once and fills the room with its
smell.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} So here is the afternoon. The twenty-four seatings on
every bell, and the ties between the bells, make a whole world.
Everything in it can be followed with your ledger, or shrunk on my cloth
to a number. One eighth leaves it. And with eighth-ends brought in from
outside, anything at all can be built.

\textbf{Crab:} That is what the old man says. The bench makes the
eighths, slowly, and after that it is all clips.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}looking at the model, a quarter round from
home{]}} Then let me put this one back where it belongs. \emph{{[}He
takes it by the tips.{]}}

\emph{{[}The model as it stands: the dark green up, the pale gold in the
front lug, the dark red at the right. Achilles lifts it and turns it a
quarter the other way: the pale gold goes back to the left lug, and the
dark red comes back from the right into the front. It drops in with a
knock: the dark green up, the dark red in front, home, as it came out of
the straw.{]}}

\emph{{[}At the same moment, up the lane, the changes from the tower
return to the plain falling scale, highest to lowest, every bell in the
place it started from. The ringers ring it again, and again, plain and
settled.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} Thank you. \emph{{[}He lays the green baize back over the
bell-tray, corner to corner, and carries the clip tin, the box of
eighth-ends and the ledger, shut, to the dresser.{]}}

\emph{{[}The falling scale sounds a last time, and then the tower's
bells stop one after another, each left standing where the ringers set
it, and the tower goes quiet. The quiet comes down the lane and in at
the window, and the applewood can be heard again, ticking in the
grate.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}putting the upper cord, the counter from
beside the teapot, her string, her tubes and her little box of rings
into her work-bag, and folding her cloth{]}} Your tray stayed quiet all
afternoon.

\textbf{Crab:} It always does, in good company. More tea? There is a cup
left in the pot, and it has been listening.

\textbf{Achilles:} Half, then, and you have the other half.

\textbf{Crab:} A half and a half. I shall be careful not to make a whole
turn of it.

\emph{{[}He pours with great care, a little into each cup, and shakes
the last drop into his own. Achilles holds his cup in both hands again,
though his hands are warm now, and the Tortoise settles deeper into her
chair by the fire.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Listen. The eaves are still going.

\textbf{Achilles:} It'll be dripping till midnight.

\emph{{[}Up the lane, the church clock begins to strike, and strikes
four.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Four, and still light. The days are getting longer.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}looking at the model in its cradle{]}} So
everything inside is paper. Only the eighths cost anything.

\textbf{Crab:} Come to the kitchen tomorrow. I have a long picture that
wants cooking down, and I should like to see how few eighths are left in
it at the end.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then what exactly is it that separates the machines
paper can follow from the ones it can't? And how few eighths does a
machine really need?

\textbf{Tortoise:} Inside the world of quarters, nothing is hard. Count
the eighths.

\emph{{[}Nobody answers her yet. The sun has gone down behind the roofs
across the lane, and the long pale light of the thaw lies in the window,
with the fire's warmer light across the hearth and its blue-and-white
tiles, every one of them square in its place. Under the green baize the
tray stands as the Crab covered it, its five bells on their pads and
every cord of it knotted where the old man knotted it; beside it the
model sits in its cradle. The passage door is shut. At the far end of
the room the print hangs on the end wall in its plain black frame, gone
grey with the rest of the wall, one more of the Crab's things. Up the
lane the tower is silent, and only the eaves go on, a drop, and another,
into the slush on the sill. Achilles's scarf lies folded over the back
of his chair, his boots stand dry by the fender, and the three of them
sit a while longer with their cups, in no hurry at all.{]}}

\hypertarget{chapter-16-inside-the-clifford-world}{%
\chapter{Chapter 16: Inside the Clifford
World}\label{chapter-16-inside-the-clifford-world}}

\emph{--- Twenty-Four Preludes and a T ---}

\emph{Part V: Engineering the Diagram}

\emph{Escher: ``Stars'' --- many-sided solids hanging in a dark space}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

Can a machine be thoroughly quantum, entangling everything it touches,
and still be followed step by step by someone with a pencil and a
notebook?

It sounds impossible. We have spent fifteen chapters learning that a
quantum state is expensive to write down. Five small quantum systems
need thirty-two numbers. A hundred need a list of numbers whose length
is itself a number with thirty-one digits, and no notebook that could
ever be built would hold it. Entanglement makes it worse, not better: an
entangled state cannot be written as one short list per system, because
the whole is not the parts. This is why nobody simulates a large quantum
computer on an ordinary one, and why anyone bothers to build one.

And yet there is a large family of quantum machines that a notebook can
follow with ease. They entangle freely. They run the protocols of the
earlier chapters: the Bell pairs of Chapter 6, the teleportation of
Chapter 10, the key-sharing of Chapter 12. Their states can be spread
over a hundred systems or a thousand. A careful clerk with a ruled book,
writing a few marks per system, can say at every moment exactly what the
machine holds and exactly what the odds of every reading are. The trick
is not to write down the state. It is to write down the tests the state
passes: the touches it would not notice.

Which machines are these? The answer is surprisingly small and
surprisingly geometric. They are the machines built from a handful of
moves: turns by a quarter and by a half. On one wire those moves make
twenty-four positions, the ways a many-sided wooden solid can sit in a
stand. On many wires they make a world, closed and complete, in which
nothing is hard.

One move leads out of that world: a turn by an eighth. It looks like a
small thing, one angle halved again. It is the whole difference between
a machine a clerk can follow and a machine nobody can. This chapter
walks round the inside of the world of quarters and halves, learns to
follow it on paper and to shrink its pictures to numbers, and then turns
the eighth that leaves it.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-twenty-four}{%
\section{§16.1 The Twenty-Four}\label{the-twenty-four}}

Chapter 15 ended at the edge of this chapter. ``Everything in The Second
Drawer is a quarter-turn or a half-turn, and the eight-drawer turn-about
needed an eighth. That looks like a small difference, one angle
halved.'' The chapter's question, in the form we can answer:
\textbf{what separates the pictures built only of quarter-turns and
half-turns from the pictures that need an eighth, and why does that
difference matter so much?}

We answer it in five steps. This section meets the quarters and halves
on one wire. The next four put them on many wires, show what they leave
unnoticed, follow them on paper and in pictures, and then turn the
eighth.

\textbf{On the blackboard.} The bit-flip \(X\) and the phase-flip \(Z\)
have been with us since the early chapters. Add their product, turned by
\(i\): \[Y\;=\;iXZ\;=\;\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix}.\]
Gottesman writes the same relation as \(\sigma_y=i\sigma_x\sigma_z\)
(his eq. (5)). The four matrices \(I,X,Y,Z\) satisfy \(X^2=Y^2=Z^2=I\),
and any two of \(X,Y,Z\) \textbf{anticommute}: \(XZ=-ZX\), and likewise
for the other pairs. Their products stay in the family up to a factor:
\(XY=iZ\), \(YZ=iX\), \(ZX=iY\).

A \textbf{Pauli string} on \(n\) wires is a tensor product of \(n\) of
these four letters, one per wire, top wire first; for instance
\(X\otimes Z\otimes I\) on three wires. The \textbf{Pauli group}
\(\mathcal P_n\) is the set of Pauli strings multiplied by one of the
four phases \(\pm1,\pm i\).

Take two wires and two strings, \(X\otimes Z\) and \(Z\otimes X\). On
each wire the letters anticommute, so exchanging the order of the
product gives \((-1)\cdot(-1)=+1\): the two strings commute. By contrast
\(X\otimes I\) and \(Z\otimes X\) disagree in sign on the first wire
only, and they anticommute. The sign is a count of disagreements.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 16.1 (the Pauli group).} For every \(n\),
\(\mathcal P_n\) is a group with \(4\cdot4^n\) elements: \(64\) on two
wires and \(256\) on three. Any two of its elements either commute or
anticommute. They anticommute exactly when the number of wires on which
both letters are different from \(I\) and from each other is odd.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} On one wire the product of two letters is a letter times
one of \(\pm1,\pm i\) (the products listed above, together with
\(P^2=I\) and \(IP=PI=P\)). So a product of two Pauli strings is a Pauli
string times a phase, and the phases multiply among \(\pm1,\pm i\); the
inverse of a phase times a string is the conjugate phase times the same
string, since every letter squares to \(I\). There are \(4^n\) strings
and four phases, and a phase times a string determines both, so
\(\lvert\mathcal P_n\rvert=4\cdot4^n\). On one wire two letters commute
when one of them is \(I\) or they are equal, and anticommute otherwise.
Reversing the order of a product of two strings reverses the order on
every wire, which contributes one \(-1\) per anticommuting wire.
\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch16/TwentyFour.py}.

Gottesman opens his account with the same count: the Pauli group
``consists of \(4\cdot4^n\) elements''.

\hypertarget{following-operators-instead-of-states}{%
\subsection{Following operators instead of
states}\label{following-operators-instead-of-states}}

Gottesman's paper of 1998 is called ``The Heisenberg Representation of
Quantum Computers'', and its idea fits in one line (his eqs. (1) and
(2)). If a machine applies a unitary \(U\) to a state \(\ket\psi\), then
for any operator \(N\), \[U N\ket\psi\;=\;UNU^{\dagger}\,U\ket\psi .\]
So after the gate, the operator \(UNU^{\dagger}\) does to the new state
exactly what \(N\) did to the old one. Instead of following the state,
follow what happens to operators: \(N\mapsto UNU^{\dagger}\). That map
respects products, \(UMNU^{\dagger}=(UMU^{\dagger})(UNU^{\dagger})\), so
it is enough to follow \(X\) and \(Z\) on each wire: every Pauli string
is a product of those, up to a phase.

For most gates this is no saving, because \(UXU^{\dagger}\) is some
large matrix. For some gates it is a great saving.

\textbf{The Clifford group} \(\mathcal C_n\) is the set of unitaries
\(U\) on \(n\) wires with
\[U P U^{\dagger}\in\mathcal P_n\qquad\text{for every }P\in\mathcal P_n .\]
Three examples are familiar. The Hadamard \(H\) sends \(X\mapsto Z\) and
\(Z\mapsto X\), and therefore \(Y=iXZ\mapsto iZX=-Y\). The phase gate
\[S\;=\;\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&i\end{pmatrix}\] sends \(X\mapsto Y\),
\(Y\mapsto -X\) and \(Z\mapsto Z\). The CNOT, control on top, sends
\[X\otimes I\mapsto X\otimes X,\quad I\otimes X\mapsto I\otimes X,\quad Z\otimes I\mapsto Z\otimes I,\quad I\otimes Z\mapsto Z\otimes Z .\]
These are the rows of Gottesman's Table 1. A word on names: Gottesman's
thesis of 1997 writes \(G\) for the Pauli group and \(N(G)\) for this
group of unitaries (the normalizer of \(G\)); his paper of 1998 writes
\(\mathcal P\) and \(N(\mathcal P)\) and says that \(N(\mathcal P)\)
``is also called the Clifford group \(\mathcal C\)''; both write \(R\)
and \(P\) for the Hadamard and the phase gate. We write
\(\mathcal P_n\), \(\mathcal C_n\), \(H\) and \(S\).

On one wire, what can a Clifford do? It must send \(X\) to a Pauli that
is Hermitian and squares to \(I\), and not to \(\pm I\), since \(X\) is
not a multiple of \(I\). It must also be traceless, as \(X\) is, which
leaves six choices: \(\pm X\), \(\pm Y\), \(\pm Z\). Draw them as the
six tips of an octahedron, with \(+X\) pointing to the front, \(+Y\) to
the right, \(+Z\) up, and each minus sign at the opposite tip. Then a
Clifford moves the tips about.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 16.2 (the twenty-four).} Up to an overall phase, the
one-wire Clifford group \(\mathcal C_1\) has exactly \(24\) elements.
Each one permutes the six tips \(\pm X,\pm Y,\pm Z\) as a rotation of
the octahedron; different elements give different rotations; every
rotation of the octahedron occurs; and \(H\) and \(S\) generate them
all.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} \emph{At most twenty-four.} A Clifford \(U\) sends \(X\)
to one of the six tips. It sends \(Z\) to a tip that anticommutes with
the image of \(X\) (conjugation keeps \(XZ=-ZX\)), so not to that tip or
its opposite: four choices. The image of \(Y=iXZ\) is then forced,
\(UYU^{\dagger}=i\,(UXU^{\dagger})(UZU^{\dagger})\). So there are at
most \(6\times4\) ways to move the tips. Two unitaries that move the
tips the same way agree up to a phase: if
\(UXU^{\dagger}=VXV^{\dagger}\) and \(UZU^{\dagger}=VZV^{\dagger}\),
then \(Q=V^{\dagger}U\) commutes with \(X\) and \(Z\), hence with
\(I,X,Y,Z\), which span all \(2\times2\) matrices, so \(Q\) is a
multiple of \(I\).

\emph{The moves are rotations.} A move sends the three axes to three
axes with signs, so it is a signed permutation of \((X,Y,Z)\), and the
forced image of \(Y\) fixes the last sign so that the determinant is
\(+1\): from \(XYZ=iI\), the images satisfy the same relation, and a
signed permutation with determinant \(-1\) would give \(-iI\). The
rotations of the octahedron are exactly the signed permutations of its
three axes with determinant \(+1\).

\emph{At least twenty-four.} \(S\) turns the octahedron a quarter about
the up--down axis, sending the front tip to the right; its powers
\(I,S,S^2,S^3\) give four different rotations that keep \(+Z\) up. \(H\)
exchanges \(+Z\) and \(+X\), \(S\) carries \(+X\) to \(+Y\), \(S^2=Z\)
carries \(+X\) to \(-X\), \(H\) carries \(-X\) to \(-Z\), and \(S\)
carries \(-X\) to \(-Y\). So the group generated by \(H\) and \(S\) can
bring any of the six tips up, and for each tip up it has the four
quarter-turns about it. That is \(6\times4\) different rotations, all
generated by \(H\) and \(S\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch16/TwentyFour.py}, which also enumerates the group.

Hein, Dür, Eisert, Raussendorf, Van den Nest and Briegel list them in
their Table 1, ``All 24 single-qubit Clifford unitaries'',
``disregarding such global phases'', each written as a product of
elementary permutations of the three axes.

Here is the octahedron. It is \textbf{not a string diagram}: its lines
are edges of a solid, not wires, and none of the rules of Chapter 8
apply to it. It is a picture of where the three Pauli axes point.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=1.45em, y=1.3em, >=stealth,
  tip/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.7pt,minimum size=1.05em,inner sep=0pt},
  lab/.style={font=\footnotesize,inner sep=1.5pt,fill=white},
  alab/.style={font=\footnotesize,inner sep=1.5pt}]
  \coordinate (U) at (0,4.4);
  \coordinate (D) at (0,-4.4);
  \coordinate (R) at (4.6,0);
  \coordinate (L) at (-4.6,0);

  \coordinate (B) at (1.7,1.4);

  \node[tip, fill=green!60] at (U) {}; \node[lab, right=6pt] at (U) {$+Z$};

\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

\emph{The octahedron of Pauli tips.} A figure of a different kind, not a
string diagram. The six tips are \(\pm X\) (red, towards the reader and
away), \(\pm Y\) (gold, right and left) and \(\pm Z\) (green, up and
down), the plus tip dark and the minus tip pale. Each one-wire Clifford
is a rotation that seats the solid again. The two arrows draw two
equations as tip moves: \(HXH^{\dagger}=Z\), the front tip carried up,
and \(SXS^{\dagger}=Y\), the front tip carried to the right.

The half-turns about the three axes are the Paulis themselves: \(X\)
fixes \(\pm X\) and swaps the other two pairs, and likewise for \(Y\)
and \(Z\). Every tip lands on itself or its opposite.

For many wires we state the answer and do not prove it.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 16.3 (the generators; Gottesman, stated, not proved).}
Every element of \(\mathcal C_n\) is, up to an overall phase, a product
of \(H\) and \(S\) on single wires and CNOTs on pairs of wires. In
Gottesman's words (1998, §3), ``\(R\), \(P\), and CNOT, applied to
arbitrary qubits or pairs of qubits, generate the full Clifford group
\(\mathcal C\).'' Hein and co-authors add that ``up to a global phase
factor any Clifford operation'' decomposes into \(O(N^2)\) such gates,
their \(N\) being our \(n\).
\end{quote}

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} Every one of these gates is a spider picture
whose turns are all quarters or halves. A red \(\pi\) dot with one leg
in and one out is \(X\) exactly, and a green \(\pi\) dot is \(Z\)
exactly (§8.2). A green dot with phase \(\pi/2\) is
\(\ket0\bra0+e^{i\pi/2}\ket1\bra1=S\), exactly. The Hadamard is the
yellow box. The green--red pair of Chapter 8 (row 64) is the CNOT, with
the number \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) when it is drawn bare: \[S\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1em, y=1em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]

  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2.4,0);

\end{tikzpicture}
,\qquad
Z\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1em, y=1em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},

\end{tikzpicture}
,\qquad
X\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1em, y=1em,
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},

\end{tikzpicture}
,\qquad
\mathrm{CNOT}\;=\;\sqrt2\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.55em, x=1em, y=1em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
  \path (0,-0.7) (0,2.3);

\end{tikzpicture}\] Reading left to right, \(Y=iXZ\) is \(i\) times a
green \(\pi\) followed by a red \(\pi\). The ``over'' of the octahedron,
the Hadamard, is Chapter 8's colour change (Theorem 8.2, row 58): a
green \(\pi\) between two yellow boxes is a red \(\pi\), exactly, which
is \(HZH=X\). \[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1em, y=1em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-0.9) (0,1.0);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (4.4,0);
  \node[hbox] at (1.0,0) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (2.2,0) {};
  \node[hbox] at (3.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1em, y=1em,
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-0.9) (0,1.0);

\end{tikzpicture}\] So every product of \(H\), \(S\) and CNOT, fed
\(\ket0\) (a red point, times \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\)) and read with
\(\bra0\) where we like, is a picture in which every turn is a multiple
of a quarter. We call such pictures \textbf{quarter-turn pictures}. Van
de Wetering's survey states the converse as well: the Clifford maps
``are precisely those linear maps that can be presented by ZX-diagrams
containing only phases that are multiples of \(\tfrac\pi2\)''. We have
shown one direction, and we use only that one.

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why single out the unitaries that
send Paulis to Paulis? Because they are exactly the gates whose effect
can be followed by following operators. A Clifford on \(n\) wires is
known, up to a phase, once we know where it sends the \(2n\) operators
\(X_1,\dots,X_n,Z_1,\dots,Z_n\) (the argument of the proof above, wire
by wire), and each of those goes to a single Pauli string. That is a
short list of signed letters, where a general gate would need a matrix
with \(4^n\) entries. Section §16.4 turns this into a notebook.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{safe-touches}{%
\section{§16.2 Safe Touches}\label{safe-touches}}

Take two wires, each in \(\ket+=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket0+\ket1)\), and
apply CZ, the gate that turns over \(\ket{11}\) and nothing else. The
result is
\[\mathrm{CZ}\ket{++}\;=\;\tfrac12\bigl(\ket{00}+\ket{01}+\ket{10}-\ket{11}\bigr).\]
Now touch it. The string \(X\otimes I\) swaps the first bit, giving
\(\tfrac12(\ket{10}+\ket{11}+\ket{00}-\ket{01})\): a different state.
The touch was noticed. But \(X\otimes Z\) swaps the first bit and turns
over every term whose second bit is \(1\):
\[\tfrac12\bigl(\ket{10}-\ket{11}+\ket{00}+\ket{01}\bigr),\] which is
the state we started with, term for term. A flip on the first wire is
noticed; the same flip with a sign on its partner is not. By symmetry
\(Z\otimes X\) goes unnoticed too. This section explains the pattern for
any number of wires joined in any way.

\textbf{On the blackboard.} A \textbf{graph} \(G=(V,E)\) is a set \(V\)
of \textbf{vertices} and a set \(E\) of \textbf{edges}, each edge an
unordered pair of different vertices. Two vertices joined by an edge are
\textbf{adjacent}, and the \textbf{neighbourhood} \(N_a\) of a vertex
\(a\) is the set of vertices adjacent to \(a\). Put one wire on each
vertex, so \(n=\lvert V\rvert\), and write \(\mathrm{CZ}_{bc}\) for the
CZ on the wires of \(b\) and \(c\). The \textbf{graph state} of \(G\) is
\[\ket G\;=\;U_G\,\ket+^{\otimes n},\qquad U_G\;=\;\prod_{\{b,c\}\in E}\mathrm{CZ}_{bc}\]
(Hein et al., eq. (24); their \(U_{ab}\) is our CZ). Every CZ is
diagonal, so the order of the product does not matter. Written out,
\[\ket G\;=\;2^{-n/2}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}(-1)^{E(x)}\ket x,\qquad E(x)=\sum_{\{b,c\}\in E}x_bx_c ,\]
every string with amplitude \(\pm2^{-n/2}\), and a minus sign when the
string has an odd number of edges with both ends at \(1\).

Our running example is the \textbf{bow tie}: five vertices, called
\textbf{bells} as in the dialogue, numbered in ket order: \(1\)
left-back, \(2\) left-front, \(3\) the \textbf{knot}, \(4\) right-back,
\(5\) right-front. Its edges are \(12\), \(13\), \(23\), \(34\), \(35\)
and \(45\): two triangles sharing the knot. We write
\(\ket{G_{\bowtie}}\) for its graph state.

For each vertex \(a\), let \[K_a\;=\;X_a\prod_{b\in N_a}Z_b ,\] an \(X\)
on \(a\) and a \(Z\) on each neighbour of \(a\). Hein and co-authors
call the \(K_a\) \textbf{correlation operators} (their Proposition 2).
On the bow tie, top wire first,
\[K_3\;=\;Z\otimes Z\otimes X\otimes Z\otimes Z,\qquad K_1\;=\;X\otimes Z\otimes Z\otimes I\otimes I .\]
The example above was the graph with two vertices and one edge, and its
\(K_1\) and \(K_2\) were \(X\otimes Z\) and \(Z\otimes X\).

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Dirac's Blackboard.}\nopagebreak

\emph{One tie at a time.} The headline of this section (Result 16.6
below) rests on one identity for one edge:
\(\mathrm{CZ}_{ab}\,X_a\,\mathrm{CZ}_{ab}=X_aZ_b\). Check it on a basis
string \(\ket{x_ax_b}\) of the two wires. The first CZ gives the sign
\((-1)^{x_ax_b}\). Then \(X_a\) flips the first bit to \(1-x_a\). The
second CZ gives \((-1)^{(1-x_a)x_b}\). The two signs multiply to
\((-1)^{x_b}\), whatever \(x_a\) was. So the net effect is: flip the
first bit, and turn over the string if the second bit is \(1\). That is
\(X_aZ_b\). A CZ on two other wires commutes with \(X_a\), and every CZ
commutes with every \(Z\), so pushing \(X_a\) through the whole of
\(U_G\) leaves one \(Z\) on each neighbour of \(a\) and nothing else:
\[U_G\,X_a\,U_G^{\dagger}\;=\;X_a\prod_{b\in N_a}Z_b\;=\;K_a .\] CZ is
its own inverse, so \(U_G^{\dagger}\) is the same product of CZs, and
the order of the CZs does not matter.
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{the-net}{%
\subsection{The net}\label{the-net}}

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} Van de Wetering's survey draws a graph state
in one step: ``every vertex becomes a Z-spider with an output attached
to it'', and every edge becomes a wire between the two spiders with a
Hadamard on it. We call that picture the \textbf{net} of \(G\). Each
vertex is a phase-free green spider with one output leg running to the
right, and one leg for each edge at that vertex. Each edge is a wire
joining two spiders, carrying a yellow box. Chapter 8 also allowed a
dashed wire for a Hadamard on a wire (row 56). We draw the box, because
the rewrites below move things through it, and because the dialogue's
ties wear yellow sleeves. We call the edges of a net \textbf{ties}.

The smallest net has two spiders and one tie. It is the state we touched
at the start of the section, with a number:
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.95em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-0.8) (0,2.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,2) -- (2.4,2);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2.4,0);
  \draw[wire] (0,2) -- (0,0);
  \node[hbox] at (0,1) {};
  \node[zsp] at (0,2) {};
  \node[zsp] at (0,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;\sqrt2\;\mathrm{CZ}\ket{++}\;=\;\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket{00}+\ket{01}+\ket{10}-\ket{11}\bigr).\]

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 16.4 (the net).} For every graph with \(v\) vertices and
\(e\) edges, the bare net equals exactly \(2^{(v-e)/2}\ket G\). For the
bow tie it is \(2^{-1/2}\ket{G_{\bowtie}}\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} Read the net as a sum over bits. A phase-free green spider
forces all its legs to agree (row 53), so each vertex \(b\) carries one
bit \(x_b\) to its output and to all of its ties. A yellow box between
bits \(x_b\) and \(x_c\) contributes the matrix entry
\(\bra{x_c}H\ket{x_b}=2^{-1/2}(-1)^{x_bx_c}\). So the net is
\(2^{-e/2}\sum_x(-1)^{E(x)}\ket x=2^{-e/2}\,2^{v/2}\ket G\).
\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch16/SafeTouches.py}, which checks
the number on random graphs.

Here is the bow tie's net. The bells are stacked in ket order, top wire
first, their outputs run to the right, and the ties are drawn as arcs on
the left: short arcs between neighbouring bells, and longer arcs from
the knot to the far bell of each wing.

\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=5.95em, x=1.2em, y=1.55em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt}]
  \draw[wire] (3,8) to[out=225,in=135,looseness=1.3] node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (3,6);
  \draw[wire] (3,6) to[out=225,in=135,looseness=1.3] node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (3,4);
  \draw[wire] (3,8) to[out=175,in=160,looseness=1.1] node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (3,4);
  \draw[wire] (3,4) to[out=225,in=135,looseness=1.3] node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (3,2);
  \draw[wire] (3,2) to[out=225,in=135,looseness=1.3] node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (3,0);
  \draw[wire] (3,4) to[out=200,in=185,looseness=1.1] node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (3,0);
  \foreach \y in {8,6,4,2,0} { \draw[wire] (3,\y) -- (6,\y); \node[zsp] at (3,\y) {}; }
  \node[sdlabel, right] at (6,8) {$1$};
  \node[sdlabel, right] at (6,6) {$2$};
  \node[sdlabel, right] at (6,4) {$3$};
  \node[sdlabel, right] at (6,2) {$4$};
  \node[sdlabel, right] at (6,0) {$5$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;2^{-1/2}\,\ket{G_{\bowtie}}\]

\hypertarget{a-half-through-a-ring-at-rest}{%
\subsection{A half through a ring at
rest}\label{a-half-through-a-ring-at-rest}}

To prove the headline in pictures we need one rule that Chapter 8 stated
only for two legs and only ``up to a scalar'': pushing a half-turn of
one colour through a phase-free spider of the other. A \textbf{clip
ring} is our name for a spider with exactly two legs sitting on a wire.
A green or red clip ring with no phase is a plain wire (§8.2); we say it
is \textbf{at rest}. A red clip ring with phase \(\pi\) is \(X\), a
green one is \(Z\).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 16.5 (a half through a ring at rest).} Let a phase-free
green spider have \(k\ge2\) legs. A red \(\pi\) on one of its legs
equals a red \(\pi\) on each of its other \(k-1\) legs, exactly, with no
number. The same holds with the colours exchanged. On the blackboard:
\(X^{\otimes k}\) exchanges the two terms of
\(\ket{0\cdots0}\bra{0\cdots0}+\ket{1\cdots1}\bra{1\cdots1}\), and so
leaves their sum unchanged.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} The derivation by the rules is the sketchbook sidebar
below. On the blackboard: bend all legs to one side, so that the spider
is the state \(\ket{0\cdots0}+\ket{1\cdots1}\) on \(k\) wires.
\(X^{\otimes k}\) fixes it, and multiplying both sides by \(X\) on the
first wire moves that \(X\) to the other \(k-1\) wires.
\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch16/SafeTouches.py}.

It is Chapter 8's \(\pi\)-commutation (Theorem 8.4, row 60) for a
phase-free spider, now with any number of legs and with its exact
number, just as Chapter 14 found the exact number of the two-legged
case.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Coecke's Sketchbook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{Deriving the push.} Here is Result 16.5 from rules the book has
stated. Stand the spider with one leg in and \(k-1\) legs out. A map
with one input is fixed by what it does to the dark point and the lit
point, the red points \(\sqrt2\ket0\) and \(\sqrt2\ket1\), because they
span the input (the principle behind row 104). Feed in a red point with
phase \(c\pi\). On the left side, the red \(\pi\) fuses with the point
first (fusion, row 57), giving a red point with phase \((c+1)\pi\); then
the phase-free green spider copies it onto its \(k-1\) outputs (copy,
row 59). On the right side, the spider copies the point with phase
\(c\pi\) first, and then each output's red \(\pi\) fuses into its copy,
giving phase \((c+1)\pi\) on every output. Both sides end with the same
\(k-1\) red points. And both paid the same price: one point in, \(k-1\)
points out, is the same copy in both orders, and fusion costs nothing.
So the prices cancel, and the rule holds with no number at all. The rule
needs the spider phase-free: a turned spider does not copy.
\end{quote}

The picture of the rule, drawn for four legs:
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.1em, y=1.1em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1.8) (0,1.9);
  \draw[wire] (-0.2,0) -- (2.6,0);
  \draw[wire] (2.6,0) -- (4.4,1.4);
  \draw[wire] (2.6,0) -- (4.4,0);
  \draw[wire] (2.6,0) -- (4.4,-1.4);
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (1.1,0) {};
  \node[zsp] at (2.6,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.1em, y=1.1em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-2.7) (0,2.7);
  \draw[wire] (-0.2,0) -- (1.0,0);
  \draw[wire] (1.0,0) -- (3.0,1.9) -- (4.8,1.9);
  \draw[wire] (1.0,0) -- (4.8,0);
  \draw[wire] (1.0,0) -- (3.0,-1.9) -- (4.8,-1.9);
  \node[zsp] at (1.0,0) {};
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (3.6,1.9) {};
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (3.6,0) {};
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi$}}] at (3.6,-1.9) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\]

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 16.6 (the stabilizers of a graph state).} For every graph
\(G\) with \(n\ge1\) vertices and every vertex \(a\), exactly,
\[K_a\ket G\;=\;\ket G .\] In pictures: on the net of \(G\) (Result
16.4), a red \(\pi\) on \(a\)'s output and a green \(\pi\) on the output
of each neighbour of \(a\) give back the bare net, with no number.
\end{quote}

This is the chapter's headline theorem. It is proved twice in §16.7,
once in each strand. We call \(K_a\) the \textbf{safe touch} at \(a\).

For the two-spider net the touch is a red \(\pi\) on the top output and
a green \(\pi\) on the bottom one: the \(X\otimes Z\) of the opening
example, which went unnoticed. §16.7 proves the headline for every
graph, in both strands, and §16.8 draws it on the bow tie, touched at
the knot.

The safe touches do more than fix \(\ket G\). They name it.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 16.7 (the stabilizer group).} For every graph \(G\) with
\(n\) vertices: (i) the \(K_a\) commute, and the products
\(K^{\mathbf b}=\prod_aK_a^{b_a}\) over the bit strings
\(\mathbf b\in\{0,1\}^n\) are \(2^n\) different elements of
\(\mathcal P_n\), forming an abelian group \(\mathcal S_G\), the
\textbf{stabilizer group} of \(\ket G\), every element of which fixes
\(\ket G\); (ii) for bit strings \(\mathbf b\in\{0,1\}^n\), the \(2^n\)
states \(Z^{\mathbf b}\ket G=\prod_aZ_a^{b_a}\ket G\) form an
orthonormal basis, and
\(K_aZ^{\mathbf b}\ket G=(-1)^{b_a}Z^{\mathbf b}\ket G\); (iii)
\(\ket G\bra G=2^{-n}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal S_G}\sigma\); (iv)
\(\ket G\) is, up to a number, the only state fixed by every \(K_a\).
\end{quote}

This is Hein et al.'s Proposition 3, with their eqs. (29) and (30);
their subsets \(W\) of vertices are our bit strings \(\mathbf b\). For
the bow tie, \(\mathcal S_{G_{\bowtie}}\) has \(32\) elements.

\emph{Proof.} (i) \(K_a\) and \(K_b\) can disagree in sign only on the
wires \(a\) and \(b\) (everywhere else both carry \(I\) or \(Z\)). On
wire \(a\), \(K_a\) has \(X\) and \(K_b\) has \(Z\) exactly when \(a\)
and \(b\) are adjacent; on wire \(b\) the same holds with the roles
exchanged. So there are zero or two anticommuting wires, and by Result
16.1 the two commute. The product \(K^{\mathbf b}\) has an \(X\) or
\(Y\) exactly on the wires \(a\) with \(b_a=1\), so different
\(\mathbf b\) give different elements, and none of them is \(-I\). Each
fixes \(\ket G\) by Result 16.6.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\item
  \(Z_c\) commutes with \(K_a\) for \(c\ne a\) and anticommutes with
  \(K_a\) for \(c=a\). So
  \(K_aZ^{\mathbf b}\ket G=(-1)^{b_a}Z^{\mathbf b}K_a\ket G=(-1)^{b_a}Z^{\mathbf b}\ket G\).
  Two different \(\mathbf b\) differ at some \(a\), where \(K_a\), which
  is Hermitian, has different eigenvalues on them, so the states are
  orthogonal. There are \(2^n\) of them, each of length one, so they are
  an orthonormal basis.
\item
  Since the \(K_a\) commute and square to \(I\), expanding the product
  \(\prod_a\tfrac12(I+K_a)\) gives each element of \(\mathcal S_G\)
  once, times \(2^{-n}\). Each factor \(\tfrac12(I+K_a)\) projects onto
  the states with \(K_a=+1\), so the product projects onto the states
  with every \(K_a=+1\). By (ii), among the basis states that is
  \(Z^{\mathbf 0}\ket G=\ket G\) alone.
\item
  A state fixed by every \(K_a\) is fixed by the projector of (iii),
  which is \(\ket G\bra G\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
  \texttt{Code/Ch16/SafeTouches.py}.
\end{enumerate}

So a graph state can be described without a single amplitude: list, for
each vertex, the letter \(X\) on the vertex and \(Z\) on its neighbours.
For five bells that is five short strings instead of thirty-two numbers.
Section §16.4 makes that description into a working notebook.

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why build graph states from
\(\ket+\) and CZ, rather than write down a general state? Because then
the whole state is described by the graph: each tie is the same simple
gate, the ties commute, and the only information is which vertices are
joined. And nothing is lost by the restriction. Section §16.3 shows that
every state the quarter-turn gates can make is a graph state with a
one-wire Clifford on each wire.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{half-a-touch}{%
\section{§16.3 Half a Touch}\label{half-a-touch}}

The safe touch \(K_a\) is a half-turn on each wire it touches. What does
half of it do?

Take the bow tie and the left-back bell, \(a=1\), with neighbours \(2\)
and \(3\). Half a turn about \(X\) is
\(e^{-i\frac\pi4X}=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(I-iX)\), and half a turn about \(Z\)
is \(e^{i\frac\pi4Z}=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(I+iZ)\). Apply
\[U\;=\;e^{-i\frac\pi4X_1}\,e^{i\frac\pi4Z_2}\,e^{i\frac\pi4Z_3}\] and
ask what the new state is fixed by. For any operator \(K\) that fixed
the old state, \(UKU^{\dagger}\) fixes the new one. Take
\(K_2=Z_1X_2Z_3\). On wire \(1\),
\(e^{-i\frac\pi4X}Z\,e^{i\frac\pi4X}=e^{-i\frac\pi2X}Z=-iXZ\), because
\(Z\) anticommutes with \(X\). On wire \(2\), likewise
\(e^{i\frac\pi4Z}X\,e^{-i\frac\pi4Z}=iZX\). So
\[UK_2U^{\dagger}\;=\;(-iX_1Z_1)(iZ_2X_2)\,Z_3\;=\;X_1Z_1\;Z_2X_2\;Z_3 .\]
That is not a safe touch of the bow tie. But it is the product
\((X_1Z_2Z_3)(Z_1X_2)\), and those are the safe touches \(K'_1\) and
\(K'_2\) of a \textbf{different graph}: the bow tie with the tie between
bells \(2\) and \(3\) removed. Half a touch did not leave the state
alone. It re-tied the net.

\textbf{On the blackboard.} For a graph \(G\) and a vertex \(a\), the
\textbf{local complement} \(\tau_a(G)\) is the graph obtained by
complementing the edges among the neighbours of \(a\): two neighbours of
\(a\) that were adjacent become non-adjacent, and two that were not
become adjacent. Nothing else changes. This is Hein et al.'s notation
(their eq. (41)); Duncan, Kissinger, Perdrix and van de Wetering, and
van de Wetering's survey, write \(G\star a\) for the same graph. Doing
it twice undoes it: \(\tau_a(\tau_a(G))=G\).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 16.8 (the LC-rule, with its phase).} For every graph
\(G\) and vertex \(a\), let
\[U^{\tau}_a\;=\;e^{-i\frac\pi4X_a}\prod_{b\in N_a}e^{i\frac\pi4Z_b}.\]
Then, exactly,
\[U^{\tau}_a\ket G\;=\;e^{i\pi(\lvert N_a\rvert-1)/4}\,\ket{\tau_a(G)},\qquad (U^{\tau}_a)^2\;=\;i^{\lvert N_a\rvert-1}K_a .\]
Two halves of the touch make the touch: at the knot of the bow tie
\((U^{\tau}_3)^2=-iK_3\), and at a wing bell \(iK_a\).
\end{quote}

Hein and co-authors state this as their Proposition 5, eqs. (42) and
(43), with \(U^{\tau}_a(G)\propto\sqrt{K_a}\). Their eq. (42) is an
equality of states determined by their stabilizers, which fixes the
phase only up to an overall factor; the phase above is ours, computed
below, with their \(e^{i\frac\pi4\sigma_z^{N_a}}\) read as the product
of one factor per neighbour.

\emph{Proof.} \emph{The stabilizers.} This is Hein et al.'s argument
(their eq. (44) and after), and the example above is one case of it.
Write \(K'_c\) for the safe touches of \(\tau_a(G)\). For a vertex \(c\)
that is not a neighbour of \(a\) (including \(a\) itself),
\(U^{\tau}_a\) commutes with \(K_c\), and \(K_c=K'_c\), because local
complementation at \(a\) changes only the edges among \(N_a\). For a
neighbour \(b\), conjugation turns the \(Z_a\) in \(K_b\) into
\(-iX_aZ_a\) and the \(X_b\) into \(iZ_bX_b\), and leaves the other
\(Z\)s alone, so
\[U^{\tau}_aK_bU^{\tau\dagger}_a\;=\;X_aZ_a\,Z_bX_b\prod_{c\in N_b\setminus\{a\}}Z_c\;=\;K'_aK'_b ,\]
where the last step compares wire by wire: the \(Z\)s of \(K'_a\) on the
other neighbours of \(a\) exactly toggle the edges from \(b\) to those
neighbours. So the new state \(U^{\tau}_a\ket G\) is fixed by every
\(K'_c\) (and \(K'_a\) itself is the image of \(K_a\)), and by Result
16.7 (iv) it is a number times \(\ket{\tau_a(G)}\). Both have length
one, so the number is a phase \(\lambda\).

\emph{The phase.} Compare the amplitudes of \(\ket{0\cdots0}\). Every
graph state has \(\braket{0\cdots0|\tau_a(G)}=2^{-n/2}\). On the other
side, \(\bra{0\cdots0}e^{i\frac\pi4Z_b}=e^{i\pi/4}\bra{0\cdots0}\) for
each neighbour, and
\(\bra{0\cdots0}\,\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(I-iX_a)\ket G=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(1-i)\,2^{-n/2}\),
since the string with a single \(1\) at \(a\) has no edge with both ends
at \(1\). So
\(\lambda\,2^{-n/2}=e^{i\pi\lvert N_a\rvert/4}\,e^{-i\pi/4}\,2^{-n/2}\).

\emph{The square.}
\(\bigl(e^{-i\frac\pi4X}\bigr)^2=e^{-i\frac\pi2X}=-iX\) and
\(\bigl(e^{i\frac\pi4Z}\bigr)^2=iZ\), so
\((U^{\tau}_a)^2=(-i)\,i^{\lvert N_a\rvert}X_a\prod_bZ_b\).
\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch16/HalfATouch.py}.

Hein and co-authors add a converse, which we state and do not prove:
``two graph states \(\ket G\) and \(\ket{G'}\) are LC-equivalent iff the
corresponding graphs are related by a sequence of local
complementations'', LC-equivalent meaning related by one-wire Cliffords
on every wire. They cite Van den Nest, Dehaene and De Moor, and Glynn,
for it.

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} A red dot with phase \(\pi/2\) and two legs
is \(\ket+\bra++i\ket-\bra-=e^{i\pi/4}e^{-i\frac\pi4X}\), and a green
dot with phase \(-\pi/2\) is
\(\mathrm{diag}(1,-i)=e^{-i\pi/4}e^{i\frac\pi4Z}\). So half a touch,
drawn as clip rings, is \(U^{\tau}_a\) times
\(e^{i\pi/4}e^{-i\pi\lvert N_a\rvert/4}\), and that number cancels the
phase of Result 16.8 exactly.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 16.9 (re-tying).} For every graph \(G\) with edge set
\(E\) and every vertex \(a\), a red clip ring turned a quarter round
(\(+\pi/2\)) on \(a\)'s output and a green clip ring turned a quarter
back (\(-\pi/2\)) on each neighbour's output send \(\ket G\) to exactly
\(\ket{\tau_a(G)}\). So do the reverse turns, a red quarter back and
green quarters round. As nets, with \(E'\) the edge set of
\(\tau_a(G)\):
\[\bigl(\text{net of }G\text{ with those clip rings}\bigr)\;=\;2^{(\lvert E'\rvert-\lvert E\rvert)/2}\,\bigl(\text{net of }\tau_a(G)\bigr).\]
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} The first form is Result 16.8 with the number just
computed. For the reverse turns the clip rings are \((U^{\tau}_a)^{-1}\)
times the inverse number, and
\((U^{\tau}_a)^{-1}\ket G=i^{1-\lvert N_a\rvert}\,U^{\tau}_aK_a\ket G\)
by the square in Result 16.8, which is
\(i^{1-\lvert N_a\rvert}e^{i\pi(\lvert N_a\rvert-1)/4}\ket{\tau_a(G)}=e^{-i\pi(\lvert N_a\rvert-1)/4}\ket{\tau_a(G)}\);
the inverse number cancels it. The net form follows from Result 16.4,
since both nets have the same \(v\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch16/HalfATouch.py}.

This equation is \textbf{proved on the blackboard and checked by
matrix}, not derived here by rewriting. Its derivation by the rules of
the calculus is due to Duncan and Perdrix. Duncan and co-authors cite it
as ``R. Duncan and S. Perdrix. Graph states and the necessity of Euler
decomposition'' (2009), and draw it as their eq. (5), with
\(X_{-\pi/2}\) on the vertex and \(Z_{\pi/2}\) on its neighbours, which
is the reverse form. Van de Wetering's survey draws it as its eq. (100).

At the left-back bell of the bow tie the neighbours are \(2\) and \(3\),
which are tied, so re-tying removes one tie and the number is
\(2^{-1/2}\):

have made it a different net. At the knot, whose four neighbours are
joined by only two ties, re-tying removes the tie inside each wing and
adds a tie from each wing bell to both bells of the other wing: the bow
tie's six ties become eight, and the number is \(2^{(8-6)/2}=2\). Add a
second quarter on each of the three rings and they fuse (row 57) into
the safe touch of Result 16.6, which the net does not notice; on the
graph, the second re-tying at the same bell undoes the first.

\hypertarget{three-re-tyings-the-pivot}{%
\subsection{Three re-tyings: the
pivot}\label{three-re-tyings-the-pivot}}

Re-tie the bow tie at the left-back bell, then at the knot, then at the
left-back bell again. Following the definition three times gives the
graph with ties \(12\), \(13\), \(14\), \(15\), \(23\), \(24\), \(25\)
and \(45\): the left-back bell now has every other bell as a neighbour,
the knot has only the left-back and left-front bells, and the two bells
have in effect exchanged their places in the graph, with the ties among
the others adjusted. Duncan et al.~give this combination a name. For
adjacent vertices \(u\) and \(v\), the \textbf{pivot} of \(G\) along the
edge \(uv\) is \[G\wedge uv\;=\;\tau_u\bigl(\tau_v(\tau_u(G))\bigr)\]
(their Definition 4.3, ``\(G\wedge uv:=G\star u\star v\star u\)''). It
is symmetric in \(u\) and \(v\). Split the other vertices by where they
are joined: \(A\), the neighbours of \(u\) alone; \(B\), the neighbours
of \(v\) alone; \(C\), the common neighbours. The pivot complements the
ties between \(A\) and \(B\), between \(A\) and \(C\), and between \(B\)
and \(C\), and exchanges the neighbourhoods of \(u\) and \(v\).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 16.10 (the pivot).} For every graph \(G\) and every edge
\(uv\), exactly, with no phase,
\[H_uH_v\prod_{c\in N_u\cap N_v}Z_c\;\ket G\;=\;\ket{G\wedge uv}.\] In
the bow tie example,
\(H_1H_3Z_2\ket{G_{\bowtie}}=\ket{G_{\bowtie}\wedge13}\).
\end{quote}

Van de Wetering's survey draws this as its eq. (101), ``applying a
Hadamard to the vertices we pivot along, and applying a Z gate to the
vertices in their common neighbourhood'', and Duncan et al.~as their eq.
(6), crediting Duncan and Perdrix (cited as ``Ross Duncan and Simon
Perdrix. Pivoting makes the ZX-calculus complete for real stabilizers'',
2014). In pictures: yellow boxes on the outputs of \(u\) and \(v\) and a
green \(\pi\) on each common neighbour's output turn the net of \(G\)
into \(2^{(\lvert E''\rvert-\lvert E\rvert)/2}\) times the net of
\(G\wedge uv\), where \(E''\) is its edge set. Again this is checked by
matrix, not derived by rewriting.

\emph{Proof.} Apply Result 16.8 three times. Follow the neighbourhoods:
at the first step \(u\)'s neighbours are \(\{v\}\cup A\cup C\); after
it, \(v\)'s are \(\{u\}\cup A\cup B\); after the second step, \(u\)'s
are \(\{v\}\cup B\cup C\). Multiply the three unitaries wire by wire. On
\(u\) they give \(e^{-i\frac\pi4X}e^{i\frac\pi4Z}e^{-i\frac\pi4X}\), and
on \(v\) they give \(e^{i\frac\pi4Z}e^{-i\frac\pi4X}e^{i\frac\pi4Z}\);
each of these equals \(-YH\), as one checks by multiplying out. Every
vertex of \(A\), \(B\) or \(C\) receives exactly two \(Z\)
quarter-turns, \(\bigl(e^{i\frac\pi4Z}\bigr)^2=iZ\). So, up to a phase,
\[\ket{G\wedge uv}\;\propto\;\bigl(Y_uY_v\,Z_AZ_B\bigr)\;H_uH_vZ_C\ket G ,\]
writing \(Z_A\) for a \(Z\) on every vertex of \(A\), and so on. The
first bracket is the product of the safe touches of \(u\) and \(v\) in
\(G\wedge uv\): there \(u\)'s neighbours are \(\{v\}\cup B\cup C\) and
\(v\)'s are \(\{u\}\cup A\cup C\), and wire by wire
\((X_uZ_vZ_BZ_C)(X_vZ_uZ_AZ_C)=(X_uZ_u)(Z_vX_v)Z_AZ_B=Y_uY_vZ_AZ_B\). So
it fixes \(\ket{G\wedge uv}\), and \(H_uH_vZ_C\ket G\) is a phase times
\(\ket{G\wedge uv}\). The phase is \(1\):
\(\bra{0\cdots0}H_uH_vZ_C\ket G=\bra{+_u+_v0\cdots0}G\rangle=\tfrac12\bigl(1+1+1-1\bigr)2^{-n/2}=2^{-n/2}\),
the same as \(\braket{0\cdots0|G\wedge uv}\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch16/HalfATouch.py}.

\hypertarget{every-state-of-the-world}{%
\subsection{Every state of the world}\label{every-state-of-the-world}}

The quarter-turn gates, started from \(\ket{0\cdots0}\), make a family
of states with many names. Aaronson and Gottesman prove that four
descriptions of it agree.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 16.11 (stabilizer states; stated, not proved).} (Aaronson
and Gottesman, Theorem 1.) For an \(n\)-qubit state \(\ket\psi\) the
following are equivalent: (i) \(\ket\psi\) can be obtained from
\(\ket0^{\otimes n}\) by CNOT, Hadamard and phase gates only; (ii) the
same, with measurements allowed too; (iii) \(\ket\psi\) is fixed by
exactly \(2^n\) Pauli operators; (iv) \(\ket\psi\) is determined by the
group \(\mathrm{Stab}(\ket\psi)\cap\mathcal P_n\) of Pauli operators
that fix it. Such states are called \textbf{stabilizer states}. There
are \[2^n\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\bigl(2^{n-k}+1\bigr)\] of them (their
Proposition 2): \(6\) on one wire, \(60\) on two, \(1080\) on three, and
\(2\,423\,520\) on five. Every stabilizer state is a graph state with a
one-wire Clifford on each wire (Hein et al., Proposition 4, which they
credit to Schlingemann and to Grassl, Klappenecker and Rötteler; van de
Wetering calls this the \textbf{GSLC} form, graph state with local
Cliffords). And every unitary quarter-turn circuit equals one ``in
canonical form'', ``11 rounds in the sequence H-C-P-C-P-C-H-P-C-P-C''
(Aaronson and Gottesman, Theorem 8), from which, ``building on a result
by Patel, Markov, and Hayes'', they obtain circuits with
\(O(n^2/\log n)\) gates.
\end{quote}

The six on one wire are the tips of the octahedron: the states fixed by
\(\pm X\), \(\pm Y\) or \(\pm Z\). The graph states of §16.2 are, by
Result 16.7, examples of (iii) and (iv). In the GSLC form every state of
the world of quarters and halves is a net with a quarter-turn picture on
each output: in the language of the dialogue, a tray of bells, each
seated one of the twenty-four ways.

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why local complementation, a
strange operation on graphs, rather than something simpler such as
deleting an edge? Because it is what the world does. Deleting an edge
needs a CZ, a gate on two wires; local complementation needs only
one-wire turns, so it is the move by which one-wire Cliffords can be
absorbed into the net. That is why the GSLC form is not unique, and why
the shrink of §16.4 can remove spiders without touching the rest.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Feynman's Notebook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{An operation older than the qubit.} Local complementation was not
invented for quantum states. Duncan, Kissinger, Perdrix and van de
Wetering credit it to Anton Kotzig, in a paper on Eulerian lines in
4-valent graphs, printed in the proceedings of the Colloquium on Graph
Theory held at Tihany in 1966, which appeared in 1968. Hein and
co-authors, writing in 2006 from Innsbruck, London, Pasadena and Leuven,
cite Bouchet for the operation, and Van den Nest, Dehaene and De Moor,
and Glynn, for its meaning in quantum terms: one-wire Cliffords on a
graph state are local complementations of its graph. The pictures came
later. Duncan and Perdrix derived the local complementation of graph
states in the ZX-calculus in a paper of 2009, ``Graph states and the
necessity of Euler decomposition'', and the pivot in ``Pivoting makes
the ZX-calculus complete for real stabilizers'', at the QPL workshop in
2014. By 2020 Duncan, Kissinger, Perdrix and van de Wetering had turned
both into the engine of a circuit simplifier: remove every interior
spider you can, by re-tying its neighbours.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-crabs-ledger}{%
\section{§16.4 The Crab's Ledger}\label{the-crabs-ledger}}

How much is there to write down, if we follow a quarter-turn machine by
its stabilizers?

Take the bow tie and write its five safe touches as five rows, one
letter per wire and a sign at the end. Then apply one Hadamard, to the
knot. By §16.1, \(H\) exchanges \(X\) and \(Z\) on its wire and turns
\(Y\) into \(-Y\). So each row changes only in the knot's column:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
row & before & after \(H_3\) \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(1\) & \(+\;X\,Z\,Z\,I\,I\) & \(+\;X\,Z\,X\,I\,I\) \\
\(2\) & \(+\;Z\,X\,Z\,I\,I\) & \(+\;Z\,X\,X\,I\,I\) \\
\(3\) & \(+\;Z\,Z\,X\,Z\,Z\) & \(+\;Z\,Z\,Z\,Z\,Z\) \\
\(4\) & \(+\;I\,I\,Z\,X\,Z\) & \(+\;I\,I\,X\,X\,Z\) \\
\(5\) & \(+\;I\,I\,Z\,Z\,X\) & \(+\;I\,I\,X\,Z\,X\) \\
\end{longtable}

Each new row fixes the new state \(H_3\ket{G_{\bowtie}}\), for the
reason in Gottesman's line: if \(K\ket\psi=\ket\psi\) then
\((UKU^{\dagger})(U\ket\psi)=U\ket\psi\). No amplitude was computed. The
new state is determined by the five rows, because they generate a group
of \(2^5\) Paulis that fix it (Result 16.11 (iii), (iv)).

\textbf{On the blackboard.} Store each letter as two bits, an \(x\)-bit
and a \(z\)-bit: \(I=00\), \(X=10\), \(Z=01\), \(Y=11\) (the pair \(11\)
stands for \(Y=iXZ\); any sign goes in the row's sign bit). A row on
\(n\) wires is then \(2n\) bits and one sign bit. The whole state is
\(n\) rows.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 16.12 (Knill's theorem; Gottesman 1998, Theorem 1,
stated).} ``Any quantum computer performing only: a) Clifford group
gates, b) measurements of Pauli group operators, and c) Clifford group
operations conditioned on classical bits, which may be the results of
earlier measurements, can be perfectly simulated in polynomial time on a
probabilistic classical computer.''
\end{quote}

Gottesman credits it to ``E. Knill, private communication''. Aaronson
and Gottesman call it ``the Gottesman-Knill theorem''. Here is the part
of its proof that concerns us, with the updates in full.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 16.13 (the ledger).} Let a stabilizer state on \(n\)
wires be recorded as \(n\) rows of signed Pauli strings that generate
its stabilizer group. Then: (i) after \(H\) on wire \(a\), each row has
its \(x\)- and \(z\)-bits on wire \(a\) exchanged, and its sign flipped
if both were \(1\); (ii) after \(S\) on wire \(a\), each row has its
sign flipped if both bits on wire \(a\) were \(1\), and then its
\(z\)-bit on wire \(a\) replaced by \(z\oplus x\); (iii) after a CNOT or
a CZ, each row changes only in the two columns of the gate; (iv) a
measurement of a Pauli string \(M\) that commutes with every row gives a
certain outcome, \(+1\) if \(M\) is in the group and \(-1\) if \(-M\)
is; a measurement of an \(M\) that anticommutes with some row gives each
outcome with probability \(\tfrac12\). The record has \(n(2n+1)\) bits.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} (i)--(iii): conjugation respects products, so it is enough
to know where the gate sends \(X\) and \(Z\) on its wires, which is
Gottesman's Table 1 (§16.1); the bit rules are those images written in
bits (the sidebar below). A gate on wires \(a\) and \(b\) conjugates a
string letter by letter, and only the letters on \(a\) and \(b\) change.
(iv) If \(M\) anticommutes with a row \(g\), then
\(\bra\psi M\ket\psi=\bra\psi Mg\ket\psi=-\bra\psi gM\ket\psi=-\bra\psi M\ket\psi\),
so \(\bra\psi M\ket\psi=0\), and the probability of reading \(+1\),
which is
\(\bigl\lVert\tfrac12(I+M)\ket\psi\bigr\rVert^2=\tfrac12\bigl(1+\bra\psi M\ket\psi\bigr)\),
is \(\tfrac12\). If \(M\) commutes with every row, then \(M\ket\psi\) is
fixed by every row, so by Result 16.11 (iv) (Result 16.7 (iv) for a
graph state) \(M\ket\psi=\lambda\ket\psi\), with \(\lambda=\pm1\) since
\(M^2=I\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch16/CrabsLedger.py},
which runs the ledger and the state vector side by side through random
quarter-turn circuits and checks every row after every gate.

On the bow tie, measuring \(K_3\) gives \(+1\) with certainty. Measuring
\(Z\) on the left-back bell gives each outcome half the time: \(Z_1\)
anticommutes with the row \(K_1\).

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Dirac's Blackboard.}\nopagebreak

\emph{The updates, bit by bit.} On one wire write a letter as \((x,z)\),
meaning \(i^{xz}X^xZ^z\), so that \((1,1)\) is \(iXZ=Y\). The Hadamard
sends \(X\mapsto Z\), \(Z\mapsto X\), \(Y\mapsto -Y\): in bits it swaps
\(x\) and \(z\), and flips the row's sign when \(x=z=1\). The phase gate
sends \(X\mapsto Y\), \(Y\mapsto -X\), \(Z\mapsto Z\):
\((1,0)\mapsto(1,1)\) with no sign, \((1,1)\mapsto(1,0)\) with a sign,
\((0,1)\) fixed. So: flip the sign when \(x=z=1\), then set
\(z:=z\oplus x\). These are Aaronson and Gottesman's rules (``set
\(r_i:=r_i\oplus x_{ia}z_{ia}\) and swap \(x_{ia}\) with \(z_{ia}\)'',
and ``\(z_{ia}:=z_{ia}\oplus x_{ia}\)''). For a CNOT from \(a\) to \(b\)
they give \(x_b:=x_b\oplus x_a\), \(z_a:=z_a\oplus z_b\), and a sign
flip when \(x_az_b(x_b\oplus z_a\oplus1)=1\). The count: \(n\) rows of
\(2n+1\) bits, \(n(2n+1)\) in all. For the bow tie, \(55\) bits against
\(32\) complex amplitudes; for a hundred bells, \(20\,100\) bits against
a list of amplitudes whose length has thirty-one digits.
\end{quote}

Aaronson and Gottesman improved the ledger. They add \(n\) more rows,
``destabilizer'' generators, at ``a cost of a factor-2 increase in the
number of bits'', \(2n(2n+1)\), and in return every measurement is
simulated in \(O(n^2)\) steps. They implemented it in a program they
called CHP (CNOT-Hadamard-Phase), which, their abstract says, ``can
handle thousands of qubits easily''. And they placed the problem
exactly. Deciding whether a given wire will read \(\ket1\) with
certainty after a given quarter-turn circuit is hard for the class
\(\oplus\mathrm{L}\) (``parity-L''), since circuits of CNOTs are a
special case; and it lies in \(\oplus\mathrm{L}\), their Theorem 4. So
it is \(\oplus\mathrm{L}\)-complete, which they read as ``strong
evidence that stabilizer circuits are not even universal for classical
computation''. We state these results and do not prove them.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Feynman's Notebook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{Whose theorem.} The result first appears as a report. Daniel
Gottesman's doctoral thesis at the California Institute of Technology,
\emph{Stabilizer Codes and Quantum Error Correction}, submitted on 21
May 1997, says in its section ``The Toffoli Gate'' that ``Knill {[}44{]}
has shown that a quantum computer using only elements from \(N(G)\) and
measurements can be simulated efficiently on a classical computer'', and
the reference reads ``E. Knill, personal communication''. The following
year Gottesman, then in the T-6 Group at Los Alamos National Laboratory,
wrote ``The Heisenberg Representation of Quantum Computers'', Los Alamos
preprint LAUR-98-2848, and stated the result as Theorem 1, ``Knill's
theorem'', citing ``E. Knill, private communication''. He drew the moral
in the next paragraph: the theorem ``implies that quantum computation is
only more powerful than classical computation when it uses gates outside
the Clifford group.'' Scott Aaronson and Gottesman, in a paper of 2004,
wrote of the conclusion ``sometimes known as the Gottesman-Knill
theorem'', and made it fast.
\end{quote}

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} A picture with no inputs and no outputs is a
number (Chapter 2). An amplitude \(\bra y C\ket{0\cdots0}\) of a
quarter-turn circuit \(C\) is such a picture: red points on the left,
red effects on the right, and \(C\) in quarter-turn spiders between. Van
de Wetering's survey (§6.5) shows how to find that number by rewriting
alone, using the two graph moves of §16.3 in a form for the inside of a
picture.

First, fuse and colour-change until the picture is a net: green spiders
joined only by ties. A spider is \textbf{interior} if it has no input or
output leg. Then:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Pull out a quarter.} An interior spider turned a quarter round
  (\(+\pi/2\)) or a quarter back (\(-\pi/2\)) can be removed: complement
  the ties among its neighbours, as in re-tying, and turn each neighbour
  a quarter the other way. A number is set aside. This is van de
  Wetering's eq. (102) and Duncan et al.'s Lemma 5.2.
\item
  \textbf{Pull out a pair of halves.} Two tied interior spiders whose
  turns are \(0\) or \(\pi\) can be removed together, by a pivot along
  their tie, with half-turns added to the neighbours (van de Wetering's
  eq. (103), Duncan et al.'s Lemma 5.3).
\item
  \textbf{A spider with no legs is a number}: a green spider with phase
  \(\alpha\) and no legs is \(1+e^{i\alpha}\), so \(2\) at rest, \(1+i\)
  at a quarter round, \(1-i\) at a quarter back, and \(0\) at a half.
\end{itemize}

We call this \textbf{the shrink}. For a closed quarter-turn picture, van
de Wetering explains, the procedure ``removes all spiders that have any
connection to another spider'', and what is left is a set of spiders
with no legs, whose product is the amplitude.

Here it is on the bow tie. Cap every output of its net with a green
effect turned a quarter round, \(\bra0+i\bra1\). Each cap fuses into its
bell (row 57), so every bell becomes an interior spider turned a quarter
round, and the picture is closed. Draw the bells as the bow tie itself:
the left wing on the left, the back bells on top, and the knot in the
middle. Pull out the left-back bell, top left: its neighbours, the
left-front bell and the knot, are tied, so the tie between them goes,
and each is turned a quarter back, which leaves both at rest; the
left-front bell is now alone. Then pull out the right-back bell in the
same way: the tie from the knot to the right-front bell goes, the knot
is turned to a quarter back, and the right-front bell comes to rest.
Each pull-out sets aside the number \(e^{i\pi/4}/2\) (the sidebar below
shows where it comes from).

\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.0em, y=1.0em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-2.7) (0,2.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.8) -- node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (0,-1.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.8) -- node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (3.0,0);
  \draw[wire] (0,-1.8) -- node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (3.0,0);
  \draw[wire] (3.0,0) -- node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (6.0,1.8);
  \draw[wire] (3.0,0) -- node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (6.0,-1.8);
  \draw[wire] (6.0,1.8) -- node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (6.0,-1.8);
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi/2$}}] at (0,1.8) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi/2$}}] at (0,-1.8) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi/2$}}] at (3.0,0) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi/2$}}] at (6.0,1.8) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi/2$}}] at (6.0,-1.8) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;\frac{e^{i\pi/4}}{2}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.0em, y=1.0em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},

  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
