\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 16.14 (the shrink of the bow tie).} Exactly,
\[\bigl(\bra0+i\bra1\bigr)^{\otimes5}\,\bigl(2^{-1/2}\ket{G_{\bowtie}}\bigr)\;=\;\left(\frac{e^{i\pi/4}}{2}\right)^{2}\cdot2\cdot(1-i)\cdot2\;=\;1+i .\]
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} In pictures, the chain above: two pull-outs, each setting
aside \(e^{i\pi/4}/2\), and three spiders with no legs, worth \(2\),
\(1-i\) and \(2\). \(\bigl(e^{i\pi/4}/2\bigr)^2=i/4\), and
\(\tfrac i4\cdot4(1-i)=1+i\). On the blackboard, the left side is
\(2^{-3}\sum_xi^{\lvert x\rvert}(-1)^{E(x)}\) over the \(32\) strings
\(x\), with \(\lvert x\rvert\) the number of \(1\)s, which also gives
\(1+i\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch16/CrabsLedger.py}, which
builds the three pictures and checks each against the one before, with
its number.

The number does not depend on the order of the pull-outs; pulling out
the knot first would give different pictures and the same \(1+i\). With
the caps at rest instead of turned, the closed net is exactly \(1\), and
pivots on pairs of halves shrink it to a number in the same way.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Coecke's Sketchbook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{Where the number comes from, and what the shrink does not do.} Sum
over the bit \(x_1\) of the pulled-out bell. Its two ties give
\(2^{-1}(-1)^{x_1(x_2+x_3)}\), and its quarter turn gives \(i^{x_1}\),
so the sum is \(\tfrac12\bigl(1+i(-1)^{x_2+x_3}\bigr)\). Check the four
cases: this equals
\(\tfrac12\sqrt2\,e^{i\pi/4}(-i)^{x_2}(-i)^{x_3}(-1)^{x_2x_3}\). The
factors \((-i)^{x_2}\) and \((-i)^{x_3}\) are the quarter-back turns on
the neighbours. The factor \((-1)^{x_2x_3}\) cancels the sign of the tie
between them, which leaves that tie's \(2^{-1/2}\) outside. In all,
\(\tfrac12\cdot\sqrt2\,e^{i\pi/4}\cdot2^{-1/2}=e^{i\pi/4}/2\). Van de
Wetering is candid that the rules in his survey are not
``scalar-accurate'', and that the Gottesman--Knill theorem ``also states
that you can efficiently calculate marginal probabilities as well, which
our procedure in its current form does not do''; for that he points to
the doubled pictures of Chapter 9. So the shrink computes amplitudes of
closed pictures, one number at a time. The ledger computes the odds of
readings. And the claim that the shrink takes polynomially many steps is
the sources' count of moves, each removing a spider; a rewrite proves an
equality, not a running time.
\end{quote}

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why keep a ledger of stabilizers
rather than of amplitudes? Because a quarter-turn gate sends each row to
a single row, so the ledger never grows: \(n\) rows before, \(n\) rows
after, each updated by a rule a clerk can apply. The amplitudes of the
same state are \(2^n\) numbers, and a gate mixes them. The ledger is
small because the world is closed: what goes in as a Pauli string comes
out as a Pauli string.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{an-eighth}{%
\section{§16.5 An Eighth}\label{an-eighth}}

So the world of quarters and halves can be followed on paper, in the
ledger or by the shrink. The eighth-turn is the gate
\[T\;=\;\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\] a green
\(\pi/4\) dot in pictures (Chapter 15, row 114). Two eighths make a
quarter: \(T^2=S\).

\textbf{On the blackboard.} Follow the front tip:
\[TXT^{\dagger}\;=\;\begin{pmatrix}0&e^{-i\pi/4}\\ e^{i\pi/4}&0\end{pmatrix}\;=\;\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(X+Y).\]

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 16.15 (\(T\) is not a Clifford).}
\(TXT^{\dagger}=(X+Y)/\sqrt2\), which is not a phase times a Pauli
string, so \(T\notin\mathcal C_1\). On the octahedron, \(T\) turns the
solid an eighth of a whole turn about the up--down axis: the front tip
\(+X\) goes to the direction \((1,1,0)/\sqrt2\), the midpoint of the
edge between the tips \(+X\) and \(+Y\). The up and down tips stay where
they are, but the four tips round the middle all land on edge midpoints,
so the solid is not seated. \(T^2=S\) is a quarter-turn, and a Clifford.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} The matrix product above, and \(X+Y\) has two non-zero
Pauli components, while a phase times a Pauli has one. \(T\) is
diagonal, so it fixes \(Z\); on the \(X\)--\(Y\) plane it acts as the
rotation by \(\pi/4\), since
\(T(\cos\varphi\,X+\sin\varphi\,Y)T^{\dagger}=\cos(\varphi+\tfrac\pi4)X+\sin(\varphi+\tfrac\pi4)Y\)
(the diagonal entries of the matrix above carry the angle).
\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch16/AnEighth.py}.

A word on names. \(T\) is often called the \(\pi/8\) gate, because
\(T=e^{i\pi/8}\,\mathrm{diag}(e^{-i\pi/8},e^{i\pi/8})\). Gottesman's
list of gates that complete the Clifford group includes ``a \(\pi/8\)
rotation of the Bloch sphere'' (1998) and ``the single-qubit \(\pi/8\)
rotation'' (thesis); those are his words. What \(T\) does to the
octahedron, and so to the sphere, is the turn by \(\pi/4\) just
computed: an eighth of a whole turn.

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} An eighth is a green spider with phase
\(\pi/4\), and the shrink cannot touch it. Cap every output of the bow
tie's net with a green effect turned an eighth,
\(\bra0+e^{i\pi/4}\bra1\). Every bell fuses into an interior spider
turned an eighth. Neither move of the shrink applies: a pull-out needs a
quarter, and a pair needs halves.
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.0em, y=1.0em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-2.7) (0,2.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.8) -- node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (0,-1.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.8) -- node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (3.0,0);
  \draw[wire] (0,-1.8) -- node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (3.0,0);
  \draw[wire] (3.0,0) -- node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (6.0,1.8);
  \draw[wire] (3.0,0) -- node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (6.0,-1.8);
  \draw[wire] (6.0,1.8) -- node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (6.0,-1.8);
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi/4$}}] at (0,1.8) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi/4$}}] at (0,-1.8) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi/4$}}] at (3.0,0) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi/4$}}] at (6.0,1.8) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi/4$}}] at (6.0,-1.8) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;\frac18\sum_{x}e^{i\pi\lvert x\rvert/4}(-1)^{E(x)}\;=\;\frac{3\sqrt2-4}{8}+\frac{\sqrt2-2}{8}\,i .\]
The picture is still a number, and the blackboard finds it by adding
\(32\) terms. The shrink stops before it starts. That is not a proof
that no clever method could find the number quickly. It is a statement
about these moves: they were built for quarters and halves.
\texttt{Code/Ch16/AnEighth.py} runs PyZX's quarter-turn simplifier on
the picture above and checks that it stops with all five eighth-turn
spiders left inside.

\hypertarget{bringing-the-eighth-in-from-outside}{%
\subsection{Bringing the eighth in from
outside}\label{bringing-the-eighth-in-from-outside}}

If the world cannot make an eighth, perhaps it can be given one, ready
made. Write
\[\ket\mu\;=\;T\ket+\;=\;\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket0+e^{i\pi/4}\ket1\bigr)\]
for the \textbf{magic state}. The name is Bravyi and Kitaev's, and so is
the idea that such states, supplied from outside, are all that
quarter-turn machines lack. Van de Wetering's survey (§5.3) gives the
\textbf{injection}, which moves the eighth from \(\ket\mu\) onto any
state.

Take a data wire in any state \(\ket\psi=\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1\) and a
second wire in \(\ket\mu\). Apply a CNOT, control on the data wire,
target on the magic wire, and read the magic wire in the basis
\(\ket0,\ket1\). Before stating the result, compute:
\[\mathrm{CNOT}\bigl(\ket\psi\ket\mu\bigr)\;=\;\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\Bigl(\bigl(\alpha\ket0+e^{i\pi/4}\beta\ket1\bigr)\ket0+\bigl(e^{i\pi/4}\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1\bigr)\ket1\Bigr).\]
If the reading is \(0\), the data wire holds
\(\alpha\ket0+e^{i\pi/4}\beta\ket1=T\ket\psi\). If it is \(1\), it holds
\(e^{i\pi/4}\bigl(\alpha\ket0+e^{-i\pi/4}\beta\ket1\bigr)=e^{i\pi/4}T^{\dagger}\ket\psi\),
the eighth turned the wrong way. A quarter mends it: \(ST^{\dagger}=T\).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 16.16 (injection).} For every data state \(\ket\psi\),
exactly: projecting the magic wire onto \(\bra0\) leaves
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}T\ket\psi\) on the data wire; projecting it onto
\(\bra1\) and then applying \(S\) leaves
\(\tfrac{e^{i\pi/4}}{\sqrt2}T\ket\psi\). The probability of reading
\(0\) on the magic wire is \(\tfrac12\), and so is the probability of
reading \(1\). Either way the data wire ends in \(T\ket\psi\), up to a
phase, and the magic state is used up.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} The computation above, with the \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\)
carried along; each branch has length \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\), so
probability \(\tfrac12\). In pictures, with the bit \(a\) of the reading
written into the phases as in Chapter 10 (row 75): the magic state is a
green \(\pi/4\) point, which is \(\sqrt2\ket\mu\); the CNOT is the
green--red pair (row 64), bare \(\mathrm{CNOT}/\sqrt2\); the reading is
a red effect with phase \(a\pi\), which is \(\sqrt2\bra a\); and the
correction is a green \(a\pi/2\) on the data wire. Together the pieces
carry \(\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2/\sqrt2=\sqrt2\). For \(a=0\) the red effect
fuses into the red dot of the pair (fusion, row 57), leaving a
phase-free red dot with two legs, which is a plain wire (§8.2); the
green point then fuses into the green dot on the data wire. For \(a=1\)
the fused red dot is a red \(\pi\) with two legs, which is \(X\); pushed
into the green point it turns the point's phase to \(-\pi/4\) and sets
aside \(e^{i\pi/4}\), since
\(X(\ket0+e^{i\pi/4}\ket1)=e^{i\pi/4}(\ket0+e^{-i\pi/4}\ket1)\)
(\(\pi\)-commutation with its number, as in Chapter 14); the point fuses
into the data wire with \(-\pi/4\), and the green quarter fuses on top,
\(-\pi/4+\pi/2=\pi/4\):
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.74em, x=1.1em, y=1.1em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1.1) (0,2.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.8) -- (5.4,1.8);
  \draw[wire] (0.3,0) -- (3.9,0);
  \draw[wire] (2.0,1.8) -- (2.0,0);
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]left:{$\pi/4$}}] at (0.3,0) {};
  \node[zsp] at (2.0,1.8) {};
  \node[xsp] at (2.0,0) {};
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]below:{$a\pi$}}] at (3.9,0) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$a\pi/2$}}] at (3.9,1.8) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;e^{ia\pi/4}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.74em, x=1.1em, y=1.1em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1.1) (0,2.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.8) -- (2.6,1.8);
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi/4$}}] at (1.3,1.8) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] and the right side is \(e^{ia\pi/4}\,T\), which is
\(\sqrt2\) times the branch on the blackboard. \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch16/AnEighth.py}, which checks both branches on a random
non-real \(\ket\psi\).

The picture shows the eighth travelling: from the magic point, through
the tie, onto the data wire. It also shows why a quarter is the right
correction: the red half on the reading flips the eighth, and the
difference between an eighth forward and an eighth back is a quarter,
which the world of quarters can supply.

Bravyi and Kitaev use different letters, and we will not borrow them.
Their \(T\) is a Clifford that turns the octahedron a third of a turn,
cycling its three axes; their \(\ket T\) is one kind of magic state, and
their \(\ket H\) another; they write a general state as
\(\ket{A_{\theta}}=2^{-1/2}(\ket0+e^{i\theta}\ket1)\) (their eq. (2)).
Our \(\ket\mu\) is their \(\ket{A_{\pi/4}}\), and it is of their
``H-type''. Van de Wetering's magic state is \(\ket0+e^{i\pi/4}\ket1\),
which is \(\sqrt2\ket\mu\).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 16.17 (magic and universality; Gottesman and
Bravyi--Kitaev, stated, not proved).} The quarter-turn gates together
with \(T\) generate a set of unitaries dense in all unitaries: in
Gottesman's words, ``the Clifford group plus an appropriate extra gate
generate a set of unitary operators dense in \(U(2^n)\)''. Bravyi and
Kitaev show (their §III) that a supply of one H-type magic state lets
quarter-turn machines apply the phase gate \(\Lambda(e^{-i\pi/4})\),
which is our \(T^{\dagger}\): ``It does not belong to the Clifford
group'', and the subgroup of \(U(2)\) it generates together with the
one-wire Cliffords ``is dense in \(U(2)\)''. Our \(\ket\mu\) is H-type
too, and it gives \(T\) directly, by the injection above. On the
octahedron, their magic states point to the centres of its faces (\(8\)
of their ``T-type'') and the midpoints of its edges (\(12\) of
``H-type''); \(\ket\mu\) points to the edge midpoint between \(+X\) and
\(+Y\).
\end{quote}

The octahedron plays a second role in their paper. Write a one-wire
mixed state as \(\tfrac12(I+\rho_xX+\rho_yY+\rho_zZ)\). If
\(\lvert\rho_x\rvert+\lvert\rho_y\rvert+\lvert\rho_z\rvert\le1\), the
point \((\rho_x,\rho_y,\rho_z)\) lies inside the octahedron whose tips
are the six stabilizer states, the state is a mixture of those six, and
a quarter-turn machine fed with it can be simulated efficiently (their
Theorem 1). Outside the octahedron things change. They show that noisy
copies of a magic state can be purified by quarter-turn operations
alone, a process now called \textbf{distillation}, provided the
polarization along a magic direction exceeds a threshold, ``about 65\%''
in their abstract. We name distillation and do not describe it.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Feynman's Notebook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{Why ``magic''.} Sergey Bravyi and Alexei Kitaev, at the Institute
for Quantum Information at Caltech, wrote ``Universal quantum
computation with ideal Clifford gates and noisy ancillas'' in 2004. They
imagined hardware in which the quarter-turn gates are nearly perfect,
protected, for instance, by the topology of exotic two-dimensional
materials whose excitations are anyons, while everything else is noisy.
Such a machine can only be as powerful as its one noisy ingredient: a
supply of ancilla qubits in some mixed state \(\rho\). Their question
was for which \(\rho\) it becomes universal. Their answer turned on
special states with two properties at once: fed to the perfect gates,
they give universality, and noisy copies of them can be purified by the
perfect gates alone. ``It is a rather surprising coincidence that one
and the same state can comprise both of these properties,'' they wrote,
``and that is the reason why we call them magic states.'' The
quarter-turn machine is a notebook's plaything; with a trickle of magic
it is a quantum computer.
\end{quote}

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why a state and not a gate? Because
the world of quarters can do everything except the eighth, including
prepare, entangle, read and correct. So the eighth need only be made
once, somewhere, as a state, perhaps slowly and with effort, and then
fed in. Injection turns a supply of states into a supply of gates. The
cost of a computation then moves to one place: how many magic states it
consumes.

\hypertarget{the-theorem-twice-16}{%
\section{§16.7 The Theorem, Twice}\label{the-theorem-twice-16}}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 16.6 (the stabilizers of a graph state), restated.} Let
\(G=(V,E)\) be a graph with \(n\ge1\) vertices,
\(\ket G=U_G\ket+^{\otimes n}\), and for each vertex \(a\) let
\(K_a=X_a\prod_{b\in N_a}Z_b\). Then for every \(a\), exactly,
\[K_a\ket G\;=\;\ket G .\]
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{diracs-blackboard-16}{%
\subsection{Dirac's Blackboard}\label{diracs-blackboard-16}}

\textbf{Step 1: the empty graph.} \(X\ket+=\ket+\), so
\(X_a\ket+^{\otimes n}=\ket+^{\otimes n}\): the start is fixed by
\(X_a\) alone.

\textbf{Step 2: through the ties.} For an edge at \(a\),
\(\mathrm{CZ}_{ab}\,X_a\,\mathrm{CZ}_{ab}=X_aZ_b\) (the Dirac's
Blackboard sidebar of §16.2: on \(\ket{x_ax_b}\) the two signs multiply
to \((-1)^{x_b}\)). For an edge \(\{b,c\}\) not at \(a\),
\(\mathrm{CZ}_{bc}\) acts on other wires and commutes with \(X_a\).
Every CZ is diagonal and commutes with every \(Z\). So, pushing \(X_a\)
through the CZs of \(U_G\) one at a time, and using
\(\mathrm{CZ}^{\dagger}=\mathrm{CZ}\),
\[U_G\,X_a\,U_G^{\dagger}\;=\;X_a\prod_{b\in N_a}Z_b\;=\;K_a .\]

\textbf{Step 3: conclude.}
\[K_a\ket G\;=\;U_GX_aU_G^{\dagger}\,U_G\ket+^{\otimes n}\;=\;U_G\,X_a\ket+^{\otimes n}\;=\;U_G\ket+^{\otimes n}\;=\;\ket G .\qquad\blacksquare\]

\hypertarget{coeckes-sketchbook-10}{%
\subsection{Coecke's Sketchbook}\label{coeckes-sketchbook-10}}

Draw the part of the net of \(G\) around the vertex \(a\): its green
spider, its output with a clip ring, and its ties, each with a yellow
box, to its neighbours \(b_1,\dots,b_k\), each with its own output and
clip ring. A short stub on each neighbour stands for its other ties,
which play no part. The touch puts a red \(\pi\) on \(a\)'s clip ring
and a green \(\pi\) on each neighbour's. Each step names its rule. In
the pictures below \(a\) is at the bottom left, two neighbours stand for
all of them, and every dot drawn on a tie carries a half, \(\pi\).

\textbf{Step 1: push the half into \(a\)} (Result 16.5, row 120).
\(a\)'s spider is phase-free, and its legs are its output and its ties.
The red \(\pi\) leaves the output and appears on every tie, next to
\(a\). The output's clip ring is left at rest.

\textbf{Step 2: through the boxes} (colour change, Theorem 8.2, row 58).
A red \(\pi\) followed by a yellow box is the yellow box followed by a
green \(\pi\): \(XH=HZ\), which is Theorem 8.2 on a two-legged dot with
\(H^2=I\) used on one side. Each half crosses its box and turns green.

\textbf{Step 3: meet the neighbour's half} (fusion, Theorem 8.1, row
57). On each tie the green \(\pi\) now stands next to the neighbour's
green spider, and slides into it. The neighbour's own clip ring carries
a green \(\pi\) too, on the other side of the spider. Fusion, read both
ways, lets the spider and its ring share their turns as they like:
together they carry \(\pi+\pi=2\pi\), which is no turn. So the neighbour
is phase-free again and its ring is at rest.

\textbf{Step 4: read off.} What is left is the untouched net, with every
clip ring at rest. A ring at rest is a plain wire (§8.2), so this is the
bare net, and nothing was set aside at any step: the push costs nothing
(Result 16.5), and so do colour change and fusion. The touched net
equals the bare net, exactly, which is \(K_a\ket G=\ket G\) multiplied
on both sides by the net's number \(2^{(v-e)/2}\) (Result 16.4).
\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch16/SafeTouches.py}, which carries
out these moves as edits of the picture, checking the value after each.

\hypertarget{the-verdict-16}{%
\subsection{The verdict}\label{the-verdict-16}}

A draw, and the chapter says so. The blackboard proof is three lines,
and Step 2 is one identity for one tie, repeated. The sketchbook proof
is one push and a slide, and it shows something the algebra compresses:
\emph{why} the \(Z\)s land where they do. The half on \(a\) runs out
along every tie, and each tie carries it to exactly one neighbour. The
pattern of the touch is the pattern of the net.

What the blackboard gives that the picture does not is everything around
the headline. That the \(K_a\) commute, that they generate \(2^n\)
touches the state does not notice, that the state is the only one they
all fix, and that the states \(Z^{\mathbf b}\ket G\) form a basis: those
are Result 16.7, proved with operators and counting. The picture proves
that each touch goes unnoticed. The algebra proves that together they
name the state.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-touched-bow-tie}{%
\section{§16.8 The Touched Bow Tie}\label{the-touched-bow-tie}}

Here is the chapter's master diagram: the net of the bow tie, with a
clip ring on every output, touched at the knot. On the blackboard it is
\[K_3\,\bigl(2^{-1/2}\ket{G_{\bowtie}}\bigr),\qquad K_3=Z\otimes Z\otimes X\otimes Z\otimes Z .\]
It is drawn with its clip rings \textbf{unfused}, so that the touch sits
on the outputs as separate pieces, one ring per bell, as the dialogue's
brass rings sit on the pulls of the bell-tray.

From top to bottom, the bells in ket order: the left-back bell, the
left-front bell, the knot, the right-back bell and the right-front bell,
each a phase-free green spider. On the left, the ties, each with its
yellow box: a short arc from the left-back bell to the left-front bell,
a short arc from the left-front bell to the knot, and a longer arc
outside them from the left-back bell to the knot; then, below, a short
arc from the knot to the right-back bell, a short arc from the
right-back bell to the right-front bell, and a longer arc outside them
from the knot to the right-front bell. On the right, each bell's pull:
an inner length from the bell to its clip ring, and an outer length from
the clip ring to the output. The knot's clip ring is a red \(\pi\). The
clip rings of the left-back, left-front, right-back and right-front
bells are green \(\pi\)s. We call the picture \textbf{The Touched Bow
Tie}.

No two ties cross, and no tie crosses a pull: the knot's four ties leave

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 16.18 (The Touched Bow Tie).} Exactly,
\[\text{The Touched Bow Tie}\;=\;2^{-1/2}\,\ket{G_{\bowtie}},\] the same
as the untouched net with every clip ring at rest. The number
\(2^{-1/2}\) is the net's own, \(2^{(5-6)/2}\) for five bells and six
ties.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} \textbf{On the blackboard.} The clip rings are
\(Z\otimes Z\otimes X\otimes Z\otimes Z=K_3\) on the outputs of the net,
which is \(2^{-1/2}\ket{G_{\bowtie}}\) (Result 16.4). By Result 16.6,
\(K_3\ket{G_{\bowtie}}=\ket{G_{\bowtie}}\).

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} The chain of §16.7 at \(a=3\), with the four
neighbours \(1,2,4,5\). The red \(\pi\) on the knot's ring goes into the
knot and out along its four ties (row 120), leaving the knot's ring at
rest. Each half crosses its yellow box and turns green (row 58): on the
arcs to the left-back and right-front bells, and on the short arcs to
the left-front and right-back bells. Each reaches a wing bell and meets
the green \(\pi\) on that bell's ring: \(\pi+\pi=0\) (row 57), four
times. The ties between the wing bells, the arcs from left-back to
left-front and from right-back to right-front, are never touched. Every
ring is at rest, the picture is the untouched net, and no number was set
aside. \(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch16/SafeTouches.py}, which
builds this picture, counts its lines, checks that it equals the
untouched net, and checks that the touch with the colours exchanged,
green on the knot and red on the wings, is not the net.

The touch changed every ring on the tray, and the net did not notice.
Touched at a wing bell instead, say the left-back, the picture has a red
\(\pi\) on that bell's ring and green \(\pi\)s on the rings of the
left-front bell and the knot only; the chain is the same, with two ties
instead of four.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{what-the-pictures-leave-to-the-blackboard-1}{%
\section{§16.9 What the Pictures Leave to the
Blackboard}\label{what-the-pictures-leave-to-the-blackboard-1}}

Take stock. The Pauli strings on \(n\) wires form a group of
\(4\cdot4^n\) elements, any two of which commute or anticommute (Result
16.1). The Cliffords are the unitaries that send Paulis to Paulis; on
one wire there are twenty-four of them, the rotations of an octahedron
(Result 16.2), and on many wires \(H\), \(S\) and CNOT generate them
(Result 16.3). In pictures a graph state is a net with a known number
(Result 16.4), and a half pushed through a phase-free spider comes out
on every other leg (Result 16.5). A graph state is fixed by its safe
touches (Result 16.6, the headline, proved twice), which generate a
group of \(2^n\) Paulis that names the state (Result 16.7). Half a touch
re-ties the net (Results 16.8 and 16.9), three re-tyings make a pivot
(Result 16.10), and every state of the world is a net with a
quarter-turn picture on each output (Result 16.11). Knill's theorem
(Result 16.12) is made practical by the ledger (Result 16.13), and a
closed quarter-turn picture shrinks to a number (Result 16.14). The
eighth is not a Clifford (Result 16.15), but a magic state brings it in
(Result 16.16), and with it every unitary can be approximated (Result
16.17). The Touched Bow Tie is the untouched net (Result 16.18).

Now the honest part. \textbf{The world of quarters and halves belongs,
in the end, to the blackboard.} The headline was a draw. But the
following have no string-diagram proof in this chapter: that the
stabilizers generate a group of \(2^n\) elements and name the state; the
exact phase of the LC-rule and of the pivot; that the ledger follows
every quarter-turn circuit, including its measurements, and with what
odds; Aaronson and Gottesman's tableau, canonical form and
\(\oplus\mathrm{L}\)-completeness; the density of the quarter-turn gates
with \(T\); and distillation. The pictures of re-tying and pivoting were
proved on the blackboard and checked by matrix, not derived by
rewriting; their derivations are Duncan and Perdrix's. The shrink is a
genuine pictorial computation, but it computes amplitudes of closed
pictures, one at a time; marginal probabilities need the doubled
pictures of Chapter 9. And its speed, like every speed, is a count of
steps taken from the sources. A rewrite proves that two processes are
equal. It proves nothing about how long anything takes, and it did not
prove that the eighth is hard: only that these moves cannot remove it.

What the pictures do show is the shape of the world. A quarter-turn
state is a net with a quarter-turn picture on each output (Result
16.11), and a quarter on one wire can be traded for a re-tying of the
net (Result 16.9). That is why the world is small: the only information
is which vertices are tied and how each output is seated. And it is why
the eighth is a different kind of thing, not a finer quarter. It leaves
the octahedron unseated, and it leaves the shrink with nothing to pull.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

The chapter's question has an answer. A machine built only of
quarter-turns and half-turns can entangle as much as it likes, and still
a clerk can follow it: not by writing down its state, which would need
more numbers than any notebook holds, but by writing down the touches
its state would not notice. Those touches form a small group, one row
per wire, and every quarter-turn gate moves each row to a single new
row. In pictures the same world is a net of spiders, and any closed
picture of it can be shrunk, spider by spider, to a number. The
eighth-turn escapes both: it sends a Pauli to a mixture of two, and it
sits inside a picture where no move can reach it. With nothing but
quarters a machine is paper. With quarters and a supply of eighths it
can approximate any computation at all. The difference matters so much
because it is the whole difference.

That leaves the next question. If the quarters are free and the eighths
are the cost, then a circuit should be written with as few eighths as
possible. Chapter 17, \emph{Compiling by Rewriting}, takes a whole
circuit, turns it into a net, and shrinks it with the moves of this
chapter. What is left behind is only its eighths. How few can it be made
to need?

\hypertarget{uxe9tude-in-simplification}{%
\chapter{Étude in Simplification}\label{uxe9tude-in-simplification}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\emph{物干しや}\\
\emph{雫寄り合ふ}\\
\emph{春隣}

\emph{monohoshi ya}\\
\emph{shizuku yoriau}\\
\emph{haru-donari}

\emph{The clothesline in rain ---}\\
\emph{drops slide into each other,}\\
\emph{and spring is next door.}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\emph{{[}The Crab's kitchen, early on the afternoon of the next day.
Rain drums on the roof of the scullery end. At the deal table the
Tortoise sits with her work-bag at her feet; on the table stand the
teapot, a stiff card, and something low and heavy under a cloth. The
back door opens, and Achilles comes in out of the rain, dripping.{]}}

\emph{{[}The kitchen he comes into is long, and warm from end to end. At
the scullery end, under the drumming roof, are the stone sink and the
one window, and the outside of the glass is covered with small drops,
each one by itself, none touching another, and new ones landing in the
spaces between. At the far end the range has been alight since before
dawn: the oven is shut, the fire door stands a finger's width ajar and
lets a warm light out across the hearth, and at the back of the hot
plate a big stockpot, its lid on, mutters to itself; the copper pans
hang on their nails on the wall behind. Between the two ends stands the
deal table, and along the long wall the dresser holds the Crab's cups
and, on its top shelf, a row of preserves in jars, each a summer's
picking cooked down to a few dark inches. Over the range, in a plain
dark frame, hangs a print: Escher's \textup{Development I}, plain
squares that change, step by step, into interlocking figures. The warmth
of the range keeps its glass clear while the window at the other end
runs with rain. It hung there before the rain set in this morning, and
it will hang there when the rain has gone.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} The thaw's turned to rain, and the rain's turned
serious. I came the field way, and most of the field came with me.

\textbf{Crab:} Off with that scarf before it waters my floor. There's a
rail on the range; hang it there and it'll be dry before you go.

\emph{{[}Achilles unwinds his scarf and hangs it on the range rail.{]}}

\emph{{[}He stays by the range a moment with his hands spread behind him
to the warmth, and the scarf on the rail begins at once to smell of warm
wet wool. Behind him, the back door has been shut on the weather, and
the rain goes back to being a sound on the roof.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} I came by the lane and only my shell got wet, which
is what it's for.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}sniffing{]}} Something in that oven smells
warm and good. What is it?

\textbf{Crab:} Three tins, set in the warm oven since dawn. Not for
eating; you'll see.

\textbf{Achilles:} ``Not for eating'' is a cruel thing to say to a wet
man in a warm kitchen.

\textbf{Crab:} There's bread and tea for eating, and you shall have
both. \emph{{[}He pours for all three, and sets the pot down at the
right-hand end of the table as the bench on its range side faces it.{]}}
Sit where you can see the beam.

\emph{{[}Achilles sits on the bench that runs along the range side of
the table, at the Tortoise's left, facing the scullery end, his back to
the range, and looks up. At the scullery end a stout beam crosses
overhead, and from hooks at its ends a long tangle of green curtain
rings and cord hangs in two lines, one above the other.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} The long picture I promised you. I tied it last night
from this card: the card's recipe, hung up in rings and cords, every
step of it. This afternoon I mean to cook it down.

\emph{{[}There are hooks at both ends of the beam: an upper left hook
and an upper right hook on the beam itself, and a lower left hook and a
lower right hook on short drops below them. Every ring in the tangle is
green. Every cord is knotted at both its ends, to a ring or to a hook;
none passes through a ring.{]}}

\emph{{[}The upper line. Its left lead runs plain from the upper left
hook to a small green ring. From that first small ring a cord in a
yellow sleeve runs to a second small ring. From the second small ring a
sleeved cord runs to a big green ring. From the big ring the upper
line's right lead runs plain to the upper right hook.{]}}

\emph{{[}The lower line. Its left lead runs plain from the lower left
hook to the first eighth ring, a green ring whose bead is set an eighth
round. From the first eighth ring a sleeved cord runs to the first plain
ring, a green ring at rest. Another runs from the first plain ring to
the second eighth ring; another from the second eighth ring to the
second plain ring; another from the second plain ring to the third
eighth ring; another from the third eighth ring to the third plain ring;
another from the third plain ring to the fourth eighth ring; and another
from the fourth eighth ring to the fourth plain ring. From the fourth
plain ring the lower line's right lead runs to the lower right hook, and
it too wears a yellow sleeve.{]}}

\emph{{[}From the big ring the ties hang down in a fan, each in its own
yellow sleeve: a tie from the big ring to the first plain ring, a tie
from the big ring to the second plain ring, a tie from the big ring to
the third plain ring, and a tie from the big ring to the fourth plain
ring. Nothing crosses.{]}}

\emph{{[}The window's grey light comes in under the beam and lies along
the lower line, cord after cord; the range's warmer light, from the far
end of the kitchen, catches the upper line, and the ties of the fan
between them take a little of each. Every yellow sleeve is a short
bright collar on its cord. In the warm air off the range nothing in the
tangle stirs, and the rain drums on the roof just above it.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} It looks like washing hung out by somebody very
particular.

\textbf{Crab:} It took me till midnight. \emph{{[}He slides the stiff
card across the table.{]}} And that is what I tied it from.

\textbf{Achilles:} I'll read it when I've stopped dripping on it.

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}lifting the cloth from the low heavy thing
beside the teapot, at the very end of the table: beneath it, a
griddle-like press with a slotted rim, and beside it a second row of
empty hooks, facing the bench{]}} And my koekpan --- you remember; still
shy. A copy goes on it, it presses, and whatever it makes hangs on those
second hooks; the thing you copied stays where it is. \emph{{[}He lays
the cloth back over it.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} I remember it jams if anyone watches it.

\textbf{Crab:} It likes being watched less than ever. I've had it longer
than I've had this kitchen, and I have never once seen it work.

\emph{{[}Under its cloth again the koekpan sits beside the teapot like a
sleeping thing: a broad flat press of old Delft iron, its face worn to a
soft shine by years of hands, its handle dark where a claw has held it,
the maker's mark cast into its rim and worn nearly smooth. With nobody
turned its way it gives off a warmth of its own, and a low sound at the
very edge of hearing, like a kettle a long way from the boil. Achilles
turns his head to catch it, and it is not there; he looks back into his
cup, and it steals up again.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}setting her work-bag on the bench beside
her{]}} I've brought my cloth, in case the pan wants company.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}wrapping both hands round his cup{]}} This
is the first thing all day that's been warmer than I am.

\textbf{Crab:} Then drink it before it changes its mind.

\emph{{[}The Crab sets a plate of bread and butter by the teapot and
draws up his own chair. Achilles eats two slices without noticing that
he has, and the colour comes back into the hands round his cup. The
Tortoise tucks her feet in under the bench, and the rain keeps up its
one sound on the scullery roof.{]}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{first-challenge-four-eighths}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{First Challenge --- \emph{Four
Eighths}}{First Challenge --- Four Eighths}}\label{first-challenge-four-eighths}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}picking up the card and reading aloud{]}}
``An eighth on the lower line, then a joiner from the upper line to the
lower. Four times over.'' \emph{{[}He counts on his fingers.{]}} Four
eighths. And yesterday every eighth was the dear part.

\textbf{Crab:} Every one of them made slowly, on the bench, and used up
the moment it's tied on. A card with four is a dear card.

\textbf{Achilles:} And a joiner?

\textbf{Tortoise:} Yesterday's joiner: a green ring on the upper line,
tied by a short length to a red ring on the lower. If the upper line is
lit, it flips the lower; if the upper is dark, it leaves the lower be.
It's the commonest step on any card.

\textbf{Achilles:} The controlled flip, from the snow. I remember it.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}pleasantly{]}} The joiners come in pairs.
What do they do to each other?

\textbf{Achilles:} They cancel. Flip and flip back. So it's just four
eighths on the lower line: a half.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Then follow the card with the upper line lit and the
lower dark, and tell me where the eighths land.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}running his finger along the card{]}} The
first eighth sees the lower line dark, so it does nothing. The first
joiner sees the upper lit and lights the lower. The second eighth sees
it lit, and turns. The second joiner darkens it again.

\textbf{Crab:} And the rest?

\textbf{Achilles:} The third eighth sees dark and does nothing; the
third joiner lights it; the fourth eighth turns; the fourth joiner
darkens it. \emph{{[}His finger stops at the end of the card.{]}} Two of
them turned. A quarter --- and on the upper line's account. \ldots Oh.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The joiners cancel only with nothing between them. On
this card there's always an eighth between.

\emph{{[}By the back door the latch lies in its keep where it lay before
Achilles lifted it, and the draught he let in has been shut out again.
But on the flags just inside the sill the rain that blew in while the
door stood open lies in a puddle, and the mat beside it is dark with
what came in on his boots.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} So it isn't a half on the lower line at all. What the
lower line gets depends on the upper. \emph{{[}He turns the card over,
as if the answer might be on the back.{]}} Then how does the card come
apart, if not in pairs?

\textbf{Tortoise:} Not apart. Into a net. \emph{{[}She lifts her
drawing-cloth out of her work-bag and spreads it on the table in front
of Achilles, its near edge on his side and its right-hand end towards
the teapot, then brings out string, her little box of rings with their
beads, each ring opening at a small hinge so that it clips on or off a
cord anywhere, and her yellow tubes, each slit along its length to clip
on.{]}} My drawing-cloth, and my rings and tubes, as ever: what I lay on
it is a picture of a thing, not the thing. And the old rule for the
tubes: a ring with a tube on every cord comes out the other colour, its
bead where it was; and two tubes in a row are no tube at all, so I may
put a pair on anywhere I like.

\emph{{[}She lays a long cord across the drawing-cloth from Achilles's
left to his right, and another below it, nearer him: the upper line and
the lower. Along the lower she lays the card's steps from the left: a
green ring with its bead set an eighth round, an eighth of the way
clockwise from the ring's far side as Achilles looks down, where a bead
at rest sits; then a red ring at rest, tied by a short string straight
up to a green ring at rest on the upper line, a joiner; then another
eighth, and another joiner; another eighth, another joiner; another
eighth, and a joiner last. What lies on the cloth: the card, step for
step, in green and red, every cord plain. Every string she ties this
afternoon she leaves slack, long enough to follow its rings wherever
they slide.{]}}

\begin{center}
\cardcloth*{The card, laid out}
\end{center}

\emph{{[}The cloth as it stands: on the lower line each red ring has a
cord running left along the line, a cord running right, and a short
string up to its green. On each of a red ring's cords the Tortoise clips
a tube and another beside it, which changes nothing. Then she draws the
ring through the near tube of every pair: the tubes go into it and are
gone, and the ring comes out green, its bead still at rest. The far tube
of each pair stays on its cord. She does the same to each red ring along
the line. What lies on the cloth now: every ring green; a tube on every
cord that runs between two rings of the lower line, and on every short
string up to the upper line; the lower line's left lead plain, its right
lead wearing the tube the last red ring left behind. What has changed:
not a red ring is left, and a tube stands wherever red used to meet the
rest. What has held: every bead, every cord's two ends, and what the
picture does.{]}}

\begin{center}
\cardcloth[reds made green]{Every ring green}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} All green now. And on the upper line, a row of plain
green rings with nothing between them but cord.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}setting a claw beside the first green ring
on the upper line{]}} Slide them together.

\emph{{[}The upper line as it stands: four green rings at rest spaced
along a plain cord, each with a sleeved string hanging down to a ring on
the lower line. The Tortoise slides them along the cord towards its
middle, the first and the second into one, then the third into those,
then the fourth, so that they meet above the third eighth. The cord does
not move and its two ends do not stir; only the rings travel, and where
they meet they knot into one green ring. At rest and at rest make rest:
the bead does not move. Every string that hung from one of the four now
hangs from that ring, and each still reaches the same ring below. What
has changed: four rings are one, and the strings fan down from it. What
has held: which ring below each string reaches, and every bead.{]}}

\begin{center}
\cardcloth[reds made green, upper rings slid together]{A fan of sleeves}
\end{center}

\emph{{[}The ring at the head of the fan now holds both leads of the
upper line, the one from the left and the one to the right. The Tortoise
clips a green ring at rest onto the left lead, which changes nothing;
clips a tube onto the lead between that ring and the ring at the head of
the fan, and another beside it, which changes nothing; and clips another
ring at rest onto the lead between the tubes. What lies on the upper
line now: the left lead to a ring, a tube, another ring, a tube, the
ring at the head of the fan, and the right lead. What has changed: the
ring at the head of the fan holds only one end. What has held:
everything the picture does.{]}}

\begin{center}
\cardcloth[reds made green, upper rings slid together, small rings put on]{Rings clipped on}
\end{center}

\emph{{[}At the window two drops high on one pane have crept near enough
to touch, and in the moment they touch they are one drop, as big as both
together. It gathers itself, and slips a little way down the glass.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}looking from the cloth up to the beam, and
back{]}} That's the tangle. Ring for ring: the small rings, the big one,
the eighths, the plain rings, and a sleeve wherever you've a tube.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Your tangle, drawn. Nothing was spent to get it: not
a bead turned, not an eighth lost or gained.

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}proudly{]}} That is just how I tied it, the way
you showed me on your cloth after tea yesterday: every ring green, a
sleeve on every tie, and no ring holding two ends. The knots are mine;
the rule was yours.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then why two small rings on the upper lead? One would
look lonely enough.

\textbf{Tortoise:} A ring may hold only one end of a line, so the big
ring had to give up the left one. One small ring alone would sit on
plain cord next to the big one, and slide straight back into it. So a
pair of tubes, and a ring between them: two sleeves in a row are no
sleeve.

\emph{{[}The Crab laughs under his breath at the lonely ring, and tops
up all three cups, Achilles's first, and pushes the plate of bread and
butter an inch nearer him. Achilles takes another slice and eats it with
his eyes on the cloth.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} And the eighths can't slide together, either. On the
lower line there's a sleeve between each eighth and the next, and a
plain ring in the way. \emph{{[}He looks up at the tangle.{]}} Four
eighths hanging there. How few can it be made to need?

\emph{{[}The Crab lifts the cloth off the koekpan.{]}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{second-challenge-cooking-down}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Second Challenge --- \emph{Cooking
Down}}{Second Challenge --- Cooking Down}}\label{second-challenge-cooking-down}}

\textbf{Crab:} Now. A copy on the pan, a press, and we shall see.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The cloth first, if you'll humour me. Your pan works
in the dark; I'd like Achilles to see one way through by daylight before
it does.

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}resigned, with a claw still on the handle{]}} By
daylight, then. Briskly.

\emph{{[}The Tortoise gathers the net off the drawing-cloth, its rings
into her box and its cords, strings and tubes into her work-bag, and on
the bare cloth lays the card out again as she did at first: the upper
line and the lower, and along the lower from the left an eighth, a
joiner, an eighth, a joiner, an eighth, a joiner, an eighth, a joiner;
every ring in its first colour, every cord plain.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Look at the second eighth. It sits between two
joiners, and nothing else does: a joiner, a turn on the lower line, a
joiner. Watch what that comes to.

\emph{{[}The second eighth as it stands: a green ring an eighth round on
the lower line, a joiner's red ring on each side of it, and above, on
the upper line, those joiners' green rings, each tied down by a short
string to its red. The Tortoise slides the two upper greens towards each
other into one, meeting above the eighth; that one ring now holds both
short strings. She slides the eighth apart, into a plain green ring on
the lower line and a small green end hanging from it by a plain cord:
the bead goes with the end, an eighth round, and the ring left on the
line is at rest. She slides the upper ring apart too, so that one part
keeps the upper line and the other holds both short strings.{]}}

\emph{{[}Now four rings sit in a square: two greens, the upper part
holding the strings and the plain ring on the lower line, and two reds,
each green tied to each red, and each ring with just one cord besides.
It is the Crab's cradle from the snow. It comes undone as the cradle
always did: the square goes, its rings unclipped into her box and its
strings into her work-bag, and in its place one red ring gathers the
greens' other cords, and one green ring, tied to it by a single cord,
gathers the reds'. What lies in that place now: on the upper line a
plain green ring, above the eighth's place, tied down to a red ring, the
hub, which lies between the lines straight below it; from the hub,
hanging out to the left, the green end, an eighth round; and from the
hub a cord down to a plain green ring on the lower line. The Tortoise
takes a small bone counter from her work-bag and sets it off the
drawing-cloth, just beyond its near edge at its right-hand end, by the
teapot. What has changed: two joiners and the eighth between them are
one hub, with the eighth hanging from it. What has held: the eighth's
turn, whole, hanging now where both lines can reach it.{]}}

\begin{center}
\cardcloth[second eighth hung]{The cradle, undone}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} It hangs from something tied to both lines at once.

\textbf{Tortoise:} A turn between two joiners hangs from a hub. The
fourth eighth sits between two joiners as well.

\emph{{[}She does the same with the fourth eighth and its two joiners,
more quickly: the upper greens into one, meeting above the eighth, the
eighth apart into a plain ring and an end, the square formed and undone,
its rings into her box and its strings into her bag; a second hub stands
on the drawing-cloth, straight below its upper ring, with its own eighth
hanging from it out to the right. A second counter goes by the teapot,
on the first.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}setting a claw at the head of the upper
line{]}} Slide them together.

\emph{{[}The cloth as it stands: on the upper line two plain green
rings, one hub's foot each, with plain cord between; on the lower line
the first eighth, the first hub's foot, the third eighth and the second
hub's foot, all green, with plain cord between. The Tortoise slides the
upper line's feet towards each other into one plain ring, meeting above
the third eighth; it is tied to both hubs now. Then along the lower line
she slides the first eighth into the first foot, and those into the
third eighth, and brings the second foot along into all of it: an eighth
and nothing and an eighth and nothing, and the bead comes to rest a
quarter round. What lies on the cloth now: one ring on the upper line,
at rest; one on the lower, a quarter round; and between them the two
hubs, each tied to both rings, each with its eighth hanging. What has
changed: two of the eighths have met on the lower line and made a
quarter. What has held: the other two, still hanging from their hubs,
untouched.{]}}

\begin{center}
\cardcloth[second eighth hung, fourth eighth hung, slid together]{Feet slid together}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Two hubs, and both hung from the same two rings.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Then they are one hub.

\emph{{[}The two hubs as they stand: each tied to the upper ring and to
the lower, each with an eighth hanging from it. The Tortoise slides each
line's ring apart, so that one part of it holds both hubs' cords; those
two parts and the two hubs make a square again, and the square comes
undone, its rings into her box and its strings into her bag, into a
single red hub, between the lines straight below the upper ring, and a
single green ring; and the green ring slides together with both hanging
ends. What lies on the cloth now: one hub, tied to the upper ring and to
the lower, and hanging from it, out to the right, one end, a quarter
round. A third counter goes by the teapot, on the other two. What has
changed: two eighths on two hubs are one quarter on one hub. What has
held: the rings on the lines, and what the whole picture does.{]}}

\emph{{[}The rain has thickened, and the window over the sink is busy
with it: all over the glass drops are meeting drops, and every meeting
leaves one where there were two. There are fewer of them on the pane
than there were, and bigger, with clear glass between.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} And a hub with a quarter hanging from it, standing on
a quarter back on each line, is a tie in a sleeve. That one I haven't a
move for; I've tried it on every way the lines can start, and it holds.

\emph{{[}The picture as it stands: the upper ring at rest, the lower a
quarter round, the hub between with its quarter hanging. The Tortoise
slides each line's ring apart so that the part holding the hub's cord is
turned a quarter back: the upper ring leaves a ring a quarter round on
its line, and the lower leaves a ring at a half. The hub stands now on
two feet a quarter back, with a quarter round hanging from it. She lifts
it away whole, feet and hub and end, unclipping the feet from the lines,
into her box of rings; and in its place ties a single sleeved string
between two green rings at rest, one on each line; and those two slide
into their neighbours on the lines. What lies on the cloth now: on the
upper line one green ring, a quarter round; on the lower, one green ring
at a half; between them one sleeved tie. No eighth anywhere. What has
changed: four eighths have become a quarter, a half and a tie. What has
held: what the card does, with the counters by the teapot.{]}}

\begin{center}
\cardcloth[second eighth hung, fourth eighth hung, slid together, one hub, sleeved tie]{Nothing hanging}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} A quarter on the upper line, a half on the lower, and
a tie between. The eighths met, and added, and there's nothing left of
them.

\textbf{Achilles:} Let me check that my way: the card, and no cloth.
Both lines dark: no eighth ever sees a lit line, so nothing turns.

\textbf{Crab:} And with the lower lit?

\textbf{Achilles:} Upper dark, lower lit: the joiners never flip it, and
every eighth sees it lit. All four: a half. Upper lit, lower dark I did
before: two, a quarter.

\textbf{Tortoise:} And both?

\textbf{Achilles:} Both lit: the first eighth turns, the first joiner
darkens the lower, the second eighth sees dark, the second joiner lights
it again, and round we go. Two again: a quarter. \emph{{[}He sits
back.{]}} A quarter whenever the upper is lit, a half when the lower is
--- and when both are, a half taken back.

\textbf{Tortoise:} And your cloth?

\textbf{Achilles:} Says the same. A quarter on the upper ring, a half on
the lower, and the tie is yesterday's tie: it gives a half when both its
ends are lit. That's the half taken back.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Your finger and my cloth agree, then, tie and all.

\emph{{[}Achilles sits back with his cup against his chest, rather
pleased with his finger, and the Tortoise nods to him over hers. For a
moment there is nothing in the kitchen but the rain on the roof and the
stockpot talking to itself at the back of the range.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} Now my pan. \emph{{[}He is already at the dresser.{]}}

\emph{{[}The Crab takes from the dresser drawer a copy of the tangle
that he tied this morning, ring for ring the same from the same card,
and lays it on the koekpan: the small rings, the big ring, the eighth
rings with their beads an eighth round, the plain rings, every sleeve.
The tangle on the beam he does not touch. He closes the press, stands at
the table's end with his back to it and to the pan, his face to the
fire, and works the handle behind him by feel.{]}}

\emph{{[}Achilles leans over the table to see what the pan is doing with
it. Without turning round, the Crab puts up a claw.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} It jams if watched. Look at the fire, or at me; my back
is very interesting.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}straightening{]}} Sorry. It's hard not to.

\textbf{Crab:} Everyone says so. That is why it jams so often.

\emph{{[}Achilles turns his eyes to the fire as he is told, and the
Tortoise turns hers there too. At the back of the hot plate the
stockpot, full to the brim at dawn and loud all morning, has sunk to a
low mutter; nobody has lifted its lid since, and what comes from under
it now smells of everything that went in, only closer. Behind their
backs, from the table, where a moment ago there was nothing at all,
comes the koekpan's low sound at the edge of hearing, like a kettle a
long way from the boil.{]}}

\emph{{[}The copy as it went on: the long tangle, ring for ring, four
eighths among its rings. The press settles with a small click, and the
Crab's claw leaves the handle. The copy is gone from the pan. On the
second row of hooks hangs something far barer: on the upper line one
green ring, its bead a quarter round, at the right of the ring as
Achilles faces the hooks; on the lower line one green ring, its bead at
a half, at the bottom of the ring, for on a hanging ring a bead at rest
stands at the top and round goes clockwise; between them a single cord
in a yellow sleeve, from the foot of the upper ring to the top of the
lower; each ring hung by its leads from the second hooks, left and
right, knotted to its band either side of its top. No eighth ring
anywhere. On the beam the long tangle has not stirred: every ring and
every sleeve where it was. What has changed: the copy, cooked down to
two rings and a tie. What has held: the tangle, untouched, and the
cloth's answer, matched.{]}}

\begin{center}
\secondhooks*[a quarter round, at a half]{What the pan made}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}looking from the second hooks to the
cloth{]}} The same. A quarter, a half, and a sleeve between. What does
it do in there?

\textbf{Crab:} It slides together what can slide, re-ties what can be
re-tied, the way you saw yesterday, and carries the eighths along until
they meet. No bead changes in there except by one of those moves. That
is all I know, and all the letter from Delft would say.

\emph{{[}Achilles looks up from the second hooks to the long tangle on
the beam, and then round over his shoulder to the print on the wall over
the range: Escher's \textup{Development I}.{]}}

\emph{{[}As he looks, a gust drops down the flue, the fire roars up for
a breath behind its door, and the glow from the gap climbs the wall and
lies across the print. For that moment it is the brightest thing at that
end of the kitchen.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Like your print over the range: plain squares that
change, step by step, into interlocking figures --- only the other way
about.

\emph{{[}For answer the Crab lifts the two rings and their sleeved cord
off the second hooks, and puts them away in the dresser drawer.{]}}

\emph{{[}He lays the cloth back over the koekpan.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} On a long card it leaves fewer eighths than it was given,
most times. But it never promises the fewest. On this one it left none.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Every move on the pan and on my cloth is one that
leaves the thing unchanged. That's why its answer can be trusted, though
nobody may watch it.

\emph{{[}She lifts the quarter ring and the half ring off the
drawing-cloth on their lines, with their sleeved tie between, and lays
them on the table just beyond the drawing-cloth's far edge, leaving it
bare; and sweeps the counters from beside the teapot into her bag.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} And the pan hands back a picture, not a recipe. Can a
picture be run just as it is, without turning it back into a card?

\emph{{[}The Crab glances at the oven.{]}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{third-challenge-the-one-way-row}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Third Challenge --- \emph{The One-Way
Row}}{Third Challenge --- The One-Way Row}}\label{third-challenge-the-one-way-row}}

\textbf{Crab:} It can. That's what's in the oven.

\emph{{[}He opens the oven door, and with a folded oven cloth lifts out
three long narrow tins, one after another, and sets them in a row on the
table at its left-hand end as Achilles sees it, side by side, a hand's
breadth apart, each with a long side towards him, the first tin nearest
him; then he hangs the oven cloth back by the range. Each has three
small domed lids along it, and on each lid a knob with a pointer,
turning against eight marks round the rim: at rest the pointer points
away from Achilles, and round is clockwise as he looks down on it. The
end lid at his left is the first.{]}}

\emph{{[}The warm smell Achilles sniffed at comes out of the oven with
them, and it turns out to be the smell of warm tin and nothing else. The
tinsmith's mark is stamped small into the end of each tin, with the word
Delft beneath it. Standing in their row on the table they tick softly as
they cool, now one and now another.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} My one-way tins, from the tinsmith two doors down from
the old man's bench in Delft. Each is a long narrow tin with three
hollows in a row: the first, the second and the last. Set together in
one tin, the hollows come out joined, each to the next.

\textbf{Achilles:} And the knobs?

\textbf{Crab:} A dial on every lid. The pointer turns in eighths: at
rest, an eighth round, a quarter round, three eighths round, a half,
three eighths back, a quarter back, an eighth back; where it stands is
that lid's setting. Lift a lid, and the hollow is read at its setting:
under the lid is a glass drop, and it shows dark or it shows lit. A
lifted lid can't be put back; that hollow is spent.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then you've three tins' worth of looking, and no
more.

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}a claw on the row{]}} Everything else I own

the second at rest, the last an eighth back.

\textbf{Achilles:} May I?

\textbf{Crab:} Lift them in order: first, second, last.

\emph{{[}The first tin as it stands: three lids down, the first pointer

\emph{{[}He lifts the second lid. The drop beneath it is dark. The last

\emph{{[}The last drop shows lit. All three lids lie on the table in

\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} The reading part, at least, a tin can show. Show him.

\textbf{Achilles:} Lit.
