\hypertarget{chapter-17-compiling-by-rewriting}{%
\chapter{Chapter 17: Compiling by
Rewriting}\label{chapter-17-compiling-by-rewriting}}

\emph{--- Étude in Simplification ---}

\emph{Part V: Engineering the Diagram}

\emph{Escher: ``Development I'' --- plain squares that change, step by
step, into interlocking figures}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

If someone hands you a recipe that works, how can you find a cheaper
recipe that does exactly the same thing, and how can you be sure that it
does?

Every cook knows the first half of the question. A recipe written in a
hurry repeats itself: it tells you to stir, then to stop, then to stir
again; it adds salt twice. A better cook reads it and writes a shorter
one. But in a kitchen the test of the new recipe is easy. You make both
dishes and taste them. If the second is as good as the first, nobody
minds how it was found.

A quantum computer is run from a recipe too, a list of small steps done
to a handful of wires, one after another. Some steps are cheap. Some are
expensive, so expensive that on the machines now being designed, the
cost of a whole computation is counted almost entirely in them. A recipe
with fewer expensive steps is a better recipe. And here the tasting
fails. A quantum recipe on a hundred wires cannot be run and compared on
paper: its table of numbers is longer than any notebook. Nor can the
machine itself be trusted to taste, because a machine that reads its own
wires disturbs them. If a shorter recipe is to be used, it has to be
\emph{known} to do the same thing, before anyone runs it.

This chapter's answer is to stop reading the recipe as a list and to
draw it. The picture forgets the order in which the steps were written
down, and keeps only how the wires are joined and turned. Then the
picture is rewritten, one small move at a time, and every move is one
that changes nothing. When no move is left, what remains is the same
process, drawn smaller. The expensive steps meet inside the picture, add
up, and sometimes vanish. Then a recipe is taken out of the small
picture again.

And the pictures give something more. A picture can be run without being
turned back into a recipe at all: prepare the wires joined as the
picture says, then read them one by one. The readings are coin tosses,
but if they are read in the right order, each reading's outcome can be
sent forward and the coins stop mattering. The order that makes that
possible turns out to be exactly the order that lets a recipe be taken
out of a picture.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{four-eighths}{%
\section{§17.1 Four Eighths}\label{four-eighths}}

Chapter 16 ended with this question: ``If the quarters are free and the
eighths are the cost, then a circuit should be written with as few
eighths as possible. Chapter 17, \emph{Compiling by Rewriting}, takes a
whole circuit, turns it into a net, and shrinks it with the moves of
this chapter. What is left behind is only its eighths. How few can it be
made to need?''

The chapter's question, in the form we can answer: \textbf{a circuit is
a recipe; how does one find a cheaper recipe that does exactly the same,
and how does one know that it does?} We answer it in four steps. This
section counts what a recipe costs and draws it as a net. Section §17.2
cooks the net down. Section §17.3 runs a net without ever turning it
back into a recipe. Section §17.4 takes a recipe out of a cooked net,
and finds the order that makes that possible.

\textbf{On the blackboard.} Recall the gates of Chapter 16, each a
\(2\times2\) matrix:
\[T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad S=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&i\end{pmatrix},\qquad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.\]
Squaring doubles the turn: \(T^2=S\), \(S^2=Z\), \(Z^2=I\), so
\(T^8=I\). On two wires, write \(\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}\) for the CNOT whose
control is the upper wire and whose target is the lower, so that
\(\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}\ket{x_1x_2}=\ket{x_1,\,x_1\oplus x_2}\) in ket
order, top wire first. It undoes itself: \(\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}^2=I\).
Products of operators are read right to left, as always; pictures and
recipes are read left to right.

Here is the recipe of this chapter, in words: \emph{an eighth on the
lower wire, then a CNOT from the upper wire to the lower; four times
over.} As a matrix,
\[U\;:=\;\bigl(\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}\,(I\otimes T)\bigr)^4 .\] The letter
\(U\) means this matrix, and nothing else, for the rest of the chapter.

Chapter 16 showed why the eighths are the cost. The gates \(H\), \(S\)
and CNOT generate the Clifford gates, which a notebook can follow, and
\(T\) is not one of them. Kissinger and van de Wetering state the
practical side: on the machines being designed to correct their own
errors, ``magic state distillation and injection allow for
fault-tolerant implementation of T gates'', but ``they typically require
an order of magnitude more resources than Clifford gates''. So they
count only the eighths. The \textbf{\(T\)-count} of a circuit built from
Clifford gates and \(T\) is its number of \(T\) and \(T^{\dagger}\)
gates; Kissinger and van de Wetering count, more generally, every phase
gate whose turn is not a multiple of a quarter, and for circuits of
\(T\) gates the two counts agree. The recipe above has \(T\)-count
\(4\).

How few can it be made to need? A first guess is tempting.

\emph{The trap.} The CNOTs come in pairs, and
\(\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}^2=I\). So perhaps they cancel, and the four eighths
all land on the lower wire: \(T^4=Z\), and the recipe is \(I\otimes Z\),
with \(T\)-count \(0\).

Follow one input and see. Start in \(\ket{10}\): the upper wire lit, the
lower dark. The first eighth sees a dark lower wire and does nothing.
The first CNOT lights the lower wire. The second eighth sees it lit and
turns the whole state by \(e^{i\pi/4}\). The second CNOT darkens the
lower wire again, so the third eighth does nothing; the third CNOT
lights it, and the fourth eighth turns by \(e^{i\pi/4}\) again; the
fourth CNOT darkens it. The state comes back as
\(e^{i\pi/2}\ket{10}=i\ket{10}\). But \((I\otimes Z)\ket{10}=\ket{10}\).
The guess is wrong: two of the four eighths turned, and they turned
because the \emph{upper} wire was lit. The CNOTs cancel only when
nothing sits between them.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Dirac's Blackboard.}\nopagebreak

\emph{The recipe, multiplied out.} Write \(w=e^{i\pi/4}\) and
\(Q=\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}(I\otimes T)\). In the basis
\(\ket{00},\ket{01},\ket{10},\ket{11}\),
\(I\otimes T=\mathrm{diag}(1,w,1,w)\), and \(\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}\)
exchanges \(\ket{10}\) and \(\ket{11}\). So \(Q\) fixes \(\ket{00}\),
sends \(\ket{01}\mapsto w\ket{01}\), \(\ket{10}\mapsto\ket{11}\) and
\(\ket{11}\mapsto w\ket{10}\). Apply it twice:
\(\ket{10}\mapsto\ket{11}\mapsto w\ket{10}\) and
\(\ket{11}\mapsto w\ket{10}\mapsto w\ket{11}\). Hence
\[Q^2=\mathrm{diag}(1,\,w^2,\,w,\,w)=\mathrm{diag}(1,\,i,\,w,\,w),\] and
squaring once more, \[U=Q^4=\mathrm{diag}(1,\,-1,\,i,\,i).\] Against it,
\(I\otimes Z=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,1,-1)\). The two agree exactly on the
inputs whose upper bit is \(0\), and differ on both inputs whose upper
bit is \(1\). And \((S\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CZ}\), with
\(\mathrm{CZ}=\mathrm{diag}(1,1,1,-1)\), is
\(\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,i,-i)\,\mathrm{diag}(1,1,1,-1)=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,i,i)\):
the recipe needs no eighth at all. Section §17.2 says why.
\end{quote}

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} A CNOT is Chapter 8's green--red pair (row
64): a green spider on the control wire and a red spider on the target
wire, joined by one cord. Drawn bare, with no number, it is
\(\mathrm{CNOT}/\sqrt2\). In this chapter we call it a \textbf{joiner},
as the dialogue does. An eighth is a green spider with phase \(\pi/4\)
(row 125). Every spider is drawn in the colours of Chapters 8 to 16, and
its phase is written beside it; a spider with no phase written is at
rest. The recipe, bare, is four joiners and four eighths:
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.83em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1.2) (0,2.6);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.8) -- (13.8,1.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (13.8,0);
  \foreach \x in {2.9,6.1,9.3,12.5} { \draw[wire] (\x,1.8) -- (\x,0); }
  \foreach \x in {1.3,4.5,7.7,10.9} { \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi/4$}}] at (\x,0) {}; }
  \foreach \x in {2.9,6.1,9.3,12.5} { \node[zsp] at (\x,1.8) {}; \node[xsp] at (\x,0) {}; }
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;\tfrac14\,U .\] Each joiner carries \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) and each
eighth carries nothing, so the number is
\(\bigl(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigr)^4=\tfrac14\).

Now look at the trap in the picture. Two joiners with nothing between
them: the two greens sit on one cord of the upper wire and slide
together (fusion, row 57), and so do the two reds on the lower wire.
What is left is a green and a red joined by two cords, which Chapter 8's
Hopf rule (row 62) takes apart, at the price of a half, and fusion
closes the loose ends back into their wires:
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.83em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
  \path (0,-0.7) (0,2.5);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.8) -- (4.6,1.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (4.6,0);
  \draw[wire] (1.5,1.8) -- (1.5,0);
  \draw[wire] (3.1,1.8) -- (3.1,0);
  \node[zsp] at (1.5,1.8) {}; \node[xsp] at (1.5,0) {};
  \node[zsp] at (3.1,1.8) {}; \node[xsp] at (3.1,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;\tfrac12\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.65em, x=1em, y=1em]
  \path (0,-0.7) (0,2.5);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.8) -- (2.4,1.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2.4,0);
\end{tikzpicture}\] which is \(\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}^2/2=I/2\). Put an
eighth between the two joiners and the reds can no longer meet: the
lower wire now reads red, green, red, and a red and a green do not fuse.
The greens on the upper wire still slide together. That is the picture's
way of saying what the blackboard found: the eighths between joiners
feel the upper wire.

\hypertarget{the-net-of-a-circuit}{%
\subsection{The net of a circuit}\label{the-net-of-a-circuit}}

Chapter 16 drew a graph state as a \textbf{net}: a phase-free green
spider for each vertex, and a \textbf{tie} carrying a yellow box for
each edge (row 119). A circuit can be drawn in the same language, with
inputs and turns added. Duncan, Kissinger, Perdrix and van de Wetering
give the precise form. Their Definition 3.1 reads: ``A ZX-diagram is
graph-like when: 1. All spiders are Z-spiders. 2. Z-spiders are only
connected via Hadamard edges. 3. There are no parallel Hadamard edges or
self-loops. 4. Every input or output is connected to a Z-spider and
every Z-spider is connected to at most one input or output.'' A Z-spider
is a green spider, and a \textbf{Hadamard edge} is a cord carrying one
yellow box (row 56). Chapter 8 also allowed a dashed cord for it; in
this chapter every Hadamard edge is drawn with its yellow box, as the
dialogue's ties wear yellow sleeves.

Here is our recipe, turned into that form in three moves, none of which
costs a number.

\emph{First, colour change} (Theorem 8.2, row 58). A red spider is a
green spider with a yellow box on every leg, exactly. Each red of a
joiner has three legs, so it becomes a green spider with a box on its
tie and a box on each side of it on the lower wire:
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.19em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
  \path (0,-0.7) (0,3.1);
  \draw[wire] (0,2.4) -- (2.8,2.4);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2.8,0);
  \draw[wire] (1.4,2.4) -- (1.4,0);
  \node[zsp] at (1.4,2.4) {}; \node[xsp] at (1.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.19em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-0.7) (0,3.1);
  \draw[wire] (0,2.4) -- (4.4,2.4);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (4.4,0);
  \draw[wire] (2.2,2.4) -- (2.2,0);
  \node[hbox] at (0.9,0) {};
  \node[hbox] at (3.5,0) {};
  \node[hbox] at (2.2,1.2) {};
  \node[zsp] at (2.2,2.4) {}; \node[zsp] at (2.2,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] Do this to all four joiners. On the lower wire every
eighth now sits between two boxes, except the first, which has the lower
input on its left; each former red is a green spider at rest. Along the
lower wire the spiders alternate, an eighth and a spider at rest, joined
by Hadamard edges, and the last spider at rest reaches the lower output
through one more box.

\emph{Second, fusion} (row 57). The four greens on the upper wire are
joined by plain cords, so they slide together into one green spider at
rest. It holds the upper input, the upper output, and four ties, one to
each former red:
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=3.35em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1.2) (0,6.6);
  \draw[wire] (0,6) -- (20.4,6);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (20.4,0);
  \foreach \x in {3.6,8.4,13.2,18.0} { \draw[wire] (10.8,6) -- node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (\x,0); }
  \foreach \x in {2.4,4.8,7.2,9.6,12.0,14.4,16.8,19.2} { \node[hbox] at (\x,0) {}; }
  \foreach \x in {1.2,6.0,10.8,15.6} { \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi/4$}}] at (\x,0) {}; }
  \foreach \x in {3.6,8.4,13.2,18.0} { \node[zsp] at (\x,0) {}; }
  \node[zsp] at (10.8,6) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] This picture is still exactly the recipe's picture,
\(\tfrac14U\). It satisfies conditions 1 to 3, but not condition 4: the
big spider on the upper wire holds two ends, the upper input and the
upper output.

\emph{Third, the dummies.} A green spider at rest with two legs is a
plain wire (row 57, as in Chapter 8), and two yellow boxes in a row are
none (\(H^2=I\), row 56). So a plain lead may be replaced, at no cost,
by a spider at rest, a box, a spider at rest and a box:
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1em, y=1em]
  \path (0,-0.7) (0,0.7);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2.4,0);
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-0.7) (0,0.7);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (6.4,0);
  \node[zsp] at (1.0,0) {};
  \node[hbox] at (2.4,0) {};
  \node[zsp] at (3.8,0) {};
  \node[hbox] at (5.2,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] Put this on the upper wire's left lead, with the
last box next to the big spider. Now the big spider is reached from the
input only through two small spiders and two Hadamard edges, and it
holds one end. Every condition holds. The result, drawn in full in
§17.7, is this chapter's master diagram, \emph{The Uncooked Net}. It is
the recipe, exactly: colour change, fusion, the spider at rest and
\(H^2=I\) are all exact, so \textbf{no number was spent}, and its value
is \(\tfrac14U\).

Nothing in these three moves used the particular recipe. Duncan and
co-authors prove that it always works, and they add two moves for
doubled ties and loops that a recipe of joiners and eighths does not
produce here.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 17.1 (every diagram has a net; Duncan, Kissinger, Perdrix
and van de Wetering, Lemma 3.2, stated).} Every ZX-diagram equals a
non-zero number times a graph-like ZX-diagram.
\end{quote}

Their Lemma 3.2 says ``Every ZX-diagram is equal to a graph-like
ZX-diagram'', and their Remark 2.2 says that throughout the paper they
``neglect (non-zero) scalar factors'', so that an equality they prove
means that the two matrices differ by a non-zero factor \(z\). We have
written the factor into the statement. For our recipe we tracked it: it
is \(1\). Their proof is the one above: colour change, fusion, the
removal of doubled ties and loops, and dummy spiders wherever a spider
holds two ends. See \texttt{Code/Ch17/FourEighths.py}, which builds
\emph{The Uncooked Net} by hand, checks it against the recipe's picture
after each of the three moves, and checks that PyZX's own graph-like
form of the recipe is the same net, spider for spider and tie for tie.

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why insist on one colour, boxes on
every tie, and one end per spider, when the recipe's picture was already
a correct picture? Because then the whole diagram is a graph with a turn
on each vertex. Nothing else is left to know. And graphs can be changed
by graph moves: the re-tying and the pivot of Chapter 16, which were
proved for nets, now apply to a circuit. The price is that the picture
no longer looks like a recipe. Section §17.4 is about paying it back.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{cooking-down}{%
\section{§17.2 Cooking Down}\label{cooking-down}}

Look again at the recipe's second eighth. It sits between the first and
second joiners, and nothing else does. Call such a stretch, a joiner, a
turn on the lower wire, a joiner, a \textbf{sandwich}.

\textbf{On the blackboard.} For any angle \(\alpha\) let
\(Z(\alpha)=\mathrm{diag}(1,e^{i\alpha})\), and let
\[\Gamma(\alpha)\;:=\;\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}\,\bigl(I\otimes Z(\alpha)\bigr)\,\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}.\]
Follow \(\ket{x_1x_2}\). The first CNOT puts \(x_1\oplus x_2\) on the
lower wire; the turn multiplies by \(e^{i\alpha(x_1\oplus x_2)}\); the
second CNOT restores \(x_2\). So
\[\Gamma(\alpha)\ket{x_1x_2}\;=\;e^{i\alpha(x_1\oplus x_2)}\ket{x_1x_2},\qquad \Gamma(\alpha)=\mathrm{diag}\bigl(1,\,e^{i\alpha},\,e^{i\alpha},\,1\bigr).\]
The sandwich turns by \(\alpha\) when the two wires disagree. It does
not care which wire is which. This is Kissinger and van de Wetering's
\textbf{phase gadget} on two wires; their eq. (8) gives it on any number
of wires, a turn by \(\alpha\) on the parity
\(x_1\oplus\cdots\oplus x_n\), and van de Wetering's survey (§5.6) calls
both the diagram and the unitary phase gadgets. The letter \(\Gamma\)
means only this two-wire gadget here.

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} Chapter 14 drew a controlled turn as a
\textbf{hub}: a phase-free red spider tied to a green spider on each
wire, with a third leg, the pendant, ending in a green spider with one
leg (row 103). Chapter 13 drew the same red hub, with nothing hanging
from it, as the parity gadget (row 102). A green spider with one leg we
call an \textbf{end}, and we say it is turned by its phase. Hang an end
turned \(\alpha\) from a hub whose two feet are at rest:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 17.2 (the sandwich).} For every angle \(\alpha\),
exactly: \[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.67em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-1.3) (0,3.9);
\draw[wire] (0,3.2) -- (5.6,3.2);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (5.6,0);
\draw[wire] (1.2,3.2) -- (1.2,0);
\draw[wire] (4.4,3.2) -- (4.4,0);
\node[zsp] at (1.2,3.2) {}; \node[xsp] at (1.2,0) {};
\node[zsp] at (4.4,3.2) {}; \node[xsp] at (4.4,0) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\alpha$}}] at (2.8,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;\overset{\text{row 57}}{=}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.67em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-1.9) (0,3.9);
\draw[wire] (0,3.2) -- (5.2,3.2);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (5.2,0);
\draw[wire] (2.6,3.2) -- (2.6,1.7);
\draw[wire] (2.6,1.7) -- (1.4,0);
\draw[wire] (2.6,1.7) -- (3.8,0);
\draw[wire] (2.6,0) -- (2.6,-1.3);
\node[zsp] at (2.6,3.2) {};
\node[zsp] at (2.6,1.7) {};
\node[xsp] at (1.4,0) {}; \node[xsp] at (3.8,0) {};
\node[zsp] at (2.6,0) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]right:{$\alpha$}}] at (2.6,-1.3) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;\overset{\text{row 61}}{=}\;2^{-1/2}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.67em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-1.3) (0,3.9);
\draw[wire] (0,3.2) -- (3.4,3.2);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (3.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,3.2) -- (1.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,1.6) -- (2.7,1.6);
\node[zsp] at (1.4,3.2) {}; \node[zsp] at (1.4,0) {};
\node[xsp] at (1.4,1.6) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]right:{$\alpha$}}] at (2.7,1.6) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] On the blackboard: the sandwich, bare, is
\(\tfrac12\Gamma(\alpha)\) (two joiners), and the hub picture is
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\Gamma(\alpha)\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} The derivation by the rules is the sketchbook sidebar
below. On the blackboard, the sandwich's two joiners carry \(\tfrac12\).
In the hub picture, each green foot copies its wire's bit onto its tie;
the red hub, a phase-free red spider with two legs in and one out, sends
\(\ket{x_1}\ket{x_2}\) to \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\ket{x_1\oplus x_2}\), as in
the proof of Result 14.5; and the end gives
\(e^{i\alpha(x_1\oplus x_2)}\). That is
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\Gamma(\alpha)\), and
\(\tfrac12=2^{-1/2}\cdot\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch17/CookingDown.py}, which checks both pictures at
\(\alpha=\pi/4\) and at a random angle.

The hub with its end is Kissinger and van de Wetering's phase gadget,
drawn with a red hub. They draw it with a green hub joined to the feet
by Hadamard edges, and to the end by a Hadamard edge; colour change (row
58) turns one drawing into the other. With the feet turned \(\alpha/2\)
and the end turned \(-\alpha/2\), it is Chapter 14's controlled turn;
with the feet at rest, all of its turn hangs from the hub.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Coecke's Sketchbook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{Deriving the sandwich.} Result 17.2 follows from rules already
stated. The two greens on the upper wire are joined by a plain cord:
slide them together (row 57), into one green holding two ties. Slide the
turned spider on the lower wire apart (row 57 backwards): a spider at
rest on the wire, with an end turned \(\alpha\) hanging from it. Slide
the upper green apart too, so that one part stays on the wire and the
other holds both ties. That is the middle picture: two greens, the part
holding the ties and the spider at rest on the lower wire, and two reds,
and every green tied to every red. Each of the four is at rest and has
exactly one other leg. That is Chapter 8's cross (Theorem 8.5, row 61),
and it comes undone to one red tied to one green, worth
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) of it. The new red gathers the greens' other legs,
so it is tied to the upper wire's spider and hung with the end: it is
the hub. The new green gathers the reds' other legs, the two halves of
the lower wire: it is the lower foot. It never looked at \(\alpha\).
\end{quote}

The same rules fuse two gadgets. Suppose two hubs are tied to the same
two spiders, with ends turned \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). On the
blackboard, \(\Gamma(\alpha)\,\Gamma(\beta)=\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)\),
since both are diagonal and their phases add.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 17.3 (two hubs on the same spiders).} For all angles
\(\alpha,\beta\), exactly, and whatever turns the two spiders on the
wires carry:
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.67em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-0.8) (0,3.9);
\draw[wire] (-0.6,3.2) -- (5.4,3.2);
\draw[wire] (-0.6,0) -- (5.4,0);
\draw[wire] (2.4,3.2) -- (1.3,1.6) -- (2.4,0);
\draw[wire] (2.4,3.2) -- (3.5,1.6) -- (2.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.3,1.6) -- (0.1,1.6);
\draw[wire] (3.5,1.6) -- (4.7,1.6);
\node[zsp] at (2.4,3.2) {}; \node[zsp] at (2.4,0) {};
\node[xsp] at (1.3,1.6) {}; \node[xsp] at (3.5,1.6) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\alpha$}}] at (0.1,1.6) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\beta$}}] at (4.7,1.6) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;2^{-1/2}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.67em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-0.8) (0,3.9);
\draw[wire] (0,3.2) -- (3.6,3.2);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (3.6,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,3.2) -- (1.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,1.6) -- (2.7,1.6);
\node[zsp] at (1.4,3.2) {}; \node[zsp] at (1.4,0) {};
\node[xsp] at (1.4,1.6) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]right:{$\alpha+\beta$}}] at (2.7,1.6) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\]
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} Slide each wire's spider apart so that one part stays on
the wire, keeping its turn, and the other part, at rest, holds both hub
ties (row 57). Those two parts and the two hubs are a cross, every one
at rest with one other leg, and the cross comes undone (row 61) at the
price \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\): a red tied to the two wire parts, and a green
gathering the two ends. The green and the ends slide together (row 57):
an end turned \(\alpha+\beta\). On the blackboard, each hub is worth
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\,e^{i\alpha(x_1\oplus x_2)}\) on the bits its feet
copy, so two hubs give \(\tfrac12e^{i(\alpha+\beta)(x_1\oplus x_2)}\)
and one hub gives \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) times the same. \(\;\blacksquare\)
See \texttt{Code/Ch17/CookingDown.py}.

Kissinger and van de Wetering call this \textbf{gadget fusion}, (GF),
and derive it from their rules (f), (h) and (b\('\)), which are fusion,
colour change and the cross for any number of legs. On the blackboard it
is, in their words, ``a well-known simplification used in
phase-polynomial circuits, where two phases acting on the same parity of
the input qubits can be summed together.''

\hypertarget{four-eighths-that-cancel}{%
\subsection{Four eighths that cancel}\label{four-eighths-that-cancel}}

Now the recipe. Its second and fourth eighths are each inside a
sandwich. Its first and third are not, but they sit on the lower wire,
next to the hubs' lower feet, where fusion reaches them.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 17.4 (four eighths that cancel).} Exactly,
\[U\;=\;\bigl(\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}\,(I\otimes T)\bigr)^4\;=\;(S\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CZ}\;=\;\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,i,i),\]
and \(U\ket{x_1x_2}=i^{\,x_2+(x_1\oplus x_2)}\ket{x_1x_2}\). The recipe
has \(T\)-count \(4\), and \((S\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CZ}\) has \(T\)-count
\(0\). In pictures, the recipe's bare picture is \(2^{-3/2}\) times the
\textbf{cooked picture}, a green spider turned a quarter on the upper
wire and a green spider turned a half on the lower, joined by one
Hadamard edge:
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.83em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-1.2) (0,2.6);
\draw[wire] (0,1.8) -- (13.8,1.8);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (13.8,0);
\foreach \x in {2.9,6.1,9.3,12.5} { \draw[wire] (\x,1.8) -- (\x,0); }
\foreach \x in {1.3,4.5,7.7,10.9} { \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi/4$}}] at (\x,0) {}; }
\foreach \x in {2.9,6.1,9.3,12.5} { \node[zsp] at (\x,1.8) {}; \node[xsp] at (\x,0) {}; }
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;2^{-3/2}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.19em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-1.2) (0,3.4);
\draw[wire] (0,2.4) -- (2.8,2.4);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2.8,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,2.4) -- (1.4,0);
\node[hbox] at (1.4,1.2) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi/2$}}] at (1.4,2.4) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi$}}] at (1.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] The cooked picture is \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}U\); no
eighth is left in it.
\end{quote}

This is the chapter's headline theorem. It is proved twice in §17.6, by
a parity count on the blackboard and by six moves in the sketchbook, the
sandwiches first.

\hypertarget{cooking-in-general}{%
\subsection{Cooking in general}\label{cooking-in-general}}

A long circuit is cooked the same way, but with more moves. Its net has
\textbf{interior} spiders, spiders with no input or output leg, and the
cook's work is to remove as many of them as possible. Duncan and
co-authors call a spider \textbf{Pauli} if its phase is a multiple of
\(\pi\) (at rest or a half), and \textbf{Clifford} if its phase is a
multiple of \(\pi/2\); a Clifford spider that is not Pauli, turned an
odd number of quarters, they call \textbf{proper Clifford}. Their two
main moves are Chapter 16's graph moves, done inside a net: re-tying at
a spider turned a quarter removes that spider (their Lemma 5.2), and a
pivot along a tie between two Pauli spiders removes both (their Lemma
5.3); a third move, their eq. (9), first adds spiders at rest on a
boundary wire, so that a spider next to the boundary becomes interior
and the pivot can reach it. \textbf{This chapter uses re-tying and the
pivot only as Chapter 16 stated them (rows 122 and 123), and does not
derive them.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 17.5 (simplification; Duncan, Kissinger, Perdrix and van
de Wetering, Theorem 5.4, stated).} There is a terminating procedure
that turns any graph-like ZX-diagram into a graph-like ZX-diagram, up to
one-wire unitaries on its inputs and outputs and up to a non-zero number
(their Remark 2.2), which contains no interior proper Clifford spider,
no pair of tied interior Pauli spiders, and no interior Pauli spider
tied to a boundary spider. If every spider of the first diagram is
Clifford, the result has no interior spider at all.
\end{quote}

Their count of the cost (their Remark 5.6): each step removes a spider
and toggles ties among the others, so for a net with vertex set \(V\)
the procedure takes at most \(O(\lvert V\rvert^3)\) elementary graph
operations; they write \(n\) for \(\lvert V\rvert\), and report that in
practice it scales far better.

The eighths survive Result 17.5: a spider turned an eighth is not
Clifford, and no move touches it. Kissinger and van de Wetering found
the way round. Their variations (P2) and (P3) of the pivot remove any
interior Pauli spider that is left, at the price of moving a
neighbouring turn out onto a gadget, a hub hanging from the net. Then
gadgets can meet. Two gadgets on the same spiders fuse, (GF), which is
Result 17.3; and a gadget tied to only one spider slides its turn into
that spider, their (ID).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 17.6 (ZX-simplify; Kissinger and van de Wetering,
Algorithm 4.3 and Definition 4.4, stated).} Starting from a graph-like
diagram: (1) re-tie until no interior proper Clifford spider is left;
(2) pivot, with (P1), (P2) and (P3), until every interior Pauli spider
is removed or moved onto a gadget; (3) remove every gadget whose turn is
a multiple of a quarter; (4) apply (ID) and (GF) wherever possible, and
if anything changed, go back to (1). The procedure terminates, since
every step removes a spider or a gadget, and for a net with vertex set
\(V\) it takes at most \(O(\lvert V\rvert^3)\) elementary graph
operations (their \(n\) is \(\lvert V\rvert\)). It ends in
\textbf{reduced gadget form}: every interior spider is non-Clifford or
part of a non-Clifford gadget, every gadget is tied to more than one
spider, and no two gadgets are tied to the same set of spiders.
\end{quote}

Result 17.6 lowers the number of eighths in the picture. It does not
promise the fewest. Nothing in it is a proof that a smaller count is
impossible, and the authors do not claim one.

\textbf{Phase teleportation.} A cooked net does not look like a circuit,
and turning it back into one is the subject of §17.4. Kissinger and van
de Wetering found a way to skip that step. Give each eighth of the
original circuit its own name, \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots\), and cook the
net with the names in place of the numbers. When (ID) or (GF) adds two
named turns, the sum can be moved onto one of the two and the other set
to \(0\), \emph{in the original circuit}, and the new circuit cooks to
the same net, so it is provably equal to the old one. In the words of
their abstract, ``Phase teleportation does not change the number or
location of non-phase gates''; only the turns change.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 17.7 (the recipe, teleported).} Keep every joiner of the
recipe where it is. Replace the first and the fourth eighths by
quarters, \(S\), and remove the second and the third. The new circuit
equals \(U\) exactly, and has \(T\)-count \(0\). So does every choice of
one quarter among the first and third places and one among the second
and fourth. But quarters in the first and third places give
\(I\otimes Z\), the trap.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} By the parity count of §17.6 (steps (1) and (2)), a turn
in the first or third place sees \(x_2\), and a turn in the second or
fourth place sees \(x_1\oplus x_2\). So one quarter in each class gives
\(i^{\,x_2}\,i^{\,x_1\oplus x_2}\), which is \(U\) by Result 17.4, and
two quarters that both see \(x_2\) give \((-1)^{x_2}\), which is
\(I\otimes Z\). \(\;\blacksquare\) PyZX's phase teleportation chooses
the first and fourth places; \texttt{Code/Ch17/CookingDown.py} checks
the circuit it returns against \(U\).

In the language of the gadgets: the first and third eighths slid
together on the lower wire, and the second and fourth added on one hub.
Two classes, a quarter each.

\textbf{What PyZX does.} Duncan and co-authors, and Kissinger and van de
Wetering, built these procedures into PyZX, an open-source Python
library. On \emph{The Uncooked Net} its \texttt{full\_reduce} leaves
exactly the cooked picture of Result 17.4, with the number \(2^{-3/2}\)
written beside it, and its \texttt{extract\_circuit} returns
\((S\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CZ}\), exactly \(U\). On twenty random circuits
of Clifford gates and eighths generated with a fixed seed, three wires
and forty gates each, \texttt{full\_reduce} kept the value exactly in
all twenty and lowered the number of eighths in eighteen.
\texttt{Code/Ch17/CookingDown.py} checks all of this against the
matrices.

On the published benchmarks the numbers are honest and mixed. Kissinger
and van de Wetering ran thirty-six benchmark circuits. They matched or
beat the previous best-known count of eighths, without extra wires, on
twenty-six of the thirty-six, and beat it on six; with a further
optimiser, TODD, run afterwards, they beat it on twenty. On twenty of
the thirty-six they got exactly the previous best, which they read as a
hint that those counts sit in ``some kind of `local optimum'\,''. Three
rows of their Table 1: the circuit \emph{nth-prime6} went from \(567\)
eighths to \(279\) (the previous best was \(400\)); \emph{mod54} from
\(28\) to \(8\), and to \(7\) with TODD (previous best \(16\));
\emph{tof3} from \(21\) to \(15\), the same as before. In their words,
``The circuits where PyZX seems to do considerably better are ones that
contain many Hadamard gates'', which hamper the older methods built on
phase polynomials. The PyZX paper adds that on \emph{nth-prime6}, ``PyZX
optimises this to a circuit with 279 T gates in less than a second.''

\textbf{Validation.} How do they know the cooked circuits are right? The
same rules check them. Compose the original circuit with the adjoint of
the optimised one, and cook the result. If the circuits are equal, the
composite is the identity, and cooking should leave bare wires.
Kissinger and van de Wetering did this for every benchmark: ``In every
case, the resulting circuit was reduced to the identity.'' When it
succeeds, the list of moves is a certificate of equality. When it fails,
nothing is proved either way; they note that ``the general problem of
circuit equality validation is QMA-hard'', citing earlier work, ``and
hence a general efficient validation strategy is unlikely to exist''.
For our recipe the check is short: the recipe followed by the adjoint of
\((S\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CZ}\) is \(U\,U^{\dagger}=I\), and PyZX cooks
its picture to two bare wires.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Feynman's Notebook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{A compiler with no gates in it.} In 2019 Ross Duncan, Aleks
Kissinger, Simon Perdrix and John van de Wetering posted
``Graph-theoretic Simplification of Quantum Circuits with the
ZX-calculus''; \emph{Quantum} published it in 2020. Their move was to
forget the gates. Turn the circuit into a graph with turns, remove every
interior spider that local complementation and pivoting can reach, and
then prove that what is left can still be turned back into a circuit.
The next month Kissinger and van de Wetering posted ``Reducing T-count
with the ZX-calculus'', which added the gadgets and phase teleportation;
revised in January 2020, it appeared in \emph{Physical Review A} that
year as ``Reducing the number of non-Clifford gates in quantum
circuits''. Both methods live in PyZX, which its authors presented at
the Quantum Physics and Logic conference of 2019, published in 2020 ---
``pronounced like `physics' without the H'', they write. Kissinger and
van de Wetering's validation caught a mistake that was not theirs: of
another group's optimised benchmark circuits, all passed but one,
qcla-mod7, which was then shown to be incorrect.
\end{quote}

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why hang a turn from a hub, instead
of leaving it on the wire where the recipe put it? Because on the wire a
turn is stuck between the joiners around it, and in a recipe of many
joiners two turns that act on the same parity may be far apart. On a
hub, the turn is attached to \emph{which wires it reads}, not to
\emph{when}. Two turns that read the same wires hang from hubs tied to
the same spiders, wherever they came from, and Result 17.3 adds them.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-one-way-row}{%
\section{§17.3 The One-Way Row}\label{the-one-way-row}}

The cook hands back a picture, not a recipe. Can a picture be run as it
is?

Take one wire in a state \(\ket\psi=a\ket0+b\ket1\) and a second wire in
\(\ket+\). Apply CZ, and then read the first wire, not in the basis
\(\ket0,\ket1\) but in a turned basis. Danos and Kashefi write
\[\ket{\pm_{\alpha}}\;=\;\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket0\pm e^{i\alpha}\ket1\bigr),\]
and a reading \(M^{\alpha}\) that projects onto \(\ket{+_{\alpha}}\) or
\(\ket{-_{\alpha}}\), with the outcome \(s=0\) for \(+\) and \(s=1\) for
\(-\). Compute.
\(\mathrm{CZ}(\ket\psi\otimes\ket+)=a\ket0\ket++b\ket1\ket-\). Reading
outcome \(s\) applies
\(\bra{\pm_{\alpha}}=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\bra0\pm e^{-i\alpha}\bra1\bigr)\)
to the first wire and leaves
\[\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(a\ket++(-1)^se^{-i\alpha}b\ket-\bigr)\;=\;\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\,H\bigl(a\ket0+(-1)^se^{-i\alpha}b\ket1\bigr)\]
on the second wire. For \(s=0\) that is
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}HZ(-\alpha)\ket\psi\); for \(s=1\) there is an extra
\(Z\) inside, and \(HZ=XH\).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 17.8 (one step).} For every state \(\ket\psi\), every
angle \(\alpha\) and each outcome \(s\in\{0,1\}\), exactly,
\[\bigl(\bra{\pm_{\alpha}}\otimes I\bigr)\,\mathrm{CZ}\,\bigl(\ket\psi\otimes\ket+\bigr)\;=\;\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\,X^{s}HZ(-\alpha)\ket\psi,\]
with \(+\) for \(s=0\) and \(-\) for \(s=1\). Each outcome has
probability \(\tfrac12\), whatever \(\ket\psi\) is.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} The computation above; \(X^{s}HZ(-\alpha)\) is unitary, so
each branch has length \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch17/OneWayRow.py}, which checks it on a random non-real
\(\ket\psi\).

The reading moved the state from one wire to the other, turned it by
\(-\alpha\), and put a yellow box on it. The price is the \(X^s\): half
the time the result comes out flipped, and the reader cannot choose
which half.

\textbf{On the blackboard: patterns.} Raussendorf and Briegel turned
this into a way of computing. Prepare many wires in \(\ket+\), join
neighbours by CZ, in a line, a square grid, or any graph, and then read
the wires one at a time. The state before any reading is the graph state
of Chapter 16, which they call a \textbf{cluster state}; their eq. (1)
says that it is fixed, up to a sign, by
\(\sigma_x^{(a)}\prod_{a'}\sigma_z^{(a')}\) over the neighbours \(a'\)
of \(a\), which is Chapter 16's safe touch. In their words, the cluster
is ``a `substrate' on which any quantum circuit can be imprinted by
one-qubit measurements''. Danos and Kashefi wrote the procedure down as
a \textbf{pattern}, a list of commands: prepare the non-input wires in
\(\ket+\); apply \(E_{ij}\), their name for the CZ on wires \(i\) and
\(j\), which we write \(\mathrm{CZ}_{ij}\), for every edge; read wire
\(i\) with \(M_i^{\alpha}\); and correct wire \(j\) with \(X_j^{s_i}\)
or \(Z_j^{s_i}\), a Pauli applied only if an earlier outcome \(s_i\) was
\(1\). The wires are the vertices of an \textbf{open graph}
\((G,V_{\mathrm{in}},V_{\mathrm{out}})\): a graph \(G\) with vertex set
\(V\), a set \(V_{\mathrm{in}}\) of inputs and a set
\(V_{\mathrm{out}}\) of outputs. Danos and Kashefi, and Duncan and
co-authors, write it \((G,I,O)\); we keep \(I\) for the identity matrix.
Every vertex not in \(V_{\mathrm{out}}\) is read, and \(N_i\) is the
neighbourhood of \(i\) (Danos and Kashefi write \(G(i)\)).

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} A pattern is a picture already. Its CZs and
\(\ket+\)s make the net of Chapter 16 (row 119). A reading's effect,
\(\bra{\pm_{\alpha}}\), is
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\bra0+e^{i(-\alpha+s\pi)}\bra1\bigr)\), which is
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) times a green end turned \(-\alpha+s\pi\): one
picture for both outcomes, with Chapter 10's bit-times-\(\pi\) phase
(row 75). So a pattern, branch by branch, is a net with a green end on
each wire that is read.\footnote{Van de Wetering's survey (§6.3) draws
  the effect of the outcome
  \(\ket{+_{XY,\alpha}}=\ket0+e^{i\alpha}\ket1\) as a green effect
  labelled \(\alpha\), and the other outcome as \(\alpha+\pi\). With
  this book's convention that the mirror conjugates (Chapter 3), the
  effect of \(\ket0+e^{i\alpha}\ket1\) is the end turned \(-\alpha\).
  The difference is one of labelling; we follow Danos and Kashefi and
  write the turn \(-\alpha\).} The one step of Result 17.8 is a spider
on the input wire, tied through a yellow box to a spider at rest on the
output wire, with an end hanging from the first. Write
\(\varphi=-\alpha\) for the end's turn. Fuse the end into its spider
(row 57): the spider on the input wire becomes a green spider turned
\(\varphi+s\pi\). The spider at rest on the output wire has two legs, so
it is a plain wire (row 57, as in Chapter 8). What is left is a green
spider turned \(\varphi+s\pi\), then a box, then a plain wire. So
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-0.8) (0,1.2);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (4.0,0);
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\varphi+s\pi$}}] at (1.2,0) {};
  \node[hbox] at (2.6,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;HZ(\varphi+s\pi)\;=\;X^{s}HZ(\varphi),\] exactly (since
\(Z(\varphi+s\pi)=Z(\varphi)Z^{s}\) and \(HZ=XH\)). The picture before
fusing, with the \(\ket+\), the CZ and the effect each drawn bare, has
the same value, and that is \(\sqrt2\) times the branch on the
blackboard: the \(\ket+\) is \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) times a green point,
the CZ is \(\sqrt2\) times its bare tie (row 119's tie), and the effect
is \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) times its end.

Conversely, van de Wetering's survey (§6.3) states that ``any graph-like
ZX-diagram can be described as a measurement fragment'', adding spiders
at rest where a turned spider carries an output. It adds the caveat at
once: such a fragment is ``post-selected'', read as if every reading
came out the right way, and ``it is in general not possible'' to write a
graph-like diagram as a pattern that can absorb the other outcomes; a
diagram with inputs and no outputs, for instance, has nowhere to send
them. We state this and do not prove it.

\hypertarget{three-dishes-in-a-row}{%
\subsection{Three dishes in a row}\label{three-dishes-in-a-row}}

Now the example that makes feed-forward necessary. Take three wires in a
row, \(1\)--\(2\)--\(3\), all prepared in \(\ket+\) and joined by
\(\mathrm{CZ}_{12}\mathrm{CZ}_{23}\): no inputs,
\(V_{\mathrm{out}}=\{3\}\). Read wire \(1\) with its end turned
\(\varphi_1=\pi/4\) (Danos and Kashefi's \(\alpha_1=-\pi/4\)), then wire
\(2\) with \(\varphi_2=0\), then wire \(3\) with \(\varphi_3=-\pi/4\).
If the first two readings both come out \(0\), Result 17.8 twice says
that wire \(3\) holds, before its reading,
\[\tfrac12\,HZ(\varphi_2)HZ(\varphi_1)\ket+\;=\;\tfrac12\,T\ket+\;=\;\tfrac12\ket\mu,\]
Chapter 16's magic state, and the reading at \(\varphi_3=-\pi/4\) finds
\(0\) with certainty: \(\bra0+e^{-i\pi/4}\bra1\) against
\(\ket0+e^{i\pi/4}\ket1\) gives \(2\), and \(\bra0-e^{-i\pi/4}\bra1\)
gives \(0\). The dialogue calls outcome \(0\) \emph{dark} and outcome
\(1\) \emph{lit}.

But the first two readings are coin tosses. If the first comes out \(1\)
and the second \(0\), wire \(3\) holds \(Z\ket\mu\) instead, and the
reading at \(-\pi/4\) finds \(1\) with certainty. The last reading has
become a coin that knows the first two. The cure is to change the later
settings according to the earlier outcomes. Here is the rule the chapter
uses, which the dialogue's Crab keeps for his tins: \textbf{if the first
reading is \(1\), turn the second setting the other way,
\(\varphi_2\mapsto-\varphi_2\), and put a half on the third,
\(\varphi_3\mapsto\varphi_3+\pi\); if the second reading is \(1\), turn
the third setting the other way.} So the third setting is
\((-1)^{s_2}\varphi_3+s_1\pi\).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 17.9 (the row, with and without feed-forward).} In the
three-wire row above, each of the four patterns \((s_1,s_2)\) of the
first two readings has probability \(\tfrac14\). Read by the rule, the
third reading is \(0\) with probability \(1\) in every pattern; the
third settings are \(-\pi/4\), \(\pi/4\), \(3\pi/4\) and \(5\pi/4\) for
\((s_1,s_2)=(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)\). Read without the rule, always at
\(-\pi/4\), the third reading is \(1\) with probability \(\tfrac12\)
overall: never after \((0,0)\), always after \((1,0)\), and with
probability \(\tfrac12\) after \((0,1)\) and after \((1,1)\). With only
the ``other way'' half of the rule it is \(1\) with probability
\(\tfrac12\); with only the ``half on'' half, \(\tfrac14\). Kept unread,
wire \(3\) holds exactly \(X^{s_2}Z^{s_1}\ket\mu\) (the branch divided
by its length), which the Paulis the first two outcomes name turn back
into \(\ket\mu\), up to a sign.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} The Dirac's Blackboard sidebar below shows where the kept
state \(X^{s_2}Z^{s_1}\ket\mu\) comes from. Each reading of it is a
two-term sum; for instance after \((1,0)\) the state is
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket0+e^{i5\pi/4}\ket1\bigr)\), and the reading
at \(3\pi/4\) gives \(\tfrac12\bigl(1+e^{i2\pi}\bigr)=1\) for outcome
\(0\). The other cases are the same kind of sum. \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch17/OneWayRow.py}, which computes every branch and every
probability above from the three-wire state.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Dirac's Blackboard.}\nopagebreak

\emph{Where the corrections come from.} Danos and Kashefi's proof of
their Theorem 1 runs on five equations, their (1)--(5), which in our
letters read: \(\bra{+_{\alpha}}Z^{s}=\bra{\pm_{\alpha}}\) (the
outcome-\(s\) effect);
\(Z_i^s\,\mathrm{CZ}_{ij}=X_j^s\,\mathrm{CZ}_{ij}\,X_j^s\);
\(X_i^s\,\mathrm{CZ}_{ij}=\mathrm{CZ}_{ij}\,Z_j^s\,X_i^s\);
\(Z_i^s\,\mathrm{CZ}_{ij}=\mathrm{CZ}_{ij}\,Z_i^s\); and
\(X_i^s\ket+_i=\ket+_i\). Run the row. Reading wire \(1\) with outcome
\(s_1\) leaves, by Result 17.8, \(X_2^{s_1}\) on wire \(2\), still in
front of \(\mathrm{CZ}_{23}\). Push it through by the third equation,
rearranged:
\(\mathrm{CZ}_{23}X_2^{s_1}=X_2^{s_1}Z_3^{s_1}\mathrm{CZ}_{23}\). So
wire \(2\) carries an \(X\) and wire \(3\) a \(Z\). The \(X\) on wire
\(2\) is absorbed by reading it at \(-\varphi_2\) instead of
\(\varphi_2\), since
\((\bra0+e^{i\theta}\bra1)X=e^{i\theta}(\bra0+e^{-i\theta}\bra1)\). The
\(Z\) on wire \(3\) commutes onward (fourth equation) and is absorbed by
adding \(\pi\) to wire \(3\)'s setting. Reading wire \(2\) leaves
\(X_3^{s_2}\), absorbed by turning wire \(3\)'s setting the other way.
These are the rule's three clauses.
\end{quote}

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} Close the row: an end on every wire, turned
\(\varphi_k+s_k\pi\). Three \(\ket+\)s, two CZs and three effects carry
\(\bigl(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigr)^3(\sqrt2)^2\bigl(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigr)^3=\tfrac14\),
so the bare picture is exactly \(4\) times the amplitude of the readings
\((s_1,s_2,s_3)\):
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-1.15em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-2.4) (0,0.8);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (6.0,0);
  \foreach \x in {0,3.0,6.0} { \draw[wire] (\x,0) -- (\x,-1.5); }
  \node[hbox] at (1.5,0) {}; \node[hbox] at (4.5,0) {};
  \foreach \x in {0,3.0,6.0} { \node[zsp] at (\x,0) {}; }
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\varphi_1+s_1\pi$}}] at (0,-1.5) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\varphi_2+s_2\pi$}}] at (3.0,-1.5) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\varphi_3+s_3\pi$}}] at (6.0,-1.5) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;4\,\bigl(\bra{\pm_{\alpha_1}}\otimes\bra{\pm_{\alpha_2}}\otimes\bra{\pm_{\alpha_3}}\bigr)\,\mathrm{CZ}_{12}\mathrm{CZ}_{23}\ket{+\!+\!+},\]
with \(\alpha_k=-\varphi_k\) and the sign of each effect set by \(s_k\).
To see the rule in the picture we need one more small rule, about a red
half meeting an end.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 17.10 (a red half against an end).} For every angle
\(\varphi\), exactly: a red spider turned \(\pi\) on the cord of a green
end turned \(\varphi\) may be taken off, if the end is turned the other
way and the number \(e^{i\varphi}\) is written beside it:
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-0.7) (0,1.3);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2.6,0);
\node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (1.1,0) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\varphi$}}] at (2.6,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;e^{i\varphi}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-0.7) (0,1.3);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.4,0);
\node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$-\varphi$}}] at (1.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] So an end at rest is unchanged, an end turned a half
stays a half with the number \(-1\), and an end turned an eighth becomes
an end turned an eighth back.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} A red \(\pi\) with two legs is \(X\) exactly (§8.2), and
\((\bra0+e^{i\varphi}\bra1)X=\bra1+e^{i\varphi}\bra0=e^{i\varphi}(\bra0+e^{-i\varphi}\bra1)\).
In the rules, this is Chapter 8's \(\pi\)-commutation (Theorem 8.4, row
60) applied to an end, with its number written. \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch17/OneWayRow.py}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 17.11 (the travelling half).} For all angles
\(\varphi_1,\varphi_2,\varphi_3\), write
\(P(\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3)\) for the closed row with its ends
turned \(\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3\). Exactly,
\[P(\varphi_1+\pi,\,\varphi_2,\,\varphi_3)\;=\;e^{i\varphi_2}\,P(\varphi_1,\,-\varphi_2,\,\varphi_3+\pi),\]
\[P(\varphi_1,\,\varphi_2+\pi,\,\varphi_3)\;=\;e^{i\varphi_3}\,P(\varphi_1,\,\varphi_2,\,-\varphi_3).\]
In pictures, the first equation is
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-1.15em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},

ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]

\foreach \x in {0,2.8,5.6} { \draw[wire] (\x,0) -- (\x,-1.5); }
\node[hbox] at (1.4,0) {}; \node[hbox] at (4.2,0) {};
\foreach \x in {0,2.8,5.6} { \node[zsp] at (\x,0) {}; }

\node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\varphi_2$}}] at (2.8,-1.5) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\varphi_3$}}] at (5.6,-1.5) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;e^{i\varphi_2}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-1.15em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]

\foreach \x in {0,2.8,5.6} { \draw[wire] (\x,0) -- (\x,-1.5); }
\node[hbox] at (1.4,0) {}; \node[hbox] at (4.2,0) {};
\foreach \x in {0,2.8,5.6} { \node[zsp] at (\x,0) {}; }
\node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\varphi_1$}}] at (0,-1.5) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$-\varphi_2$}}] at (2.8,-1.5) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\varphi_3+\pi$}}] at (5.6,-1.5) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\]
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} The derivation is the sketchbook sidebar below: the half
from the first end travels to the second wire's spider and on to the
third, turning the second end the other way (Result 17.10) and landing
on the third end as a half. The second equation is the same journey, one
step shorter. \(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch17/OneWayRow.py},
which builds both sides for random angles and compares them as numbers.

Result 17.11 is the rule. Suppose the first reading is \(1\). By the
first equation, the picture of that branch, read at the settings the
rule prescribes, \(-\varphi_2\) and \(\varphi_3+\pi\), equals
\(e^{-i\varphi_2}\) times the picture with the first reading \(0\) and
the original settings, since the two halves on the third end add to a
whole turn. The same holds for the second reading and the second
equation. So every branch has, for each third outcome, the amplitude of
branch \((0,0)\) times a number of length \(1\). Branch \((0,0)\) never
reads \(1\) at the third wire; so no branch does.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Coecke's Sketchbook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{The travelling half.} Leave the ends unfused, so every spider on
the row is at rest. Slide the half off the first end, turned
\(\varphi_1+\pi\), onto its cord (row 57 backwards), then through the
first spider onto its tie (row 57). Through the yellow box it turns red
(row 58). It meets the second spider, at rest, and comes out on every
other leg (row 120): a red half on the second end's cord, and one on the
tie to the third spider. On the cord it turns the second end the other
way, setting aside \(e^{i\varphi_2}\) (Result 17.10). On the tie,
through the box, it turns green again, passes through the third spider
and fuses with the third end: a half. If both of the first two ends are
lit, push the second end's half first, so that the second spider is
still at rest when the first half arrives. The warning: this is an
equality of numbers, branch by branch. It does not say how the odds are
shared out; Result 17.8 does.
\end{quote}

Danos and Kashefi proved that this works on any open graph with the
right kind of order. Their Definition 2 is quoted in §17.4; here is
their theorem.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 17.12 (determinism; Danos and Kashefi, Theorem 1,
stated).} If an open graph \((G,V_{\mathrm{in}},V_{\mathrm{out}})\) has
a flow \((f,\prec)\) (§17.4), then the pattern that prepares \(\ket+\)
on every non-input, applies \(\mathrm{CZ}_{ij}\) on every edge, and
then, for each non-output \(i\) in the order \(\prec\), reads \(i\) with
\(M_i^{\alpha_i}\) and applies the corrections
\[X_{f(i)}^{s_i}\prod_{k\in N_{f(i)}\setminus\{i\}}Z_k^{s_i},\] is
runnable, and \textbf{uniformly and strongly deterministic}: every
branch gives the same map, for every choice of the angles \(\alpha_i\).
Danos and Kashefi call that map the unitary embedding the pattern
realizes.
\end{quote}

In the row, \(f(1)=2\) and \(f(2)=3\): the reading of wire \(1\)
corrects wire \(2\) by an \(X\) and wire \(3\), the other neighbour of
wire \(2\), by a \(Z\); the reading of wire \(2\) corrects wire \(3\) by
an \(X\). A correction on a wire that is still to be read is absorbed
into its setting, as the sidebar showed, and a correction on an output
is applied. In the picture, the \(X_{f(i)}\) is the red half arriving at
\(f(i)\), and the \(Z_k\) are the green halves it sends on to the other
neighbours of \(f(i)\). Danos and Kashefi give the same intuition in
words: their eq. (2) converts ``an anachronical \(Z\) correction at
\(i\)'' into ``a `future' \(X\) correction, the one sent to \(f(i)\)'',
and a ``\,`past' \(X\) correction'', sent back until it is absorbed by a
preparation.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Feynman's Notebook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{Measurements only.} Robert Raussendorf and Hans J. Briegel, at the
Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität in Munich, posted ``Quantum computing via
measurements only'' in October 2000; \emph{Physical Review Letters}
printed it in 2001 as ``A one-way quantum computer''. Their picture of
the laboratory was a lattice of neutral atoms held in ``periodic
micropotentials'', entangled all at once by ``controlled collisions
between atoms in neighboring potential wells'', then read one atom at a
time. They noted that single-atom occupation of a three-dimensional
optical lattice had been reported with a filling factor of \(0.44\),
above the percolation threshold of \(0.31\), so a cluster bounded only
by the trap could exist. Each reading destroys entanglement as it goes.
Their conclusion: ``Cluster states are thus one-way quantum computers
and the measurements form the program.'' Vincent Danos and Elham Kashefi
asked in 2005 which patterns can be made deterministic, and answered
with flow; the paper appeared in \emph{Physical Review A} in 2006. Van
de Wetering's survey adds that ``the development of the ZX-calculus was
originally motivated by the desire to describe MBQC in a better way'',
citing Ross Duncan's ``A graphical approach to measurement-based quantum
computing'' (2013).
\end{quote}

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why read in a turned basis,
\(\ket{\pm_{\alpha}}\), and not in \(\ket0,\ket1\)? Because a reading in
\(\ket0,\ket1\) only cuts a wire out of the graph (Raussendorf and
Briegel: measurements of \(\sigma_z\) ``effectively remove'' qubits),
and a reading in \(\ket\pm\) only moves the state along. The turn
\(\alpha\) is the only place where the program can enter. With it, one
step is a turn and a yellow box, and turns and yellow boxes make every
one-wire gate.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{out-again}{%
\section{§17.4 Out Again}\label{out-again}}

The tins of the dialogue were read in an order, first, second, last, and
the rule sent each outcome forward. What exactly must be true of a graph
for such an order to exist?

\textbf{On the blackboard: flow.} Danos and Kashefi's Definition 2
reads: ``An open graph state \((G,I,O)\) has flow if there exists a map
\(f:O^c\to I^c\) (from measured qubits to prepared qubits) and a partial
order \(>\) over \(V\) such that for all \(i\in O^c\): (F0)
\((i,f(i))\in G\); (F1) \(f(i)>i\); (F2) for all neighbours of \(f(i)\)
except \(i\) (\(k\in G(f(i))\smallsetminus\{i\}\)), we also have
\(k>i\).'' In our letters: an open graph
\((G,V_{\mathrm{in}},V_{\mathrm{out}})\) has a \textbf{flow}
\((f,\prec)\) if \(f\) sends each vertex not in \(V_{\mathrm{out}}\) to
a vertex not in \(V_{\mathrm{in}}\), and \(\prec\) is a partial order on
\(V\), such that for every \(i\notin V_{\mathrm{out}}\):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  (F0) \(f(i)\in N_i\): the correction goes to a neighbour;
\item
  (F1) \(i\prec f(i)\): the neighbour is read later, or not at all;
\item
  (F2) \(i\prec k\) for every \(k\in N_{f(i)}\setminus\{i\}\): the other
  neighbours of \(f(i)\), which receive the \(Z\) corrections, are later
  too.
\end{itemize}

The row has a flow: \(f(1)=2\), \(f(2)=3\), with \(1\prec2\prec3\).
Check (F2): the neighbours of \(2\) other than \(1\) are \(\{3\}\), and
\(1\prec3\); wire \(3\) has no neighbour other than \(2\).

Here is a graph that has none. Take three vertices \(a\), \(b\), \(c\),
with edges \(a\)--\(c\) and \(b\)--\(c\), a \textbf{V} with its corner
at \(c\); read \(a\) and \(b\), and keep \(c\) as the output. Danos and
Kashefi draw this graph as their Fig. 2, with \(a\) an input.

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} Close the V with ends on \(a\) and \(b\),
and leave \(c\)'s output open. A lit reading on \(a\) sends its half
through \(c\), which is at rest, and out on \(c\)'s other legs: onto
\(c\)'s output, as a red half, and along the tie to \(b\), where it
lands on \(b\)'s end as a green half. Exactly, with no number:
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-2.4) (0,2.4);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.6) -- node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (2.6,0);
  \draw[wire] (0,-1.6) -- node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (2.6,0);
  \draw[wire] (-1.5,1.6) -- (0,1.6);
  \draw[wire] (-1.5,-1.6) -- (0,-1.6);
  \draw[wire] (2.6,0) -- (4.4,0);
  \node[zsp] at (0,1.6) {}; \node[zsp] at (0,-1.6) {}; \node[zsp] at (2.6,0) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\varphi_a+\pi$}}] at (-1.5,1.6) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\varphi_b$}}] at (-1.5,-1.6) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-2.4) (0,2.4);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.6) -- node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (2.6,0);
  \draw[wire] (0,-1.6) -- node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (2.6,0);
  \draw[wire] (-1.5,1.6) -- (0,1.6);
  \draw[wire] (-1.5,-1.6) -- (0,-1.6);
  \draw[wire] (2.6,0) -- (5.4,0);
  \node[zsp] at (0,1.6) {}; \node[zsp] at (0,-1.6) {}; \node[zsp] at (2.6,0) {};
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (4.2,0) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\varphi_a$}}] at (-1.5,1.6) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\varphi_b+\pi$}}] at (-1.5,-1.6) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] (rows 57, 58 and 120, as in the travelling half). So
\(a\)'s outcome has to be known before \(b\) is read. By the same
picture turned over, \(b\)'s outcome has to be known before \(a\) is
read. Each has to go before the other.

The blackboard makes this exact, and for a weaker kind of order too.
Browne, Kashefi, Mhalla and Perdrix introduced \textbf{generalised
flow}, or \textbf{gFlow}, in 2007; we take the definition from Duncan
and co-authors, who cite them (their ref. {[}8{]}). For a set \(A\) of
vertices, its \textbf{odd neighbourhood} \(\mathrm{Odd}(A)\) is the set
of vertices with an odd number of neighbours in \(A\). A gFlow
\((g,\prec)\) sends each vertex \(u\) not in \(V_{\mathrm{out}}\) to a
set \(g(u)\) of vertices not in \(V_{\mathrm{in}}\), such that
\(u\in\mathrm{Odd}(g(u))\); \(u\prec v\) for every \(v\in g(u)\); and
\(u\prec v\) for every \(v\ne u\) in \(\mathrm{Odd}(g(u))\) (their
Definition B.2). A flow is a gFlow with \(g(u)=\{f(u)\}\): then
\(\mathrm{Odd}(g(u))=N_{f(u)}\), and the conditions are (F0) to (F2). In
the picture, \(g(u)\) is the set of spiders a lit half from \(u\) is
sent through, and \(\mathrm{Odd}(g(u))\) the set of ends it lands on.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 17.13 (the V has no order).} The V, with
\(V_{\mathrm{out}}=\{c\}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{in}}\) empty or \(\{a\}\),
has no flow and no gFlow.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} The only neighbour of \(a\) is \(c\), so
\(a\in\mathrm{Odd}(g(a))\) forces \(c\in g(a)\). The only neighbour of
\(b\) is \(c\) as well, so then \(b\in\mathrm{Odd}(g(a))\), and
\(b\ne a\) forces \(a\prec b\). The same argument with \(a\) and \(b\)
exchanged forces \(b\prec a\). A partial order cannot have both. A flow
is a gFlow, so there is no flow either. \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch17/OutAgain.py}, which also searches every order by brute
force.

This is Danos and Kashefi's Fig. 2, ``an open graph state with no
flow''.\footnote{Danos and Kashefi add that the pattern on this graph
  can still be made deterministic if \(b\) is read at the fixed angle
  \(\pi/2\); but then it is deterministic only at that angle, and so, in
  their words, ``not uniformly deterministic''.} Result 17.13 says
nothing about the V beyond this: no order of readings makes its
corrections work for every setting.

\hypertarget{taking-a-recipe-out}{%
\subsection{Taking a recipe out}\label{taking-a-recipe-out}}

A cooked net is a picture of a unitary, and Result 17.12 says how to
\emph{run} it if it has a flow. Duncan and co-authors used the same kind
of order to take a \emph{circuit} out of it.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 17.14 (nets from circuits keep an order; Duncan,
Kissinger, Perdrix and van de Wetering, Lemma 3.7, Theorem 4.5 and
Corollary 5.5, stated).} (i) The net that Lemma 3.2's procedure makes
from a circuit has a \textbf{focused gFlow}, a gFlow in which
\(\mathrm{Odd}(g(u))\) contains no non-output other than \(u\) (their
Definition 3.4, which they credit to Mhalla, Murao, Perdrix, Someya and
Turner). (ii) If an open graph has a focused gFlow, then it still has a
gFlow after a local complementation at an interior vertex \(u\) followed
by deleting \(u\), and after a pivot along an edge between two interior
vertices followed by deleting both. (iii) So the procedure of Result
17.5 keeps a focused gFlow. By their Remark 3.6, an open graph has a
gFlow if and only if it has a focused one.
\end{quote}

Part (i) is easy to see on \emph{The Uncooked Net}: it has a flow that
runs along the wires. Send each spider to the next spider on its own
wire, the first small spider to the second, the second to the big
spider, and each lower spider to the one on its right; order the upper
wire's two small spiders first, then the lower wire's spiders from left
to right, then the big spider. Each of (F0) to (F2) is a check against
the drawing in §17.7. Duncan and co-authors prove (i) exactly this way:
a circuit's net has a causal flow (their Definition B.1, credited to
Danos and Kashefi), which is a gFlow (their Theorem B.3). Part (iii)
covers re-tying and the pivot, and only those. For the gadget moves of
Result 17.6, van de Wetering's survey says that the extraction algorithm
of Backens, Miller-Bakewell, de Felice, Lobski and van de Wetering,
``There and back again: A circuit extraction tale'' (a preprint of 2020,
its ref. {[}13{]}), ``further generalises this approach by being able to
deal with phase gadgets''; we have not read that paper, and claim
nothing more about it. On the twenty random circuits of §17.2, PyZX's
gFlow finder found an ordinary gFlow after cooking on sixteen, and none
on the four whose cooked nets kept a gadget; PyZX took a circuit out of
all twenty.

\textbf{On the blackboard: extraction.} Duncan and co-authors take the
circuit out from the right. Keep a \textbf{frontier}, one spider for
each wire, starting at the outputs. A turn on a frontier spider slides
off onto its output as a phase gate. A Hadamard edge between two
frontier spiders is a CZ, and comes off as one. What remains between the
frontier and the spiders behind it is a set of Hadamard edges, described
by a matrix \(B\) with a row for each frontier spider and a column for
each spider behind, with entry \(1\) where they are tied: the
\textbf{biadjacency matrix}. Van de Wetering's survey writes it \(P\)
and Duncan and co-authors write it \(M\); we write \(B\). Adding one row
of \(B\) to another, over \(\mathbb F_2\), where \(1+1=0\), is a CNOT on
the two wires (their Proposition 7.1). Gaussian elimination turns part
of \(B\) into rows with a single \(1\); a frontier spider with a single
tie to one spider behind it, and no turn, is a plain wire through a
yellow box, and the frontier moves one step left. The existence of a
gFlow guarantees that some row can always be reduced so, which is what
makes the procedure finish (their §7; they remark that knowing a gFlow
exists is enough, without computing it).

Here is the smallest case, one row operation. Two spiders behind, on the
inputs, and two frontier spiders, on the outputs, with
\[B=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}:\] the upper frontier spider is
tied to both spiders behind, the lower only to the lower one. Adding the
second row to the first gives \(I\).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 17.15 (a joiner at the ends).} Exactly, with no number:
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.19em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-0.7) (0,3.1);

\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (5.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (4.0,2.4);

\node[hbox] at (2.7,0) {};

\node[zsp] at (4.0,2.4) {}; \node[zsp] at (4.0,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.19em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-0.7) (0,3.1);
\draw[wire] (0,2.4) -- (7.0,2.4);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (7.0,0);
\draw[wire] (5.6,2.4) -- (5.6,0);
\node[hbox] at (2.7,2.4) {};
\node[hbox] at (2.7,0) {};
\node[zsp] at (1.4,2.4) {}; \node[zsp] at (1.4,0) {};
\node[zsp] at (4.0,2.4) {}; \node[zsp] at (4.0,0) {};
\node[zsp] at (5.6,2.4) {}; \node[xsp] at (5.6,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] The joiner has its green on the upper wire and its
red on the lower. The same picture with the joiner the other way up is
not equal to the left side.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} Sum over bits. On the left, the spiders behind copy the
input bits \(x_1,x_2\), the frontier spiders carry output bits
\(y_1,y_2\), and the three boxes give
\(2^{-3/2}(-1)^{x_1y_1+x_2y_1+x_2y_2}\). On the right, the picture
before the joiner is \(H\otimes H\) exactly, since each wire is a spider
at rest, a box and a spider at rest; so the right side is
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}(H\otimes H)\). Now
\((H\otimes H)\ket{x_1x_2}=\tfrac12\sum_z(-1)^{x_1z_1+x_2z_2}\ket{z_1z_2}\),
and the CNOT sends \(\ket{z_1z_2}\) to \(\ket{z_1,z_1\oplus z_2}\).
Writing \(y_1=z_1\) and \(y_2=z_1\oplus z_2\), so that
\(z_2=y_1\oplus y_2\), the sign is \((-1)^{x_1y_1+x_2(y_1\oplus y_2)}\),
which is the left side's, and the numbers agree:
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\cdot\tfrac12=2^{-3/2}\). With the joiner the other way
up the same computation gives the sign
\((-1)^{x_1(y_1\oplus y_2)+x_2y_2}\), which differs at \(x=(1,0)\),
\(y=(0,1)\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch17/OutAgain.py}.

Duncan and co-authors state Proposition 7.1 for any diagram and any pair
of frontier rows, and add that a focused gFlow survives the step. We
have proved only this instance, which is the one the dialogue's cloth
uses.

Now the recipe itself. The cooked picture has no spider behind its
frontier: both of its spiders hold an output.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 17.16 (the recipe taken out).} Exactly: the cooked
picture equals a Hadamard edge between two spiders at rest, followed by
a green quarter on the upper wire and a green half on the lower,

\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(S\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CZ}\). The new recipe is: a CZ,

\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} Slide each turn off its spider toward the output (row 57
backwards). A phase-free green spider on each wire, joined by a yellow
box, is \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\mathrm{CZ}\): each spider copies its bit onto
the tie, and the box gives
\(\bra{x_2}H\ket{x_1}=2^{-1/2}(-1)^{x_1x_2}\); this is the computation
of Result 16.4 with an input leg on each spider. A green \(\pi/2\) with
two legs is \(S\), and a green \(\pi\) is \(Z\) (§16.1).
\(\;\blacksquare\) PyZX's \texttt{extract\_circuit} returns the same
three gates; see \texttt{Code/Ch17/OutAgain.py}.

For a general circuit, one thing is lost on the way out.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 17.17 (extraction; Duncan, Kissinger, Perdrix and van de
Wetering, §7, stated).} If a graph-like diagram has a gFlow, the
frontier procedure takes a circuit out of it. For a net cooked from a
circuit by Result 17.5, the circuit taken out equals the original
\textbf{up to a global phase}: a number \(r\) with \(\lvert r\rvert=1\).
\end{quote}

The global phase is the one place in this chapter's own computations
where a number is not tracked; the stated Results 17.1 and 17.5 carry
their sources' non-zero number. Duncan and co-authors neglect non-zero
numbers throughout (their Remark 2.2), and they explain why that is
harmless here: if two unitaries differ by a factor \(z\), then
\(\lvert z\rvert=1\), so neglecting numbers will, ``at worst'', give an
output that differs from the input by a global phase. On the twenty
random circuits of §17.2, every extracted circuit was the original times
such an \(r\), and none was exactly equal;
\texttt{Code/Ch17/OutAgain.py} asserts \(\lvert r\rvert=1\) in each. Our
recipe's extraction happens to be exact.

Why not take a circuit out of \emph{any} picture of a unitary? Van de
Wetering's survey (§6.6) gives the reason to doubt it can be done fast.
The promise that a picture is unitary ``is a global property of the
diagram'': large parts of it may be far from unitary and be cancelled
only by a later part, so an algorithm ``would somehow have to be using
knowledge about the global structure of the diagram''; and deciding
whether a closed picture is non-zero ``comes awfully close to being a
QMA-complete problem''. The survey states the argument as a reason for
doubt, not as a proof, and so do we. The hope, it says, is local
structure, and the best-known algorithm, which it credits to Backens and
co-authors, ``can extract a circuit out of any ZX-diagram that has a
gflow, a combinatorial property \ldots{} that corresponds to the
possibility of consistently feed-forwarding Pauli errors from
measurement outcomes''.

\textbf{The synthesis.} That last phrase joins the two halves of this
chapter. The order in which a pattern can be read, every half sent
forward, is an order in which a cooked net can be taken out again as a
recipe, frontier by frontier from the outputs. A net made from a circuit
starts with such an order (Result 17.14 (i)); re-tying and the pivot
keep it (Result 17.14 (iii)). The frontier moves from the outputs toward
the inputs, the gFlow order read backwards. We claim that a gFlow is
\emph{enough} for extraction, which is Duncan and co-authors' theorem,
and nothing more: PyZX also takes circuits out of cooked nets that keep
gadgets and have no ordinary gFlow, and the algorithm that covers them
is the one we have not read.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Coecke's Sketchbook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{What the pictures of this section do not say.} Result 17.15 is an
equality of pictures with its number; it is not an algorithm, and it
does not say which row operations to choose. Gaussian elimination
chooses them, and Gaussian elimination is the blackboard's. The frontier
is the picture's: it is the line in the drawing between what has become
recipe and what is still net, and it moves left one spider at a time.
Result 17.13 is the other kind of statement a picture cannot make on its
own. The drawing of the V shows a half from \(a\) landing on \(b\)'s end
and a half from \(b\) landing on \(a\)'s; it takes a small argument
about all possible orders, on the blackboard, to conclude that no order
exists. Pictures show what a move does. That no sequence of moves can
succeed is a claim about every sequence, and it needs a proof about
every sequence.
\end{quote}

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why an order on the vertices, and
not simply a rule for each reading? Because a correction can only go to
a wire that has not been read yet, and one correction can reach several
wires, as \(Z_3\) did in the row. So the corrections must fit together:
every wire that a reading's half lands on must come later than that
reading. Flow asks for this with one target per reading, gFlow with a
set. Anything weaker, and the V shows what goes wrong.

\hypertarget{the-theorem-twice-17}{%
\section{§17.6 The Theorem, Twice}\label{the-theorem-twice-17}}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 17.4 (four eighths that cancel), restated.} With
\(\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}\) the CNOT whose control is the upper wire,
exactly,
\[U\;=\;\bigl(\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}\,(I\otimes T)\bigr)^4\;=\;(S\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CZ},\]
and the recipe's bare picture is \(2^{-3/2}\) times the cooked picture.
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{diracs-blackboard-17}{%
\subsection{Dirac's Blackboard}\label{diracs-blackboard-17}}

Every gate in the recipe sends a basis state to a basis state times a
phase, so it is enough to follow \(\ket{x_1x_2}\).

\textbf{Step 1: the joiners.} A CNOT adds the upper bit to the lower and
leaves the upper bit alone. So after \(k\) joiners the lower wire
carries \(x_2\oplus(k\bmod2)\,x_1\), and after four it carries \(x_2\)
again: the recipe returns every basis state to itself, times a phase.

\textbf{Step 2: what each eighth sees.} The \(k\)-th eighth acts after
\(k-1\) joiners. So the first and third eighths see \(x_2\), and the
second and fourth see \(x_1\oplus x_2\).

\textbf{Step 3: the phases.} An eighth multiplies by \(e^{i\pi/4}\) when
the bit it sees is \(1\). In all,
\[U\ket{x_1x_2}\;=\;e^{i\frac\pi4\left(2x_2+2(x_1\oplus x_2)\right)}\ket{x_1x_2}\;=\;i^{\,x_2+(x_1\oplus x_2)}\ket{x_1x_2}.\]

\textbf{Step 4: read it as gates.} For bits,
\(x_1\oplus x_2=x_1+x_2-2x_1x_2\). So
\[i^{\,x_2+(x_1\oplus x_2)}\;=\;i^{\,x_1}\,i^{\,2x_2}\,i^{-2x_1x_2}\;=\;i^{\,x_1}\,(-1)^{x_2}\,(-1)^{x_1x_2},\]
which is \(S\) on the upper wire, \(Z\) on the lower, and CZ:
\(U=(S\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CZ}\). The four values are \(1,-1,i,i\) on
\(\ket{00},\ket{01},\ket{10},\ket{11}\). \(\;\blacksquare\)
