  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi/2$}}] at (3.3,3.2) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi$}}] at (3.3,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\]

\textbf{Step (v): slide together} (row 57). The quarter and the half
slide back into the spiders at the ends of the Hadamard edge:
\[\;=\;2^{-3/2}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.19em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1.2) (0,3.4);
  \draw[wire] (0,2.4) -- (2.8,2.4);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2.8,0);
  \draw[wire] (1.4,2.4) -- (1.4,0);
  \node[hbox] at (1.4,1.2) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi/2$}}] at (1.4,2.4) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi$}}] at (1.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\]

\textbf{Step (vi): read off.} The cooked picture is
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(S\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CZ}\) (Result 17.16). The
recipe's picture, \(\tfrac14U\), equals
\(2^{-3/2}\cdot\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(S\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CZ}=\tfrac14(S\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CZ}\).
So \(U=(S\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CZ}\), and no eighth is left.
\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch17/CookingDown.py}, which checks
every picture of this chain against the one before, with its number.

\hypertarget{the-verdict-17}{%
\subsection{The verdict}\label{the-verdict-17}}

The blackboard wins, and the chapter says so. The parity count is four
short steps and needs nothing but the fact that a CNOT adds bits. The
sketchbook takes six moves and three numbers, and one of its moves, step
(iv), is not a rewrite at all: the quarter hub and the Hadamard edge
were matched by evaluating both, because this book has derived no chain
of moves from the one to the other. A skeptic of pictures may say the
proof leans on the blackboard at its hinge, and the skeptic is right.

What the pictures show is \emph{why} the eighths cancel, and where. The
second and fourth eighths hang from hubs tied to the same two wires, so
they read the same parity and add; the first and third slide together on
the lower wire, because they read the same bit. That is the blackboard's
step 2, made visible: two classes, a quarter each. And the pictures win
where the blackboard's count breaks. Put a Hadamard in the middle of the
recipe, and the lower wire no longer carries a parity of the inputs; the
bookkeeping of steps 1 and 2 stops. The gadget moves do not care: a hub
is a hub wherever it came from. That is where Kissinger and van de
Wetering found their gains, on circuits ``that contain many Hadamard
gates''. We state that from their results, and have not proved it here.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-uncooked-net}{%
\section{§17.7 The Uncooked Net}\label{the-uncooked-net}}

Here is the chapter's master diagram: the graph-like net of the recipe,
built in §17.1, before any cooking. Every spider is green. Every tie
between spiders is a Hadamard edge, drawn with its yellow box, as the
ties of the Crab's tangle wear yellow sleeves.

On the upper wire, from left to right: the upper input's lead, running
plain to a small spider at rest; a Hadamard edge to a second small
spider at rest; a Hadamard edge to the big spider at rest, which is the
four controls slid together; and the upper output's lead, running plain
from the big spider. On the lower wire, from left to right: the lower
input's lead, running plain to the first eighth; then, alternating, a
Hadamard edge to the first spider at rest (the first joiner's target), a
Hadamard edge to the second eighth, a Hadamard edge to the second spider
at rest, and so on, through the fourth eighth and the fourth spider at
rest; and the lower output's lead, which carries one yellow box from the
fourth spider at rest to the output. From the big spider, four ties fan
down, each a Hadamard edge, one to each spider at rest on the lower
wire. No two lines cross. We call the picture \textbf{The Uncooked Net}.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, x=1.3em, y=1.1em,

  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \draw[wire] (0,6) -- (2.4,6);

    { \draw[wire] (\a,0) -- node[hbox,pos=0.5]{} (\b,0); }

  \node[zsp] at (2.4,6) {};
  \node[zsp] at (5.4,6) {};
  \node[zsp] at (10.8,6) {};
  \foreach \x in {1.2,6.0,10.8,15.6} { \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi/4$}}] at (\x,0) {}; }
  \foreach \x in {3.6,8.4,13.2,18.0} { \node[zsp] at (\x,0) {}; }
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 17.18 (The Uncooked Net).} Exactly,
\[\text{The Uncooked Net}\;=\;\tfrac14\,U\;=\;2^{-3/2}\times\text{the cooked picture}.\]
It has four eighths, so its picture's count is the recipe's \(T\)-count,
\(4\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} \textbf{On the blackboard.} It is the recipe's bare
picture after colour change, fusion and the two dummies of §17.1, each
of which is exact, and the recipe's picture is \(\tfrac14U\), with \(U\)
as computed in §17.6. One can also sum over the bits of the net's eleven
spiders directly, with a sign \((-1)^{xy}\) and a factor
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) for each yellow box between bits \(x\) and \(y\);
the sum gives the same matrix. \textbf{In the sketchbook.} The chain of
§17.6, run on the recipe's picture, which is this net up to the exact
moves of §17.1 (rows 56, 57 and 58). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch17/FourEighths.py}, which builds this picture and checks
it against the recipe's picture; and \texttt{Code/Ch17/CookingDown.py},
where PyZX's \texttt{full\_reduce} cooks the net by its own moves,
re-tyings, pivots and gadget moves, to the cooked picture with the
number \(2^{-3/2}\) written beside it, and \texttt{extract\_circuit}
returns \((S\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CZ}\).

The net has fifteen vertices: its two inputs and two outputs, and eleven
spiders, four of them eighths. It is what the dialogue's tangle hangs
as, under the beam: a long picture, drawn with nothing spent, and
nothing yet gained.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{what-a-rewrite-does-not-promise}{%
\section{§17.8 What a Rewrite Does Not
Promise}\label{what-a-rewrite-does-not-promise}}

Take stock. Every diagram is a non-zero number times a net (Result
17.1), and for a circuit the number can be tracked; our recipe of four
eighths is \emph{The Uncooked Net}, exactly (Result 17.18). A turn
between two joiners hangs from a hub (Result 17.2), and two hubs on the
same spiders add (Result 17.3), so the recipe's four eighths meet and
become none (Result 17.4, proved twice). Re-tying and the pivot clear a
net of its interior quarters and halves (Result 17.5), and gadgets carry
the eighths together (Result 17.6); phase teleportation writes the
result back into the original circuit (Result 17.7). A pattern is a
picture read wire by wire (Result 17.8); its readings are coin tosses
(Result 17.9), but a lit half travels forward (Results 17.10 and 17.11),
and with a flow the corrections make every branch the same (Result
17.12). The V has no such order (Result 17.13). A net from a circuit has
one, and re-tyings and pivots keep it (Result 17.14); a joiner at the
ends unties a doubled tie (Result 17.15), our recipe comes out exactly
(Result 17.16), and a general circuit comes out up to a global phase
(Result 17.17).

Now the honest part. \textbf{A rewrite proves that two processes are
equal, and nothing else.} No move in this chapter proves that a count of
eighths is the least possible. PyZX's numbers are what a heuristic
found, and they beat, match or lose to other methods circuit by circuit:
on twenty of the thirty-six benchmarks they came out exactly where the
previous best already was. No move proves a running time; the
\(O(\lvert V\rvert^3)\) bounds are the sources' counts of steps, and the
speeds are measurements. Extraction of a general diagram is not claimed
to be efficient, and the survey gives reasons to doubt it. The headline
itself was won by the blackboard, and the sketchbook's proof leaned on
it at step (iv). Re-tying and the pivot were used as Chapter 16 stated
them; their derivations by the rules are in Duncan and co-authors'
Appendix B.3, and are not in this book. And every picture in the chapter
is exact, number included, except for extraction in general, which gives
the circuit back up to a global phase.

What the pictures do give is a kind of freedom. A recipe fixes when each
step is done; a net forgets it and keeps only which wires are joined and
how each is turned. That forgetting is what lets two eighths written far
apart find each other on a hub. And the same forgetting explains the
one-way machine: a net can be read in any order that its ties allow, and
the order that makes the readings safe is the order that lets a recipe
be written down again.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

The chapter's question has an answer. A cheaper recipe is found by
drawing the recipe as a net, which costs nothing, and cooking the net:
sliding like spiders together, re-tying, and hanging turns from hubs
until the turns that read the same wires meet and add. It is known to do
the same thing because every move is an equality, and the moves
themselves are the certificate; the same moves, run on the old recipe
followed by the new one reversed, cook it down to bare wires. The cooked
net can then be run by reading, if its readings can be sent forward in
order, or taken back out as a recipe by the same order, frontier by
frontier. For our recipe the four eighths vanished, and the recipe that
came out needs none.

But every picture in this chapter was noiseless. Every joiner joined,
and every reading read what the state held. Real hardware is not like
that: now and then a reading comes out false. Chapter 18, \emph{Against
Noise}, answers with a plain remedy: make copies, and take a vote. The
picture of making copies is one this book already knows. Its encoder is
a single green spider.

\hypertarget{ricercar-with-repeats}{%
\chapter{Ricercar with Repeats}\label{ricercar-with-repeats}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\emph{鈴はただ}\\
\emph{隣に問ふや}\\
\emph{虎落笛}

\emph{suzu wa tada}\\
\emph{tonari ni tou ya}\\
\emph{mogaribue}

\emph{The little bell asks}\\
\emph{only of its neighbours ---}\\
\emph{the fence whistles all night.}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\emph{{[}The Crab's front hall, on a late-winter evening, the day after
the kitchen. The storm is at its height. The Tortoise is already in, by
the hall table, perfectly dry. In the corner by the stairs, on the
settle, something is curled that may be asleep and may not. The knocker
goes, and the Crab opens the front door on a wet Achilles and a great
deal of wind.{]}}

\emph{{[}The hall the wind comes into is long and narrow and lit early,
and the Crab keeps it, like most things he owns, in threes. There are
three lamps: one on its bracket by the front door, one on the hall table
halfway down, and one on its bracket by the kitchen door at the far end,
where the hall clock ticks on the wall. There are three coat-pegs by the
door, and three steps up to the landing where the stairs turn. In the
corner at the foot of them stands the old settle, with a cushion at its
end. The open door lets the whole storm in at once, and all three flames
flatten and gutter together; for a moment the hall is half in the dark,
and which of the three would stay in, nobody could have said. Over the
door the fanlight's three panes rattle in their frame, and the rain
comes at them in handfuls; at the narrow window beside the door it
stands in drops on the glass; along the floor the draught comes feeling
in over the worn sill, past a squat iron doorstop, across the flags. On
the wall above the settle hangs a print in a plain dark frame: Escher's
\textup{Order and Chaos}, a regular star-shaped solid at the centre,
with broken things scattered round it. The table lamp reaches it only at
a slant and leaves its lower corner in shadow. It hung there before the
storm got up this morning, and it will hang there when the storm has
blown itself out. On the settle beneath it the cushion keeps a dent that
is, looked at again, quite smooth, and there is a warmth in that corner
that may be the house's own. The clock ticks on under the wind, heard in
the lulls and lost in the gusts.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} In, in, before the door takes you with it!

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}getting the door shut behind him with his
shoulder{]}} I had the wind at my back the whole length of the lane and
the rain in my face all the way. I don't know how it managed both.

\textbf{Crab:} Weather like this keeps to no side. Off with that scarf;
it's making a pond.

\emph{{[}Achilles unwinds his scarf, soaked through, and hangs it on a
coat-peg by the door.{]}}

\emph{{[}With the door shut the three flames stand up again one at a
time, the one by the door last, and the hall comes back into its light.
Under the peg the scarf begins at once to drip onto the mat, and
Achilles stamps the wet out of his boots and blows into his hands.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}to the Tortoise{]}} And how are you dry?

\textbf{Tortoise:} The shell again. It's what it's for.

\textbf{Achilles:} One day I'll borrow it.

\textbf{Tortoise:} One day I'll lend it, and you'll find it heavier than
it looks.

\emph{{[}Achilles turns from the door and stops. Down the whole length
of the hall, at head height, runs a line of cords and curtain rings,
along the wall the hall table stands against.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}proudly{]}} My storm line. I strung it this
morning, for the storm. A message goes in here at the front door, runs
the length of the hall with the draught at it all the way, and comes out
at the kitchen.

\emph{{[}At the door end the line hangs from the front-door hook, which
also holds a brass dial under a hinged cover; at the kitchen end, from
the kitchen-door hook, which also holds a small lidded glass. Every ring
on the line hangs upright, facing into the hall, with a bead on its
band, and every bead sits stiff on its band wherever it is turned and
stands at rest at the top of its ring; turned a half, a bead stands at
the ring's foot. Every cord is knotted at both its ends, to a ring or to

\emph{{[}From the door end. The lead-in runs from the front-door hook to

\emph{{[}Mid-hall. From the first weather ring a cord runs on to a green

\emph{{[}Towards the kitchen. From the first tell ring a cord runs to a

\textbf{Achilles:} It looks like the rigging of a very small ship.

\textbf{Crab:} The rings and the bells are from Delft, from the
bellfounder across the canal from the old man's bench. He says a line
like this will carry a message through any weather worth the name.
Tonight I mean to find out.

\emph{{[}The three lamps light the line in three reaches: the one by the

\emph{{[}Achilles, turning to take it all in, sees the settle in the

\textbf{Achilles:} Oh --- and you're here too. How do you find the

\textbf{Cat:} \emph{{[}not troubling to open more than one eye{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} That's no sort of---

\textbf{Tortoise:} A loose question buys a loose answer. It always has,

\textbf{Crab:} There's tea on the hall table, and bread and cheese.

\textbf{Achilles:} As I said?

\textbf{Crab:} Yesterday, at my kitchen door, going out into the rain.
You'll see.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}a slice of bread in one hand, the cup in the

\textbf{Crab:} Most good advice begins as a joke. The trick is to hear

\emph{{[}Achilles laughs under his breath and lowers himself onto the

add, so the ring's bead, which was at rest, now stands a quarter round.
What lies on the cloth now: one green ring turned a quarter round, its
three cords running from it, and at the end of each cord nothing at all.
What has changed: the ring has taken the turn into itself. What has
held: one ring, with all three cords still on it. No turned point has
come out anywhere.{]}}

\begin{center}
\partcloth[pushed in]{the turned point}{Taken in}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} But I wanted three points, each a quarter round, one
at the end of each cord. You've given me one ring, turned, holding all
three.

\textbf{Tortoise:} You remember the press from Delft. It copied its own
kind, and made a pair of every other.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}slowly{]}} So the three cords aren't three
copies. They're one turn, shared out along three cords, and not one of
them has it alone. \ldots Oh. You can't copy a turn; you can only spread
it.

\emph{{[}Over the front door, the lamp at the corner of the lane comes
in through the fanlight's three panes of old rippled glass, not as a
lamp but as one blur of light laid across all three. Each pane has a
share of it; not one of them has the lamp.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}looking up from the cloth to the storm line,
and along it to the door{]}} Just inside the front door, a green ring:
one lead in, and three strands out. That's your parting ring.

\begin{center}
\stormline*{Strung for the storm}
\end{center}

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}with a little bow to his line{]}} It is. It
spreads whatever comes in from the dial over all three strands, and
copies nothing it shouldn't. And that is why nobody looks at my strands,
ever. A look at any one of them spoils a turned message on all three.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}gathering the turned ring off the
drawing-cloth into her box, and its cords into her work-bag{]}} So a
message on the line isn't three messages. It's one message, hanging on
three strands.

\textbf{Achilles:} But then how does anyone vote? To vote you must look
at each copy, and you've said looking spoils a turned one.

\emph{{[}The Crab only smiles, and looks down the hall at the bells.{]}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{second-challenge-the-blind-vote}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Second Challenge --- \emph{The Blind
Vote}}{Second Challenge --- The Blind Vote}}\label{second-challenge-the-blind-vote}}

\textbf{Crab:} Nobody looks. We listen. \emph{{[}He goes to stand
mid-hall, below the tell rings.{]}} My bells. Each one hangs from two
strands side by side, tied up to their tell rings. It rings when those
two strands disagree, one dark and one lit, and keeps quiet when they
agree; and it never tells which is which.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then what use is it? I'd want to know which strand is
which.

\textbf{Tortoise:} That's the one thing you mustn't want. A bell that
told you which would be a look.

\textbf{Achilles:} So it only hears whether the two agree. A strange
thing to put to a bell.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Ask the pair, not the one.

\emph{{[}Along the foot of the front door the draught has found the one
place where the old sill has worn away from the door's edge, and there,
and only there, it whistles, thin and high. Everywhere else along the
door, where wood meets wood true, there is no sound at all. It is the
same thin note on a mild night as on a bitter one, wet or dry; it sounds
only where two edges fail to meet.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}moving along to the red rings nearest the
kitchen{]}} And these are my mending rings. I turn their beads with my
own claw, a half at a time, and a bead I've turned stays where I put it
until I turn it back. My rule goes by the bells and nothing else: both
silent, I touch nothing; the first bell alone, I turn the first mending
ring; both bells, the middle one; the second bell alone, the third.

\emph{{[}He lifts the lidded glass down from the kitchen-door hook.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} And my kitchen glass, which reads what comes out. Its lid
has the same six marks as the door dial: lift it at a mark, and the
glass shows clear if the message is the one at that mark, cloudy if it's
that mark's opposite --- dark and lit, at rest and a half, a quarter
round and a quarter back. If the message is neither the mark nor its
opposite, it comes up clear or cloudy like a tossed coin.

\textbf{Achilles:} So the one who sent it lifts it at the mark he sent.

\textbf{Crab:} And clear means it came through as sent. A message goes
once and is read once. \emph{{[}He hangs the glass back on its hook, lid
down.{]}} The glass's lid goes back afterwards, unlike my tins; the
message it read is spent.

\textbf{Achilles:} Let me send one.

\textbf{Crab:} Set it where I can't see. I don't want to know what
you've sent. I'll mend it all the same.

\emph{{[}Achilles goes to the front door and lifts the dial's cover with
his back to the room, turns the pointer, and lets the cover fall. The
line as it stands: the pointer at his secret mark under the cover; every
weather ring, tell ring and mending ring at rest; the bells hanging
still; the glass on its hook, lid down, clear. He lets the dial's catch
go, and it clicks. Nothing visible runs along the cords; they hardly
stir. Down by the door the weather rings hang in the draught. Neither
bell makes a sound. The Crab's claws stay folded. What has changed: the
message has gone in, and waits now at the mending rings. What has held:
every bead at rest, and both bells silent.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} Not a sound. I touch nothing.

\emph{{[}Achilles walks the length of the hall to the kitchen door, and
lifts the lid of the glass at his mark. The glass stays clear.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Clear. It came through as I sent it. I set a quarter
round, and nobody knew.

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}resetting the glass: lid down, clear{]}} A quiet
run. The draught was kind to you. Again.

\emph{{[}Achilles, grinning, finishes his tea in one long swallow and
hands the cup to the Tortoise, who fills it again and keeps it warm
between her hands for him. The Crab, who has not sat down once since the
knocker went, still does not.{]}}

\emph{{[}Achilles goes back to the door and sets the dial under its
cover again. The Crab runs a claw along his mending rings without
looking up at them: every bead at rest, where he left it. The line as it
stands: the pointer at Achilles's secret mark; every bead at rest; the
bells still; the glass reset. Achilles lets the catch go.{]}}

\emph{{[}A gust shoves in under the front door, and the draught goes
hard along the floor and up. Down by the door the middle weather ring's
bead is flung round a half as the message passes it, and falls back to
rest behind it: too quick, from where the company stands, for anyone
there to say which ring it was. Mid-hall the first bell rings; then the
second, too. Then both fall still. What has changed: both bells have
spoken. What has held: every bead that anyone can see, at rest; and the
message, whatever it is, waiting at the mending rings.{]}}

\emph{{[}Every head in the hall turns, for no reason anyone could give,
toward the settle in the corner; and then back.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Both! Which strand was it? Let me just see which
strand it was --- \emph{{[}He hurries up the hall from the door to the
tell rings and reaches up toward the middle one.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}hurrying along the line from his mending rings
and catching his wrist, gently{]}} No.~A look at any one strand spoils a
turned message on all three, and yours may be turned. I don't know what
you sent, and I won't learn it that way.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then how will you know what to mend?

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}a claw lifted toward the bells, not the
strands{]}} Ask the pair, not the one.

\textbf{Crab:} Both bells rang. So the middle strand disagrees with both
its neighbours, and it's the middle I mend.

\emph{{[}The middle mending ring as it stands: its bead at rest, like
its neighbours'. The Crab goes back along the line to it and turns the
bead round a half with one claw, and takes the claw away. The bead stays
at the half. The first and third mending rings he does not touch, and he
has not so much as glanced at a strand. What has changed: one bead, by a
half. What has held: the other mending rings; the mark under the dial's
cover; and what the Crab knows of the message, which is nothing.{]}}

\emph{{[}Achilles goes down the hall to the kitchen door and lifts the
glass's lid at his mark. The glass stays clear.{]}}

\begin{center}
\stormline[middle mending ring at a half, glass clear]{Lifted at the kitchen}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Clear. \emph{{[}He stares at it.{]}} A quarter round
again, through a gust, and it came out exactly as I sent it. And you
mended it without knowing what it was.

\emph{{[}Out in the lane the gale drops, all at once, into its one lull
of the evening. In the sudden quiet the table lamp's flame stands up
tall and perfectly still, and its light reaches across the hall and
lies, for the first time tonight, full on the print above the
settle.{]}}

\emph{{[}The Tortoise turns in her chair and looks across the hall, her
glance passing over the settle without resting there, to the print on
the wall opposite the storm line: Escher's \textup{Order and Chaos}.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Like your print: a regular star-shaped solid at the
centre, with broken things scattered round it. The storm breaks what it
likes; the middle keeps.

\textbf{Achilles:} But how? The bells heard the gust. Why didn't they
hear the message too? It was right there on the strands they're tied to.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}as Achilles lets the glass's lid back down
and comes back up the hall to her shoulder{]}} The cloth can show you.

\emph{{[}On the bare drawing-cloth she lays out ring for ring the line
that hangs above her head, its door end at her left and its first strand
furthest from her, as the first hangs nearest the wall: a lead in to a
green ring; from it three strands, and on each strand in order a red
ring, a green ring and a red ring; the three strands meeting again in a
last green ring, and a lead out. Between the strands she lays two red
rings, each a little towards the kitchen end from the green rings of the
strands it lies between and tied to them, as the bells hang below the
gaps in the hall. Every cord of hers runs where one of his does, and
every bead is at rest. Every tie she leaves slack, long enough to follow
its rings wherever they slide.{]}}

\begin{center}
\linecloth*{On the cloth, at rest}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Your storm line, drawn.

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}coming up the hall from his mending rings to the
table, and looking from the cloth to the hall and back{]}} Ring for
ring.

\emph{{[}The gale has come back to the door, and the flames bow to it
again. The Crab draws up a kitchen chair at last and sits, elbows on the
table, and Achilles leans in over the Tortoise's shoulder with a slice
of bread forgotten in his hand.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Now this evening's second run. A weather ring the
gust turned, I draw at a half; a bell that rang, at a half; a mending
ring you turned, at a half.

\emph{{[}The cloth as it stands: every bead at rest. She turns beads
round a half: on the middle strand's red ring nearest the door, on each
bell's ring, and on the middle strand's red ring nearest the kitchen.
Nothing else moves. What has changed: those beads, each by a half. What
has held: every green ring at rest, the first and third strands' red
rings at rest, and every cord.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} And the rule for a half that meets a ring at rest. A
red half on one cord of a green ring at rest goes through it, and comes
out on every other cord of that ring. Watch the gust's half.

\emph{{[}The middle strand as it stands: the red weather ring at a half;
the green tell ring at rest, with the weather cord coming in, the
mending cord going out, and the ties to both bells running from it. The
Tortoise slides the weather ring's half along its cord into the tell
ring. The tell ring's bead does not move. The half goes through it and
comes out on every other cord of it at once: a red half on the tie to
the first bell, a red half on the tie to the second bell, and a red half
on the cord onward to the mending ring. The weather ring is left at
rest. What has changed: the one half has become a half on each of the
tell ring's other cords. What has held: the tell ring at rest; and the
first and third strands, untouched.{]}}

\begin{center}
\linecloth[halves set, gust's half sent through]{Gone through}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Into both bells at once. And on into the mending
ring.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Red meets red, and their beads add. Two halves make
none.

\emph{{[}She slides the half on each tie down into its bell. Each bell
was at a half, and a half and a half make a whole turn, which is rest.
She slides the half on the mending cord into the middle mending ring: it
was at a half, and a half more brings it too to rest. What lies on the
cloth now: every red ring at rest, the weather rings, the bells and the
mending rings alike. What has changed: the gust's half, the bells'
halves and the Crab's half have met and cancelled. What has held: the
green rings, all at rest, and every cord.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} So my half went to meet the gust's.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Exactly there. And a red ring at rest on a strand is
only cord. So now the green rings may slide together along bare cord.

\emph{{[}The cloth as it stands: along each strand, green rings at rest
with bare cord between them; the bells, at rest, lying between the
strands. The Tortoise slides the first tell ring along the first
strand's bare cord into the parting ring; then the joining ring, along
the first strand's cord from the kitchen end, into the same ring. That
ring now holds the lead in, the lead out, the first bell's tie from the
first strand, and the middle and third strands at both their ends. She
slides the middle tell ring into it along the middle strand's cord from
the door end; what is left of the middle strand now runs from that ring
back to itself, a loop, and a loop comes off, so she lifts it off into
her work-bag. She does the same with the third tell ring, and the third
strand's loop. What lies on the cloth now: one green ring at rest, with
the lead in and the lead out on it, and each bell tied twice to it. What
has changed: every green ring has gone into one, and the strands' loops
are gone. What has held: every bead at rest, and every tie of each bell
still where it runs.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} And a bell at rest, tied twice to one green ring and
to nothing else, comes off it.

\emph{{[}She lifts the first bell off into her box of rings, its ties
into her work-bag, and then the second. What lies on the cloth now: one
green ring at rest, with a lead in and a lead out, and nothing else; and
a green ring at rest with only a lead in and a lead out is just cord.
She unclips the ring into her box, knotting the lead in to the lead out
where it held them, and draws the cord straight: a plain cord from the
door end to the kitchen end. What has changed: the whole storm line,
gust and bells and mending, has come down to one plain cord. What has
held: whatever goes in at one end comes out at the other, untouched.{]}}

\begin{center}
\linecloth[halves set, gust's half sent through, halves slid in, green rings slid together, bells off, drawn straight]{Drawn straight}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} A plain cord. \emph{{[}He looks up at the line, and
back.{]}} So what you're saying is that the bells only ever heard the
gust.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The gust, and where it was. Never your message.

\textbf{Achilles:} Because whatever I set, the parting ring hangs it on
the strands as all-dark and all-lit together, so much of each. A gust on
the middle strand spoils both the same way: in each, the middle differs
from its neighbours. So the bells hear the gust, and my message never
comes into it.

\textbf{Crab:} Just so.

\textbf{Achilles:} Ask the pair, not the one.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}delighted, looking up at the bells{]}} So
nothing can get past the bells.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Will you send me one more, and let me stand by the
middle strand?

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{third-challenge-the-turn-the-bells-miss}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Third Challenge --- \emph{The Turn the Bells
Miss}}{Third Challenge --- The Turn the Bells Miss}}\label{third-challenge-the-turn-the-bells-miss}}

\emph{{[}The middle mending ring as it stands: at a half, where the Crab
left it. He goes along to it and turns it back round a half, and it
stands at rest again, like its neighbours; he knows where he left it,
and has no need to look at a strand to do it. He resets the glass: lid
down, clear.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} Everything back as it was. \emph{{[}He comes back up the
hall to the table, and watches the Tortoise take her place mid-hall, by
the middle tell ring.{]}} You won't look at it?

\textbf{Tortoise:} I shan't look at anything. I may turn something.

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}uneasily{]}} Turning's not looking. I suppose.

\emph{{[}The Tortoise gives him a look of perfect mildness and folds her
claws in front of her. Achilles, on his way to the door, pats the Crab
on the shoulder in passing, and the Crab smooths down his waistcoat as
if that had been the trouble.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}at the dial{]}} Setting. \emph{{[}He turns
the pointer under the cover and lets the cover fall.{]}} Secret again.

\emph{{[}The line as it stands: the pointer at Achilles's secret mark;
every bead at rest; the bells still; the glass reset. Achilles lets the
catch go. As the message reaches mid-hall, the Tortoise puts one claw to
the middle tell ring and turns its green bead round a half, and holds it
there while the message goes by. The ring does not move on its cords;
only its bead turns. Neither bell makes a sound. The Crab, watching the
bells and nothing else, keeps his claws folded. What has changed: the
middle tell ring's bead, at a half. What has held: both bells silent,
and every other bead at rest.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} Silent, both. Nothing to mend.

\emph{{[}Achilles walks down the hall to the kitchen door and lifts the
glass's lid at his mark. The glass clouds over.{]}}

\begin{center}
\stormline[middle tell ring at a half, glass cloudy]{Turned in passing}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Cloudy! \ldots Oh. The bells never heard a thing, and
it's spoilt all the same.

\emph{{[}The middle tell ring as it stands: its bead at a half, under
the Tortoise's claw. She turns it back round a half, to rest, as the
Crab had it, and takes her claw away. The cords have not stirred.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} There. And had you sent dark or lit, the glass would
have come up clear. My kind of turn does nothing at all to dark and lit;
it spoils only the turned ones.

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}staring at his bells{]}} Then my storm line is
half deaf.

\emph{{[}At the front door the draught whistles at its worn place as it
has all evening, and the three flames bow to every gust it brings. But
the damp has never needed the door. It has come in through the walls
without a sound, and nothing in the hall has bowed to it: behind the
coat-pegs the plaster has bloomed dark in a patch the size of a hand,
the bread on the plate has gone soft at the crust, and Achilles's scarf
on its peg is no drier than when he hung it.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} But why didn't they ring? She turned the middle
strand, and they're both tied to it.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The gust makes a strand disagree with its neighbours,
and the bells hear that. My turn makes it disagree with nothing: it
turns the message round, and the bells were never asked about that.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then what would hear it?

\textbf{Tortoise:} The same line in the other colour. \emph{{[}She goes
back to her chair at the hall table, Achilles letting the glass's lid
back down over the cloud and coming up the hall to her shoulder, and
takes her yellow tubes from her bag.{]}} My yellow tubes, as ever. A
ring with a tube on every cord comes out the other colour, its bead
where it was; and two tubes in a row are no tube at all, so I may put a
pair on anywhere I like.

\emph{{[}She lifts the plain cord off the drawing-cloth into her
work-bag, and on the bare cloth lays a fresh parting ring, its lead
coming in from her left as on the line: a green ring at rest, a lead in,
three strands out. On each of its cords she slides a pair of tubes,
which changes nothing. Then she draws the ring through the near tube of
every pair: the tubes go into it and are gone, and the ring comes out
red, its bead still at rest. The far tube of each pair stays on its
cord. What lies on the cloth now: a red ring at rest, with a tube on its
lead in and a tube on each strand. What has changed: the ring's colour.
What has held: its bead, its cords, and everything the picture does.{]}}

\begin{center}
\tubecloth*[pairs put on, drawn through]{a fresh parting ring}{Come out red}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} The same ring, asking in the other colour. Hang a
whole line from it, and its bells hear my kind of turn.

\textbf{Achilles:} And the gust?

\textbf{Tortoise:} They're deaf to the gust. So we lay both.

\emph{{[}She lifts the red ring off the drawing-cloth into her box, its
cords and tubes into her work-bag, and on the bare cloth lays a green
parting ring, its lead coming in from her left, a lead in and three
strands out. On each of the three strands she slides a tube, and past
each tube she sets another green parting ring, each with three strands
of its own. What lies on the cloth now: one ring spreading to three,
three tubes, and three rings each spreading to three: nine strands, in
groups of three.{]}}

\begin{center}
\tubecloth{nine strands}{Spread out again}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Nine strands for one message!

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}laying a pair of bells along each group, as
on the Crab's line, and across the groups one more pair, for the other
kind of turn{]}} Each group of three hears a gust on its own strands.
The pair across the groups hears my kind of turn, on any strand of the
nine.

\textbf{Crab:} And a turn that's part the one kind and part the other?
Storms aren't tidy, and my draught doesn't choose.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Whatever turns one strand is a sum of four parts: no
turn, the gust's kind, my kind, and both at once. The bells on the nine
sort out each part, and the mending undoes each. Undo every part, and
you have undone the sum.

\textbf{Crab:} Then I'll hang a bell that asks \emph{everything}.
\emph{{[}He goes to the hall-table drawer.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Everything? What would a bell like that ask?

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{fourth-challenge-what-a-bell-may-ask}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Fourth Challenge --- \emph{What a Bell May
Ask}}{Fourth Challenge --- What a Bell May Ask}}\label{fourth-challenge-what-a-bell-may-ask}}

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}coming back from the drawer with a small brass
bell on a spring clip{]}} This. My clip-bell, from the same bellfounder
in Delft; he sent it with the others, as a sample. It has no ties at
all: it clips straight onto one ring, and it rings when that one strand
is lit, and keeps quiet when it's dark.

\textbf{Achilles:} It asks a single strand, straight out.

\emph{{[}The clip-bell lies in his claw like something out of a
jeweller's window: no bigger than a thimble, its brass as bright as a
new coin, the founder's mark stamped small on its shoulder, and its clip
so fine that it trembles when the Crab breathes on it. Of all the things
from Delft in the hall, it is the prettiest.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}proudly, clipping it to the first tell ring{]}}
Ask the one, not the pair.

\emph{{[}The first tell ring as it stands: green, at rest, the first
strand's cords on either side of it and the first bell's tie hanging
from it. The Crab springs the clip-bell onto the foot of its band, and
the little bell hangs straight down from the clip. The ring does not
move on its cords; nothing is tied or untied. The bells below hang as
they were. What has changed: a small bell rides now on the first
strand's tell ring. What has held: every cord, and every bead.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} Why ask a pair a riddle when you can ask one strand
straight?

\textbf{Tortoise:} Send him one, Achilles. Dark.

\emph{{[}The Crab goes down to the kitchen door and resets the glass:
lid down, and the cloud the last message left in it clears, until the
glass stands clear again. Achilles goes to the front door, sets the dial
to dark, openly, and lets the catch go. The clip-bell hangs silent; the
tied bells are silent; the Crab touches nothing. Achilles walks down to
the kitchen door and lifts the glass's lid at dark. The glass stays
clear.{]}}

\begin{center}
\stormline[clip-bell on the first tell ring, glass clear]{Clipped on}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Dark, and clear.

\emph{{[}The Crab resets the glass. Achilles goes back to the door, sets
the dial to lit, and lets the catch go. The clip-bell rings; the tied
bells stay silent; the Crab touches nothing. Achilles walks down to the
glass again and lifts the lid at lit. The glass stays clear.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}triumphant{]}} It told me the message itself!
Lit, and it said lit, and the glass as clear as water.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Now let me set one. \emph{{[}The Crab resets the
glass. The Tortoise goes to the dial, lifts the cover with her back to
the room, turns the pointer, and lets the cover fall.{]}} Achilles, let
it go.

\emph{{[}The line as it stands: the pointer at the Tortoise's secret
mark; every bead at rest; the clip-bell on the first tell ring, still;
the tied bells still; the glass reset. Achilles comes back to the door
and lets the catch go. The clip-bell rings. The tied bells stay silent,
and the Crab touches nothing. The Tortoise walks to the kitchen door and
lifts the glass's lid at her mark. The glass clouds over. What has
changed: the clip-bell has spoken, and the glass is cloudy. What has
held: no gust, no tied bell ringing, no claw on a mending ring. Nothing
touched the message but the clip-bell's question.{]}}

\begin{center}
\stormline[clip-bell on, glass cloudy]{Lifted at her mark}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} A quarter round. Cloudy.

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}stricken{]}} But it rang! It said lit!

\textbf{Tortoise:} It said the first strand was lit, and to say so it
had to make it so, on all three. After that your message was lit and
nothing else, and a lit message read at a quarter round is a tossed
coin: it comes up cloudy as often as clear.

\textbf{Tortoise:} A bell that can tell you the message spoils every
turned one.

\textbf{Achilles:} So even when the glass comes up clear after that
bell, it's clear by luck.

\emph{{[}Achilles, still by the front door where he let the catch go,
puts his face close to the narrow window beside it to see how the lane
is faring, and his own breath fogs the pane before he can make out
anything at all. He draws back, and the fog goes, and there is the lane
again, rain and lamplight.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}slowly{]}} Then it's a look after all. A look
with a bell on it. \emph{{[}He regards the clip-bell ruefully.{]}} Well.
It's a very pretty bell.

\emph{{[}The clip-bell as it stands: on the first tell ring. The Crab
comes back along the hall to it, springs the clip open and lifts it off.
The ring hangs as it was, green, at rest, the first bell's tie still
hanging from it; the tied bells below have not stirred. He puts the
clip-bell back in the hall-table drawer, and shuts it. What has changed:
the one-strand bell is gone from the line. What has held: every cord and
every bead, as they were before it came.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} Ask the pair, not the one.

\emph{{[}In the shut drawer the clip-bell knocks once against the wood
as it settles, and is quiet. It is a pretty sample among the odd buttons
now, and the hall is a little plainer without it.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Then what may a bell ask, at all?

\textbf{Tortoise:} Anything whose answer is the same whatever the
message. Whether two strands agree is such a question. Whether one
strand is lit is not.

\textbf{Achilles:} And must it always be two strands at a time?

\textbf{Tortoise:} Not at all. \emph{{[}Back in her chair from the
kitchen door, where she has let the glass's lid back down over the
cloud, and with Achilles come up the hall to her shoulder again, she
lifts the nine strands off the drawing-cloth, their rings into her box
and the rest into her work-bag, and on the bare cloth lays strands
crosswise and lengthwise in a square weave. At every crossing she lays a
bell of one colour, tied to the four lengths of strand that meet there;
in the middle of every little square, a bell of the other colour, tied
to the four lengths round it.{]}} Bells that ask four at once, and never
the one.

\textbf{Achilles:} And your tins, Crab. If a vote of three is good, what
about a vote of three votes?

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}turning the pages of the ledger{]}} I tried it,
last night, on the top shelf: three tins to a message, a vote in each
tin, and then a vote of the three. About two in a thousand went wrong.

\textbf{Achilles:} One in ten for a hollow, three in a hundred for a
vote, two in a thousand for a vote of votes. Vote on the votes again,
and again, and it goes to nothing!

\textbf{Tortoise:} While the damp is less than a half. Above that, every
vote makes it worse.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}working it{]}} At six in ten a hollow, two
of the three go false more often than not. So the vote is wrong more
often than a single hollow is. \ldots Worse, yes.

\textbf{Crab:} Then pray for a mild damp. \emph{{[}He closes the
ledger.{]}}

\emph{{[}He goes through to the kitchen and comes back with the kettle,
and freshens the pot. Achilles cuts himself another piece of cheese, and
the Tortoise holds out her cup without looking up from the cloth. Down
by the stairs the draught passes over the settle and stirs nothing
there, if there is anything there to stir.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} And when a thing is safe inside its three strands, or
its weave, how do you \emph{do} anything with it? Join two, say, without
unwrapping them?

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{fifth-challenge-split-and-merge}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Fifth Challenge --- \emph{Split and
Merge}}{Fifth Challenge --- Split and Merge}}\label{fifth-challenge-split-and-merge}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} With a joiner. \emph{{[}She lifts the weave off the
drawing-cloth into her box and her work-bag; lays a long cord across the
bare cloth from her left to her right, the upper line, and another below
it, nearer her, the lower; and takes a joiner from her box and clips it
across them, its green ring on the upper line and its red ring on the
lower a little to the right, so that the string between them slants.{]}}
My joiner, the one you know: a green ring on the upper line, tied by a
short string to a red ring on the lower. Upper lit, it flips the lower;
upper dark, it leaves the lower be.

\begin{center}
\splitcloth*{Clipped across}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} But a joiner reaches right into both lines. Wouldn't
it unwrap them?

\textbf{Tortoise:} Look at it again.

\emph{{[}The joiner as it stands: the upper line running into the green
ring and out again; the lower line running into the red ring and out
again; the short string between them. The Tortoise loosens the short
string at the red ring and draws it out long, so that it drops a little
from the green ring, runs level beside the upper line for a way, and
then drops to the red ring, and knots it again where it was. No ring has
moved; no bead has turned; every cord ends where it ended. What has
changed: only how it lies. The green ring now has one line coming in and
two going out, the upper line and the long string beside it; the red
ring has two coming in, the long string and the lower line, and one
going out.{]}}

\begin{center}
\splitcloth[drawn out]{Drawn out long}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} A split and a merge. The green ring splits the upper
line in two, like your parting ring with two strands instead of three.
The red ring merges the second of them with the lower line: it puts a
question to the two of them, in the other colour, and answers.

\emph{{[}Where the rain has been driven in under the front door, a thin
shine of water has been spreading over the flags all evening. It reaches
the iron doorstop and parts round it, and on the far side its two edges
find each other again and are one shine, going on as before.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} It answers? How?

\textbf{Tortoise:} Like a bell: silent, or ringing. My cloth can't ring.
Have you a penny?

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}producing one from his waistcoat pocket{]}} My
pocket penny, honest as they come; I've tossed it for the last slice of
cheese for years. Heads, your merge is silent; tails, it rings.

\textbf{Tortoise:} For a joiner, the merge answers like a fair penny,
whatever the two messages. Toss it.

\emph{{[}The Crab tosses. The penny turns over and over in the
lamplight, and he claps it onto the back of his claw: heads.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} Heads. Silent.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Then the split and the merge are a plain joiner, just
as they lie. Again.

\emph{{[}He tosses again. The penny turns, and lands: tails.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} Tails. It rings.

\emph{{[}The joiner as it stands: the split and the merge, every bead at
rest. The Tortoise sets a green ring turned a half on the long string,
on its level run, just before it turns down to the red ring, on the
merge's first cord in. She slides it back along the string, away from
the red ring, into the green ring the string came from: green meets
green, and the split's bead now stands at a half. Then she slides the
split apart along the upper line: the split is left at rest, and a green
ring at a half sits on the upper line just past it. What has changed:
the half has moved from between the rings onto the upper line. What has
held: the red ring, the lower line, the long string, and every knot.{]}}

\begin{center}
\splitcloth[drawn out, half on the string, slid into the split, slid apart]{Slid back and apart}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Tails leaves a half behind. It isn't lost; it's only
sitting on the upper line, where a hand can reach it.

\textbf{Crab:} Then my hand goes where it goes on my storm line.
\emph{{[}He sets a green ring turned a half on the upper line, beside
hers, on the side away from the split.{]}}

\emph{{[}The upper line as it stands: two green rings, each at a half,
plain cord between them. The Tortoise slides one into the other. A half
and a half make none, and the ring that is left stands at rest, with
only the upper line through it: just cord, and she unclips it into her

What has changed: the half is gone. What has held: the joiner,
whole.{]}}

\begin{center}
\splitcloth[drawn out, half on the string, slid into the split, slid apart, crab's half beside, slid together]{Nothing left over}
\end{center}

\textbf{Crab:} A joiner again.

\textbf{Achilles:} So joining two protected things is a split, and a
merge, and a penny, and a hand.

\textbf{Tortoise:} And look what the rest of the evening was. Your
parting ring splits one message three ways. A bell merges two strands
and answers whether they agree. A joiner is a split and a merge.
Everything tonight was one ring, asked in two colours.

\emph{{[}Between gusts the three flames stand up together, and the hall
is lit from end to end by one light in which nobody could say where one

\emph{{[}The Crab puts the penny back in his waistcoat pocket. The

\textbf{Crab:} The last of the pot. \emph{{[}He shares it out, three

\emph{{[}Achilles takes it without argument and holds it in both hands,
and the Tortoise, her work-bag on her knee, leans back in the hall

\textbf{Achilles:} Listen to it out there. It hasn't let up once all

\textbf{Crab:} Nor will it before morning. You'll not go out into that.
There's a bed made up at the top of the stairs.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}glancing at his scarf on its peg{]}} My
scarf thanks you. It's still wet through.

\emph{{[}A clock in the hall strikes eight.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Eight. The storm has made a long evening of it.

\emph{{[}Up the lane, a breath behind as it always is in wet weather,
the church clock strikes eight too, the sound of it torn about by the
wind. Achilles yawns, and does not trouble to hide it.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}looking up at the storm line{]}} I'll leave it
up while the storm lasts. Every message tonight came through it, and
nobody looked.

\textbf{Achilles:} Set in secret, turned by a gust, mended by a claw
that never knew what it mended. And out it came, exactly.

\emph{{[}Every head in the hall turns toward the settle in the corner by
the stairs.{]}}

\emph{{[}The settle keeps its small mystery to the last. The cushion at
its end holds a dent that is, looked at again, quite smooth; the warmth
in that corner may be something curled there, or only the house's own,
gathered into the corner out of the wind; and what may be an ear, or may
be a fold in the cushion's cover, has not quite lain down all evening.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}softly, to the Crab{]}} All evening you've
asked nothing but pairs.

\textbf{Crab:} And never one thing, straight. \emph{{[}He crosses to the
settle.{]}} One question, then, and a straight one. Through all that
storm --- Cat, asleep, or awake?

\textbf{Cat:} Asleep.

\emph{{[}The Cat settles to its one answer; and as the rest of it goes
from the settle --- the curled warmth, the tucked paws, the one ear that
never quite lay down --- the last of it to fade is the grin, which hangs
a moment over the empty cushion, and then is gone too.{]}}

\emph{{[}The settle is only a settle now: an old bench at the foot of
the stairs, and a cushion with one plain dent in it, the warmth going
slowly out of it. Outside the storm is at its height still and means to
be till morning; it throws the rain at the fanlight and leans on the
front door, and the draught whistles thin at its one worn place along
the sill. Inside, the three lamps burn upright and steady. Down the
length of the hall the storm line hangs as the Crab strung it this
morning, from the front-door hook to the kitchen-door hook, every cord
knotted where he knotted it: the lead-in and the first lengths in the
door lamp's light, the lengths about the tell rings and the ties down to
the bells in the light from the table, the last lengths and the lead-out
by the kitchen. Now that nobody is attending to it, it may be giving off
its low note again under the wind, or it may not. On the table the tins
stand stacked on their tray beside the ledger, and the Tortoise's
work-bag sits closed at her feet; on its peg Achilles's scarf drips more
slowly onto the mat. Above the settle the print hangs in its plain dark
frame, the table lamp's light no more than an edge on it again, one more
of the Crab's things. At the top of the stairs a bed is made up and
waiting. Nobody goes up to it yet: Achilles sits on the lowest step with
the last of his tea in his hands, and the Crab looks along his line from
end to end, and does not look at any one strand of it.{]}}

\hypertarget{chapter-18-against-noise}{%
\chapter{Chapter 18: Against Noise}\label{chapter-18-against-noise}}

\emph{--- Ricercar with Repeats ---}

\emph{Part V: Engineering the Diagram}

\emph{Escher: ``Order and Chaos'' --- a regular star-shaped solid at the
centre, with broken things scattered round it}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

How can a message that nobody is allowed to look at travel through a
storm that turns it at random, and still arrive exactly as it was sent?

People have always had an answer to half of this question. When a line
is bad, you say the thing three times. A clerk who cannot afford a
mistake writes the figure into three ledgers, and if one of them later
disagrees with the other two, he trusts the two. A computer does the
same, silently and all the time. Gottesman points out, in a footnote,
that an ordinary digital computer ``is using a repetition code'': each
bit is held by many electrons, and after each step the bit is set back
to whatever most of them say.

A quantum message breaks both halves of that answer. The first half,
\emph{say it three times}, fails because a quantum state cannot be
copied. Chapter 11 proved it: no process makes two copies of every
state. The second half, \emph{trust the two that agree}, fails because
to find out which copies agree you would have to look at them, and a
look at a quantum message is not a harmless glance. It is a measurement,
and a measurement changes the thing it measures. So the clerk's method
is forbidden twice over.

And the storm is worse than the clerk's. A figure in a ledger is either
right or wrong. A quantum message can be turned by any small amount, in
any direction, and a turn of one part in a thousand is already a
different message. There seems to be a whole continuum of ways to go
wrong, and no finite list of repairs.

Yet the thing can be done, and done exactly. This chapter shows how. The
message is not copied, it is \emph{spread}: one message is carried by
three wires together, in a way that is not three copies. Nobody asks the
wires what they hold. Instead, each question asks whether two of the
wires \emph{agree}, and the answer to that question turns out to be the
same whatever the message is. So the questions hear the storm and never
the message. And the continuum of possible damage turns out to be an
illusion of the blackboard's description: every small turn is a sum of a
few whole ones, and whatever repairs the whole ones repairs their sums.

The price is paid in wires, and in a condition on the storm. If the
storm is too strong, the repair does more harm than good. Where exactly
that line falls is one of the great practical questions of the subject,
and the pictures of this book cannot answer it. We will say so when we
get there.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{three-for-one}{%
\section{§18.1 Three for One}\label{three-for-one}}

Chapter 17 ended with a promise: ``Real hardware is not like that: now
and then a reading comes out false. Chapter 18, \emph{Against Noise},
answers with a plain remedy: make copies, and take a vote. The picture
of making copies is one this book already knows. Its encoder is a single
green spider.''

The chapter's question, in the form we can answer: \textbf{a message
that must not be looked at is sent through noise that turns it at
random; how can it arrive exactly as sent?} We answer it in five steps.
This section says what noise is, counts what a vote buys, and draws the
one copier that does not clone. §18.2 votes without looking. §18.3 finds
the kind of noise the vote cannot hear, and builds the nine-wire code
that hears both kinds. §18.4 asks which questions a code may ask at all,
and states what is known about building a whole machine this way. §18.5
joins two protected messages without unwrapping them.

\hypertarget{noise}{%
\subsection{Noise}\label{noise}}

\textbf{On the blackboard.} Recall the Pauli matrices, in Gottesman's
Table 1:
\[X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y=iXZ=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}.\]
Gottesman calls \(X\) the \emph{bit flip}, \(Z\) the \emph{phase flip},
and \(Y\) both at once. Chapter 9 taught us that a process that may go
more than one way is a \textbf{channel}, written in Kraus form:
\(\rho\mapsto\sum_iE_i\rho E_i^{\dagger}\) with
\(\sum_iE_i^{\dagger}E_i=I\) (Gottesman's eq. (23); Chapter 9, row 70).
The three channels of this chapter each leave a wire alone with
probability \(1-p\) and do something to it with probability \(p\):
\[\mathcal N^X_p(\rho)=(1-p)\,\rho+p\,X\rho X,\qquad \mathcal N^Z_p(\rho)=(1-p)\,\rho+p\,Z\rho Z,\]
\[\mathcal N^{\mathrm{dep}}_p(\rho)=(1-p)\,\rho+\tfrac p3\bigl(X\rho X+Y\rho Y+Z\rho Z\bigr).\]
The first is the \textbf{bit-flip channel}, the second the
\textbf{phase-flip channel}, the third the \textbf{depolarizing
channel}. Their Kraus operators are \(\sqrt{1-p}\,I\) and \(\sqrt p\)
times a Pauli (for the third, \(\sqrt{p/3}\) times each of the three),
and \(\sum_iE_i^{\dagger}E_i=(1-p)I+pI=I\) because every Pauli squares
to \(I\). Noise on \(n\) wires is \textbf{independent} when it is the
channel \(\mathcal N_p\) on each wire separately,
\((\mathcal N_p)^{\otimes n}\).

A small calculation shows what the two flips do. The dialogue's door
dial has six marks. Read as states, they are dark \(\ket0\), lit
\(\ket1\), at rest \(\ket+\), a half \(\ket-\), a quarter round
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket0+i\ket1)\) and a quarter back
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket0-i\ket1)\). A bit flip exchanges dark and lit,
and it leaves at rest alone: \(X\ket+=\ket+\). On a quarter round it
gives
\[X\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket0+i\ket1\bigr)=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket1+i\ket0\bigr)=i\cdot\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket0-i\ket1\bigr),\]
a quarter back, up to the overall number \(i\), which changes nothing a
reading can see. A phase flip does the opposite: it leaves dark and lit
alone and exchanges at rest with a half, and a quarter round with a
quarter back. So \(\mathcal N^X_p\) never harms a message set at rest,
and \(\mathcal N^Z_p\) never harms a message set dark or lit. Neither is
harmless for all six marks.

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} A red spider turned \(\pi\) with two legs is
\(X\), exactly (Chapter 8, §8.2), and a green spider turned \(\pi\) with
two legs is \(Z\). Chapter 9 drew a channel on \textbf{doubled} wires
(rows 66 and 70): a wire and its mirror copy, the mirror carrying the
conjugate, and a process \(A\) drawn as \(A\) on the wire and \(\bar A\)
on the mirror. The matrix \(X\) is real, so \(\bar X=X\), and its mirror
copy is again a red half. A channel with two Kraus operators is a sum of
two doubled pictures, each with its weight. Here is the bit-flip
channel, the wire on top and its mirror copy below:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.1 (the bit flip, doubled).} For every \(p\), exactly,
\[\mathcal N^X_p\;=\;(1-p)\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em]
\path (0,-1.3) (0,1.3);
\draw[wire] (0,0.6) -- (2.6,0.6);
\draw[wire] (0,-0.6) -- (2.6,-0.6);
\end{tikzpicture}
\;+\;p\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-1.3) (0,1.5);
\draw[wire] (0,0.6) -- (2.6,0.6);
\draw[wire] (0,-0.6) -- (2.6,-0.6);
\node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (1.3,0.6) {};
\node[xsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi$}}] at (1.3,-0.6) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] The phase-flip channel is the same with green
halves, and the depolarizing channel is a weighted sum of four doubled
pictures.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} In doubled form a state
\(\rho=\sum_{ij}\rho_{ij}\ket i\bra j\) is the vector
\(\sum_{ij}\rho_{ij}\ket i\otimes\ket j\), the ket on the wire and the
conjugated bra on the mirror (Chapter 9, row 66), and a process \(A\)
acts as \(A\otimes\bar A\), which sends it to \(A\rho A^{\dagger}\). The
right-hand side acts as \((1-p)\,I\otimes I+p\,X\otimes X\), which sends
\(\rho\) to \((1-p)\rho+pX\rho X\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch18/ThreeForOne.py}, which checks it on a random non-real
density matrix.

This is the only doubled picture in the chapter. A sum of two pictures
is not one picture, and the rules of the sketchbook rewrite pictures,
not sums. So from here on we work \textbf{branch by branch}: we follow
one Kraus operator at a time, a definite pattern of flips, drawn
undoubled with Chapter 10's bit-labelled phases (row 75). A red spider
turned \(e\pi\), with \(e\) a bit, is \(X^e\): no flip when \(e=0\), a
flip when \(e=1\). One picture covers every branch. The probabilities of
the branches, and their sums, stay on the blackboard.

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why describe noise by a list of
things that might happen, each with a probability, rather than by one
``noisy'' operation? Because the wire is not the only thing that knows
what happened. A gust that flips a wire leaves a trace in the air that
flipped it, and that trace is gone for good: we cannot undo a flip we
cannot identify. The Kraus form says exactly this. It lists the things
that might have happened, as if the environment kept a record, and it
forgets the record.

\hypertarget{a-vote}{%
\subsection{A vote}\label{a-vote}}

Before the quantum case, the classical one, whose numbers the dialogue's
tins carry. A bit is written three times. The damp turns each of the
three independently, either way, with probability \(p\). We read all
three and trust the majority.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.2 (the vote of three).} For every \(p\) with
\(0\le p\le1\), and whichever way the bit was set, the majority of the
three is wrong with probability exactly \[F(p)\;=\;3p^2-2p^3 .\] At
\(p=\tfrac1{10}\), \(F(p)=0.028\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} The majority is wrong exactly when two or three of the
three are turned: \(3p^2(1-p)+p^3=3p^2-2p^3\). Nothing in the count
depends on which way the bit was set. \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch18/ThreeForOne.py}, which enumerates the eight patterns
for a bit set dark and a bit set lit, at \(p=\tfrac1{10}\), at
\(p=0.37\) and at a random \(p\).

The letter \(F\) means this function for the rest of the chapter. The
vote turns a failure rate of one in ten into about three in a hundred.
It needs no cleverness: only copies, and a count.

\hypertarget{the-one-copier-there-is}{%
\subsection{The one copier there is}\label{the-one-copier-there-is}}

The quantum version of the clerk's method would be Gottesman's eq. (3):
send \(\ket\psi\) to \(\ket\psi\otimes\ket\psi\otimes\ket\psi\). His
Theorem 1 forbids it: ``There is no quantum operation that takes a state
\(\ket\psi\) to \(\ket\psi\otimes\ket\psi\) for all states
\(\ket\psi\).'' Chapter 11 proved this in several forms (Results 11.1
and 11.3), and Gottesman's proof is the one we met first, linearity: a
map that copies \(\ket\psi\) and \(\ket\varphi\) sends their sum to
\(\ket\psi\ket\psi+\ket\varphi\ket\varphi\), not to the copy of the sum.

What linearity does allow is to copy a \emph{basis}. Chapter 11's copier
\(\delta=\ket{00}\bra0+\ket{11}\bra1\) copies \(\ket0\) and \(\ket1\)
and nothing else (row 81). Here is its three-legged cousin.

\textbf{On the blackboard.} Let
\[\mathrm{Enc}\;:=\;\ket{000}\bra0+\ket{111}\bra1 .\] It is an
\(8\times2\) matrix, with a \(1\) in the rows of \(\ket{000}\) and
\(\ket{111}\). The letter \(\mathrm{Enc}\) means this matrix, and
nothing else, for the rest of the chapter. On a general message,
\[\mathrm{Enc}\bigl(\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1\bigr)\;=\;\alpha\ket{000}+\beta\ket{111}.\]
Compare the forbidden clone,
\(\bigl(\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1\bigr)^{\otimes3}=\alpha^3\ket{000}+\alpha^2\beta\ket{001}+\dots+\beta^3\ket{111}\),
which has eight terms. The two agree only when one of \(\alpha\),
\(\beta\) is zero: for dark and lit messages, and for no other. The
message a quarter round, \(\alpha=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) and
\(\beta=\tfrac{i}{\sqrt2}\), becomes
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket{000}+i\ket{111}\bigr)\): not three
quarter-round wires, but one quarter-round message written across three
wires at once. It is the classical repetition code of Gottesman's eqs.
(1) and (2), \(0\mapsto000\) and \(1\mapsto111\), applied to the basis
and extended by linearity. Finally,
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\mathrm{Enc}=\ket0\braket{000|000}\bra0+\ket1\braket{111|111}\bra1=I\):
the encoder loses nothing.

The \textbf{code space} of the encoder is the image of \(\mathrm{Enc}\),
the two-dimensional space spanned by \(\ket{000}\) and \(\ket{111}\). We
write \(\mathcal Q\) for a code space; Gottesman writes \(C\).

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} A green spider at rest with one leg in and
three legs out is, by its definition in Chapter 8 (row 53),
\(\ket{000}\bra0+\ket{111}\bra1\). That is all.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.3 (the encoder is a spider).} Exactly, with no number,
\[\mathrm{Enc}\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
\path (0,-1.6) (0,1.6);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (2.4,1.2) -- (3.4,1.2);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (3.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (2.4,-1.2) -- (3.4,-1.2);
\node[zsp] at (1.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] and \[\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\mathrm{Enc}\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
\path (0,-1.6) (0,1.6);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (2.4,1.2) -- (3.6,1.2) -- (4.6,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (4.6,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (2.4,-1.2) -- (3.6,-1.2) -- (4.6,0);
\draw[wire] (4.6,0) -- (6.0,0);
\node[zsp] at (1.4,0) {};
\node[zsp] at (4.6,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em]
\path (0,-1.6) (0,1.6);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2.4,0);
\end{tikzpicture}\] The mirror image of the encoder, a green spider with
three legs in and one out, is \(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} The first equation is row 53 with three outputs. For the
second: the two spiders share a leg, so they slide together into one
green spider (fusion, row 57); the other two shared legs become loops
from that spider to itself, and a self-loop on a green spider goes, with
the number \(1\) (row 90; the Dirac's Blackboard sidebar of §18.2 checks
the number for a spider of any phase). What is left is a green spider at
rest with two legs, a plain wire (row 57). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch18/ThreeForOne.py}, where PyZX's \texttt{full\_reduce}
takes the right-hand picture to a bare wire with the number \(1\).

The mirror image is the second meaning of a picture that Chapter 3 gave
us: turn it left to right, and conjugate. The encoder is real, so
conjugating changes nothing. (Its three legs out are not three legs of a
cup, and no cup is drawn in this chapter; where the book draws one, the
convention of Chapter 6 holds: the cup is \(\ket{00}+\ket{11}\),
unnormalized, and the Bell state is
\(\ket{\Phi^+}=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\,\)cup.)

Now feed it a message. A dark or lit message is a \textbf{red point}:
Chapter 8's red spider with one leg, at rest for dark and turned a half
for lit. Bare, a red point at rest is \(\ket++\ket-=\sqrt2\ket0\) and a
red point turned \(\pi\) is \(\ket+-\ket-=\sqrt2\ket1\) (row 54). A
turned message is a \textbf{green point}: a green spider with one leg,
turned \(\varphi\), which is \(\ket0+e^{i\varphi}\ket1\) (row 53).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.4 (copy and spread).} Let \(a\) be a bit. Exactly:
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-1.6) (0,1.6);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.6,0);
\draw[wire] (1.6,0) -- (2.6,1.2) -- (3.6,1.2);
\draw[wire] (1.6,0) -- (3.6,0);
\draw[wire] (1.6,0) -- (2.6,-1.2) -- (3.6,-1.2);
\node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$a\pi$}}] at (0,0) {};
\node[zsp] at (1.6,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;\tfrac12\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-1.6) (0,1.6);
\draw[wire] (0,1.2) -- (1.6,1.2);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.6,0);
\draw[wire] (0,-1.2) -- (1.6,-1.2);
\node[xsp,label={[ph]left:{$a\pi$}}] at (0,1.2) {};
\node[xsp,label={[ph]left:{$a\pi$}}] at (0,0) {};
\node[xsp,label={[ph]left:{$a\pi$}}] at (0,-1.2) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\qquad\qquad
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-1.6) (0,1.6);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.6,0);
\draw[wire] (1.6,0) -- (2.6,1.2) -- (3.6,1.2);
\draw[wire] (1.6,0) -- (3.6,0);
\draw[wire] (1.6,0) -- (2.6,-1.2) -- (3.6,-1.2);
\node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\varphi$}}] at (0,0) {};
\node[zsp] at (1.6,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-1.6) (0,1.6);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.6,1.2) -- (2.4,1.2);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2.4,0);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.6,-1.2) -- (2.4,-1.2);
\node[zsp,label={[ph]left:{$\varphi$}}] at (0,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] A dark or lit point comes out as three points of the
same kind, worth twice the one, so the number \(\tfrac12\) goes to one
side. A green point turned \(\varphi\) is not copied: it slides into the
encoder, and what comes out is one green spider turned \(\varphi\) with
three legs, \(\ket{000}+e^{i\varphi}\ket{111}\). For every \(\varphi\)
this is not three points of any kind: it is entangled.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} On the blackboard:
\(\mathrm{Enc}\,\sqrt2\ket a=\sqrt2\ket{aaa}\), and three red points
give \((\sqrt2)^3\ket{aaa}\), which is twice as much. The green point:
\(\mathrm{Enc}(\ket0+e^{i\varphi}\ket1)=\ket{000}+e^{i\varphi}\ket{111}\),
which is the green spider turned \(\varphi\) with three outputs (row
53); and it has rank \(2\) across the cut between its first wire and the
other two, while three points have rank \(1\) there (Chapter 11, row
87). The derivation of the first equation by the rules is the Coecke's
Sketchbook sidebar below; the second is fusion (row 57).
\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch18/ThreeForOne.py}.

This is Chapter 11's complementarity again (row 82), now with three
legs: red points copy through a green spider, green points fuse into it.
The encoder copies a message exactly when the message is dark or lit,
and for every other message it does something no copier could do: it
spreads one message across three wires.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Coecke's Sketchbook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{The number of a copy.} Chapter 8 stated copy (Theorem 8.3) for a
green spider with one leg in and two out: a red point at rest,
\(\sqrt2\ket0\) bare, comes out as two red points with the number
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) beside them. Chapter 11 (row 81) made it exact. For
three legs, slide the encoder apart (fusion backwards, row 57) into two
copiers in a row: the first with one leg in and two out, the second on
its lower output. The point meets the first copier and becomes two
points, with the number \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\). The lower of them meets the
second copier and becomes two more, with another \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\).
Three points, and \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\cdot\tfrac1{\sqrt2}=\tfrac12\). The
same steps work for a point turned a half, since copy holds for both red
points. They do not work for a green point: a green point and a green
spider are the same colour, and fusion comes first. The warning in the
picture: the rule copies \textbf{points of the other colour}, and only
those.
\end{quote}

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why take the encoder that copies
dark and lit, and not some cleverer map? Because it is the only kind of
copying that linearity allows: an encoder that copies \(\ket0\) and
\(\ket1\) is fixed on a basis, and so it is \(\mathrm{Enc}\). Whatever a
vote can do for dark and lit messages, this encoder does. The whole
chapter is about what it does for the others.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-blind-vote}{%
\section{§18.2 The Blind Vote}\label{the-blind-vote}}

The clerk votes by reading. He opens each ledger, sees the figure, and
trusts the two that match. We may not read: a reading of one wire of
\(\alpha\ket{000}+\beta\ket{111}\) answers \(0\) with probability
\(|\alpha|^2\) and leaves \(\ket{000}\) behind, and the message is gone
(Chapter 9's Born rule). So the vote must be taken in a different way.
We shall not ask any wire what it holds. We shall ask two wires whether
they \textbf{agree}.

\hypertarget{asking-a-pair}{%
\subsection{Asking a pair}\label{asking-a-pair}}

\textbf{On the blackboard.} The operator \(Z_1Z_2=Z\otimes Z\otimes I\)
multiplies \(\ket{x_1x_2x_3}\) by \((-1)^{x_1\oplus x_2}\): by \(+1\)
when the first two bits agree, by \(-1\) when they differ. It does not
care what the bits are, only whether they match. Its two projectors are
\[\tfrac12\bigl(I+Z_1Z_2\bigr)\;\;(\text{the pair agrees}),\qquad \tfrac12\bigl(I-Z_1Z_2\bigr)\;\;(\text{the pair disagrees}),\]
and a look with these two projectors, in the sense of Chapter 9, is
Gottesman's measurement of \(Z\otimes Z\otimes I\) (his eq. (39)). The
second check asks the second and third wires, with \(Z_2Z_3\). We write
\(s_1\) for the answer of the first check and \(s_2\) for the second:
\(0\) for ``agree'', \(1\) for ``disagree''. Both together have four
outcomes \(s=(s_1,s_2)\), with projectors
\[P_s\;=\;\tfrac14\bigl(I+(-1)^{s_1}Z_1Z_2\bigr)\bigl(I+(-1)^{s_2}Z_2Z_3\bigr).\]
The two factors commute, each is a projector, and one checks that
\(P_sP_{s'}=[s=s']\,P_s\) and \(\sum_sP_s=I\). Here and below,
\([s=s']\) is \(1\) when the statement in brackets is true and \(0\)
when it is false; we do not write it \(\delta\), because \(\delta\) is
Chapter 11's copier. The four outcomes are called the \textbf{syndrome}.

Now the small calculation that makes the whole chapter work. On the code
space, \(Z_1Z_2\ket{000}=\ket{000}\) and \(Z_1Z_2\ket{111}=\ket{111}\):
both basis words have their first two bits in agreement. So \(Z_1Z_2\)
leaves every \(\alpha\ket{000}+\beta\ket{111}\) alone, and the first
check answers ``agree'' with certainty, whatever \(\alpha\) and
\(\beta\) are. The answer carries no news of the message.

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} Chapter 12 drew the parity of two classical
wires as a red dot (row 96), and Chapter 13 hung a red hub from green
feet on quantum wires and wrote its number (row 102). Here is the
smallest case. On each of two wires put a green spider at rest with
three legs, two along the wire and one tie; tie both to one red spider
turned \(s\pi\), which has only those two legs. We call the red spider a
\textbf{bell}, after the dialogue's, and the two green spiders its
\textbf{tell rings}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.5 (a bell asks a pair).} For each bit \(s\), exactly,
with no number:
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.71em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-0.6) (0,2.2);
\draw[wire] (0,1.6) -- (3.8,1.6);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (3.8,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,1.6) -- (2.7,0.8);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (2.7,0.8);
\node[zsp] at (1.4,1.6) {};
\node[zsp] at (1.4,0) {};
\node[xsp,label={[ph]right:{$s\pi$}}] at (2.7,0.8) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;\tfrac12\bigl(I+(-1)^{s}\,Z\otimes Z\bigr).\] Two such bells, on
the first and second wires and on the second and third, are the four
projectors \(P_s\) at once.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} Follow a basis state \(\ket{x_1x_2}\). Each green spider
copies its bit onto its tie (row 53), so the bell receives
\(\ket{x_1x_2}\) on its two legs. Bare, the bell is the effect
\(\bra{++}+e^{is\pi}\bra{--}\) (row 54), and
\(\braket{++|x_1x_2}=\tfrac12\),
\(\braket{--|x_1x_2}=\tfrac12(-1)^{x_1\oplus x_2}\). So the picture
multiplies \(\ket{x_1x_2}\) by
\(\tfrac12\bigl(1+(-1)^{s}(-1)^{x_1\oplus x_2}\bigr)\), which is the
projector. For the second sentence: put the second bell after the first;
the two green spiders on the middle wire are joined by a plain wire, so
they slide together into one green spider with two ties (row 57), and
the product of the two projectors is \(P_s\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch18/BlindVote.py}.
