The number is exactly \(1\) here only because the bell has two legs.
With \(w\) legs the same computation gives \(2^{1-w/2}\) times the
projector; we will need that in §18.4.

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why ask whether two wires agree,
and not simply ask one wire what it holds? Because the question ``what
does wire one hold?'' has a different answer for \(\ket{000}\) and for
\(\ket{111}\), and a question with different answers on the two words of
the code must separate them: after it is asked, \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\)
are no longer in the same state. The question ``do wires one and two
agree?'' has the \emph{same} answer on both words. Questions of that
kind leave a superposition of the two words alone, and §18.4 shows, with
Knill and Laflamme's theorem, that they are the only questions a code
may ask.

\hypertarget{the-bells-hear-the-gust}{%
\subsection{The bells hear the gust}\label{the-bells-hear-the-gust}}

Now let the storm in. A \textbf{gust pattern} is a string of three bits
\(e=e_1e_2e_3\), with \(e_k=1\) when wire \(k\) is flipped; the gust
itself is \(X^e=X^{e_1}\otimes X^{e_2}\otimes X^{e_3}\). Write
\(\bar e\) for \(e\) with every bit flipped. The \textbf{syndrome map}
sends a gust pattern to the pair of answers it would produce,
\[\sigma(e)\;=\;\bigl(e_1\oplus e_2,\;e_2\oplus e_3\bigr).\] The letter
\(\sigma\) means only this map in this chapter.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.6 (the bells hear the gust, not the message).} For
every gust pattern \(e\in\{0,1\}^3\), every outcome \(s\) and every
message,
\[P_s\,X^{e}\,\mathrm{Enc}\;=\;[\,s=\sigma(e)\,]\;X^{e}\,\mathrm{Enc}.\]
So the checks answer \(\sigma(e)\) with probability \(1\), and they do
not disturb the state.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.}
\(X^e\mathrm{Enc}(\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1)=\alpha\ket e+\beta\ket{\bar e}\).
The first check multiplies \(\ket e\) by \((-1)^{e_1\oplus e_2}\) and
\(\ket{\bar e}\) by
\((-1)^{(1\oplus e_1)\oplus(1\oplus e_2)}=(-1)^{e_1\oplus e_2}\), the
same sign; likewise the second. So \(\alpha\ket e+\beta\ket{\bar e}\)
lies wholly in the range of \(P_{\sigma(e)}\), and the other three
projectors send it to \(0\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch18/BlindVote.py}, which checks all eight patterns and all
four outcomes.

Here is the dialogue's headline run, in coordinates. The message is set
a quarter round, \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket0+i\ket1)\). The encoder spreads
it: \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket{000}+i\ket{111})\). A gust turns the middle
wire, \(e=010\): the state becomes
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket{010}+i\ket{101})\). On \(\ket{010}\) the first
pair disagrees and so does the second; on \(\ket{101}\), the same. Both
bells ring: \(s=11\), with certainty, and the state is untouched. The
bells have said ``the middle wire differs from both its neighbours'',
and nothing at all about \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) or \(i\).

So the mending is a table. For each outcome, flip back the one wire that
would have caused it:
\[c(00)=000,\qquad c(10)=100,\qquad c(11)=010,\qquad c(01)=001.\] The
correction is \(X^{c(s)}\). In the example, \(X^{010}\) turns
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket{010}+i\ket{101})\) back into
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket{000}+i\ket{111})\), which is the spread message
exactly. Nobody has looked at it.

\hypertarget{one-gust-mended-blind}{%
\subsection{One gust, mended blind}\label{one-gust-mended-blind}}

Put the pieces in a row: spread, weather, ask, mend, and join. The
joining step is the mirror image of the encoder,
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\). We should say plainly what that means.
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\) is not a device one can build on its own: it
sends \(\ket{000}\) to \(\ket0\) and \(\ket{111}\) to \(\ket1\) and
every other basis word to \(0\), so it is the picture of the \emph{good
branch} of a decoder, the branch in which the three wires are back in
the code space. A real decoder must also do something with the other
branches; we do not draw one. Every statement below says what happens in
the good branch, and says that the others have amplitude \(0\).

The gusts we correct are the single ones,
\(\mathcal E_X=\{I,X_1,X_2,X_3\}\), which are \(X^e\) for
\(e\in\{000,100,010,001\}\).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.7 (one gust, mended blind; the headline).} For every
\(X^e\in\mathcal E_X\) and every outcome \(s\), exactly,
\[\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\,X^{c(s)}\,P_s\,X^{e}\,\mathrm{Enc}\;=\;[\,s=\sigma(e)\,]\;I .\]
In words: in the one branch that occurs, \(s=\sigma(e)\), the message
comes back exactly, with the number \(1\); every other branch is exactly
\(0\), and so has probability \(0\). It holds for every message, since
both sides are linear. The same statement as a picture: \emph{The Storm
Line} (§18.8), with its weather rings turned \(e_k\pi\), its bells
\(s_j\pi\) and its mending rings \(c_k\pi\) where \(c=c(s)\), equals
\([s=\sigma(e)]\) times a bare wire:
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.1em, y=1.0em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-3.6) (0,3.6);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (2.6,2.6) -- (3.6,2.6);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (3.6,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (2.6,-2.6) -- (3.6,-2.6);
\foreach \y in {2.6,0,-2.6} {
\draw[wire] (3.6,\y) -- (6.0,\y);
\draw[wire] (6.0,\y) -- (10.4,\y);
\draw[wire] (10.4,\y) -- (12.2,\y) -- (13.4,0);
}
\draw[wire] (6.0,2.6) -- (7.6,1.3);
\draw[wire] (6.0,0) -- (7.6,1.3);
\draw[wire] (6.0,0) -- (7.6,-1.3);
\draw[wire] (6.0,-2.6) -- (7.6,-1.3);
\draw[wire] (13.4,0) -- (14.8,0);
\node[zsp] at (1.4,0) {};
\node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$e_1\pi$}}] at (3.6,2.6) {};
\node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$e_2\pi$}}] at (3.6,0) {};
\node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$e_3\pi$}}] at (3.6,-2.6) {};
\node[zsp] at (6.0,2.6) {};
\node[zsp] at (6.0,0) {};
\node[zsp] at (6.0,-2.6) {};
\node[xsp,label={[ph]right:{$s_1\pi$}}] at (7.6,1.3) {};
\node[xsp,label={[ph]right:{$s_2\pi$}}] at (7.6,-1.3) {};
\node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$c_1\pi$}}] at (10.4,2.6) {};
\node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$c_2\pi$}}] at (10.4,0) {};
\node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$c_3\pi$}}] at (10.4,-2.6) {};
\node[zsp] at (13.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;[\,s=\sigma(e)\,]\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.1em, y=1.0em]
\path (0,-3.6) (0,3.6);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2.4,0);
\end{tikzpicture}\]
\end{quote}

It is proved twice in §18.7. The blackboard's proof is Result 18.6 plus
two facts: on \(\mathcal E_X\) the map \(\sigma\) is one-to-one, and
\(c(\sigma(e))=e\), so \(X^{c(s)}X^e=I\) in the branch that occurs. The
picture reading, which is the reason the picture has the shape it has:
the spread message runs left to right along the three strands; each
weather ring is \(X^{e_k}\) (Chapter 8, §8.2, with row 75's bit); the
tell rings and the two bells are the checks of Result 18.5, slid
together on the middle strand; each mending ring is \(X^{c_k}\); and the
joining ring is \(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\). Every piece is exact with no
number, so the whole picture \emph{is}
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}X^{c}P_sX^{e}\mathrm{Enc}\), exactly.

The picture proof needs one rule the book has not yet stated. It is
about a bell whose two ties both end on the same green spider, which is
what happens when the tell rings are slid together.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.8 (the double-tied bell).} For every angle \(\theta\),
every angle \(\varphi\), and a green spider with any number of other
legs, exactly:
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-2.6) (0,1.0);
\draw[wire] (-1.4,0) -- (1.4,0);
\draw[wire] (0,0) to[out=-125,in=125] (0,-1.9);
\draw[wire] (0,0) to[out=-55,in=55] (0,-1.9);
\node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\varphi$}}] at (0,0) {};
\node[xsp,label={[ph]right:{$\theta$}}] at (0,-1.9) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;\frac{1+e^{i\theta}}{2}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-2.6) (0,1.0);
\draw[wire] (-1.4,0) -- (1.4,0);
\node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\varphi$}}] at (0,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] The red spider has exactly the two legs drawn, both
tied to the one green spider. A bell at rest comes off with the number
\(1\); a bell turned a half takes the whole picture to \(0\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} On the blackboard: the green spider holds all its legs at
one bit \(x\), with the factor \(e^{i\varphi x}\) (row 53), so the bell
sees \(\ket{xx}\), and
\(\braket{++|xx}+e^{i\theta}\braket{--|xx}=\tfrac12+\tfrac12e^{i\theta}\)
for both values of \(x\). The number does not depend on \(x\), so it
comes out in front. By the rules, the Coecke's Sketchbook sidebar below.
\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch18/BlindVote.py}, which checks it
at \(\theta=0\), at \(\theta=\pi\) and at a random \(\theta\).

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Coecke's Sketchbook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{The double-tied bell, by the rules.} Four moves. First, fusion
backwards (row 57), twice: peel the bell's turn off onto a red point
turned \(\theta\), leaving a red spider at rest that holds the two ties
and a cord to the point; and peel off from the green spider a part at
rest that holds the two ties, joined by one cord to the rest. Second,
the two parts at rest are now joined by two wires and each has one other
leg: Chapter 8's Hopf law (Theorem 8.6, row 62) cuts both ties at the
price \(\tfrac12\). Third, the red spider, left with one leg, fuses with
the red point (row 57) into a red spider with no legs, turned
\(\theta\), which is the number \(1+e^{i\theta}\) (row 54). Fourth, the
green part at rest, left with one leg, fuses back (row 57). Total:
\(\tfrac12(1+e^{i\theta})\). The warning: the rule needs \emph{both}
ties on \emph{one} green spider. A bell tied to two different spiders
does not come off; it is a question still being asked.
\end{quote}

With Result 18.8 the sketchbook proves the headline in five moves, which
§18.7 draws. In outline: each weather ring's half passes through its
tell ring (row 120) and lands in the bells tied to that strand and in
its mending ring (row 57); in the branch \(s=\sigma(e)\) with \(c=e\)
every red ring is left at rest; the tell rings and the joining ring
slide into the parting ring along bare strands; each bell is then tied
twice to one green spider and comes off with the number \(1\); and what
is left is a bare wire.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Dirac's Blackboard.}\nopagebreak

\emph{The headline in four lines, and a loop that costs nothing.} (1)
\(X^e\mathrm{Enc}(\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1)=\alpha\ket e+\beta\ket{\bar e}\).
(2) \(Z_1Z_2\) and \(Z_2Z_3\) give \(\ket e\) and \(\ket{\bar e}\) the
same signs, \((-1)^{e_1\oplus e_2}\) and \((-1)^{e_2\oplus e_3}\), so
\(P_s\) multiplies the whole state by \([s=\sigma(e)]\) and never
separates \(\alpha\) from \(\beta\). (3) On \(\mathcal E_X\),
\(\sigma(000)=00\), \(\sigma(100)=10\), \(\sigma(010)=11\),
\(\sigma(001)=01\): one-to-one, with \(c(\sigma(e))=e\), so
\(X^{c(s)}X^e=I\) in the branch that occurs. (4)
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\mathrm{Enc}=I\). On the dialogue's message,
\(\alpha=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\), \(\beta=\tfrac i{\sqrt2}\), \(e=010\): line
(1) gives \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket{010}+i\ket{101})\), line (2) gives
\(s=11\), line (3) turns the middle wire back, line (4) returns
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket0+i\ket1)\). The loop: a green spider turned
\(\varphi\) with a plain wire from one of its legs to another is
\(\sum_xe^{i\varphi x}\ket{x\cdots x}\bra{x\cdots x}\) with two of the
\(x\)'s joined, and joining them sums \(\braket{a|x}\braket{a|x}\) over
\(a\), which is \(1\). So the loop goes with the number \(1\) (row 90),
for every \(\varphi\).
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{what-the-vote-cannot-do}{%
\subsection{What the vote cannot do}\label{what-the-vote-cannot-do}}

The headline is about single gusts. Two gusts fool the bells, and they
fool them in a definite way.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.9 (what the vote cannot do).} For every gust pattern
\(e\in\{0,1\}^3\) and every outcome \(s\), exactly,
\[\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\,X^{c(s)}\,P_s\,X^{e}\,\mathrm{Enc}\;=\;[\,s=\sigma(e)\,]\;X^{[\mathrm{wt}(e)\ge2]},\]
where \(\mathrm{wt}(e)\) is the number of \(1\)s in \(e\). With two or
three gusts, the branch that occurs returns the message flipped,
\(X\ket\psi\), with certainty.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} Result 18.6 holds for all eight patterns. Flipping every
bit of \(e\) does not change \(\sigma(e)\), so
\(\sigma(e)=\sigma(\bar e)\); exactly one of \(e\) and \(\bar e\) has
weight at most \(1\), and \(c\) picks that one. If
\(\mathrm{wt}(e)\ge2\) then \(c(\sigma(e))=\bar e\), and
\(X^{\bar e}X^e=X\otimes X\otimes X\), which the code sees as
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}X^{\otimes3}\mathrm{Enc}=X\). \(\;\blacksquare\)
See \texttt{Code/Ch18/BlindVote.py}.

This is the classical vote exactly: two wrong copies outvote one right
one. For a dark or lit message the result is the wrong bit; for a
message a quarter round it is a quarter back, and for a message at rest
it is harmless, since \(X\ket+=\ket+\).

\hypertarget{every-mixture-of-gusts}{%
\subsection{Every mixture of gusts}\label{every-mixture-of-gusts}}

The headline is branch by branch and gust by gust. Real weather is a
channel, and a channel's Kraus operators need not be single Paulis: a
small unwanted turn is a sum of \(I\) and an \(X\) with complex weights.
Linearity takes care of all of them at once.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.10 (every mixture of single gusts).} For every \(E\)
in \(\operatorname{span}\mathcal E_X\), that is, every
\(E=\sum_ea_e\,X^e\) with complex numbers \(a_e\) and \(e\) running over
the four single-gust patterns \(000,100,010,001\), and for every \(s\),
\[X^{c(s)}\,P_s\,E\,\mathrm{Enc}\;=\;a_{\sigma^{-1}(s)}\,\mathrm{Enc},\]
where \(\sigma^{-1}(s)\) is the one single-gust pattern with syndrome
\(s\). So with the recovery channel
\(\mathcal R(\rho)=\sum_sX^{c(s)}P_s\,\rho\,P_sX^{c(s)}\), every channel
whose Kraus operators all lie in \(\operatorname{span}\mathcal E_X\) is
undone exactly on the code space:
\(\mathcal R\bigl(\sum_iE_i\,\mathrm{Enc}\,\rho\,\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}E_i^{\dagger}\bigr)=\mathrm{Enc}\,\rho\,\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} The operator statement is Result 18.7 applied to each
term, with \(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\) removed: Result 18.6 and
\(X^{c(\sigma(e))}X^e=I\) give
\(X^{c(s)}P_sX^e\mathrm{Enc}=[s=\sigma(e)]\,\mathrm{Enc}\) on
\(\mathcal E_X\). For the channel, apply it to each Kraus operator
\(E_i=\sum_ea_{i,e}X^e\): the output is
\(\sum_s\sum_i|a_{i,\sigma^{-1}(s)}|^2\,\mathrm{Enc}\,\rho\,\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\).
Since the channel preserves trace on the code,
\(\sum_i\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}E_i^{\dagger}E_i\mathrm{Enc}=I\), and
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}X^eX^{e'}\mathrm{Enc}=[e=e']\,I\) for
single-gust patterns (for two different single-gust patterns,
\(e\oplus e'\) has weight \(1\) or \(2\), and
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}X^{f}\mathrm{Enc}=0\) unless \(f\) is \(000\) or
\(111\); this is also the \(C=I_4\) of §18.4), so
\(\sum_i\sum_e|a_{i,e}|^2=1\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch18/BlindVote.py}, which builds five random non-real Kraus
operators in \(\operatorname{span}\mathcal E_X\) and checks that
\(\mathcal R\) restores a random non-real \(\rho\) exactly.

This is Gottesman's Theorem 2 in its first case, and we meet it in full
in §18.3. The continuum of small turns is not a continuum of problems:
whatever repairs \(I\), \(X_1\), \(X_2\) and \(X_3\) repairs every
combination of them, because the checks force each branch onto one of
the four.

\hypertarget{the-noise-of-a-storm-counted}{%
\subsection{The noise of a storm,
counted}\label{the-noise-of-a-storm-counted}}

Finally the probabilities. Independent bit flips on the three wires,
\((\mathcal N^X_p)^{\otimes3}\), have Kraus operators
\(\sqrt{p^{\mathrm{wt}(e)}(1-p)^{3-\mathrm{wt}(e)}}\,X^e\) for all eight
\(e\). Their Kraus operators do not all lie in
\(\operatorname{span}\mathcal E_X\), and Result 18.9 says what the
others do.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.11 (the logical bit flip).} For every \(p\) with
\(0\le p\le1\), encoding, independent bit flips of probability \(p\) on
each wire, the recovery \(\mathcal R\) and the good-branch decoder
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\) together act on the message as the bit-flip
channel \(\mathcal N^X_{p_L}\) with \[p_L\;=\;F(p)\;=\;3p^2-2p^3 .\]
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} By Result 18.9 each pattern \(e\) gives \(I\) if
\(\mathrm{wt}(e)\le1\) and \(X\) if \(\mathrm{wt}(e)\ge2\), in its one
branch. So the message is flipped with the total probability of two or
three flips, which is \(F(p)\) of Result 18.2. \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch18/ThreeForOne.py}, which compares the two \(4\times4\)
superoperators at \(p=\tfrac1{10}\), \(p=0.37\) and a random \(p\).

The quantum code does exactly what the tins do, and no better: at
\(p=\tfrac1{10}\) it turns one flip in ten into \(0.028\). It has also
done something the tins could never do, which is to carry a message a
quarter round.

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why a table of corrections
\(c(s)\), fixed in advance, and not a correction chosen by looking at
the result? Because there is nothing to look at. The syndrome is the
only information the checks release, and Result 18.6 says it is a
function of the gust alone. A mending rule can depend only on what is
known, and what is known is \(s\). When \(p<\tfrac12\), the table names
the most likely gust behind each syndrome, since each syndrome comes
from one pattern \(e\) of weight at most \(1\) and from \(\bar e\), of
weight at least \(2\). That is also the rule of the tins: trust the
majority.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-turn-the-bells-miss}{%
\section{§18.3 The Turn the Bells Miss}\label{the-turn-the-bells-miss}}

A gust flips a wire. But §18.1 met two kinds of flip, and the bells were
built to hear only one of them. What happens to a \textbf{phase flip},
\(Z\), on one of the three wires?

\textbf{On the blackboard.} \(Z_k\) multiplies \(\ket{x_1x_2x_3}\) by
\((-1)^{x_k}\). On the code space it gives \(\ket{000}\) the sign \(+1\)
and \(\ket{111}\) the sign \(-1\), whichever wire \(k\) it hits:
\[Z_k\,\mathrm{Enc}\bigl(\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1\bigr)\;=\;\alpha\ket{000}-\beta\ket{111}\;=\;\mathrm{Enc}\,Z\bigl(\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1\bigr).\]
The result is still in the code space. Both checks answer ``agree'',
since \(Z_1Z_2\) and \(Z_2Z_3\) commute with \(Z_k\) and fix the code
space; so nothing is mended, and the message arrives phase-flipped.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.12 (a phase flip passes unheard).} For \(k=1,2,3\) and
every outcome \(s\), exactly,
\[\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\,X^{c(s)}\,P_s\,Z_k\,\mathrm{Enc}\;=\;[\,s=00\,]\;Z .\]
As a picture: \emph{The Storm Line} with every weather ring, bell and
mending ring at rest, and a green half on the middle tell ring, equals a
green half on a wire, with the number \(1\):
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.0em, y=0.9em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-3.6) (0,3.6);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (2.6,2.6) -- (3.6,2.6);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (3.6,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (2.6,-2.6) -- (3.6,-2.6);
\foreach \y in {2.6,0,-2.6} {
\draw[wire] (3.6,\y) -- (6.0,\y);
\draw[wire] (6.0,\y) -- (10.4,\y);
\draw[wire] (10.4,\y) -- (12.2,\y) -- (13.4,0);
}
\draw[wire] (6.0,2.6) -- (7.6,1.3);
\draw[wire] (6.0,0) -- (7.6,1.3);
\draw[wire] (6.0,0) -- (7.6,-1.3);
\draw[wire] (6.0,-2.6) -- (7.6,-1.3);
\draw[wire] (13.4,0) -- (14.8,0);
\node[zsp] at (1.4,0) {};
\foreach \y in {2.6,0,-2.6} { \node[xsp] at (3.6,\y) {}; \node[xsp] at (10.4,\y) {}; }
\node[zsp] at (6.0,2.6) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$\pi$}}] at (6.0,0) {};
\node[zsp] at (6.0,-2.6) {};
\node[xsp] at (7.6,1.3) {};
\node[xsp] at (7.6,-1.3) {};
\node[zsp] at (13.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.0em, y=0.9em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-3.6) (0,3.6);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2.8,0);
\node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (1.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\]
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} On the blackboard:
\(P_sZ_k\mathrm{Enc}=Z_kP_s\mathrm{Enc}=[s=00]\,Z_k\mathrm{Enc}\), since
\(Z_k\) commutes with both checks and the code space lies in the range
of \(P_{00}\) (Result 18.6 with \(e=000\)); then \(c(00)=000\) and
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}Z_k\mathrm{Enc}=\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\mathrm{Enc}Z=Z\).
By the rules, for the middle wire as drawn: every red ring at rest with
two legs is bare cord (row 57). Slide, along bare cords, the first tell
ring into the parting ring along the first weather cord, then the
joining ring into it along the first mending cord, then the middle tell
ring, carrying its half, along the middle weather cord, and the third
tell ring along the third (row 57; the phases add, so the parting ring
is now turned \(\pi\)). The middle and third mending cords are now
loops, which go (row 90). Each bell, at rest, is tied twice to the one
green spider and comes off with the number \(1\) (Result 18.8). What is
left is a green spider turned \(\pi\) with two legs, which is \(Z\).
\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch18/NineStrands.py}, where PyZX's
\texttt{full\_reduce} leaves exactly one green spider turned \(\pi\) on
the storm line with this labelling, with the number \(1\).

The picture says it vividly: a green half and the green tell ring are
the same colour, so the half does not \emph{pass through} the tell ring,
it \emph{fuses into it}, and a spider turned a half has nothing to say
to the bells hanging from it. A dark or lit message comes through
unharmed, since \(Z\ket0=\ket0\) and \(Z\ket1=-\ket1\), the same message
up to the overall number \(-1\). A message at rest arrives as a half,
and a quarter round as a quarter back. The code that corrects every
single bit flip is blind to every single phase flip.

\hypertarget{the-other-colour}{%
\subsection{The other colour}\label{the-other-colour}}

Chapter 8's colour change (row 58) says that a spider with a yellow box
on every leg is the spider of the other colour. On the blackboard, a
yellow box is \(H\), and \(HXH=Z\). So the whole construction can be
repeated with the colours exchanged.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.13 (the phase-flip code).} Let
\(\mathrm{Enc}'=H^{\otimes3}\,\mathrm{Enc}\,H\), with checks \(X_1X_2\)
and \(X_2X_3\), projectors \(P'_s=H^{\otimes3}P_sH^{\otimes3}\) and
corrections \(Z^{c(s)}\). Exactly:
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-1.6) (0,1.6);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (2.4,1.2) -- (3.4,1.2);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (3.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (2.4,-1.2) -- (3.4,-1.2);
\node[xsp] at (1.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-1.6) (0,1.6);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2.4,0);
\draw[wire] (2.4,0) -- (3.4,1.2) -- (5.4,1.2);
\draw[wire] (2.4,0) -- (5.4,0);
\draw[wire] (2.4,0) -- (3.4,-1.2) -- (5.4,-1.2);
\node[hbox] at (1.0,0) {};
\node[hbox] at (4.4,1.2) {};
\node[hbox] at (4.4,0) {};
\node[hbox] at (4.4,-1.2) {};
\node[zsp] at (2.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;\mathrm{Enc}',\]
\[\mathrm{Enc}'^{\dagger}\,Z^{c(s)}\,P'_s\,Z^{e}\,\mathrm{Enc}'\;=\;[\,s=\sigma(e)\,]\;I\]
for every single phase flip \(Z^e\), \(e\in\{000,100,010,001\}\), and
every \(s\). The red spider sends \(\ket+\) to \(\ket{+++}\) and
\(\ket-\) to \(\ket{---}\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} The picture is colour change (row 58), exact. For the
rest, conjugate: \(H^{\otimes3}Z^eH^{\otimes3}=X^e\) and
\(H^{\otimes3}X^{c}H^{\otimes3}=Z^{c}\), so
\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Enc}'^{\dagger}Z^{c(s)}P'_sZ^e\mathrm{Enc}'&\;=\;H\bigl(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}X^{c(s)}P_sX^e\mathrm{Enc}\bigr)H\\&\;=\;[\,s=\sigma(e)\,]\,HH\;=\;[\,s=\sigma(e)\,]\,I\end{aligned}\]
by Result 18.7. \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch18/NineStrands.py}, where PyZX turns the red spider green
with a yellow box on every leg by its own move, and checks the
correction for all four single phase flips.

Its code space is spanned by \(\ket{+++}\) and \(\ket{---}\). It is the
code of Knill and Laflamme's eq. (15), written there without
normalization as \((\ket0+\ket1)(\ket0+\ket1)(\ket0+\ket1)\) and
\((\ket0-\ket1)(\ket0-\ket1)(\ket0-\ket1)\), ``such that if one qubit is
corrupted by the environment, then it is possible to detect it by using
a majority rule''. Their encoding sends \(\ket0\) to the first word and
\(\ket1\) to the second; the red spider sends \(\ket+\) and \(\ket-\) to
the same two words, normalized, so the two differ by the one yellow box
on the input. And of course the phase-flip code is blind to bit flips,
by Result 18.12 in the other colour.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Coecke's Sketchbook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{The whole storm line in the other colour.} Put two yellow boxes in
a row on every cord of \emph{The Storm Line} and on each lead; two boxes
in a row are no box (row 56), so the picture has not changed. Now every
spider has a box on every leg, and colour change (row 58) turns each
into the other colour, turn kept. The green parting ring becomes red:
\(\mathrm{Enc}'\) itself (Result 18.13). The red weather rings become
green: phase flips. The green tell rings become red, the red bells
green: checks of \(X_1X_2\) and \(X_2X_3\). The mending rings become
green: \(Z^{c}\). The joining ring becomes red, and on each lead one box
is left over, at the far end. So the storm line in the new colours is
the old one with a yellow box before it and one after. Every proof of
§18.2 runs in the new colours with no change but the names, because
every rule of Chapter 8 holds with the colours swapped. What the picture
does \emph{not} say is which code to use. That depends on which way the
storm turns things, and the storm is physics, not a picture.
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{nine-strands}{%
\subsection{Nine strands}\label{nine-strands}}

To hear both kinds of turn, use both codes, one inside the other. Spread
the message three ways against phase flips, then spread each of the
three against bit flips.

\textbf{On the blackboard.} Let
\[\mathrm{Enc}_9\;=\;\mathrm{Enc}^{\otimes3}\,H^{\otimes3}\,\mathrm{Enc},\]
a \(512\times2\) matrix from one wire to nine. Follow \(\ket0\):
\(\mathrm{Enc}\ket0=\ket{000}\), then \(H^{\otimes3}\) gives
\(\ket{+++}=2^{-3/2}(\ket0+\ket1)^{\otimes3}\), then each
\(\ket0+\ket1\) is spread to \(\ket{000}+\ket{111}\). And \(\ket1\) goes
the same way with minus signs:
\[\mathrm{Enc}_9\ket0=\tfrac1{2\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket{000}+\ket{111}\bigr)^{\otimes3},\qquad \mathrm{Enc}_9\ket1=\tfrac1{2\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket{000}-\ket{111}\bigr)^{\otimes3}.\]
These are Gottesman's eqs. (9) and (10), divided by \(2\sqrt2\), which
makes them unit vectors: the \textbf{nine-qubit code}, which Gottesman
calls ``a variant of the repetition code'', credited to Shor (his ref.
{[}43{]}). The inner layer is three bit-flip codes, one on each block of
three wires; the outer layer is the phase-flip code across the blocks.
The checks are Gottesman's Table 2, eight of them: \(Z_1Z_2\),
\(Z_2Z_3\), \(Z_4Z_5\), \(Z_5Z_6\), \(Z_7Z_8\), \(Z_8Z_9\) inside the
blocks, and across them \(X_1X_2X_3X_4X_5X_6\) and
\(X_4X_5X_6X_7X_8X_9\), his eqs. (42) and (43).

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} Each factor is a picture we have.
\(\mathrm{Enc}\) is a green spider with three legs out; \(H^{\otimes3}\)
is a yellow box on each; \(\mathrm{Enc}^{\otimes3}\) is three more green
spiders. So Shor's encoder is green, yellow, green:
\[\mathrm{Enc}_9\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.1em, y=0.8em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-5.4) (0,5.4);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.4,0);
  \draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (2.6,3.9) -- (5.2,3.9);
  \draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (5.2,0);
  \draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (2.6,-3.9) -- (5.2,-3.9);
  \node[hbox] at (3.9,3.9) {};
  \node[hbox] at (3.9,0) {};
  \node[hbox] at (3.9,-3.9) {};
  \foreach \y in {3.9,0,-3.9} {
    \draw[wire] (5.2,\y) -- (6.2,\y+1.3) -- (7.4,\y+1.3);
    \draw[wire] (5.2,\y) -- (7.4,\y);
    \draw[wire] (5.2,\y) -- (6.2,\y-1.3) -- (7.4,\y-1.3);
    \node[zsp] at (5.2,\y) {};
  }
  \node[zsp] at (1.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] exactly, with no number: the \(\tfrac1{2\sqrt2}\) is
already inside the three yellow boxes, \(1/\sqrt2\) each, as the
blackboard shows. The picture's middle cords carry a yellow box each;
these are Chapter 8's Hadamard edges (row 56).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.14 (Shor's nine).} Exactly:
\(\mathrm{Enc}_9^{\dagger}\mathrm{Enc}_9=I\); the eight checks of Table
2 commute and fix every state \(\mathrm{Enc}_9\ket\psi\); and the
twenty-eight single-wire operators \(I\), \(X_k\), \(Y_k\), \(Z_k\)
(\(k=1,\dots,9\)) produce twenty-two different syndromes: one for \(I\),
nine for the \(X_k\), three for the \(Z_k\) and nine for the \(Y_k\).
Measuring the checks and applying the correction for the syndrome
returns \(\mathrm{Enc}_9\ket\psi\) after every one of the twenty-eight,
up to an overall number \(r\) with \(|r|=1\), a global phase of the code
state, the same for every \(\ket\psi\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} The first claim: slide each inner green spider into its
mirror image (Result 18.3), which leaves three bare wires; the boxes
meet in pairs and cancel (row 56); what is left is Result 18.3 once
more. On the blackboard it is
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}H^{\otimes3}(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\mathrm{Enc})^{\otimes3}H^{\otimes3}\mathrm{Enc}=I\).
The syndromes: an \(X\) on wire \(k\) rings the two checks of its block
exactly as in §18.2, which gives nine different answers, and commutes
with the two long checks. A \(Z\) on any wire of a block is, on the
code, a phase flip of that block's spread message (Result 18.12), which
the two long checks see as the bit flip of the outer code that it is
after the boxes (Result 18.13); all three wires of a block give the same
answer, so three answers. \(Y_k=iX_kZ_k\) rings both kinds, nine more.
The corrections: an \(X\) is undone within its block (Result 18.7); a
\(Z\) is undone by a \(Z\) on any wire of its block, since two \(Z\)s in
one block act on the code as \(Z_1Z_2\) does, as nothing; a \(Y\) by
both; and the factor \(i\) in \(Y=iXZ\), with the order of the two
corrections, leaves a number \(r\) with \(|r|=1\). \(\;\blacksquare\)
See \texttt{Code/Ch18/NineStrands.py}, which checks the twenty-eight one
by one, asserting \(|r|=1\) for each.

The three \(Z\)s of a block share one syndrome, and the code does not
mind, because they do the same thing to it. Gottesman calls such a code
\textbf{degenerate}: ``different errors look the same when acting on the
coding subspace''. We return to this in §18.4.

The nine-qubit code corrects twenty-eight operators. But a real error on
one wire is rarely one of them: it is a small turn by some angle about
some axis. Here Gottesman's Theorem 2, which he credits to Shor and to
Steane (his refs. {[}43{]} and {[}46{]}), finishes the job:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Gottesman's Theorem 2 (quoted).} ``If a quantum code corrects
errors A and B, it also corrects any linear combination of A and B. In
particular, if it corrects all weight t Pauli errors, then the code
corrects all t-qubit errors.''
\end{quote}

Every \(2\times2\) matrix is a combination of \(I\), \(X\), \(Y\) and
\(Z\). So Shor's code corrects \emph{every} error on any one of its nine
wires, whatever it is, by the argument of Result 18.10: the checks force
each branch onto one of the Paulis, and each is mended. The single-wire
depolarizing channel \(\mathcal N^{\mathrm{dep}}_p\), with Kraus
operators \(\sqrt{1-p}\,I\) and \(\sqrt{p/3}\) times \(X\), \(Y\) and
\(Z\), is undone exactly on any one wire. Independent depolarizing noise
on all nine wires is another matter: its branches with errors on two
wires are not all corrected, and we do not compute the rate at which the
code then fails.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Feynman's Notebook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{Nine for one.} The code of this section is P. W. Shor's.
Gottesman's survey, posted in 2009, introduces it as ``a variant of the
repetition code'' and cites P. W. Shor, ``Scheme for reducing
decoherence in quantum memory'', \emph{Physical Review A} 52 (1995). The
next year brought the seven-qubit code, which Gottesman cites to A. M.
Steane, ``Error correcting codes in quantum theory'', \emph{Physical
Review Letters} 77 (1996), and whose stabilizer is his Table 3: the
parity checks of the classical seven-bit Hamming code, written once with
\(Z\) and once with \(X\). The general recipe for building quantum codes
out of two classical ones, Gottesman writes, ``is known as the CSS
construction after its inventors Calderbank, Shor, and Steane'', and he
cites A. R. Calderbank and P. W. Shor, ``Good quantum error-correcting
codes exist'', \emph{Physical Review A} 54 (1996), together with
Steane's paper in the \emph{Proceedings of the Royal Society of London}
A 452 (1996). Shor's code costs nine wires for one; Steane's, seven; and
there is a code with five, Gottesman's Table 4. Section 18.4 quotes the
bound that rules out four.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{what-a-bell-may-ask}{%
\section{§18.4 What a Bell May Ask}\label{what-a-bell-may-ask}}

The bells of §18.2 ask pairs. Why not ask more? A bell that could tell
us \emph{which way} a wire is set would tell us more about the storm,
and more is surely better. Let us try it before we reason about it.

\hypertarget{a-bell-that-asks-the-one}{%
\subsection{A bell that asks the one}\label{a-bell-that-asks-the-one}}

Hang a bell on the first wire alone: it asks ``is wire one dark or
lit?'', with projectors \(\tfrac12(I+Z_1)\) and \(\tfrac12(I-Z_1)\). The
dialogue's clip-bell is this bell. Send the spread message
\(\alpha\ket{000}+\beta\ket{111}\) past it.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  A dark message, \(\alpha=1\): the bell is silent with certainty, and
  the state is untouched.
\item
  A lit message, \(\beta=1\): the bell rings with certainty, and the
  state is untouched.
\item
  A message a quarter round, \(\alpha=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\),
  \(\beta=\tfrac i{\sqrt2}\): \(\tfrac12(I+Z_1)\) keeps
  \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\ket{000}\) and \(\tfrac12(I-Z_1)\) keeps
  \(\tfrac i{\sqrt2}\ket{111}\). So the bell rings with probability
  \(\tfrac12\), and afterwards the three wires hold \(\ket{000}\) or
  \(\ket{111}\). The message is now dark or lit. Read at the mark it was
  sent at, a quarter round, it is found there with probability
  \(|\braket{\text{quarter round}|0}|^2=\tfrac12\), whichever way the
  bell went.
\end{itemize}

For dark and lit messages the one-wire bell is excellent: it even
\emph{tells} us the message. That is the trap. A question whose answer
depends on the message has, by that fact, split the message into its
answers, and for every message that is not dark or lit the split is
damage. The bells of §18.2 did not have this problem because their
answers were the same on \(\ket{000}\) and \(\ket{111}\). What is needed
is a test that says, of any list of errors, whether some recovery undoes
all of them. Knill and Laflamme gave one.

\hypertarget{the-knilllaflamme-conditions}{%
\subsection{The Knill--Laflamme
conditions}\label{the-knilllaflamme-conditions}}

Let \(\mathcal Q\) be a code space with an orthonormal basis of
codewords \(\ket{\psi_i}\), and let \(\mathcal E\) be a list of errors
\(E_a\). The code \textbf{corrects} \(\mathcal E\) when one recovery
operation undoes every \(E_a\) on every state of \(\mathcal Q\). Knill
and Laflamme's phrasing is that the code ``can be extended to an
\(\mathcal A\)-correcting code'', with \(\mathcal A\) their name for the
errors; we keep the letters \(E_a\).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.15 (Knill and Laflamme, Theorem 3.2; Gottesman,
Theorem 3; stated).} A code corrects the errors \(\{E_a\}\) if and only
if, for all codewords \(\ket{\psi_i}\), \(\ket{\psi_j}\) with \(i\ne j\)
and all \(E_a\), \(E_b\),
\[\bra{\psi_i}E_a^{\dagger}E_b\ket{\psi_i}\;=\;\bra{\psi_j}E_a^{\dagger}E_b\ket{\psi_j},\qquad\bra{\psi_i}E_a^{\dagger}E_b\ket{\psi_j}\;=\;0,\]
which are Knill and Laflamme's (19) and (20). Gottesman writes the same
two conditions as one, his (30):
\(\bra{\psi_i}E_a^{\dagger}E_b\ket{\psi_j}=C_{ab}\,[i=j]\), where
\(C_{ab}\) is a Hermitian matrix that does not depend on \(i\) and
\(j\); and, for a linear space \(\mathcal E\) of errors, as his (29):
\(\bra\psi E^{\dagger}E\ket\psi=C(E)\) for every \(E\in\mathcal E\) and
every unit vector \(\ket\psi\in\mathcal Q\), with \(C(E)\) independent
of \(\ket\psi\). If the code has an encoder \(\mathrm{Enc}\) with
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\mathrm{Enc}=I\) whose columns are the
codewords, the condition is
\[\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\,E_a^{\dagger}E_b\,\mathrm{Enc}\;=\;C_{ab}\,I .\]
\end{quote}

We state the theorem and do not prove it; the proofs are Knill and
Laflamme's §3 and Gottesman's §2.2. The last line is ours, and it is one
sentence: the \((i,j)\) entry of
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}E_a^{\dagger}E_b\mathrm{Enc}\) is
\(\bra{\psi_i}E_a^{\dagger}E_b\ket{\psi_j}\), so (30) says exactly that
this matrix is \(C_{ab}\) times the identity. Read it as a statement
about questions. \(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}E_a^{\dagger}E_b\mathrm{Enc}\)
is what the pair of errors looks like \emph{from inside the code}. The
condition asks that it look like a number: the same on every message,
and never mixing one message with another. Whatever the errors reveal,
they reveal about themselves.

\textbf{In the sketchbook.}
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}E_a^{\dagger}E_b\mathrm{Enc}\) is a closed-off
picture: the parting ring, whatever the errors draw on the strands, and
the joining ring. The condition says that it must come down to \textbf{a
number times a bare wire}. A question that reads the message leaves
something on the wire that is not a number.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.16 (what the three strands may be asked).} Exactly:
(a) for the single gusts \(\mathcal E_X=\{I,X_1,X_2,X_3\}\),
\(\;\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}X^{e}X^{e'}\mathrm{Enc}=[e=e']\,I\), so
\(C=I_4\) and the conditions hold; (b) for \(\{I,Z_1\}\) the conditions
fail: \(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}Z_1\mathrm{Enc}=Z\), which is not a number
times \(I\); they fail too for the clip-bell's projector,
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\tfrac12(I+Z_1)\mathrm{Enc}=\ket0\bra0\); (c)
for the twenty-eight operators \(I,X_k,Y_k,Z_k\) on Shor's nine wires
the conditions hold, and the \(28\times28\) matrix \(C\) has rank
\(22\). As pictures:
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-1.6) (0,1.9);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (2.4,1.2) -- (4.4,1.2) -- (5.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (5.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (2.4,-1.2) -- (4.4,-1.2) -- (5.4,0);
\draw[wire] (5.4,0) -- (6.8,0);
\node[zsp] at (1.4,0) {};
\node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (3.4,1.2) {};
\node[zsp] at (5.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;0,\] \[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-1.6) (0,1.9);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (2.4,1.2) -- (4.4,1.2) -- (5.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (5.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (2.4,-1.2) -- (4.4,-1.2) -- (5.4,0);
\draw[wire] (5.4,0) -- (6.8,0);
\node[zsp] at (1.4,0) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (3.4,1.2) {};
\node[zsp] at (5.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-1.6) (0,1.9);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2.8,0);
\node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (1.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\]
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} (a) \(X^eX^{e'}=X^{e\oplus e'}\), and
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}X^{f}\mathrm{Enc}\) is \(I\) for \(f=000\),
\(X\) for \(f=111\) and \(0\) otherwise, since \(X^f\) moves
\(\ket{000}\) and \(\ket{111}\) out of the code space unless \(f\) is
\(000\) or \(111\). For two single-gust patterns, \(e\oplus e'\) is
\(000\) when \(e=e'\) and has weight \(1\) or \(2\) otherwise. (b)
\(Z_1\mathrm{Enc}=\mathrm{Enc}Z\) (§18.3), and
\(\tfrac12(I+Z_1)\mathrm{Enc}=\mathrm{Enc}\,\tfrac12(I+Z)\). (c) By
computation, in the code. The pictures: in the first, slide the joining
ring into the parting ring along the bare middle strand (row 57). The
lower strand becomes a loop, which goes (row 90); the upper strand
becomes a red half tied twice to the one green spider, and Result 18.8
at a half gives \(0\). In the second, the green half on the upper strand
fuses in as well, and what is left is a green spider turned \(\pi\) with
two legs: \(Z\), a wire that still carries a question.
\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch18/WhatABellMayAsk.py}, where
PyZX's \texttt{full\_reduce} takes each of the sixteen pictures of (a)
to a bare wire with the number \(1\) or to \(0\), and leaves one green
spider turned \(\pi\) for \(Z_1\).

Part (b) is the clip-bell. For a dark or lit message it looked harmless;
the conditions look past that, at every message at once, and see that
\(\ket{000}\) and \(\ket{111}\) get different numbers. Part (c) has a
new feature. Shor's code corrects the twenty-eight operators, but \(C\)
is not invertible: \(Z_1\), \(Z_2\) and \(Z_3\) act on the code in the
same way, so their rows of \(C\) are equal. Gottesman: ``If the matrix
\(C_{ab}\) in (30) has maximum rank, the code is called nondegenerate.
If not, as for the nine-qubit code, the code is degenerate.'' A
degenerate code need not tell errors apart; it need only undo them.

\hypertarget{counting-what-a-code-can-do}{%
\subsection{Counting what a code can
do}\label{counting-what-a-code-can-do}}

A code with \(n\) wires carrying \(k\) messages is written
\([[n,k,d]]\), with double brackets to tell it from a classical code.
The \textbf{distance} \(d\) is, in Gottesman's second definition, the
least weight of a Pauli product \(E\) for which \(\bra\psi E\ket\psi\)
depends on which code state \(\ket\psi\) it is taken in (his (34)): the
lightest error whose effect some question on the code could notice. A
code of odd distance \(d\) corrects every error on at most \((d-1)/2\)
wires (Gottesman, §§2.2--2.3; stated, not proved here). Two bounds from
Gottesman's §2.2 limit what is possible, and we state them without
proof. For a nondegenerate code, counting states gives the
\textbf{quantum Hamming bound}, his (35):
\[\sum_{j=0}^{(d-1)/2}3^j\binom nj\;2^k\;\le\;2^n ,\] since each error
on \(j\) wires is one of \(3^j\binom nj\) Pauli strings and each must
send the code to its own orthogonal copy. With \(k=1\) and \(d=3\) it
reads \((1+3n)\,2\le2^n\), which first holds at \(n=5\). Gottesman adds
that ``we do not know of any codes that beat it''. The
\textbf{Knill--Laflamme bound}, also called the quantum Singleton bound,
his (38), ``applies even to degenerate quantum codes'':
\[n-k\;\ge\;2d-2 .\] A \([[4,1,3]]\) code would violate it, so no code
that carries one message and corrects every error on one wire can do it
with fewer than five wires, and the \([[5,1,3]]\) code of Gottesman's
Table 4 ``really is optimal''.

\hypertarget{stabilizers}{%
\subsection{Stabilizers}\label{stabilizers}}

The checks of Shor's code generate a group, and the group fixes the
code. Gottesman's §2.3 turns this into a general construction. The
\textbf{Pauli group} on \(n\) wires is the set of products of \(I\),
\(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\), one on each wire, times \(\pm1\) or \(\pm i\); the
\textbf{weight} of such a product is the number of wires on which it is
not \(I\). A \textbf{stabilizer} is a subgroup \(\mathcal S\) of it in
which any two elements commute and which does not contain \(-I\); its
code \(\mathcal Q_{\mathcal S}\) is the set of states \(\ket\psi\) with
\(M\ket\psi=\ket\psi\) for every \(M\in\mathcal S\). The
\textbf{normalizer} \(N(\mathcal S)\) is the set of Pauli products that
commute with every element of \(\mathcal S\). Its elements outside
\(\mathcal S\) act on the code without being noticed by any check: they
are the code's own logical operations, and so they are the errors it
cannot catch.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.17 (Gottesman, Theorem 5; stated).} Let \(\mathcal S\)
be a subgroup of order \(2^g\) of the \(n\)-wire Pauli group whose
elements commute, with \(-I\notin\mathcal S\), and let \(d\) be the
least weight of an element of \(N(\mathcal S)\setminus\mathcal S\). Then
\(\mathcal Q_{\mathcal S}\) is an \([[n,\,n-g,\,d]]\) code.
\end{quote}

Here \(g\) is the number of independent checks; Gottesman calls it
\(a\), a letter this chapter keeps for errors. Our examples, said
plainly:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{The bit-flip code is \([[3,1,1]]\).} Its stabilizer is
  \(\{I,Z_1Z_2,Z_2Z_3,Z_1Z_3\}\), of order \(2^2\), so \(k=3-2=1\). And
  \(Z_1\) commutes with all four and is not one of them: a single phase
  flip is a logical operation, as §18.3 found. Its weight is \(1\), so
  \(d=1\). The code corrects every single bit flip and no single phase
  flip, and the distance counts the worst kind.
\item
  \textbf{Shor's code is \([[9,1,3]]\)}, with the eight generators of
  Table 2; the seven-qubit code of Table 3 is \([[7,1,3]]\), with six;
  the five-qubit code of Table 4 is \([[5,1,3]]\), with four.
\item
  \textbf{CSS codes.} Table 3 is built from the classical seven-bit
  Hamming code, its parity checks written once with \(Z\) and once with
  \(X\). Gottesman's general form uses two classical codes, one for each
  kind of check, ``known as the CSS construction after its inventors
  Calderbank, Shor, and Steane''.
\end{itemize}

The first item is our own count; \texttt{Code/Ch18/WhatABellMayAsk.py}
checks it, and checks, for the generators of Tables 2, 3 and 4 alike,
that no Pauli product of weight \(2\) or less lies in
\(N(\mathcal S)\setminus\mathcal S\) and that one of weight \(3\) does.

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} A check of a stabilizer code is a Pauli
product, and a product of \(Z\)s is a bell with more ties. Put a green
spider at rest on each of \(w\) wires and tie all of them to one red
spider turned \(s\pi\), the \textbf{hub}. The ties must cross the wires
in between to reach it; a crossing joins nothing.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.18 (a check of weight \(w\)).} For every \(w\ge1\) and
each bit \(s\), exactly, \(w\) green spiders at rest tied to one red hub
turned \(s\pi\) equal
\[2^{\,1-w/2}\cdot\tfrac12\bigl(I+(-1)^{s}Z^{\otimes w}\bigr).\] For
\(w=4\): \[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.40em, x=1.2em, y=1.0em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-2.5) (0,4.0);
\foreach \y in {3.3,2.2,1.1,0} { \draw[wire] (0,\y) -- (5.2,\y); }
\foreach \x/\y in {3.2/3.3,2.4/2.2,1.6/1.1,0.8/0} { \draw[wire] (\x,\y) -- (4.4,-1.6); \node[zsp] at (\x,\y) {}; }
\node[xsp,label={[ph]right:{$s\pi$}}] at (4.4,-1.6) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12\bigl(I+(-1)^{s}Z\otimes Z\otimes Z\otimes Z\bigr).\]
A check made of \(X\)s is the same with the colours swapped, with the
same number.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} As for Result 18.5: the feet copy \(\ket x\) onto the
ties, and the hub gives
\(\braket{+\cdots+|x}+(-1)^s\braket{-\cdots-|x}=2^{-w/2}\bigl(1+(-1)^{s}(-1)^{|x|}\bigr)\),
where \(|x|\) is the number of \(1\)s in \(x\). For the colours swapped:
put a yellow box on every leg of every spider and pairs of boxes on the
ties (rows 56, 58); on the blackboard this is conjugation by
\(H^{\otimes w}\), which turns \(Z^{\otimes w}\) into \(X^{\otimes w}\)
and keeps the number. \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch18/WhatABellMayAsk.py}, which checks \(w=2,3,4\) and both
values of \(s\), and lets PyZX's \texttt{full\_reduce} show that the
check followed by itself is \(2^{1-w/2}\) times the check.

At \(w=2\) the number is exactly \(1\), which is why the bells of §18.2
needed none. At \(w=4\) it is \(\tfrac12\).

\hypertarget{a-weave-on-a-torus}{%
\subsection{A weave on a torus}\label{a-weave-on-a-torus}}

Kitaev's §1 builds a code in which every check has weight at most four
and every wire is asked by at most four checks. In our letters: take an
\(\ell\times\ell\) square grid drawn on a torus, so that the right edge
is glued to the left and the top to the bottom, and put a wire on every
edge of the grid, so \(n=2\ell^2\). For each vertex \(v\), let \(A_v\)
be the product of \(X\) on the four edges that meet at \(v\), its
\textbf{star}; for each face \(f\), let \(B_f\) be the product of \(Z\)
on the four edges around it. Kitaev writes \(A_s\), \(B_p\),
\(\sigma^x\), \(\sigma^z\) and \(k\); we write \(A_v\), \(B_f\), \(X\),
\(Z\) and \(\ell\), because \(s\), \(p\), \(\sigma\) and \(k\) already
have jobs here.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.19 (the toric code; Kitaev, §1).} The \(A_v\) and
\(B_f\) all commute. They satisfy exactly two relations,
\(\prod_vA_v=I\) and \(\prod_fB_f=I\), so \(2\ell^2-2\) of them are
independent, and the states fixed by all of them form a space of
dimension \(2^{2\ell^2-(2\ell^2-2)}=4\): two protected messages. Kitaev
calls it ``a toric code''. An error that is not detected and not
harmless must contain a loop that goes around the torus, so it acts on
at least \(\ell\) wires.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof of the first sentence.} A star and a face share either no
edge or two, as Kitaev notes, and \(X\) and \(Z\) anticommute on each
shared edge, so \(A_v\) and \(B_f\) meet an even number of sign changes
and commute. Two stars, or two faces, are made of one kind of Pauli and
commute. The rest we take from Kitaev: the count of relations, the
dimension (which he derives two ways, once by counting independent
checks, as in Theorem 5, and once by finding the operators that act on
the protected space) and the loops. \(\;\blacksquare\) Here is the count
at \(\ell=2\): eight wires, four vertices, four faces; eight checks with
two relations, six independent; by Theorem 5, \([[8,\,8-6,\,d]]\), a
space of dimension \(2^2=4\). See \texttt{Code/Ch18/WhatABellMayAsk.py},
which builds the checks over the two-element field for \(\ell=2\), \(4\)
and \(5\) and finds the same \(4\) each time.

In the sketchbook every \(B_f\) is a weight-four hub, red, with green
feet on the four edges of a face, and every \(A_v\) is its
colour-swapped twin on the four edges of a star, each with the number
\(\tfrac12\) of Result 18.18. Drawn over the grid, the checks are a
weave of hubs, each tied to four neighbouring wires. Kitaev's point is
locality. His toric codes are ``local check codes'': each check involves
at most four wires, and each wire is in at most four checks, however
large \(\ell\) is. By his loop argument the distance is at least
\(\ell\), so the code is certain to correct every error on fewer than
\(\ell/2\) wires; Kitaev adds that it ``corrects almost any multiple
error'' on a number of wires proportional to \(\ell^2\).

\textbf{The surface code.} Fowler, Mariantoni, Martinis and Cleland
describe what grew from this. ``The surface codes evolved from an
invention of Alexei Kitaev known as toric codes''; the torus ``turned
out to be unnecessary, and planar versions (thus `surface codes') were
developed by Bravyi and Kitaev as well as Freedman and Meyer''. They
report a tolerance of ``a per-operation error rate as high as about
1\%'', against ``per-step thresholds of about \(2\times10^{-5}\)'' for
the Steane and Bacon--Shor codes laid out on two-dimensional grids with
nearest-neighbour coupling. The price is wires: ``It takes a minimum of
thirteen physical qubits to implement a single logical qubit'', and a
reasonably fault-tolerant one ``takes of order \(10^3\) to \(10^4\)
physical qubits''. In their own simulations (§VII), with errors of
several kinds injected into every step of the checking circuit at a rate
set by \(p\), they find a threshold they call \(p_{th}=0.57\%\): below
it the logical error rate falls exponentially as the code's distance
grows, and above it a larger code does worse.

\hypertarget{the-threshold}{%
\subsection{The threshold}\label{the-threshold}}

Everything so far assumed that the storm hits only the wires. In a real
machine the bells are made of the same stuff as the wires, and the hand
that mends can slip. A code whose repairs make more errors than they
catch is worse than no code. The theorem that makes quantum computing
possible in principle says that below a certain error rate this can be
beaten, at a modest cost.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.20 (the threshold theorem; Gottesman, Theorem 10;
stated, not proved).} In the book's letters: ``There is a threshold
error rate \(p_T\). Suppose we have a local stochastic error model with
\(p_i\le p<p_T\). Then for any ideal circuit \(\mathcal C\), and any
\(\epsilon>0\), there exists a fault-tolerant circuit \(\mathcal C'\)
which, when it undergoes the error model, produces an output which has
statistical distance at most \(\epsilon\) from the output of
\(\mathcal C\). \(\mathcal C'\) has a number of qubits and a number of
timesteps which are at most \(\mathrm{polylog}(|\mathcal C|/\epsilon)\)
times bigger than the number of qubits and timesteps in \(\mathcal C\),
where \(|\mathcal C|\) is the number of locations in \(\mathcal C\).''
\end{quote}

Here \(p_i\) bounds the probability of a fault at location \(i\) of the
circuit. Gottesman proves it by \textbf{concatenation}: encode every
wire in a code that corrects \(t\) errors, then encode every wire of
\emph{that} in the same code, and so on, \(L\) levels deep. If one level
turns an error rate \(p\) into at most \(Ap^{t+1}\), his (86) gives,
after \(j\) levels, \(p^{(j)}\le A\bigl(p^{(j-1)}\bigr)^{t+1}\) with
\(p_T=1/A^{1/t}\), and his (87):
\[p^{(j)}/p_T\;\le\;\bigl(p/p_T\bigr)^{(t+1)^j}.\] Below \(p_T\) the
error falls doubly exponentially in the number of levels, while the size
grows only exponentially in it; that is where the \(\mathrm{polylog}\)
comes from. We do not reproduce the proof, whose hard part is to show
that each level really does turn \(p\) into \(Ap^{t+1}\) when every
gate, including those of the checks and the mending, is noisy.

What is \(p_T\)? Each answer below is its source's, with its date.
Gottesman (2009) quotes a proven lower bound of
\(p_T\ge2.73\times10^{-5}\) for the seven-qubit code; simulations by
Knill with ``a threshold \(p_T\) of as high as 5\%, depending on the
details of the error model''; and ``the current best rigorous lower
bound'', \(10^{-3}\). Kitaev (1997), in a footnote: ``Actually, the
threshold is not known. Estimates vary from 1/300 to \(10^{-6}\).''
Fowler and co-authors (2012), for the surface code under their error
model: \(0.57\%\) per step. These numbers are not in conflict: they
answer different questions, about different codes and different models
of noise.

There is no picture of this theorem (row 143). A rewrite proves that two
processes are equal. The threshold is an inequality between
probabilities, a statement about a whole family of circuits as they
grow, and nothing in the sketchbook can say it.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Dirac's Blackboard.}\nopagebreak

\emph{A vote of votes: a toy, not the theorem.} Take the classical vote
of Result 18.2 and apply it to its own output: write each bit three
times, write each of those three times, and vote twice. The failure rate
becomes \(F(F(p))\). At \(p=\tfrac1{10}\): \(F(0.1)=0.028\), and
\(F(0.028)=3(0.028)^2-2(0.028)^3=0.002352-0.000043904=0.002308096\).
Each level roughly squares the rate and multiplies it by three. But
\(F(p)-p=p(1-p)(2p-1)\), which is negative for \(0<p<\tfrac12\) and
positive for \(\tfrac12<p<1\); since \(F\) is increasing on \([0,1]\)
(\(F'(p)=6p(1-p)\ge0\)), the levels drive every \(p\) below \(\tfrac12\)
down towards \(0\) and every \(p\) above \(\tfrac12\) up towards \(1\).
At \(p=0.6\), \(F(0.6)=0.648\): voting makes it worse. So the toy has a
threshold, \(\tfrac12\). It is a toy: its votes are counted without
error, and it knows only bit flips. Gottesman's threshold is far smaller
because his counting is itself done by noisy gates.
\end{quote}

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Feynman's Notebook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{Conditions, a torus, and a threshold.} E. Knill and R. Laflamme
posted ``A theory of quantum error-correcting codes'' in April 1996, as
Los Alamos report LA-UR-96-1300 (journal version, per Gottesman:
\emph{Physical Review A} 55, 1997). Gottesman credits his Theorem 3 to
it and to C. Bennett, D. DiVincenzo, J. Smolin and W. Wootters
(\emph{Physical Review A} 54, 1996). In July 1997 A. Yu. Kitaev posted
``Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons''. He asked why a magnet
remembers: a flipped spin is flipped back by its neighbours, and ``This
process is quite similar to the standard error correction procedure for
the repetition code. We may say that errors are being corrected at the
physical level.'' His quantum answer begins with the toric codes of his
§1. Gottesman credits the threshold theorem to D. Aharonov and M.
Ben-Or; to A. Y. Kitaev, ``Quantum error correction with imperfect
gates''; and to E. Knill, R. Laflamme and W. H. Zurek; and notes that
``Shor presented the first protocols for fault-tolerant quantum
computation'' (his ref. {[}44{]}, dated 1996). For codes ``based on
topological constructions'' he cites E. Dennis, A. Kitaev, A. Landahl
and J. Preskill, \emph{Journal of Mathematical Physics} 43 (2002).
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{split-and-merge}{%
\section{§18.5 Split and Merge}\label{split-and-merge}}

A message spread over a weave of wires is safe. But a computer must also
\emph{act} on its messages, and two messages in two separate weaves must
sometimes be joined, by a CNOT, say, without unwrapping either of them.
Unwrapping would expose them to the storm at the worst moment. In the
surface code this is done by \textbf{lattice surgery}: two patches of
the weave are joined along an edge and then cut apart again, and each
such step acts on the protected messages in a definite way. De Beaudrap
and Horsman showed that the steps are spiders.

We use their letters with one change. They write \(U_S\), \(U_R\),
\(K_{j,S}\) and \(K_{j,R}\) for the smooth and rough operations; we
write \(U_{\mathrm{sm}}\), \(U_{\mathrm{ro}}\), \(K_{j,\mathrm{sm}}\)
and \(K_{j,\mathrm{ro}}\), because in this book \(S\) is the phase gate
and \(\mathcal R\) is the recovery. The bit \(j\) is a merge's outcome.

\textbf{On the blackboard.} A \textbf{split} takes one protected message
into two. The smooth split and the rough split act on it as
\[U_{\mathrm{sm}}\;=\;\ket{00}\bra0+\ket{11}\bra1,\qquad U_{\mathrm{ro}}\;=\;\ket{++}\bra{+}+\ket{--}\bra{-} .\]
The first is Chapter 11's copier \(\delta\) (row 81); the second is its
twin in the other basis. A \textbf{merge} takes two messages into one
and, as it does so, answers a question with a bit \(j\). The smooth
merge has the two outcomes
\[K_{0,\mathrm{sm}}\;=\;\ket0\bra{00}+\ket1\bra{11},\qquad K_{1,\mathrm{sm}}\;=\;\ket0\bra{10}+\ket1\bra{01},\]
and the rough merge the two outcomes
\[K_{0,\mathrm{ro}}\;=\;\ket+\bra{++}+\ket-\bra{--},\qquad K_{1,\mathrm{ro}}\;=\;\ket+\bra{-+}+\ket-\bra{+-}.\]
In the negative branches the merge acts after a flip of its first input:
\(K_{1,\mathrm{sm}}=K_{0,\mathrm{sm}}(X\otimes I)\) and
\(K_{1,\mathrm{ro}}=K_{0,\mathrm{ro}}(Z\otimes I)\). For each merge
\(K_0^{\dagger}K_0+K_1^{\dagger}K_1=I\), so the two outcomes are the two
branches of one channel, with Kraus operators \(K_0\) and \(K_1\). The
form of \(K_{1,\mathrm{sm}}\) and \(K_{1,\mathrm{ro}}\) depends on a
convention. De Beaudrap and Horsman give two, according to whether ``the
Pauli frame of the child memory'' is adapted ``to agree with the second
parent memory'' or with the first; we use the first of their two, which
is the one written above.

A small calculation shows what a smooth merge asks. On \(\ket{ab}\),
\(K_{0,\mathrm{sm}}\) is non-zero only when \(a=b\) and
\(K_{1,\mathrm{sm}}\) only when \(a\ne b\). So the outcome is
\(j=a\oplus b\), with certainty: the smooth merge asks whether two
messages agree, which is exactly the question of the bells.

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} Each of the four is a spider with three
legs, at rest.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.21 (splits and merges are spiders; de Beaudrap and
Horsman, Lemma 1 and Corollary 2).} Exactly, with no number:
\[U_{\mathrm{sm}}=
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
\path (0,-1.0) (0,1.0);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.2,0);
\draw[wire] (1.2,0) -- (2.0,0.6) -- (2.6,0.6);
\draw[wire] (1.2,0) -- (2.0,-0.6) -- (2.6,-0.6);
\node[zsp] at (1.2,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture},
\quad
K_{0,\mathrm{sm}}=
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
\path (0,-1.0) (0,1.0);
\draw[wire] (0,0.6) -- (0.6,0.6) -- (1.4,0);
\draw[wire] (0,-0.6) -- (0.6,-0.6) -- (1.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (2.6,0);
\node[zsp] at (1.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] \[K_{0,\mathrm{ro}}=
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
\path (0,-1.0) (0,1.0);
\draw[wire] (0,0.6) -- (0.6,0.6) -- (1.4,0);
\draw[wire] (0,-0.6) -- (0.6,-0.6) -- (1.4,0);
\draw[wire] (1.4,0) -- (2.6,0);
\node[xsp] at (1.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture},
\quad
U_{\mathrm{ro}}=
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
\path (0,-1.0) (0,1.0);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.2,0);
\draw[wire] (1.2,0) -- (2.0,0.6) -- (2.6,0.6);
\draw[wire] (1.2,0) -- (2.0,-0.6) -- (2.6,-0.6);
\node[xsp] at (1.2,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] De Beaudrap and Horsman's Lemma 1 says that the
effect on the logical state of a smooth split, and of ``the positive
branch'' of a smooth merge, is the green three-legged spider at rest,
and the same for rough operations and red. Their Corollary 2 says that
the positive branches of lattice surgery ``provide a model for the
equational theory of the ZX calculus without projections'', with spiders
of two or three legs at rest.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof of the equalities.} Each is row 53 or row 54 with three
legs, the red ones with the normalized \(\ket\pm\) of Chapter 8. That
surgery on a surface code acts on the protected message by these
matrices is de Beaudrap and Horsman's result, which we state and do not
prove. \(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch18/SplitAndMerge.py}.

The negative branch is where the pictures earn their keep.
\(K_{1,\mathrm{ro}}=K_{0,\mathrm{ro}}(Z\otimes I)\), and \(Z\) is a
green half.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.22 (the negative branch; de Beaudrap and Horsman,
Lemma 3 and Corollary 4).} In the first of their two conventions,
exactly: the negative branch of a rough merge is the red merge with a
green half on its first incoming leg, and the negative branch of a
smooth merge is the green merge with a red half on its first incoming
leg: \[K_{1,\mathrm{ro}}=
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-1.2) (0,1.5);
\draw[wire] (0,0.7) -- (1.6,0.7) -- (2.4,0);
\draw[wire] (0,-0.7) -- (1.6,-0.7) -- (2.4,0);
\draw[wire] (2.4,0) -- (3.6,0);
\node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (0.8,0.7) {};
\node[xsp] at (2.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture},
\qquad
K_{1,\mathrm{sm}}=
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-1.2) (0,1.5);
\draw[wire] (0,0.7) -- (1.6,0.7) -- (2.4,0);
\draw[wire] (0,-0.7) -- (1.6,-0.7) -- (2.4,0);
\draw[wire] (2.4,0) -- (3.6,0);
\node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (0.8,0.7) {};
\node[zsp] at (2.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}.\] In their other convention the half sits on the
second incoming leg.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} \(K_{1,\mathrm{ro}}=K_{0,\mathrm{ro}}(Z\otimes I)\) and
\(K_{1,\mathrm{sm}}=K_{0,\mathrm{sm}}(X\otimes I)\), as one checks on
the four basis states; a two-legged green half is \(Z\) and a two-legged
red half is \(X\) (Chapter 8, §8.2). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch18/SplitAndMerge.py}.

A merge is not always a coin. Merge two messages both at rest,
\(\ket{++}\), roughly: \(K_{0,\mathrm{ro}}\ket{++}=\ket+\) and
\(K_{1,\mathrm{ro}}\ket{++}=0\), so the outcome is \(j=0\) with
probability \(1\). What the coin depends on is the question and the
messages. For the joiner, it turns out, the coin is fair whatever the
messages are.

\hypertarget{a-joiner-by-surgery}{%
\subsection{A joiner by surgery}\label{a-joiner-by-surgery}}

Chapter 8's joiner (row 64) is a green spider on the upper wire, a red
spider on the lower wire, and one plain cord between them; bare, it is
\(\mathrm{CNOT}/\sqrt2\). Read it again with Result 18.21 in hand. The
green spider has one leg in and two out: it is a smooth split of the
upper message. The red spider has two legs in and one out: it is a rough
merge of the split's second half with the lower message. De Beaudrap and
Horsman note that ``the standard lattice-surgical realisation of CNOT''
is exactly this composition, ``Omitting the correction operations needed
to realise CNOT deterministically'', and credit it to Horsman, Fowler,
Devitt and Van Meter (their ref. {[}30{]}).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.23 (a joiner by surgery).} For \(j=0,1\), exactly,
\[\bigl(I\otimes K_{j,\mathrm{ro}}\bigr)\bigl(U_{\mathrm{sm}}\otimes I\bigr)\;=\;\bigl(Z^{j}\otimes I\bigr)\,\frac{\mathrm{CNOT}}{\sqrt2}\;=\;\frac{\mathrm{CNOT}}{\sqrt2}\,\bigl(Z^{j}\otimes I\bigr).\]
Each branch occurs with probability \(\tfrac12\) for every input,
product or entangled, and a green half on the upper wire after the
negative branch mends it: both branches then give the CNOT. As a
picture, the negative branch and its mending are
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.71em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-0.8) (0,2.4);
\draw[wire] (0,1.6) -- (4.2,1.6);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (4.2,0);
\draw[wire] (1.0,1.6) -- (3.2,0);
\node[zsp] at (1.0,1.6) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]right:{$\pi$}}] at (2.1,0.8) {};
\node[xsp] at (3.2,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.71em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-0.8) (0,2.4);
\draw[wire] (0,1.6) -- (4.2,1.6);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (4.2,0);
\draw[wire] (1.0,1.6) -- (2.6,0);
\node[zsp] at (1.0,1.6) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (3.2,1.6) {};
\node[xsp] at (2.6,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture},
\qquad
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.71em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
\path (0,-0.8) (0,2.4);
\draw[wire] (0,1.6) -- (5.0,1.6);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (5.0,0);
\draw[wire] (1.0,1.6) -- (2.6,0);
\node[zsp] at (1.0,1.6) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (3.0,1.6) {};
\node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi$}}] at (4.2,1.6) {};
\node[xsp] at (2.6,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=0.71em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
\path (0,-0.8) (0,2.4);
\draw[wire] (0,1.6) -- (3.6,1.6);
\draw[wire] (0,0) -- (3.6,0);
\draw[wire] (1.0,1.6) -- (2.6,0);
\node[zsp] at (1.0,1.6) {};
\node[xsp] at (2.6,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}.\]
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} On the blackboard: follow \(\ket{ab}\). The split gives
\(\ket{a}\ket{a}\ket{b}\); the rough merge of the last two sends
\(\ket{ab}\) to \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\ket{a\oplus b}\) (for \(j=0\), since
\(\braket{++|ab}=\tfrac12\),
\(\braket{--|ab}=\tfrac12(-1)^{a\oplus b}\), and
\(\tfrac12(\ket++(-1)^{a\oplus b}\ket-)=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\ket{a\oplus b}\)).
So the \(j=0\) branch sends \(\ket{ab}\) to
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\ket{a}\ket{a\oplus b}\), which is
\(\mathrm{CNOT}/\sqrt2\). The \(j=1\) branch is the same after \(Z\) on
the split's second output, which the split turns into \(Z\) on its
input: \(U_{\mathrm{sm}}Z=(I\otimes Z)U_{\mathrm{sm}}\). A \(Z\) on the
control commutes with the CNOT. For every unit vector \(\ket\psi\),
\(\bigl\|(Z^j\otimes I)\,\mathrm{CNOT}\ket\psi/\sqrt2\bigr\|^2=\tfrac12\),
since \((Z^j\otimes I)\,\mathrm{CNOT}\) is unitary. By the rules: in the
negative branch the green half sits on the merge's first incoming leg,
which is the split's second output (Result 18.22). It fuses into the
split (row 57), and fusion backwards (row 57) puts it out again on the
split's upper output; that is the first picture. The mending half then
meets it on the upper wire, and two green halves fuse to a whole turn,
which is rest: a bare wire (row 57). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch18/SplitAndMerge.py}, which checks both branches, the
probability \(\tfrac12\) on five random product inputs and one random
entangled one, the certain bare rough merge on \(\ket{++}\), and lets
PyZX's \texttt{full\_reduce} bring the surgery picture and the circuit
picture of the CNOT to the same picture.

The coin is fair for the joiner because each of its branches is a
unitary divided by \(\sqrt2\). That is also why the bare joiner of
Chapter 8 carried the number \(1/\sqrt2\). De Beaudrap and Horsman put
it this way: the subnormalisation of their diagrams ``is a feature of ZX
notation, not a bug'', since it records ``the 2-norms of the Kraus
operators''. Their Theorem 5 makes it general: lattice surgery
procedures ``model randomly-constructed simple ZX diagrams'', in which
each merge is one of its two branch pictures, ``and the probability of
each diagram is given by its 2-norm''. We state it and do not prove it.

\hypertarget{one-kind-of-ring}{%
\subsection{One kind of ring}\label{one-kind-of-ring}}

Look back at what the chapter has built. The parting ring spreads one
message over three wires: it is \(\ket{000}\bra0+\ket{111}\bra1\), a
green spider. A bell asks two wires whether they agree: two green
spiders and a red one. A smooth split is a green spider, a merge is a
spider of either colour, and a CNOT between two protected messages is a
split and a merge. The phase-flip code is the same spiders in the other
colour, and Shor's code is the two stacked with yellow boxes between.
Every move of error correction, copying, asking and joining, is made of
one kind of map,
\(\ket{0\cdots0}\bra{0\cdots0}+\ket{1\cdots1}\bra{1\cdots1}\), and its
colour-changed twin. That is the reason this book has been able to draw
every step.

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why describe a merge by its two
Kraus operators rather than by ``the'' operation it performs? Because it
has no single operation. A merge is a measurement: it answers with a
bit, and the bit is not chosen by anyone. Writing both branches keeps
the answer in view, and the answer is what tells the mending hand what
to do. Hiding it, as a positive-branch picture alone would, would make
lattice surgery look deterministic, and it is not.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Feynman's Notebook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{Surgery on a weave.} Lattice surgery was introduced by C. Horsman,
A. G. Fowler, S. Devitt and R. Van Meter in ``Surface code quantum
computing by lattice surgery'', \emph{New Journal of Physics} 14 (2012),
123011; de Beaudrap and Horsman call it ``the original paper on lattice
surgery'', and it already described splitting one patch into several at
once. Niel de Beaudrap and Dominic Horsman posted ``The ZX calculus is a
language for surface code lattice surgery'' in 2017, and it was accepted
in \emph{Quantum} in 2019. Their contribution was to say what the
operations do \emph{to the protected message} in every branch, including
the unlucky ones: ``we can prove what effect such operations have on the
encoded data, and how they interact with each other''. The spiders this
book has drawn since Chapter 8 turned out, in their hands, to be a
literal description of how the patches of a surface code are cut and
joined.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-theorem-twice-18}{%
\section{§18.7 The Theorem, Twice}\label{the-theorem-twice-18}}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.7 (one gust, mended blind), restated.} With
\(\mathrm{Enc}=\ket{000}\bra0+\ket{111}\bra1\), the checks \(P_s\), the
syndrome map \(\sigma(e)=(e_1\oplus e_2,\,e_2\oplus e_3)\) and the
corrections \(c(00)=000\), \(c(10)=100\), \(c(11)=010\), \(c(01)=001\):
for every \(X^e\in\mathcal E_X=\{I,X_1,X_2,X_3\}\) and every outcome
\(s\), exactly,
\[\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\,X^{c(s)}\,P_s\,X^{e}\,\mathrm{Enc}\;=\;[\,s=\sigma(e)\,]\;I .\]
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{diracs-blackboard-18}{%
\subsection{Dirac's Blackboard}\label{diracs-blackboard-18}}

Let \(\ket\psi=\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1\) be any message, and write
\(\bar e\) for \(e\) with every bit flipped.

\textbf{Step 1: spread, then the gust.}
\(\mathrm{Enc}\ket\psi=\alpha\ket{000}+\beta\ket{111}\). A gust \(X^e\)
flips the bits where \(e\) has a \(1\), so \(X^e\ket{000}=\ket e\) and
\(X^e\ket{111}=\ket{\bar e}\):
\[X^e\,\mathrm{Enc}\ket\psi\;=\;\alpha\ket e+\beta\ket{\bar e}.\]

\textbf{Step 2: the checks.} \(Z_1Z_2\ket x=(-1)^{x_1\oplus x_2}\ket x\)
for every basis word \(x\). Flipping both bits does not change their
parity, so \(Z_1Z_2\) multiplies \(\ket e\) and \(\ket{\bar e}\) by the
same sign, \((-1)^{e_1\oplus e_2}\); likewise \(Z_2Z_3\), with
\((-1)^{e_2\oplus e_3}\). Hence
\[\begin{aligned}\tfrac12\bigl(I+(-1)^{s_1}Z_1Z_2\bigr)\bigl(\alpha\ket e+\beta\ket{\bar e}\bigr)&\;=\;\tfrac12\bigl(1+(-1)^{s_1+e_1\oplus e_2}\bigr)\bigl(\alpha\ket e+\beta\ket{\bar e}\bigr)\\&\;=\;[\,s_1=e_1\oplus e_2\,]\bigl(\alpha\ket e+\beta\ket{\bar e}\bigr),\end{aligned}\]
and with the second factor,
\[P_s\,X^e\,\mathrm{Enc}\ket\psi\;=\;[\,s=\sigma(e)\,]\bigl(\alpha\ket e+\beta\ket{\bar e}\bigr).\]
The number in front is the same for \(\alpha\) and for \(\beta\): the
checks never separate them.

\textbf{Step 3: the mending.} If \(s\ne\sigma(e)\), the state is already
\(0\), and so is everything after. If \(s=\sigma(e)\): on the four
single-gust patterns, \(\sigma(000)=00\), \(\sigma(100)=10\),
\(\sigma(010)=11\) and \(\sigma(001)=01\), four different answers, and
the table \(c\) was built as the inverse of this list, so
\(c(\sigma(e))=e\). Then \(X^{c(s)}X^e=X^eX^e=I\), and
\[X^{c(s)}\,P_s\,X^e\,\mathrm{Enc}\ket\psi\;=\;\alpha\ket{000}+\beta\ket{111}.\]

\textbf{Step 4: the join.}
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\bigl(\alpha\ket{000}+\beta\ket{111}\bigr)=\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1=\ket\psi\).

So
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}X^{c(s)}P_sX^e\mathrm{Enc}\ket\psi=[s=\sigma(e)]\ket\psi\)
for every \(\ket\psi\), which is the operator equation.
\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch18/BlindVote.py}, which checks it
for all four gusts and all four outcomes, and the full statement of
Result 18.9 for all eight patterns.

\hypertarget{coeckes-sketchbook-12}{%
\subsection{Coecke's Sketchbook}\label{coeckes-sketchbook-12}}

Start from \emph{The Storm Line} as drawn in Result 18.7: the parting
ring, one weather ring \(e_k\pi\) on each strand, the tell rings with
the two bells \(s_1\pi\) and \(s_2\pi\) hanging from them, one mending
ring \(c_k\pi\) on each strand, and the joining ring. The picture
\emph{is} \(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}X^{c}P_sX^e\mathrm{Enc}\), exactly, by
the reading of §18.2. Every step below names its rule; every number is
written. We write \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) for the two bits of
\(\sigma(e)\).

\textbf{Step (i): each gust's half goes where its ties go} (row 120,
then row 57). The weather ring on strand \(k\) sits on one leg of the
tell ring \(t_k\), which is green and at rest. A red half on one leg of
a green spider at rest comes out as a red half on every other leg, with
the number \(1\) (row 120; if \(e_k=0\) there is no half, and nothing
moves). The weather ring is left at rest. On the strand, the half meets
the mending ring and fuses into it (row 57): it becomes
\((c_k+e_k)\pi\). On each tie, it meets the bell at the tie's end and
fuses into it: the first bell, tied to strands one and two, receives
\(e_1+e_2\), and the second receives \(e_2+e_3\). So the bells are now
\((s_1+\sigma_1)\pi\) and \((s_2+\sigma_2)\pi\), turns being counted
modulo a whole turn.
