\hypertarget{the-verdict-18}{%
\subsection{The verdict}\label{the-verdict-18}}

The blackboard wins, and the chapter says so. Its proof is four steps,
each a line: the gust moves both words of the code, the checks see the
same parity in both, the table undoes the gust, and the encoder's mirror
undoes the encoder. The sketchbook needs five moves, a path chosen with
care so that every ring slid along is bare, and a rule, Result 18.8,
that had to be derived first from Hopf and fusion. Nothing in the
picture proof is hard, but there is more of it.

What the picture shows, and the algebra hides, is \emph{where a gust
goes}. On the blackboard \(\sigma\) is a formula,
\((e_1\oplus e_2,\,e_2\oplus e_3)\). In the picture of step (i) it is
the drawing: a gust's half goes into exactly the bells tied to its
strand, and on into its own mending ring, and nowhere else. The ties
\emph{are} the syndrome map. The same picture shows why the checks
cannot hurt the message: they hang from green spiders at rest, which
pass a red half on without looking at what flows along the strand. The
pictures win outright elsewhere in the chapter: on phase flips, where
colour change turns the whole code into its twin in one move (§18.3),
and on surgery, where the negative branch's half slides back through the
split to where the mending hand can reach it (§18.5). The
Knill--Laflamme conditions are a draw: the picture closes each question
to a number times a bare wire, but the matrix \(C_{ab}\) of those
numbers, and its rank, are the blackboard's. And every probability in
the chapter, \(p_L\) and the threshold among them, belongs to the
blackboard alone.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-storm-line}{%
\section{§18.8 The Storm Line}\label{the-storm-line}}

Here is the chapter's master diagram: one whole round of the bit-flip
code, drawn once for every case. It spreads the message, meets the
weather, asks the two checks, mends, and joins. Its bits make it one
picture for all branches (row 75): \(e_k\) says whether the weather
turned strand \(k\), \(s_j\) is the answer of bell \(j\), and \(c_k\)
says whether the mending hand turned strand \(k\) back.

Walk it from left to right. The lead-in runs from the input to the
parting ring, a green spider at rest. Three strands leave the parting
ring, the first on top, and each is drawn in four lengths: from the
parting ring to its weather ring, a red spider turned \(e_k\pi\); from
the weather ring to its tell ring, a green spider at rest; from the tell
ring to its mending ring, a red spider turned \(c_k\pi\); and from the
mending ring to the joining ring, a green spider at rest. Between the
first and middle strands hangs the first bell, a red spider turned
\(s_1\pi\), with a tie to each of the first two tell rings; between the
middle and third strands hangs the second bell, turned \(s_2\pi\), tied
to the middle and third tell rings. So the middle tell ring holds two
ties and each outer tell ring holds one. The lead-out runs from the
joining ring to the output. No two lines cross. Every ring is drawn
whether its bit is \(0\) or \(1\), and every tie is a plain cord; there
is no yellow box anywhere. We call the picture \textbf{The Storm Line}.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, x=1.2em, y=1.05em,

The picture has fifteen vertices: the input, the output, and thirteen
spiders, five green and eight red. Every piece of it is exact with no
number: the parting ring is \(\mathrm{Enc}\) (Result 18.3), each weather
and mending ring is \(X^{e_k}\) or \(X^{c_k}\), the tell rings and bells
are \(P_s\) (Result 18.5), and the joining ring is
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}\). So the whole is
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}X^{c}P_sX^{e}\mathrm{Enc}\). With the mending
hand following the table, \(c=c(s)\), it is the headline. With the
mending bits left free, it says what every mending does.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 18.24 (The Storm Line).} For all bits \(e_1,e_2,e_3\),
\(s_1,s_2\) and \(c_1,c_2,c_3\), exactly,
\[\text{The Storm Line}\;=\;[\,s=\sigma(e)\,]\cdot\begin{cases}I&\text{if }e\oplus c=000,\\ X&\text{if }e\oplus c=111,\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\]
With \(c=c(s)\) and \(X^e\in\mathcal E_X\) it is Result 18.7; with
\(c=c(s)\) and any \(e\) it is Result 18.9.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} \textbf{On the blackboard.} By Result 18.6,
\(P_sX^e\mathrm{Enc}=[s=\sigma(e)]\,X^e\mathrm{Enc}\). Then
\(X^cX^e=X^{e\oplus c}\), and
\(\mathrm{Enc}^{\dagger}X^{f}\mathrm{Enc}\) is \(I\) for \(f=000\),
\(X\) for \(f=111\), and \(0\) otherwise (the proof of Result 18.16).
\textbf{In the sketchbook.} Step (i) of §18.7 holds for every labelling:
the bells become \((s_j+\sigma_j)\pi\) and the mending rings
\((c_k+e_k)\pi\). If \(s\ne\sigma(e)\), the last picture of §18.7 gives
\(0\). If \(s=\sigma(e)\), both bells are at rest, and there are three
cases, by the weight of \(e\oplus c\). If it is \(000\), steps (ii) to
(v) give the bare wire. If it is \(111\), every mending ring is a half:
slide the tell rings into the parting ring along the bare weather cords
(row 57), and the bells come off with the number \(1\) (Result 18.8);
push the first strand's half through the joining ring, which is at rest
(row 120): it comes out on the other two strands, where it fuses with
their halves to rest (row 57), and on the lead-out; the three strands
are now bare, so the joining ring slides into the parting ring, the two
loops go (row 90), and what is left is a red half on a wire, \(X\),
number \(1\). If the weight of \(e\oplus c\) is \(1\) or \(2\), push
each mending ring's half back through its tell ring (row 120): it lands
on that strand's weather cord and on the ties, and the bells become
\(\sigma_j(e\oplus c)\,\pi\), which is a half for at least one of them,
since \(\sigma\) vanishes only on \(000\) and \(111\). The mending cords
are now bare: slide the tell rings into the \emph{joining} ring along
them (row 57), and each bell is tied twice to it; a bell at a half gives
\(0\) (Result 18.8). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch18/BlindVote.py}, which builds this picture in PyZX,
counts its vertices and cords, checks its value against the formula for
every one of the \(2^8\) labellings, and lets \texttt{full\_reduce}
derive the bare wire, a single \(X\) with the number \(1\), or \(0\).

It is what the dialogue's storm line hangs as, the length of the Crab's
front hall: rings and bells and cords, the message going in at the door
and coming out at the kitchen, and nobody looking at it on the way.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{what-a-rewrite-cannot-carry}{%
\section{§18.9 What a Rewrite Cannot
Carry}\label{what-a-rewrite-cannot-carry}}

Take stock. Noise is a channel, and a channel is a sum of branches
(Result 18.1). The classical vote of three fails with probability
\(F(p)=3p^2-2p^3\) (Result 18.2). The one copier that linearity allows
is a green spider, which copies dark and lit messages and spreads every
other (Results 18.3 and 18.4). A bell asks two wires whether they agree
(Result 18.5), and its answer depends on the gust and not on the message
(Result 18.6), so a single gust is mended blind, exactly (Result 18.7,
proved twice). A bell tied twice to one spider comes off with
\((1+e^{i\theta})/2\) (Result 18.8). Two gusts win the vote (Result
18.9); every mixture of single gusts is mended (Result 18.10); and
independent flips become a logical flip of probability \(F(p)\) (Result
18.11). A phase flip passes the bells unheard (Result 18.12), colour
change gives the code that hears it (Result 18.13), and Shor's nine
wires hear both (Result 18.14). A code may ask only questions whose
answers do not depend on the message (Results 18.15 and 18.16);
stabilizer codes (Result 18.17) ask them with checks of any weight
(Result 18.18), and Kitaev's toric code asks them locally (Result
18.19). Below a threshold, codes within codes make a computation as
reliable as we like (Result 18.20). Splits and merges are spiders
(Results 18.21 and 18.22), and a joiner is one of each, mended by a half
(Result 18.23). \emph{The Storm Line} says what every mending does
(Result 18.24).

Now the honest part. \textbf{A rewrite proves that two processes are
equal, and nothing else.} No picture in this chapter proves a threshold:
Result 18.20 is Gottesman's, stated and not proved, and row 143 has no
picture. No picture proves a distance, or that a code is the best of its
kind: the quantum Hamming and Knill--Laflamme bounds, Theorem 5 and
Kitaev's count are quoted, and the distances we checked, the \(1\) of
\([[3,1,1]]\) in the text and the \(3\) of the nine-, seven- and
five-wire codes in \texttt{Code/Ch18/WhatABellMayAsk.py}, were found by
listing operators, not by drawing. The Knill--Laflamme theorem is
stated; the pictures of Result 18.16 only evaluate its conditions on
examples. De Beaudrap and Horsman's lemmas are claims about what surgery
does to a patch of a real surface code; what we checked is that the
matrices they name are spiders. Every probability in the chapter,
\(F(p)\), the fair coin of the joiner and every threshold figure, was
computed or quoted on the blackboard. The joining ring was only ever the
good branch of a decoder. And the headline itself went to the
blackboard.

What the pictures do give is a way of seeing the whole construction as
one thing. The checks hang from green spiders at rest, and a green
spider at rest passes a red half from any leg to all the others: that
one fact is why the bells hear the gust, why they hear it on exactly the
strands they are tied to, and why they learn nothing of the message.
Change the colour and the same fact makes the phase-flip code. Change
the reading and it makes lattice surgery. Every picture in the chapter
is exact, number included. The only ``up to'' is the overall number
\(r\) with \(|r|=1\) that Shor's code may leave on a corrected state,
and that is a global phase, which no reading can see.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

The chapter's question has an answer. A message that must not be looked
at survives a storm that turns it at random by being spread, not copied,
over several wires by a green spider; by being questioned only about
whether its wires agree, never about what they hold; and by being mended
by a table that reads only those answers. The storm's continuum of small
turns collapses, under the questions, into a few whole ones, each undone
exactly. Against both kinds of turn it takes nine wires, or seven, or
five. And if the hardware's own mistakes are rare enough, below a
threshold whose value is still argued over, codes inside codes make a
whole computation as reliable as we please.

Every theorem in this book has been proved twice, once on the blackboard
and once in the sketchbook, and this chapter has said plainly, more than
once, where the second proof was the longer one. The last chapter turns
to the pictures themselves. Chapter 19, \emph{Logic of Pictures}, asks
whether ``proved twice'' is always possible, and what the pictures'
rules are when they are read as axioms.

\hypertarget{sinfonia-in-a-closed-box}{%
\chapter{Sinfonia in a Closed Box}\label{sinfonia-in-a-closed-box}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\emph{閉ぢし箱}\\
\emph{喉を鳴らすや}\\
\emph{冬籠}

\emph{tojishi hako}\\
\emph{nodo o narasu ya}\\
\emph{fuyugomori}

\emph{The closed box, purring ---}\\
\emph{and all of us shut indoors}\\
\emph{till the winter's done.}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\emph{{[}The Crab's music room, towards eleven on the night of the
storm. The curtains are drawn and the door to the hall is shut. The Crab
sits by the fire with a lute across his knees; its case stands shut on a
low stool in the middle of the room, between the pianos and the fire.
The Anteater, who came in an hour ago wet through, has the chair nearest
the fire, and his coat hangs over another beside it. The Tortoise is at
the table with her work-bag. Achilles has the chair nearest the
case.{]}}

\emph{{[}Nearly everything in the Crab's music room was bought as a pair
and has stayed one, and at night, with the curtains drawn, the pairs
close in round the fire: the two upright pianos side by side against the
long wall, their lids down; the two music stands beside them; a lamp lit
at either end of the table; and on the mantelpiece the two clocks by one
maker, which do not keep step, their ticks falling anyhow under the
noise of the weather. The one tall window has its heavy curtains drawn
across it, a damask of leaves, and behind them the rain comes at the
house in handfuls. Over the mantel, between the clocks, hangs Escher's
\textup{Print Gallery} in a plain frame: a man in a gallery, looking at
a print that holds the gallery he stands in. The firelight reaches no
higher than the foot of the frame, and the lamps on the table leave the
rest of it in a half-dark. It hung there before the storm got up, and it
will hang there when the storm has blown itself out. The fire is
new-made with wood that came in wet, and it hisses and sulks: a flame
stands up at one end of a log and lies down again, another starts where
nobody was looking, and which log has caught, nobody could yet say. The
Anteater's coat steams on its chair, the red earth of Aunt Hillary's
hill not quite washed out of its hem, and it hangs a little crooked,
dragged down on one side by something heavy in an inner pocket. On its
low stool the lute case stands shut, a maker's mark burned into the wood
beside its clasp; the side of it towards the fire is warm, as anything
standing so near that fire would be, and whether there is anything in it
but its lining, the case does not say. Across the Crab's knees lies the
lute that came out of it, pear-backed, with a rose cut in its belly as
fine as lace, and in its bent-back pegbox a peg for every string: the
top string alone, fine as a hair, and under it the pairs, each a shade
heavier and darker than the pair above, down to the lowest, the two
strings of every pair so alike and so close that only a hair's breadth
of air between them says there are two.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} Nobody could sleep through that wind, so I thought I'd do
something useful with the damp. This is my lute, from a workshop in
Füssen, on the Lech, where they have been making nothing else for longer
than anyone remembers. The top string runs alone, and every course under
it is a pair: two strings side by side, tuned to one note and struck
together, so the pair sounds as one. A night like this puts them out,
and puts each pair out with itself.

\emph{{[}He shuts his eyes and sounds the top string by itself: one
note, a shade flat. He turns its peg a hair and sounds it again, and the
note comes up to pitch. What has changed: one string's note. What has
held: every other string on the lute, untouched.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} The first course, a single string.

\textbf{Achilles:} I never went up, you know. The bed looked lovely, and
the wind said no.

\textbf{Crab:} Nor did I. \emph{{[}Eyes still shut, he sounds the pair
of strings just below the top string, both together.{]}} The second
course.

\emph{{[}The two strings of the pair sound almost one note, and not
quite: their two pitches beat against each other in a slow waver, like a
wheel with a loose spoke. The Crab turns one peg of the pair a hair. The
waver slows, slows, and stops, and the two strings sound as one note.
What has changed: one string's pitch, and the waver gone out of the
pair. What has held: its twin, which he never touched; the single string
above; every pair below.{]}}

\textbf{Anteater:} You have a good ear, Mr Crab. I have been sitting in
my own steam this last hour, and I could not have told you anything was
wrong.

\textbf{Crab:} There's always something wrong with a lute. The trick is
to have it all wrong together. \emph{{[}The next pair, sounded together;
one peg turned a hair; the waver gone.{]}} The third course. You came
from Aunt Hillary's, Doctor?

\textbf{Anteater:} Straight from her, and wet through at every step. She
has sealed every door in the hill against the storm: every chamber shut
on its own, with its own ants in it and its own air. You could not get a
message from one room of her to the next tonight if you begged.

\emph{{[}Under the talk, the rain on the house, which a moment ago was
only a noise, can be heard for what it is: a great many drops, each
striking once, somewhere on the roof or the wall, and on its own, and
out of all of them one steady hiss that no single drop makes. The
Anteater turns his face to the fire and shuts his eyes, like somebody
listening to a voice he knows.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} And she's content with that?

\textbf{Anteater:} She is never more herself than when she is shut up in
pieces. \emph{{[}He reaches to his coat where it hangs, draws a small
bundle from its deep inner pocket, and unwraps a brass lamp, tarnished
and cold.{]}} Madam Tortoise, your lamp: the Genie's, from your top
shelf. You asked me to bring it when I came, and I have kept it drier
than I kept myself.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Thank you, Doctor. \emph{{[}She takes it and sets it
beside her work-bag.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} The Genie's lamp? What for?

\textbf{Tortoise:} Perhaps for nothing.

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}another pair sounded; a peg; the waver gone{]}}
The fourth course.

\emph{{[}From the shut case on its stool comes a purr.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \ldots Did your case just purr?

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}opening his eyes{]}} I put the lute down an hour
ago and shut the case, to keep the damp out of the lining. Empty. I'd
swear to it.

\textbf{Achilles:} The Cat was on the hall settle at eight, and nobody
saw it go anywhere. \emph{{[}He leans towards the case.{]}} Cat? How are
you getting on in there?

\textbf{Cat:} \emph{{[}from inside the case{]}} Asleep, mostly. And a
little awake, round the edges.

\emph{{[}The case as it stands: shut, its brass clasp down. The Crab
lays the lute across his knees, leans from his chair, and sets a
claw-tip under the clasp; it lifts a hair's breadth. The Tortoise's hand
comes down, gently, over his claw, and the clasp settles back. What has
changed: nothing in the case, and nothing on it. What has held: the lid,
down.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Open it and you've asked it.

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}drawing his claw back{]}} \ldots So I have. And
one doesn't ask a guest whether it's asleep. \emph{{[}He takes up the
lute again.{]}} It may keep the lining; it's velvet from Lyon, and it
was never meant for anything half so warm. \emph{{[}A pair sounded; a
peg; the waver gone.{]}} The fifth course.

\textbf{Achilles:} You tune them with your eyes shut. Is that for the
ear?

\textbf{Crab:} It's for the strings. Stare at a string and it won't
settle: it goes sharp from nerves. Try.

\emph{{[}Achilles fixes his eyes on the next pair while the Crab sounds
it. The waver comes and goes and will not stop; the Crab turns the peg,
and the pitch slides past where it should rest, and back, and past
again. Achilles looks away, into the fire. The Crab turns the peg a
hair, and the pair settles into one note. What has changed: one string
of the pair, brought to its twin. What has held: the lute, whole, and
none the worse for being looked at.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} The sixth course. You see.

\textbf{Achilles:} I see I'd better not.

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}eyes shut again; two more pairs, each a peg
turned and a waver gone{]}} The seventh course. The eighth course.
There's cocoa on the hob if anyone wants it. I've left the storm line up
in the hall, and I'll not go out to it till this wind is done.

\textbf{Tortoise:} I'll pour. \emph{{[}She pours the cocoa and hands the
cups round.{]}}

\emph{{[}The Anteater takes his cup in both hands and holds it under his
nose for the steam. Achilles, his feet drawn up under him in the chair
nearest the case, blows on his cocoa and watches the case over the rim;
and the Tortoise, sitting down again with the last cup, glances across
the table at Achilles.{]}}

\textbf{Anteater:} Near eleven, and not one of us abed.

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}another pair; a peg; the waver gone{]}} The
ninth course. \emph{{[}The last pair, the deepest, sounded together: a
longer waver, slow as breathing, and then one low note.{]}} And the
lowest course. There. \emph{{[}He sweeps a claw once across the whole
lute, the single top string and every pair beneath it, and they sound
together as one chord.{]}} In tune, for as long as the storm lets it be.

\emph{{[}The storm booms in the chimney, and goes on booming. Now that
nobody is looking at it, the lute on the Crab's knee seems to answer the
wind each time, a murmur somewhere among the pairs, too low to be sure
of; the moment anyone turns to listen for it, there is only the
storm.{]}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{first-challenge-every-card-balances}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{First Challenge --- \emph{Every Card
Balances}}{First Challenge --- Every Card Balances}}\label{first-challenge-every-card-balances}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}bringing a squared pack of plain cards out
of her work-bag{]}} While you all talked this evening, I wrote down
every move we have made with pictures since the first evening we sat
down together, one move to a card. On each card there's a picture on the
left and a picture on the right, with ``is'' between them; and under the
right-hand picture its number, when it has one, a size in words or a
little dial for a turn of the whole. It's the rules of the house, Mr
Crab, in one pack.

\textbf{Crab:} The rules of my own house, dealt to me. I've never been
dealt my house before.

\textbf{Achilles:} And if one of them is wrong?

\textbf{Anteater:} At which level are you asking? A card by itself, or a
card with a picture all round it, doing its work in company?

\textbf{Achilles:} By itself, first. \emph{{[}He takes out his pad.{]}}
My pad: I'll work both sides of every card in numbers, and give it a
tick here when they come out the same. A tick on the pad, never on your
cards. Deal.

\emph{{[}The Tortoise sets the Genie's lamp on the mantel beside the
left-hand clock, out of the way, and sits down again with the deck.{]}}

\emph{{[}The deck as it stands: squared and face down in the Tortoise's
hand; Achilles's pad blank but for a ruled margin. She turns the top
card face up on the table, the right way up for Achilles, who sits
across the table from her: a cord with a box and then another box on it
is the two boxes run together; two cords, one above the other, each with
its box, are the boxes side by side. Achilles bends over it, works the
left side and the right side on his pad, and makes a small tick in the
margin. What has changed: one card face up, one tick on the pad. What
has held: the rest of the deck, face down in her hand.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} One after another, and side by side.

\textbf{Achilles:} That's the least they could do. Tick.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}the next card face up{]}} The crossing.
\emph{{[}And the next.{]}} The bend. The bent cord is the pair,
unweighted: both ends dark or both ends lit, with no number in front.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}working{]}} Dark with dark, lit with lit,
and nothing to shrink it. And pulled straight it's a plain cord, with no
number to pay. Tick, and tick.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Sliding together: two rings of one colour on a plain
cord are one ring, and their beads add.

\textbf{Achilles:} An eighth and a quarter make three eighths, either
side. Tick. You'll trip me somewhere; there's always one card that's
wrong.

\emph{{[}The deal goes on. Card by card she turns them up: the tube that
changes a ring's colour; two tubes that are no tube; a point copied
through a ring of the other colour, its number written under; a half
passing a turn of the other colour, with a dial under the right-hand
side; the cross undone, with its number; a loop that comes off. For
each, Achilles works the two sides on his pad, frowning, and for each he
makes his tick. The ticks go down the margin in a column; the face-up
cards spread across the table; the pack in her hand grows thin.{]}}

\begin{center}
\rulecard*{half passing}{Face up on the table}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Two cords are none.

\textbf{Achilles:} A green ring and a red ring joined by two cords, the
same as the two rings apart? \emph{{[}He works it.{]}} No, they're not.
They come to half as much. \emph{{[}He looks up, pleased.{]}} There's
your wrong card.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Look under the right-hand picture.

\textbf{Achilles:} ``Halved.'' \ldots Oh. It's written there. Tick.
Without that half it would be wrong by double, and a closed picture is
nothing but its number.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Which is why every card carries its number.

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}with half an eye on the case{]}} Nothing's
stirred in there.

\emph{{[}The fire has taken at last, log by log, and burns now in many
places at once, each flame going its own way on its own log and none of
them like its neighbour. Achilles's eyes go from his pad to the case and
back to his pad; across the table, between one card and the next, the
Tortoise's go to Achilles. The case stands as it stood, warm on its fire
side, and keeps its own counsel.{]}}

\textbf{Anteater:} You have ticked a great many cards alone, Achilles.
But a card is never used alone. In a proof it sits in the middle of a
picture, with things before it and after it and beside it.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then let me put one in company. \emph{{[}He takes the
sliding card and, on his pad, draws a box before it, a box after it, and
a third box on a cord running alongside; he works the whole with the
card's left side inside it, and again with its right side.{]}} The same.
Anything that stands round the card stands round both its sides alike,
so it can't tell them apart. Tick, in company.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Now the mirror card. There's one more way to look at
a card: hold it up to the lamp and read it from behind, through the
paper, and left and right change places, and every turn reads the other
way round. That is the mirror, and it costs nothing to look.

\emph{{[}The mirror card as it stands, face up: on the left a box with
its turns, then ``is'', then on the right the same box drawn the other
way about, every turn reversed. She lifts it and holds it between the
table lamp and Achilles, its inked face turned away from him, so that
the lamp shines through the thin card and the pictures show through
backwards. From his side the right-hand picture now stands on the left
and the left on the right, and every bead that read a quarter round
reads a quarter back. What has changed: which side is which, and which
way every turn goes. What has held: the card itself, its ``is'', every
cord and ring on it.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} It's the same card, with its two sides changed over.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}holding the sliding card to the lamp the
same way{]}} And this one?

\begin{center}
\rulecard[through]{sliding}{Held to the lamp}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Two rings sliding into one, the beads turned the
other way round and still adding. The sliding card again, with other
turns.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}holding up the card of the half passing a
turn of the other colour{]}} And this?

\emph{{[}From behind, each picture has crossed to the other side of the
card, and in each the half now stands on the other side of the turn it
passes; the little dial has crossed with its picture, and stands now
under the left-hand one, pointing the other way round.{]}}

\begin{center}
\rulecard[through]{half passing}{Read from behind}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} The half on the other side of the turn, and the dial
turned back. That's the same card read in the other order, and you wrote
it both ways. All three are cards I've ticked already.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Hold any of them to the lamp, and what you see from
behind is a card of the deck.

\emph{{[}Where the two curtains meet across the window, the draught has
turned the edge of one of them back a hand's breadth, and its back
shows: the same damask leaves as on its face, turned the other way
about, the pale and the dark changed over. It is a curtain from either
side, and the Crab chose it for that.{]}}

\emph{{[}She turns up the last card: letting go, and reading. Achilles
works it and makes the last tick at the foot of the column; then he
gathers the spread cards into one pack and knocks its edges square on
the table. What has changed: every card has its tick, and the column on
his pad is full. What has held: every card, just as she wrote it.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}handing her the squared deck{]}} Whatever
the pictures say, the numbers say.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Every card balances.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then the numbers can check every picture. Can the
pictures check every number?

\textbf{Tortoise:} Not in your kitchen yesterday, Mr Crab. Do you
remember the hub with a quarter hanging from it?

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{second-challenge-the-hinge}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Second Challenge --- \emph{The
Hinge}}{Second Challenge --- The Hinge}}\label{second-challenge-the-hinge}}

\textbf{Crab:} Remember it! I have a card in my recipe box for every
dish that came out of that afternoon, and a blank one where that one
goes.

\textbf{Tortoise:} A hub with a quarter hanging from it, standing on a
quarter back on each line, is a tie in a sleeve. Yesterday I hadn't a
move for it.

\textbf{Achilles:} My numbers settled it, though. Both pictures came to
the same on every way the lines could start.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Your numbers checked it; my cards never reached it.
Either the deck is a card short, or I wasn't clever enough. I would
rather it were the deck.

\textbf{Achilles:} So what you're saying is the deck was wrong.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Short, not wrong. You've just ticked every card in
it. \emph{{[}She takes a blank card and a pencil.{]}}

\emph{{[}The card as it starts: blank. On the left she draws one cord
with three rings on it in a row: a green ring, its bead a quarter round;
a red ring, a quarter round; a green ring, a quarter round. She writes
``is''. On the right she draws a plain cord with a single yellow tube on
it, and under the tube a small dial, its arrow turned an eighth round.
What has changed: a blank card holds a rule. What has held: the deck
beside it, as Achilles ticked it.{]}}

\begin{center}
\rulecard{new}{No longer blank}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Green, red, green, a quarter each: glass, steel,
glass! One click each, with the clock, and your ball stood just where
the brass needle's two clicks had left it. The night the snow lay, Crab.

\textbf{Crab:} My lamp-black ball. I opened its shutter that night, and
it has never turned true since. It sits in the cabinet still.

\textbf{Achilles:} But the ball never showed an eighth of anything.
\emph{{[}He works the card on his pad.{]}} There. The three quarters
make the tube, and turn the whole an eighth round besides; a ball can't
show a turn of the whole, and the numbers can. Tick.

\emph{{[}Behind the drawn curtains and the cloud, the sky has wheeled a
good eighth of the way round since eight o'clock; or the house has, with
this room and everything in it, which comes to the same. Nothing in the
room shows it: not the fire, not the cocoa in the cups, not one string
of the lute.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} I have never got that card out of the other cards,
and those who have looked hardest say it can't be got out of theirs. So
it goes in as a card of its own: given, not got. \emph{{[}She lays it on
the deck.{]}}

\textbf{Anteater:} A new rule for the house, and at this hour of the
night.

\emph{{[}He says it fondly, as of a grandchild up long past its bedtime,
and holds out his cup; the Crab fills it from the pot on the hob and
sets the pot back to keep warm. Achilles stretches his feet towards the
fire, his pad on his knee, and his eyes go to the case before they go
back to the cards.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} And three small ones come out of it. \emph{{[}She
draws three more cards quickly, and pencils a small cross in the top
right-hand corner of each.{]}} The cross means taken from the others,
not given. Three quarters back, green, red, green, is the tube with the
whole an eighth back. A green turn passes a red point at rest untouched,
and a red point at a half by turning the whole by the same turn. And a
green point a quarter round is a red point a quarter back, with the
whole an eighth round.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}working each on his pad{]}} Tick. Tick. And
tick.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}drawing her cloth out of her work-bag and
spreading it on the table in front of her, its near edge on her side, so
that what lies on it reads left to right, upper and lower, as she looks
down at it from her chair; Achilles, across the table, sees it the other
way up{]}} My drawing-cloth, with my rings and cords and yellow tubes,
as ever: what lies on it is a picture of a thing, not the thing.
\emph{{[}She sets her little box of rings beside the cloth, and brings
out a little packet of paper dials. Each ring opens at a small hinge,
and each tube at a slit, so that either clips on or off a cord anywhere;
on her cloth, as ever, a bead at rest sits at its ring's far side as she
looks down, and a turn goes round clockwise.{]}} And these are new
tonight: slips. A bead turns one ring; a slip laid in the corner of the
cloth turns the whole picture, and two slips that cancel are taken away
together.

\emph{{[}She lays the hub as it stood in the Crab's kitchen just before
she lifted it away whole, without the rest of that picture round it: two
plain cords across the cloth, one above the other; on each a green ring,
its bead a quarter back; from each of those a short tie running to one
red ring between the cords, at rest, the hub; and from the hub a short
cord running out and down to the right, to a green point lying on the
cloth, its bead a quarter round. The corner of the cloth, its far
right-hand corner, is empty.{]}}

\begin{center}
\hingecloth*{Laid out flat}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} The hub, as it stood yesterday. Now the new cards.

\emph{{[}The point as it stands, lying out to the right of the hub:
green, a quarter round, on its short cord from the hub. The Tortoise
lifts it off the end of the cord into her box and ties on in its place a
red point, its bead a quarter back; then she sets a slip's arrow an
eighth round and lays it in the corner. What has changed: the point's
colour and its bead, and the corner, which holds one slip now. What has
held: the hub, the two feet, both lines, and what the picture does; the
crossed card says so.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} A red point on a red hub. Red into red?

\textbf{Tortoise:} Red into red.

\emph{{[}The red point, a quarter back, lies out to the right of the red
hub on its short cord. She slides it up the cord into the hub: the cord
is gone, the point is gone into the ring, and the hub's bead, which
stood at rest, now stands a quarter back. What has changed: the hub has
lost its short cord and taken the point's turn. What has held: the hub's
two ties to the feet, the feet, and the one slip in the corner.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} So now the hub is only a red ring a quarter back,
sitting on the tie between the two feet.

\emph{{[}Each foot as it stands: a green ring a quarter back on its
line, tied to the hub. She slides the upper foot apart along its own
tie: a green ring at rest stays on the upper line, and a green ring a
quarter back sits on the tie just below it. Then the lower foot, the
same way: a green ring at rest on the lower line, and a green ring a
quarter back on the tie just above it. What has changed: the feet stand
at rest, and their turns have moved onto the tie. What has held: each
line, the red ring in the middle, and the corner; nothing goes to the
corner for this.{]}}

\begin{center}
\hingecloth[red point, slid into the hub, feet slid apart]{Feet at rest}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}reading the tie from top to bottom{]}} Green
a quarter back, red a quarter back, green a quarter back. That's your
new card seen through.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The crossed one.

\emph{{[}The three rings on the tie as they stand: green, red, green, a
quarter back each, in a row between the two rings at rest. She lifts the
three off together into her box and slides a single yellow tube onto the
tie in their place; then she sets a second slip's arrow an eighth back
and lays it in the corner beside the first. What has changed: three
rings have become one tube, and the corner holds two slips. What has
held: the ring at rest on each line, and the tie's two ends.{]}}

\textbf{Anteater:} And your two slips, Madam? One says an eighth round,
and one an eighth back.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Then they go together.

\emph{{[}The corner as it stands: two slips, their arrows turned
opposite ways. She picks them up one on the other and puts them in her
bag. What has changed: the corner is empty. What has held: everything on
the cloth, on each line a green ring at rest, and between them a tie
with a tube on it.{]}}

\begin{center}
\hingecloth[red point, slid into the hub, feet slid apart, tube, slips gone]{The corner empty}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} A sleeved tie. \ldots Oh. The eighth the ball
couldn't show: the slips were carrying it the whole way, and it
cancelled.

\textbf{Crab:} Yesterday's gap, shut. \emph{{[}He reaches for the new
card.{]}} I'm copying that into my recipe box tonight, and its three
little crossed ones with it.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Whatever the numbers say, the pictures can say.

\textbf{Achilles:} With the right cards, you mean. Yesterday you were a
card short. And one card mended one gap: how do you know there isn't
another gap, waiting for another card?

\textbf{Crab:} Will they do it for something I've not seen?

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{third-challenge-same-number-same-picture}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Third Challenge --- \emph{Same Number, Same
Picture}}{Third Challenge --- Same Number, Same Picture}}\label{third-challenge-same-number-same-picture}}

\textbf{Crab:} A dare, then, and I'll hold the stakes. Achilles, you
name two pictures whose numbers agree, anything you please, chosen with
your pad and not with her cloth. Madam Tortoise gets from one to the
other by her cards alone.

\emph{{[}The Crab settles back in his chair, very pleased to be holding
the stakes of anything. The fire has drawn itself up into a steady rank
of flames along the logs, each standing where it stands and drawing
evenly; and under them the embers have begun to glow in small cells,
each brightening and dimming on its own, and the whole bed of them one
steady red.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}working on his pad for a while, then turning
it face down{]}} Here's one. A tube, then a quarter round, three times
over, on one cord; and a bare cord with the whole turned an eighth
round. My pad says they're the same. Get from one to the other with your
cards, and don't look at my numbers.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Agreed. \emph{{[}She clears the cloth: the rings of
the sleeved tie into her box, and its tie, tube and all, into her
work-bag with the cords of the lines.{]}}

\emph{{[}She lays a single cord across the cloth, and on it, from left
to right: a yellow tube, a green ring a quarter round, a tube, a green
ring a quarter round, a tube, a green ring a quarter round. The corner
is empty.{]}}

\begin{center}
\darecloth*{Achilles's dare}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} Nothing in that picture says ``an eighth''. I chose
it for that.

\emph{{[}The cord as it stands. The Tortoise takes the first tube, the
green ring after it and the tube after that, a ring with a tube on each
of its cords, and draws the ring through both tubes: the tubes are gone
into it, and it comes out red, its bead still a quarter round. What has
changed: the ring's colour, and two tubes fewer on the cord. What has
held: the ring's bead, and everything to the right of it.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} A red quarter round. And this tube I read by the new
card, backwards.

\emph{{[}The one tube left on the cord sits between two green quarters.
She lifts it off into her work-bag and threads in its place a green
ring, a red ring and a green ring, each a quarter round, and lays a slip
in the corner with its arrow an eighth back. The cord now reads: red
quarter, green quarter, green quarter, red quarter, green quarter, green
quarter. What has changed: one tube has become three rings, and the
corner holds a slip. What has held: the rest of the cord, and what it
does.{]}}

\begin{center}
\darecloth[drawn through, card backwards]{Read backwards}
\end{center}

\textbf{Anteater:} You have made it longer.

\textbf{Tortoise:} To make it shorter. \emph{{[}Green beside green,
twice over: she slides each pair of green quarters together, the
left-hand ring into the right-hand one, and each pair becomes one green
ring at a half. The cord reads red quarter, green half, red quarter,
green half.{]}}

\emph{{[}The first green half as it stands, with a red quarter round
just after it. She slides the half along the cord, past the red ring to
just beyond it: as it passes, the red ring's bead swings from a quarter
round to a quarter back, and she lays a second slip in the corner, its
arrow a quarter round. The cord reads now: red quarter round, red
quarter back, green half, green half. What has changed: the half has
gone by, and the ring it passed turns the other way. What has held: the
half itself, and every ring's colour.{]}}

\begin{center}
\darecloth[drawn through, card backwards, halves, half passed]{Slid past}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} A red quarter round and a red quarter back, side by
side.

\emph{{[}She slides the two red rings together: a quarter round and a
quarter back make rest, and the ring at rest, with only the cord through
it, slips off into her box. Then the two green halves: a half and a half
make a whole turn, which is rest, and that ring slips off into her box
too. What lies there now is a bare cord, not a ring on it. In the corner
lie a slip an eighth back and a slip a quarter round; she lays them one
on the other, puts them in her work-bag, and lays a single slip in their
place, its arrow an eighth round. What has changed: every ring and tube
gone, and two slips become one. What has held: the cord's two ends.{]}}

\begin{center}
\darecloth[drawn through, card backwards, halves, half passed, bare cord, one slip]{A new slip}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} A bare cord, and the whole turned an eighth round.
May I look at your pad now?

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}turning it over{]}} A bare cord, the whole
an eighth round. I lose, and I'm glad of it.

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}crowing{]}} Whatever the numbers say, the
pictures can say.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Given the right cards, Mr Crab. And they aren't the
same cards for every kind of picture.

\emph{{[}On the nearer music stand lies a piece for the lute, written
out in the letters a lute-player reads, which tell the fingers where to
go; on the other stand lies the same piece in notes, which tell the ear
what it will hear. The Crab copied the letters out of the notes himself,
one winter, bar by bar, and has never found a bar that would not go.{]}}

\textbf{Anteater:} At which level, then? Are the right cards for small
questions the right cards for large ones?

\textbf{Tortoise:} It goes by the kind of picture, not the size. For
pictures that turn only by quarters, a right deck was found some years
ago. For pictures with eighth turns the right deck was found only
lately, and for any turn at all there's one too.

\textbf{Achilles:} And pictures that let go, like the one the Cat's in?

\textbf{Tortoise:} With quarter turns, yes. With eighths, the people who
had found the eighth-turn deck left that one open. And none of those
decks is quite my deck, so I'll not promise more than I've shown you
tonight.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}looking at the case{]}} Then whatever I
could work out about the Cat, you could draw. But I can't work out
whether it's asleep.

\textbf{Tortoise:} No one can, from outside. So what can a closed box
tell anyone?

\emph{{[}Every eye in the room goes to the case, and the case gives
nothing back: a shut lid, a clasp with no claw near it, and a warmth on
its fire side that would do as well for something curled inside as for
the fire alone. Asleep or awake, it has let the room wonder since
eleven.{]}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{fourth-challenge-one-answer-out}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Fourth Challenge --- \emph{One Answer
Out}}{Fourth Challenge --- One Answer Out}}\label{fourth-challenge-one-answer-out}}

\textbf{Achilles:} It can tell me I've watched it all evening. I haven't
taken my eyes off it since the purr.

\textbf{Tortoise:} I know. I've been watching you.

\textbf{Achilles:} Me? What for?

\textbf{Tortoise:} Because you were watching the box. Let me lay the
three of us out. \emph{{[}She clears the cloth, the bare cord into her
work-bag and its slip after it, and brings out more rings.{]}} The read
ring you know: a green ring that takes a cord and its copy and gives out
one single cord, the answer. And a cord let go is tied to its own copy,
as ever; when I want a picture's odds and not only its shape, I lay it
twice, as it is and seen through, one under the other.

\emph{{[}She lays it out. At the top, the Cat's cord, starting from a
green point at rest. Below it, Achilles's page: a cord starting from a
red point at rest, blank. Below that, her own page, the same. On the
Cat's cord she threads a green ring and ties it by a short tie to a red
ring on Achilles's page: his look. Further along Achilles's page she
threads a green ring and ties it to a red ring on her own page: her
look. Then she lays the whole again beneath, seen through, but not as a
card is held to the lamp: left and right stay as they were, and the rows
come in the other order, so that her own page's copy lies nearest the
middle, Achilles's below it and the Cat's lowest, with a clear row left
between the layers; every bead keeps its rest at its ring's far side,
and turns the other way round. Every bead is at rest, so bead for bead
the copy looks just like the picture above it. She ties each page's
cord, at its right-hand end, to its own copy's cord, with a knot where
the cord turns down, her page's turn inside Achilles's: let go. And she
brings the Cat's cord and its copy together into a read ring in the
clear row, from which a cord runs off to the right-hand edge of the
cloth.{]}}

\begin{center}
\boxcloth*{Pages and looks}
\end{center}

\textbf{Achilles:} And which of those is me?

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}her finger on the upper layer{]}} The middle
cord is your page. The Cat, as it was: evenly asleep and awake. Your
look copies the Cat onto your page; my look copies your page onto mine.
Both pages let go, and the Cat's cord read.

\textbf{Achilles:} That's us. That's this whole room.

\emph{{[}Achilles looks from the cloth to the case; the Tortoise, across
the table, looks from the cloth to Achilles; the Crab looks at the pair
of them; and the Anteater, warming his hands, looks at everybody. On the
mantel the two clocks tick on out of step, as though neither had noticed
the other all evening.{]}}

\emph{{[}The cloth as it stands: on each layer, each page starts at a
red point at rest, joined by plain cord to the red ring of a look. The
Tortoise slides each red point along its cord into the red ring beside
it, red into red, both at rest; and each ring, left at rest on its cord,
slips off into her box. Four times over: on each page, as it is and seen
through. What has changed: the red points and red rings are gone, and
each look's short tie runs on as plain cord from its green ring to
wherever the page went. What has held: the green rings, the let-go
cords, the read ring.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} My page is gone into your ring, and yours into
nowhere.

\emph{{[}On each layer now: the Cat's green point, Achilles's green ring
on the Cat's cord, and her green ring, all at rest and joined by plain
cord. She slides them together, his look's ring and hers along the cord
to the Cat's point, where they meet: the Cat's point, his look's ring
and hers become one green ring at rest, with a cord to the read ring and
the let-go cords running down to the same kind of ring on the copy
below. The same on the copy. What has changed: the whole company on each
layer has become one ring. What has held: the read ring, and the let-go
cords between the layers.{]}}

\begin{center}
\boxcloth[red points slid in, slid together]{Slid together}
\end{center}

\textbf{Anteater:} Two rings now, one above and one below, and joined
more ways than one.

\emph{{[}The two green rings as they stand: joined by the let-go cords,
and each running to the read ring. She slides the upper ring down a
let-go cord into the lower: green into green, one ring; and what is left
of the let-go cords now runs from that ring round and back into it, a
loop. Then she slides the read ring in along the copy's cord, and the
upper layer's cord, still running to it, becomes a loop too. She lifts
the loops off into her work-bag. What lies on the cloth: one green ring
at rest, just where the Cat's point lay on the copy, with a cord running
from it to the cloth's edge, and no slip in the corner. What has
changed: every look, every page, every copy, gone. What has held: the
ring's rest, which was the Cat's point's, and the cord out to the
edge.{]}}

\begin{center}
\boxcloth[red points slid in, slid together, loops off]{Loops lifted off}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} There's the Cat's own point, on the answer's cord,
just as it lay before anybody looked.

\textbf{Achilles:} But I looked! My page has it written down. That has
to count for something.

\textbf{Tortoise:} It counts on your page. And your page is let go; it
doesn't come out of the box.

\emph{{[}Not a word said in this room tonight has got out of it: not
through the shut door, not through the drawn curtains, not up the
chimney against that wind. Anyone out in the lane, if anybody were fool
enough to be out in the lane, would know of the whole room one thing
only: a patch of warm light on the wet cobbles, where the curtains do
not quite meet.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}working on his pad{]}} Evenly asleep and
awake before anyone looked. After my look, and your look at me, and both
pages let go: evenly asleep and awake. \ldots Oh. My watching changed
nothing anyone outside could hear. Then no look can ever change a closed
box's odds!

\textbf{Tortoise:} Not any look. Yours copied asleep-or-awake, and mine
only watched you. A look that asked the Cat some other question could
change them.

\emph{{[}From the case, a purr.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}taking up the lute{]}} Then here is what a
closed box gives out.

\emph{{[}The lute as it stands, lying across his knees belly up, its
neck to his left, so that, seen from his chair, the top string is the
farthest from him and the lowest pair the nearest: every pair in tune,
the top string alone above them. Eyes shut, the Crab sounds the pairs
one after another, from just under the top string down to the lowest,
each pair's two strings sounding one note. Then he lays a claw flat
across every string to still them, lifts it, and plucks the top string
alone. What has changed: where there were many notes one after another,
there is one, and it hangs in the room. What has held: every string, in
tune, as he tuned it.{]}}

\begin{center}
\crablute*[top string sounding]{Plucked alone}
\end{center}

\textbf{Tortoise:} Those pairs of strings are like my cords and their
copies: two, sounding as one. The top string is like the answer, which
has no copy, as a record has none. Only a likeness, mind: a copy turns
every bead the other way, and a twin string only agrees.

\emph{{[}In the grate the logs, burned through where they crossed,
settle into the embers together with a soft sound and a lift of sparks,
and burn on, lower and quieter than before. The Anteater leans to the
hearth and warms his hands at them.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Then any machine's a closed box like that. It starts,
it runs, and it gives out one answer, with odds.

\textbf{Crab:} And if the answer's wrong?

\textbf{Achilles:} Say it's right two times in three. Run it three times
and take the majority. All three right, eight times in twenty-seven;
just two right, in three ways, twelve times more. Twenty times in
twenty-seven.

\textbf{Crab:} Better than two in three?

\textbf{Achilles:} Two in three is eighteen in twenty-seven, so better.
And your cloth found the Cat's odds without a single number.

\textbf{Anteater:} The pad and the cloth, agreeing again.

\textbf{Achilles:} Whatever the numbers say, the pictures can say.

\textbf{Crab:} With the right cards.

\textbf{Anteater:} And if someone outside the room could undo the whole
room, you and your page and all? Aunt Hillary's wardens can.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{fifth-challenge-watchers-watched}{%
\section{\texorpdfstring{Fifth Challenge --- \emph{Watchers
Watched}}{Fifth Challenge --- Watchers Watched}}\label{fifth-challenge-watchers-watched}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Undo a room? What wardens?

\textbf{Anteater:} Aunt Hillary keeps two sealed chambers for a game she
is very fond of, and she plays it on nights like this. In one chamber an
ant tosses a weighted coin: heads one time in three, tails the other
two. On heads she sets a little token pointing down and sends it through
a hatch into the other chamber. On tails she sets it crosswise, half
down and half up.

\textbf{Tortoise:} And in the other chamber?

\textbf{Anteater:} An ant there looks at the token, and finds it lying
one way or the other, down or up. Then both hatches are sealed. Outside
each chamber sits a warden, who can undo the whole chamber, ant and
token and memory and all, back into one thing, and ask it a single
question: ``ok, or not?''

\textbf{Achilles:} Undo an ant's memory? And the ant never knows?

\textbf{Anteater:} She saw what she saw; I don't doubt an ant for a
moment. That is the difficulty. Each of them reasons from what she is
certain of.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Such as?

\textbf{Anteater:} The looking ant, if she saw the token up, is certain
the coin came down tails, for heads never sends it up. The tossing ant,
on tails, is certain that the looker's warden will hear ``not ok''. And
the tosser's warden, on hearing ``ok'', is certain the looking ant saw
it up.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then chain them. The tosser's warden hears ``ok'', so
the looking ant saw it up, so the coin was tails, so the looker's warden
hears ``not ok''. They can never both hear ``ok''.

\textbf{Anteater:} Aunt Hillary has played it round after round. One
round in twelve, both hear ``ok''.

\textbf{Achilles:} \ldots Then somebody's certainty is wrong. Whose?

\textbf{Anteater:} At which level are you asking? The ants', the
wardens', or Aunt Hillary's own, who holds the lot? Three natural things
were assumed: that her arithmetic holds in every chamber, the wardens'
included; that those who are certain do not contradict one another; and
that each ant saw one thing, and one thing only. The story does not say
which to give up, and neither will she.

\emph{{[}Round the case, the room; round the room, the shut house; round
the house, the storm. Each is shut on the one inside it, and each has of
the one inside only what gets through: the room, a purr now and then;
the house, a murmur of voices behind a door; the storm, a patch of light
it cannot get in at.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Well, nobody in this room can undo anybody. You've
only watched me, Tortoise.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Only watched. I haven't the hands to undo a whole
Achilles.

\textbf{Crab:} Nor I a Cat, it seems.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then let me ask something bigger than a room.
Tortoise, your lamp?

\textbf{Tortoise:} The Genie's lamp, on the mantel where I put it. Rub
it once, and he comes.

\emph{{[}Achilles takes the lamp down from the mantel. It is as it has
been all evening: brass, tarnished, cold, its wick dry, never lit. He
rubs its side once with his palm. The lamp does not warm; but from its
spout comes a breath of pale mist that, instead of fading, gathers and
rises and thickens, and there between the table and the fire stands the
Genie, brushing a little damp from his sleeves. The lamp in Achilles's
hands is as cold and dull as before. What is new is one more at the
table.{]}}

\textbf{Genie:} The Office of Wishes. One query, the evening's only one:
say it exactly, and say it once.

\emph{{[}While he speaks the light in the room seems to draw in towards
the table: the lamps at either end lean their flames a little inward,
and the glow of the fire reaches further across the floor than it did,
towards the old brass in Achilles's hands. The Crab sits very upright,
as a host does when a guest has come in by some way other than the
door.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Two players, in two rooms that cannot speak to each
other, sharing whatever pairs they like, and a referee who sets them any
game he pleases. I want a way to tell, for every such game, whether they
can win it every time or at best half the time.

\textbf{Genie:} A way to answer every question of a kind is a question
about questions, and not mine to grant. Referred. \emph{{[}He tilts his
head, as though listening up a stairwell, and straightens at once.{]}}

\emph{{[}In the chimney the wind goes up the flue with a single boom,
and the echo of it comes back down before the boom has finished, so that
the two are heard as one sound. The embers brighten and dim in the same
instant.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Referred where?

\textbf{Genie:} To the Meta-Genie, and above him, and above that, as
high as it goes; and it goes up without end. The answer has come down
already.

\textbf{Crab:} Already? From as high as it goes?

\textbf{Genie:} At once. It always does. The answer is no: there is no
such way.

\textbf{Achilles:} No way at all? For every game?

\textbf{Genie:} For every machine, the Office can set a game that the
pair win every time if the machine ever stops, and win at best half the
time if it never does. So a way to tell every time from half the time,
for every game, would tell of every machine whether it ever stops.
Nothing tells that; the Office has it from very high up.

\textbf{Achilles:} Then my query's spent, and on a no.

\textbf{Genie:} A query answered is a query spent. The Office is exact.

\emph{{[}The Genie thins to mist from the feet up, and the mist draws
itself back into the spout of the lamp in Achilles's hands, the last
wisp of it going in like a breath taken. The lamp is as it was: cold,
dull, unlit. What has changed: one fewer at the table, and a query
spent. What has held: the lamp. Achilles sets it down on the table.{]}}

\emph{{[}The light goes back to its places: the lamps' flames stand
straight again, and the firelight draws back to the hearth. Achilles
sits down again in the chair nearest the case and holds his hands out to
the embers; his eyes go back to the case, and across the table the
Tortoise's go to him.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} You've watched that case all night, Achilles, and
I've watched you watching it. Who has been watching me, I couldn't tell
you.

\emph{{[}Outside, the wind drops into a lull. In the quiet a flame
stands up tall out of the embers, and for as long as it stands its light
climbs the chimney-breast and lies full across the print over the
mantel.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}looking up at the print over the mantel,
between the clocks: Escher's \textup{Print Gallery}{]}} Your print,
Crab: a man in a gallery, looking at a print that holds the gallery he
stands in. I've been sitting in it all night.

\textbf{Crab:} \emph{{[}after a silence{]}} Then what have we got, out
of the whole night?

\textbf{Tortoise:} Every card balances.

\textbf{Anteater:} That much we ticked.

\textbf{Tortoise:} With the right cards, the pictures can say anything
the numbers can about a closed picture. And a closed box gives out one
answer, with odds that no watcher who only takes note can change.

\textbf{Achilles:} And the Genie's kind of question?

\textbf{Tortoise:} No way, drawn or worked, answers every question of
that kind. And the Doctor's story doesn't say which of the three to give
up.

\emph{{[}In the grate the logs have burned down into one bed of fire,
and there is no telling any more where one of them lay and where
another; the whole of it glows at once, and the room is warm into its
corners. The storm has not let up, and the house leans into it and does
not mind.{]}}

\emph{{[}On the mantel the two clocks strike twelve, the one beginning
before the other has done, so that the strokes fall in between one
another.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} Midnight, by both of them, more or less.

\textbf{Anteater:} \emph{{[}feeling the sleeve of his coat where it
hangs{]}} And my coat has dried. Aunt Hillary will be unsealing her
doors by morning, one chamber at a time.

\emph{{[}The Crab lays the lute on the table beside the stool where its
case stands, every string still.{]}}

\textbf{Crab:} The last of the cocoa. \emph{{[}He shares it out, and
gives Achilles the fuller cup.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Thank you. \emph{{[}He holds the cup and does not
drink; his eyes have gone back to the case.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} You've watched it all night. Ask it.

\textbf{Crab:} Ask it, Achilles. I shan't touch the clasp.

\emph{{[}For a moment the whole room looks at the case, and the case
stands on its low stool as it has stood all night, warm on its fire
side, shut as the Crab shut it. There may be something curled on the
velvet from Lyon, or there may be only velvet; asleep or awake, the room
has let it be both through all the storm.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Cat --- asleep or awake?

\textbf{Cat:} Awake.

\emph{{[}The lid stays down. The purr stops; over the closed case a grin
shows for a moment, the last of the Cat to go, and then is gone too.{]}}

\emph{{[}The case is only a case now: a lute case on a low stool, shut,
with velvet from Lyon inside it, asked its one question and done with
being asked. Beside it on the table the lute lies as the Crab laid it,
strung as he strung it: the top string alone, and beneath it the pairs,
each two strings side by side, down to the lowest, all of them still.
The Genie's lamp stands among the cups, a piece of old brass and nothing
more. In the grate the one bed of fire has gone low and red under a skin
of ash, and gives its warmth out steadily to the whole room. Outside the
storm is up still, throwing the rain at the curtained window and booming
in the chimney, and means to be till morning; inside, the two clocks
tick on out of step into the first minutes of the day. Over the mantel
the print hangs in its plain frame, the firelight no higher than the
foot of it again, one more of the Crab's things. Nobody goes up to bed.
Achilles sits in the chair nearest the case with his cup in both hands;
the Anteater's coat hangs dry on its chair, and the Anteater dozes
beside it; the Crab has his feet to the fire; the Tortoise, her work-bag
on her knee, has stopped watching Achilles; and for the first time all
night nobody in the room is watching anybody at all.{]}}

\hypertarget{chapter-19-logic-of-pictures}{%
\chapter{Chapter 19: Logic of
Pictures}\label{chapter-19-logic-of-pictures}}

\emph{--- Sinfonia in a Closed Box ---}

\emph{Part VI: Foundations}

\emph{Escher: ``Print Gallery'' --- a man in a gallery, looking at a
print that holds the gallery he stands in}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

If two pictures always give the same numbers, can the rules always turn
one into the other?

Imagine two clerks who keep the accounts of one house. The first keeps
them in figures. The second keeps them in drawings, and he has a short
list of moves he is allowed to make on a drawing: slide this, join that,
take a loop away. Whenever the draughtsman says ``these two drawings
come to the same thing'', the clerk of figures can check him by adding
up. So far, so safe. The question of this chapter runs the other way.
Whenever the figures say that two drawings come to the same thing, can
the draughtsman get from one drawing to the other \emph{by his own moves
alone}, without once borrowing the other clerk's sums?

It is not an idle question, because this book has been keeping its
accounts in exactly this double way. Every chapter proved its main
result twice, once in figures and once in drawings. Most of the time the
drawings managed on their own. But not always. More than once the
sketchbook reached a step it could not take by moves, and it crossed the
gap by working out both sides in figures and noting that they agreed.
Two chapters ago it said so plainly, and admitted that a skeptic who
distrusted pictures would be right to point at that step.

So is the gap in the drawings, or only in the list of moves? If one more
move would close it, is there always one more move? Could there be a
list that never needs to borrow at all? And if there is, what does such
a list buy, and what can no list of moves ever buy?

These questions have answers, and most of them are recent. People found
lists of moves that never need to borrow, for one kind of drawing after
another, in a burst of papers between 2013 and 2019; for one kind, the
authors of the last of those papers left the question open. There is
also a second part of the story: some questions about quantum systems
cannot be settled by any procedure at all, drawn or computed; and some
questions about watchers who watch other watchers turn out to have no
consistent answer unless something natural is given up.

And at the very end there is a box, closed, with something asleep inside
it, and a person watching the box, and another person watching him. We
will ask what a closed box can tell anyone, and whether it matters who
was watching.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{every-card-balances}{%
\section{§19.1 Every Card Balances}\label{every-card-balances}}

Chapter 18 ended with this: ``Every theorem in this book has been proved
twice, once on the blackboard and once in the sketchbook, and this
chapter has said plainly, more than once, where the second proof was the
longer one. The last chapter turns to the pictures themselves. Chapter
19, \emph{Logic of Pictures}, asks whether `proved twice' is always
possible, and what the pictures' rules are when they are read as
axioms.''

The chapter's question, in the form we can answer: \textbf{if two
pictures have the same matrix, can the rules of the calculus always
rewrite the one into the other?} We answer it in five steps. This
section names what we have been drawing since Chapter 1, lists the rules
as a deck of cards, and proves that every card is true. §19.2 finds one
card the deck was missing, adds it, and uses it to close a gap that
Chapter 17 left open; that is the chapter's headline. §19.3 states what
is known about the general question, kind of picture by kind of picture,
and works one example with the cards alone. §19.4 asks what a closed
picture of a whole computation tells us, and defines the class of
problems quantum computers are said to solve. §19.5 lists, with sources,
what pictures cannot do. The master diagram in §19.8 is a closed box
with a Cat in it, and §19.9 watches the watchers.

\hypertarget{what-we-have-been-drawing}{%
\subsection{What we have been drawing}\label{what-we-have-been-drawing}}

Since Chapter 1 we have drawn two kinds of thing: \textbf{wires}, which
stand for systems (a qubit, a pair of qubits, a classical bit), and
\textbf{boxes}, which stand for processes that take some systems in and
put some systems out. We had two ways of putting pictures together:
\emph{one after another}, joining the outputs of the first to the inputs
of the second, and \emph{side by side}, stacking two pictures with no
wire between them (Chapter 4). A picture with no wires going in and none
going out is a number (Chapter 2). A picture can be reflected left to
right, which is its \textbf{mirror} (Chapter 3). From Chapter 6 a wire
could bend: the \textbf{cup} is a state on two wires and the
\textbf{cap} an effect on two wires, and an S-shaped bend pulls straight
(row 42, yanking). And from Chapter 8 on, the boxes we cared most about
were spiders, whose matrices depend only on which leg is joined to which
(row 63).

Mathematicians have a name for any collection of systems and processes
that can be put together in these ways. We will call it \textbf{a theory
of processes}. A \emph{category} is the part that composes one after
another; a \emph{monoidal} category adds side by side; \emph{compact
closed} adds the cups and caps with yanking; and \emph{dagger} adds the
mirror. So what we have been drawing is a \textbf{dagger compact closed
category}. The name is long and the idea is the one the reader has been
using since the first chapter: systems, processes, two ways to combine
them, bends that yank, and a mirror.

\textbf{On the blackboard.} The theory we have used throughout is the
one in which a system of \(k\) qubits is the space \(\mathbb C^{2^k}\)
and a process is a matrix. ``One after another'' is the matrix product,
written right to left: the picture with \(g\) first and \(f\) after it
is \(f\circ g\). ``Side by side'' is the Kronecker product \(\otimes\),
top wire first. The mirror of a process \(f\) is its adjoint
\(f^{\dagger}\), the conjugate transpose, and two laws tie it to the two
ways of combining:
\[(f\circ g)^{\dagger}=g^{\dagger}\circ f^{\dagger},\qquad (f\otimes g)^{\dagger}=f^{\dagger}\otimes g^{\dagger}.\]
The cup and the cap are, as always in this book, \textbf{unnormalized}:
\[\text{cup}=\ket{00}+\ket{11},\qquad \text{cap}=\bra{00}+\bra{11},\qquad \ket{\Phi^+}=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\,\text{cup},\]
so that yanking, \((\text{cap}\otimes I)(I\otimes\text{cup})=I\), holds
with no number. Selinger's survey states that ``the category FdHilb of
finite dimensional Hilbert spaces is dagger compact closed'', ``with
\(f^{\dagger}\) the usual linear algebra adjoint'' (his Example 7.11).
FdHilb is the grown-up name for ``finite-dimensional complex vector
spaces and the matrices between them'', which is our blackboard.

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} Nothing new is drawn. The cup is a wire bent
so that both ends point right; the cap, a wire bent so that both ends
point left: \[\text{cup}\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em]
  \path (0,-1) (0,1);
  \sdcup{1}{0.6}{-0.6}
  \draw[wire] (1,0.6) -- (2.4,0.6);
  \draw[wire] (1,-0.6) -- (2.4,-0.6);
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;\ket{00}+\ket{11},\qquad
\text{cap}\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em]
  \path (0,-1) (0,1);
  \draw[wire] (0,0.6) -- (1.4,0.6);
  \draw[wire] (0,-0.6) -- (1.4,-0.6);
  \sdcap{1.4}{0.6}{-0.6}
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;\bra{00}+\bra{11}.\] What is new is the claim that the mirror of a
whole picture is always the adjoint of its matrix. For a single box this
is how Chapter 3 defined the mirror. For a picture built of many pieces
it is a fact to be proved, and here is an example of what it says. A box
\(K\), then a green spider turned \(\alpha\) with one leg in and two
out; in the mirror, the spider comes first, with two legs in and one
out, turned \(-\alpha\), and then the mirror of \(K\):
\[\text{mirror of}\;\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1.5) (0,1.7);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (3.4,0);
  \draw[wire] (3.4,0) -- (4.4,0.9) -- (5.4,0.9);
  \draw[wire] (3.4,0) -- (4.4,-0.9) -- (5.4,-0.9);
  \node[sdbox] at (1.3,0) {$K$};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\alpha$}}] at (3.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;\;=\;\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1.5) (0,1.7);
  \draw[wire] (0,0.9) -- (1,0.9) -- (2,0);
  \draw[wire] (0,-0.9) -- (1,-0.9) -- (2,0);
  \draw[wire] (2,0) -- (5.4,0);
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$-\alpha$}}] at (2,0) {};
  \node[sdbox] at (4.1,0) {$K^{\dagger}$};
\end{tikzpicture}\] The matrix of the left picture is
\(Z_{1\to2}(\alpha)\,K\), where
\(Z_{1\to2}(\alpha)=\ket{00}\bra0+e^{i\alpha}\ket{11}\bra1\) is the
spider of row 53. Its adjoint is
\(K^{\dagger}\bigl(\ket0\bra{00}+e^{-i\alpha}\ket1\bra{11}\bigr)\),
which is the matrix of the right picture, read left to right. The order
has reversed, the legs have swapped sides, and the turn has changed
sign. Does that happen for every picture, however large?

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 19.1 (the mirror is the dagger).} For every picture \(D\)
built from wires, boxes, spiders, yellow boxes, cups, caps and
crossings, let the mirror of \(D\) be its reflection left to right, with
every spider's turn \(\alpha\) replaced by \(-\alpha\) and every box
\(K\) by its mirror \(K^{\dagger}\). Then the matrix of the mirror of
\(D\) is the adjoint of the matrix of \(D\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} By the way \(D\) is built. For the single pieces: the
adjoint of a green spider with \(m\) legs in, \(k\) out and turn
\(\alpha\) is
\(\bigl(\ket{0\cdots0}\bra{0\cdots0}+e^{i\alpha}\ket{1\cdots1}\bra{1\cdots1}\bigr)^{\dagger}\),
which is the green spider with \(k\) legs in, \(m\) out and turn
\(-\alpha\); the same for red, with \(\ket{\pm}\) in place of
\(\ket0,\ket1\) (rows 53, 54). \(H^{\dagger}=H\). The adjoint of the cup
is the cap, and a crossing is its own mirror, as a matrix and as a
picture. A box's mirror is \(K^{\dagger}\) by Chapter 3's definition.
For the two ways of combining: the mirror of ``\(g\), then \(f\)'' is
``the mirror of \(f\), then the mirror of \(g\)'', and
\((f\circ g)^{\dagger}=g^{\dagger}\circ f^{\dagger}\); the mirror of a
side-by-side picture keeps top above bottom, and
\((f\otimes g)^{\dagger}=f^{\dagger}\otimes g^{\dagger}\).
\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch19/EveryCardBalances.py}, which
takes pictures with random turns on every spider and checks that PyZX's
mirror of each has the conjugate transpose as its matrix.

Selinger puts the same thing in one phrase: the graphical language of a
dagger category comes ``with the dagger of a diagram taken to be its
mirror image''.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Dirac's Blackboard.}\nopagebreak

\emph{Three reflections, kept apart.} The book has three ways of turning
a process over, and they are easy to confuse. The \textbf{transpose}
\(A^{T}\) is what you get by bending both of a box's wires round (row
43): entries swapped, no conjugation. The \textbf{conjugate} \(\bar A\)
is what the mirror copy of a doubled wire carries (row 66): every entry
conjugated, nothing swapped. The \textbf{adjoint}
\(A^{\dagger}=\bar A^{T}\) is the mirror, Result 19.1: both at once. On
a spider they look like this. Take
\(Z_{1\to2}(\alpha)=\ket{00}\bra0+e^{i\alpha}\ket{11}\bra1\). Its
transpose is \(\ket0\bra{00}+e^{i\alpha}\ket1\bra{11}\), the same spider
bent round, turn kept. Its conjugate is
\(\ket{00}\bra0+e^{-i\alpha}\ket{11}\bra1\), the same shape, turn
reversed. Its adjoint is \(\ket0\bra{00}+e^{-i\alpha}\ket1\bra{11}\):
bent round \emph{and} reversed. For a spider, bending is free (row 63),
so the mirror of a spider is the conjugate of a spider. For a general
box it is not: \(\bar A\) and \(A^{\dagger}\) are different matrices,
and only the second is the mirror.
\end{quote}

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why name the structure at all, when
every example in the book is matrices? Because a name says which facts
the pictures use. Every move with bends and mirrors that we have made
depends only on the laws above, not on the entries of any matrix.
Anything proved with those moves alone is true in \emph{every} theory
with those laws, not only in ours.

That last sentence is itself a theorem, and a different one from the
chapter's question. Selinger states it for compact closed categories
(his Theorem 4.33): an equation ``follows from the axioms of compact
closed categories if and only if it holds, up to isomorphism of
diagrams, in the graphical language''; for the dagger version he says
the same holds ``up to isomorphism (for dagger compact closed
categories)'', ``proved by the same method''. He adds a caveat (4.34):
``The special case of diagrams over a simple signature was proven by
Kelly and Laplaza'', and ``The general case does not appear in the
literature.'' That result is about \emph{every} theory of processes at
once, with the boxes left as unknowns. The chapter's question is about
\emph{one} theory, the qubits, and about particular boxes, the spiders,
whose matrices we know. The two must be kept apart: the first is called
coherence, and the second, the one this chapter is about, is called
completeness.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Feynman's Notebook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{Who named what the reader was drawing.} The idea that quantum
protocols live in a category with bends and a mirror was put forward by
Samson Abramsky and Bob Coecke in ``A categorical semantics of quantum
protocols'', posted in February 2004. They called the structure a
``strongly compact closed category''. Peter Selinger's survey of
graphical languages (2009) uses the name that has stuck, ``dagger
compact closed category'', and credits the definition to that paper and
to his own ``Dagger compact closed categories and completely positive
maps'' of 2007. The pictures themselves are older than the quantum
reading of them: Selinger credits the coherence of compact closed
pictures, for the simplest case, to G. M. Kelly and M. L. Laplaza's
``Coherence for compact closed categories'' (1980). What was new was the
claim, in the abstract of Abramsky and Coecke's paper, that ``the
essential structures found in key quantum information protocols such as
teleportation'' ``can be captured at this abstract level'': the bends
and a way of adding. Chapter 6 of this book made the same claim with a
yank.
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{the-deck}{%
\subsection{The deck}\label{the-deck}}

The rules of the calculus, as the book has used them, can be written one
to a card, each card an equation between two pictures with its number.
Here is the deck. Every card was dealt in an earlier chapter, and its
row in the Rosetta Table is given.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Wiring.} One after another and side by side (Chapters 1 and
  4); the crossing (Chapter 4); the bend and its yank, cup and cap
  unnormalized (rows 39--42); the mirror (Chapter 3, and Result 19.1).
\item
  \textbf{Only the connectivity counts} (row 63): pieces may be slid,
  stretched and bent as long as the same legs stay joined.
\item
  \textbf{Fusion} (row 57): two spiders of one colour joined by a plain
  wire slide together, and their turns add. Exact.
\item
  \textbf{Identity} (Chapter 8): a spider at rest with two legs is a
  bare wire.
\item
  \textbf{Colour change} (row 58): a spider with a yellow box on every
  leg is the other colour, same turn. \textbf{Two yellow boxes} in a row
  are none (row 56).
\item
  \textbf{Copy} (rows 59, 81): a red point at rest or at a half, fed
  into a green spider at rest with one leg in and \(k\) out, comes out
  as \(k\) red points, times \(2^{(1-k)/2}\); so \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) for
  two out. And the colours swapped.
\item
