  \textbf{A half passes the other colour} (row 60, with Chapter 14's
  number): \(Z(\pi)X(\alpha)=e^{i\alpha}X(-\alpha)Z(\pi)\), and the
  colours swapped.
\item
  \textbf{Bialgebra} (row 61), with the number \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\), and
  \textbf{Hopf} (row 62), with the number \(\tfrac12\).
\item
  \textbf{A loop comes off} (row 90): a plain wire from a spider back to
  itself may be removed, number \(1\).
\item
  \textbf{Letting go and reading} (rows 67, 68), and \textbf{causality}
  (row 72), for doubled pictures (Chapter 9).
\end{itemize}

Here \(Z(\alpha)=\mathrm{diag}(1,e^{i\alpha})\) and
\(X(\alpha)=HZ(\alpha)H\) are the two-legged green and red spiders,
bare, and a \emph{point} is a spider with one leg: a green point at rest
is \(\ket0+\ket1\), a red point at rest is \(\sqrt2\ket0\) and a red
point at a half is \(\sqrt2\ket1\). One more card will join the deck in
§19.2.

Every card carries its number. That matters, and here is why. The Hopf
card, as Chapter 8 first dealt it, said that a green spider and a red
spider joined by two wires are the same as the two spiders apart, ``up
to'' a number. With its number written, it reads
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
  \path (0,-1.2) (0,1.2);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.2,0);
  \draw[wire] (1.2,0) to[out=60,in=120] (3.6,0);
  \draw[wire] (1.2,0) to[out=-60,in=-120] (3.6,0);
  \draw[wire] (3.6,0) -- (4.8,0);
  \node[zsp] at (1.2,0) {};
  \node[xsp] at (3.6,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;\tfrac12\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
  \path (0,-1.2) (0,1.2);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.2,0);
  \node[zsp] at (1.2,0) {};
  \draw[wire] (2.4,0) -- (3.6,0);
  \node[xsp] at (2.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] On the blackboard: the green spider with one leg in
and two out is \(\ket{00}\bra0+\ket{11}\bra1\), and the red one with two
in and one out sends \(\ket{00}\) and \(\ket{11}\) both to
\(\tfrac12(\ket++\ket-)=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\ket0\). So the left side is
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\ket0(\bra0+\bra1)\), and the right side is
\(\tfrac12\cdot\sqrt2\ket0\,(\bra0+\bra1)\), the same. Now suppose the
card had been dealt without its \(\tfrac12\), and feed a green point at
rest into both sides. The left side gives
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\ket0\cdot2=\sqrt2\ket0\). The right side, without the
\(\tfrac12\), gives \(\sqrt2\ket0\cdot2=2\sqrt2\ket0\). A chain of moves
using that card would ``prove'' that \(\sqrt2\ket0=2\sqrt2\ket0\). For
shapes of processes that is harmless; for numbers it is fatal, and a
closed picture \emph{is} a number. So the cards must balance, number and
all.

There is a second worry, which the Anteater of the dialogue puts as a
question about levels. A card is checked by itself. But in a proof it is
used inside a larger picture, with other pieces all round it. Is a card
that is true alone still true in company?

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 19.2 (soundness: every card balances).} Write
\([\![ D]\!]\) for the matrix of a picture \(D\). (a) For every card of
the deck, and every choice of the turns written on it, the two sides
have the same matrix, number included. (b) If
\([\![ D]\!]=[\![ D']\!]\), then for any pictures \(K\), \(L\) and \(M\)
that fit around them, the picture ``\(K\), then \(D\) beside \(L\), then
\(M\)'' and the same picture with \(D'\) in place of \(D\) have the same
matrix. So every chain of moves by the cards proves an equation of
matrices.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} (a) One card at a time. Each card was proved as an
equation of matrices, with its number and for every turn, in the chapter
that dealt it (the rows listed above), and the yank in Chapter 6. (b) By
the way pictures are read, \([\![\cdot]\!]\) turns ``one after another''
into the matrix product and ``side by side'' into the Kronecker product.
So the matrix of the larger picture is
\([\![ M]\!]\,([\![ D]\!]\otimes[\![ L]\!])\,[\![ K]\!]\), and it does
not change when \([\![ D]\!]\) is replaced by the equal matrix
\([\![ D']\!]\). A chain of moves is a list of such replacements, so its
first and last pictures have the same matrix. \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch19/EveryCardBalances.py}, which checks every card with
random turns, and then again with each side wrapped in random non-real
boxes on the left, on the right and alongside.

The sources say this the same way. Backens: ``By considering the rewrite
rules one-by-one, it is not too difficult to show that the ZX-calculus
is sound''. Jeandel, Perdrix and Vilmart: ``It's routine to prove the
soundness of the axioms''. Van de Wetering's survey (§7.3) explains why
checking the cards is enough: the matrix of a picture is defined piece
by piece, and equal pieces make equal wholes.

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} Soundness says: \emph{every card balances}.
A card may be laid anywhere in a picture, and the picture keeps its
value. That is what gives the sketchbook the right to call a chain of
rewrites a proof. The strand's other half is Result 19.1 read as a card
game: hold any card up to the light and read it from behind, and what
you see, left and right exchanged and every turn reversed, is again a
true card, because the mirror of both sides is the adjoint of both
sides.

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why ask that every card hold
\emph{exactly}, number included, when many papers on the calculus drop
the numbers? Because this book reads probabilities off closed pictures,
and a closed picture is nothing but its number. A deck that is sound
only ``up to a number'' can prove any closed picture equal to any other
non-zero one. Where we quote such a paper we will say so.

Soundness has a partner, recalled from Chapter 8. Theorem 8.7 there
stated, with Coecke and Duncan, that the calculus is \textbf{universal}:
every pure state, every unitary and every post-selected measurement on
any number of qubits can be drawn with spiders and yellow boxes. Van de
Wetering (§7.3) calls this ``fullness'' of the map from pictures to
matrices: every matrix of that kind is the matrix of some picture.
Soundness says that the pictures never say anything false. Universality
says that they can name anything. Neither says that the rules can prove
every true equation. That is the third property, and it is the chapter's
question.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-hinge}{%
\section{§19.2 The Hinge}\label{the-hinge}}

Here is a place where the deck ran out. In Chapter 17's proof twice of
the phase-polynomial circuit (§17.6), the sketchbook's step (iv) had to
replace one small picture by another. The first was Chapter 14's
controlled turn at \(\alpha=-\pi\) (row 103): on each of two wires a
green spider turned a quarter back, \(-\tfrac\pi2\), each tied to one
red hub at rest, and from the hub hangs a green point turned a quarter
round, \(\tfrac\pi2\). We call it \(\mathrm{Hub}\). The second is two
green spiders at rest, one on each wire, joined by a wire with a yellow
box on it (Chapter 16's Hadamard edge). We call it \(\mathrm{Tie}\):
\[\mathrm{Hub}\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.67em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1.3) (0,4.5);
  \draw[wire] (0,3.2) -- (4.4,3.2);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (4.4,0);
  \draw[wire] (1.4,3.2) -- (1.4,0);
  \draw[wire] (1.4,1.6) -- (2.8,1.6);
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$-\pi/2$}}] at (1.4,3.2) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$-\pi/2$}}] at (1.4,0) {};
  \node[xsp] at (1.4,1.6) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]right:{$\pi/2$}}] at (2.8,1.6) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\qquad\qquad
\mathrm{Tie}\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=1.67em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1.3) (0,4.5);
  \draw[wire] (0,3.2) -- (2.8,3.2);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2.8,0);
  \draw[wire] (1.4,3.2) -- (1.4,0);
  \node[hbox] at (1.4,1.6) {};
  \node[zsp] at (1.4,3.2) {};
  \node[zsp] at (1.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] Both have the same matrix,
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\mathrm{CZ}\), where
\(\mathrm{CZ}=\mathrm{diag}(1,1,1,-1)\). Chapter 17 knew this, and
wrote: ``This step is a translation, checked by evaluating both sides,
not a rewrite: we derive no chain of moves from the quarter hub to the
Hadamard edge here''. Its verdict added that a skeptic of pictures ``may
say the proof leans on the blackboard at its hinge, and the skeptic is
right.''

So here is a concrete case of the chapter's question: two pictures with
the same matrix, and no chain of cards known to the book that joins
them. Either the deck is missing a card, or we have not been clever
enough. This section shows that one card closes the gap.

\hypertarget{the-euler-card}{%
\subsection{The Euler card}\label{the-euler-card}}

Chapter 3 found, in §3.6 (``Three turns''), that a quarter-turn about
\(z\), a quarter-turn about \(x\) and a quarter-turn about \(z\) make
the Hadamard box: \(SVS=e^{i\pi/4}H\), with \(S=\mathrm{diag}(1,i)\) and
\(V=HSH\). In spiders, \(S\) is a green spider turned \(\tfrac\pi2\) and
\(V\) is a red one.

\textbf{On the blackboard.} \(Z(\tfrac\pi2)=\mathrm{diag}(1,i)\) and
\(X(\tfrac\pi2)=\tfrac12\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1+i&1-i\\1-i&1+i\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\).
Multiplying \(X(\tfrac\pi2)\) on the right by \(Z(\tfrac\pi2)\)
multiplies its second column by \(i\), giving
\(\tfrac12\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1+i&1+i\\1-i&-1+i\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\);
multiplying on the left by \(Z(\tfrac\pi2)\) multiplies the second row
by \(i\):
\[Z(\tfrac\pi2)\,X(\tfrac\pi2)\,Z(\tfrac\pi2)\;=\;\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1+i&1+i\\1+i&-1-i\end{pmatrix}\;=\;\tfrac{1+i}{\sqrt2}\,H\;=\;e^{i\pi/4}\,H .\]

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} A green spider turned a quarter round, a red
spider turned a quarter round and a green spider turned a quarter round,
in a row on one wire, are the yellow box, with the whole turned an
eighth round:
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-0.8) (0,1.2);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (7.2,0);
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi/2$}}] at (1.4,0) {};
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi/2$}}] at (3.6,0) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\pi/2$}}] at (5.8,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;e^{i\pi/4}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-0.8) (0,1.2);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2.8,0);
  \node[hbox] at (1.4,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\]

\begin{quote}
\textbf{The Euler card (row 145).}
\(Z(\tfrac\pi2)\,X(\tfrac\pi2)\,Z(\tfrac\pi2)=e^{i\pi/4}H\), drawn as
above, is \textbf{added to the deck as a rule}. It is true (the
computation above), so the deck stays sound.
\end{quote}

Why \emph{add} it, when it is true and the blackboard proves it in a
line? Because a card in the deck is a move the sketchbook may make
without asking the blackboard, and until now this one was not in the
deck. Could it have been got from the other cards? The book has derived
no such chain, and the sources say that in Backens's calculus it cannot
be: ``The Euler decomposition rule cannot be derived from any
combination of the other ZX-calculus rules'', she writes (§3.3), citing
Duncan and Perdrix's paper of 2009 on ``the necessity of Euler
decomposition''. She also notes that the rule ``is special in that it
does not have a category-theoretical meaning, but follows from the fact
that any unitary single qubit operator can be decomposed as a sequence
of three rotations around two orthogonal axes''. Van de Wetering's
survey goes further and \emph{defines} the yellow box by this equation
(his eq. (44)), and Jeandel, Perdrix and Vilmart's rule set contains it
too. Backens states her calculus with numbers dropped; our card carries
its number, \(e^{i\pi/4}\).

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why this rule and not something
simpler, such as ``two yellow boxes are none''? We have that one already
(row 56), and it only relates yellow boxes to each other. Colour change
(row 58) relates a yellow box to spiders, but only when a spider is
dressed in boxes on every leg. The Euler card is the one rule that says
what a yellow box \emph{is} in terms of spiders alone. Without it the
yellow box is a separate piece that the spiders can push around but
never take apart.

Three smaller cards follow from the new one. They are not new rules:
each is derived from cards already in the deck, and each is marked so.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 19.3 (the mirror Euler; derived).} Three quarter turns
back, green, red, green, are the yellow box with the whole turned an
eighth back:
\[Z(-\tfrac\pi2)\,X(-\tfrac\pi2)\,Z(-\tfrac\pi2)\;=\;e^{-i\pi/4}H .\]
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} On the blackboard, take the adjoint of both sides of the
Euler card: \(Z(\alpha)^{\dagger}=Z(-\alpha)\),
\(X(\alpha)^{\dagger}=X(-\alpha)\), \(H^{\dagger}=H\), and the row of
three reads the same backwards. In the sketchbook, by the cards alone,
as the sidebar below does it. \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch19/TheHinge.py}.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Coecke's Sketchbook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{The mirror Euler, by the cards.} By Result 19.1 the mirror of the
Euler card is a true equation, and one might simply hold the card up to
the light. But a true equation is not yet a move: a card must be
\emph{derived} from cards in the deck. Here is the derivation. Start
with the three quarters back on one wire: green, red, green, all
\(-\tfrac\pi2\). After them, put two yellow boxes in a row, which is no
box at all (row 56). Now read the first of the two boxes by the Euler
card backwards: it becomes \(e^{-i\pi/4}\) times green, red, green, all
\(+\tfrac\pi2\). In the middle, a green quarter back meets a green
quarter round: they slide together to a green spider at rest (row 57),
which is bare wire (Chapter 8's identity card). That brings a red
quarter back next to a red quarter round: the same again. That brings
the first green quarter back next to the last green quarter round: the
same again. What is left is one yellow box, and the number
\(e^{-i\pi/4}\). The pairs vanish from the inside out, like a zip.
\end{quote}

Two lemmas about points come next. The first says what a green turn does
to a red point at rest or at a half. For an example take a red point at
a half, \(\sqrt2\ket1\), followed by a green quarter round,
\(Z(\tfrac\pi2)=\mathrm{diag}(1,i)\). The result is \(i\sqrt2\ket1\):
the same point, with the whole turned a quarter round.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 19.4 (Lemma P: a green turn passes a basis point;
derived).} For \(c\in\{0,1\}\) and every \(\alpha\),
\(Z(\alpha)\,\sqrt2\ket c=e^{ic\alpha}\,\sqrt2\ket c\). In pictures: a
red point turned \(c\pi\), followed by a green spider turned \(\alpha\),
is the same red point with the whole turned by \(c\alpha\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} On the blackboard, \(Z(\alpha)\) is diagonal with entries
\(1\) and \(e^{i\alpha}\). In the sketchbook: slide the green spider
apart into a green spider at rest on the wire with a green \(\alpha\)
point hanging from it (row 57 backwards); the red point copies through
the green spider at rest (row 81), one copy on the wire and one on the
hanging leg, with the number \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\); the copy on the
hanging leg now meets the green \(\alpha\) point, and the two make a
closed picture with no wire left open, which is a number (Chapter 2). It
is
\(\sqrt2\bra c\bigl(\ket0+e^{i\alpha}\ket1\bigr)=\sqrt2\,e^{ic\alpha}\),
as in Chapter 14's ``ledger of the lemma''. The total is
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\cdot\sqrt2\,e^{ic\alpha}=e^{ic\alpha}\):
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-2.2) (0,1.2);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (3.6,0);
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$c\pi$}}] at (0,0) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$\alpha$}}] at (2.2,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;\overset{\text{row 57}}{=}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-2.2) (0,1.2);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (3.6,0);
  \draw[wire] (2.2,0) -- (2.2,-1.5);
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$c\pi$}}] at (0,0) {};
  \node[zsp] at (2.2,0) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]right:{$\alpha$}}] at (2.2,-1.5) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;\overset{\text{row 81}}{=}\;\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-2.2) (0,1.2);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.4,0);
  \draw[wire] (0,-1.5) -- (1.8,-1.5);
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$c\pi$}}] at (0,0) {};
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]left:{$c\pi$}}] at (0,-1.5) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]right:{$\alpha$}}] at (1.8,-1.5) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;e^{ic\alpha}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-2.2) (0,1.2);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.4,0);
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$c\pi$}}] at (0,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] \(\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch19/TheHinge.py},
which checks it for random \(\alpha\) and both values of \(c\).

The second lemma is about the point hanging from \(\mathrm{Hub}\): a
green point turned a quarter round, \(\ket0+i\ket1\). It has the wrong
colour for anything we want to do with a red hub. Can it be traded for a
red point?

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 19.5 (Lemma A: a quarter point changes colour; derived).}
A red point turned a quarter back is \(e^{-i\pi/4}\) times a green point
turned a quarter round:
\(X(-\tfrac\pi2)\,\sqrt2\ket0=e^{-i\pi/4}\bigl(\ket0+i\ket1\bigr)\).
Equivalently, a green \(\tfrac\pi2\) point is \(e^{i\pi/4}\) times a red
\(-\tfrac\pi2\) point.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} On the blackboard,
\(X(-\tfrac\pi2)=\tfrac12\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1-i&1+i\\1+i&1-i\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\),
so
\(X(-\tfrac\pi2)\sqrt2\ket0=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl((1-i)\ket0+(1+i)\ket1\bigr)\),
and \(\tfrac{1-i}{\sqrt2}=e^{-i\pi/4}\),
\(\tfrac{1+i}{\sqrt2}=e^{-i\pi/4}\,i\). In the sketchbook, five moves.
Slide the red point apart into a red point at rest and a red spider
turned \(-\tfrac\pi2\) on its wire (row 57 backwards). Put a green
quarter round and a green quarter back side by side at each end of that
red spider (row 57 backwards and the identity card); the red spider now
sits between two green quarters back, and by the mirror Euler (Result
19.3) the three are \(e^{-i\pi/4}\) times a yellow box. So the wire
reads: red point at rest, green \(\tfrac\pi2\), yellow box, green
\(\tfrac\pi2\), with the number \(e^{-i\pi/4}\). The first green quarter
passes the red point at rest with the number \(1\) (Result 19.4,
\(c=0\)). The yellow box turns the red point at rest into a green point
at rest (row 58). The last green quarter fuses into it (row 57):
\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-0.8) (0,1.2);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.4,0);
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$-\pi/2$}}] at (0,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;\overset{\text{row 57}}{=}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-0.8) (0,1.2);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (3.4,0);
  \node[xsp] at (0,0) {};
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$-\pi/2$}}] at (2.0,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;\overset{\text{19.3}}{=}\;e^{-i\pi/4}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  hbox/.style={draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=yellow!85,minimum size=0.8em,inner sep=1pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-0.8) (0,1.2);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (7.4,0);
  \node[xsp] at (0,0) {};

\textbf{In the sketchbook,} then, the deck now holds one new card,
given, and three derived from it, and the two lemmas are exactly what
\(\mathrm{Hub}\) needs: Lemma A turns its hanging point red, so that it
can fuse into the red hub, and then the hub's tie reads as three quarter
turns back, which the mirror Euler turns into a yellow box.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 19.6 (the hinge; the headline).}
\(\mathrm{Hub}=\mathrm{Tie}\), exactly, with the number \(1\). Both are
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\,\mathrm{CZ}\).
\end{quote}

It is proved twice in §19.7: on the blackboard in two lines, and in the
sketchbook in five moves, each by a card of the deck. With it, Chapter
17's step (iv) is no longer a translation: it is a rewrite.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Dirac's Blackboard.}\nopagebreak

\emph{The hinge in two lines.} Let \(x=(x_1,x_2)\) be a basis word on
the two wires. Each foot of \(\mathrm{Hub}\) is a green spider, so it
passes \(\ket{x_k}\) along its wire and copies the bit \(x_k\) onto its
tie, with the turn \(e^{-i\frac\pi2x_k}\). The red hub at rest, fed
\(x_1\) and \(x_2\) on two legs, puts out
\(2^{-1/2}\ket{x_1\oplus x_2}\) on its third, and the hanging point
closes that with \(e^{i\frac\pi2(x_1\oplus x_2)}\); this is row 129's
hub, \(2^{-1/2}\Gamma(\tfrac\pi2)\). So
\[\mathrm{Hub}\ket x=2^{-1/2}\,e^{\,i\frac\pi2\,(x_1\oplus x_2-x_1-x_2)}\ket x=2^{-1/2}(-1)^{x_1x_2}\ket x ,\]
because \(x_1+x_2-(x_1\oplus x_2)=2x_1x_2\). And
\(\mathrm{Tie}\ket x=\bra{x_2}H\ket{x_1}\ket x=2^{-1/2}(-1)^{x_1x_2}\ket x\).
Both are \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\mathrm{CZ}\). The whole proof is the identity
for the carry of a one-bit sum: add two bits, subtract their parity, and
you are left with twice their product.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{same-number-same-picture}{%
\section{§19.3 Same Number, Same
Picture}\label{same-number-same-picture}}

One card closed one gap. Is there always one more card? Before the
general answer, a dare: name two pictures with the same matrix, chosen
with nothing but the blackboard in mind, and see whether the deck can
join them.

\hypertarget{a-dare}{%
\subsection{A dare}\label{a-dare}}

Take a yellow box followed by a green quarter round, three times over,
on one wire. On the blackboard the picture is \(SHSHSH=(SH)^3\), with
\(S=Z(\tfrac\pi2)=\mathrm{diag}(1,i)\) (the picture reads left to right,
the product right to left). Now
\[SH=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\i&-i\end{pmatrix},\qquad (SH)^2=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1+i&1-i\\1+i&-1+i\end{pmatrix},\]
\[(SH)^3=\tfrac{2+2i}{2\sqrt2}\,I=e^{i\pi/4}\,I .\] The six pieces do
nothing at all, except turn the whole by an eighth. Nothing in the
picture suggests it. Can the cards find it?

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 19.7 (a tube and a quarter, three times over).}
\((SH)^3=e^{i\pi/4}I\), and the deck derives it: the picture of a yellow
box and a green quarter round, three times over, rewrites by the cards
to a bare wire with the number \(e^{i\pi/4}\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} The blackboard did it above. In the sketchbook, five
moves, each by one card, with the pictures read left to right.
\textbf{(i)} The first yellow box, green quarter and yellow box are a
green spider with a box on each leg: colour change makes it a red
quarter round (row 58). \textbf{(ii)} The next yellow box is replaced by
the Euler card read backwards, \(e^{-i\pi/4}\) times green, red, green
quarters round (row 145). \textbf{(iii)} Neighbours of one colour fuse
(row 57): the wire now reads red \(\tfrac\pi2\), green \(\pi\), red
\(\tfrac\pi2\), green \(\pi\). \textbf{(iv)} The first green half passes
the red quarter after it: the quarter is reversed and the whole turns a
quarter round, \(e^{i\pi/2}\) (row 60, with Chapter 14's number; on the
blackboard, \(X(\tfrac\pi2)Z(\pi)=e^{i\pi/2}Z(\pi)X(-\tfrac\pi2)\)).
\textbf{(v)} The two red quarters, round and back, fuse to rest, and so
do the two green halves, which make a whole turn; spiders at rest with
two legs are bare wire (row 57 and the identity card). The numbers:
\(e^{-i\pi/4}\,e^{i\pi/2}=e^{i\pi/4}\).

Step (ii) is the Euler card again. The chain needed it, and at no point
did the sketchbook look at a matrix. That is one dare won. The general
question is whether every dare can be won.

\hypertarget{completeness}{%
\subsection{Completeness}\label{completeness}}

\textbf{On the blackboard.} Fix a kind of picture: say, those whose
spiders are turned only by multiples of \(\tfrac\pi2\), or of
\(\tfrac\pi4\), or by anything at all. A deck of cards is
\textbf{complete} for that kind if, for every two pictures \(D_1\) and
\(D_2\) of that kind,
\[[\![ D_1]\!]=[\![ D_2]\!]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad D_1\text{ rewrites to }D_2\text{ by the cards of the deck.}\]
Soundness (Result 19.2) is the arrow the other way. Van de Wetering
(§7.3) puts it in the language of §19.1: soundness says the map
\([\![\cdot]\!]\) from pictures to matrices is well defined;
universality says it is \emph{full}, every matrix of the kind is hit;
completeness says it is \emph{faithful}, no two pictures that the cards
cannot join are sent to the same matrix. He is plain about his own rule
set: ``The ruleset we presented in Figure 1 is not complete''.

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} Completeness says: \textbf{same number, same
picture}, \emph{with the right cards}. If the blackboard says two
pictures agree, the sketchbook can get from one to the other without
borrowing anything from the blackboard. It says a chain \emph{exists};
it does not say how long the chain is, or how to find it.

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why fix a \emph{kind} of picture
first, instead of asking for one deck that works for everything? Because
the answer depends on the kind. Van de Wetering's Figure 1, which
suffices for turns by quarters, is not enough for turns by eighths
(§19.5 shows an equation that his survey says it cannot prove), and each
kind has needed its own deck, found in its own paper. A definition that
did not name the kind could not say which of those papers answered it.

Here is what is known, by kind, quoted from the papers that proved it.
None of it is proved in this book.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 19.8 (completeness, by kind; stated, not proved).} (a)
\emph{Turns by multiples of \(\tfrac\pi2\) (the Clifford pictures).}
Miriam Backens (Oxford, 2013), Theorem 21: ``The ZX-calculus is complete
for stabilizer quantum mechanics.'' Her rule set includes the Euler
rule, and it ignores non-zero numbers: ``Since global phases have no
physical effect and the normalization of pure states is fixed, we will
ignore them'' (her §3.3). (b) \emph{Turns by multiples of \(\tfrac\pi4\)
(Clifford+T).} Emmanuel Jeandel, Simon Perdrix and Renaud Vilmart
(posted May 2017), Theorem 1: ``The \(\frac\pi4\)-fragment of the
ZX-Calculus as presented in Figure 1 is complete: for any two diagrams
\(D_1\), \(D_2\) in the \(\frac\pi4\)-fragment of the ZX-Calculus,
\([\![ D_1]\!]=[\![ D_2]\!]\) iff \(ZX_{\pi/4}\vdash D_1=D_2\).'' Their
Figure 1 is a ``Set of rules for the ZX-Calculus with scalars''. (c)
\emph{Any turns.} Kang Feng Ng and Quanlong Wang (Oxford, 2017), Theorem
5.2: ``The ZX-calculus is complete for universal pure qubit quantum
mechanics: If \([\![ D_1]\!]=[\![ D_2]\!]\), then
\(ZX\vdash D_1=D_2\)''. Their language is extended ``with two new
symbols (although in principle they could be eliminated \ldots)''. (d)
\emph{With letting go (Chapter 9's doubled pictures).} Titouan Carette,
Emmanuel Jeandel, Simon Perdrix and Renaud Vilmart (Nancy, 2019),
Corollary 1 (of Theorem 1): ``Given a \(\dagger\)-CC \(C\) with enough
isometries, if \(G\) is a \(\dagger\)-CC universal complete graphical
language for \(C\) then \(G^{\top}\) is a universal complete language
for CPM(\(C\)).'' Their superscript is the ground symbol, which we write
\(\top\) as for the book's discard (row 67). They show that the turns by
multiples of \(\tfrac\pi2\), with letting go, meet the condition (their
§4.2), and that the turns by multiples of \(\tfrac\pi4\) do not; for
these, ``we leave open the complete axiomatisation of quantum operations
for this fragment'' (their §4.3).
\end{quote}

Read the scope of each with care. In (b), Jeandel, Perdrix and Vilmart
reached completeness ``by adding two new axioms to the language'', but
\emph{two} is counted against their own Figure 1, not against this
book's deck, and we do not count cards against theirs. Whether the
book's deck, with the Euler card, is the same as any of these rule sets
we have not checked, and do not claim. In (d), ``\(\dagger\)-CC'' is
their abbreviation for a dagger compact closed category, the structure
of §19.1, and CPM(\(C\)) is the doubled construction of Chapter 9. The
words ``enough isometries'' name a technical condition (their Definition
10) that the kind of picture must meet for the discard to be added this
simply.

This also corrects a sentence of Chapter 8. Theorem 8.7 there said that
within the Clifford pictures ``any two diagrams denoting the same map
can be turned into one another by the rules alone, with no return to
matrices (Backens).'' That is right, with two qualifications we can now
state: Backens's rules include the Euler rule, which the book's deck
lacked until §19.2; and her rules, like van de Wetering's Figure 1
(``these rules are only correct up to non-zero scalar''), ignore
non-zero numbers, which the book's cards do not.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Feynman's Notebook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{The completeness race.} Van de Wetering's survey (2020, §9.1)
tells the story, dating each paper by its first posting on the arXiv.
Coecke and Duncan introduced the calculus in a 2007 preprint, and more
formally in 2008; the Hadamard box was then a piece of its own. Duncan
and Perdrix saw in 2009 that its decomposition into turns was needed for
completeness. Backens proved the Clifford case in 2013. The next step
came through a different calculus, the ZW-calculus, for which
Hadzihasanovic found a complete rule set ``in the beginning of 2015''.
In May 2017 Jeandel, Perdrix and Vilmart used it to settle Clifford+T.
In June 2017 Ng and Wang, at Oxford, settled the case of any turns,
through a modified ZW-calculus from Hadzihasanovic's thesis. In January
2018 each side answered the other: Jeandel, Perdrix and Vilmart with any
turns, Ng and Wang with Clifford+T. Van de Wetering calls it an
``entangled'' history, and the word is fair: within a year, two groups
each did both, each in the other's wake.
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{an-instance-with-letting-go}{%
\subsection{An instance with letting
go}\label{an-instance-with-letting-go}}

Part (d) is about doubled pictures, with a wire and its mirror copy and
a cap that lets them go (Chapter 9). Here is the simplest dare of that
kind. On a wire, a green spider turned \(a\), a red one turned \(b\) and
a green one turned \(c\); on its mirror copy, which carries the
conjugate process, the same three turned \(-a\), \(-b\), \(-c\); then
let the wire go, which is a cap joining the wire to its copy. The
blackboard says that a unitary, then letting go, is just letting go
(causality, row 72):
\(\operatorname{tr}(U\rho U^{\dagger})=\operatorname{tr}\rho\). Does the
sketchbook agree without being told?

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 19.9 (letting go after any turn).} For all turns \(a\),
\(b\), \(c\), exactly: a green, a red and a green spider turned \(a\),
\(b\), \(c\) on a wire, the same turned \(-a\), \(-b\), \(-c\) on its
mirror copy, and then the cap, equal the bare cap.
\end{quote}

\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-2.4) (0,2.4);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.2) -- (7.0,1.2);
  \draw[wire] (0,-1.2) -- (7.0,-1.2);
  \sdcap{7.0}{1.2}{-1.2}
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$a$}}] at (1.4,1.2) {};
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]above:{$b$}}] at (3.6,1.2) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]above:{$c$}}] at (5.8,1.2) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$-a$}}] at (1.4,-1.2) {};
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]below:{$-b$}}] at (3.6,-1.2) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]below:{$-c$}}] at (5.8,-1.2) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em]
  \path (0,-2.4) (0,2.4);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.2) -- (1.2,1.2);
  \draw[wire] (0,-1.2) -- (1.2,-1.2);
  \sdcap{1.2}{1.2}{-1.2}
\end{tikzpicture}\]

\emph{Proof.} The cap is unnormalized, \(\bra{00}+\bra{11}\), and as a
picture it is a green spider at rest with two legs, bent (rows 40, 63).
So the green \(c\) next to it slides into it (row 57), and so does the
green \(-c\) from the other side: the turns add to rest. Now the cap is
bare again, and the red \(b\) and red \(-b\) are joined through it by a
plain wire, so they fuse to a red spider at rest, which is bare wire
(row 57, identity). The same happens to the green \(a\) and \(-a\). What
is left is the bare cap. Every move is exact, with no number. On the
blackboard: \(\bigl(\text{cap}\bigr)(U\otimes\bar U)=\text{cap}\) for
every unitary \(U\), since
\(\sum_i\bra{ii}(U\otimes\bar U)=\sum_{i,j,k}U_{ij}\bar U_{ik}\bra{jk}=\sum_{j,k}(U^{\dagger}U)_{kj}\bra{jk}\),
and \(U^{\dagger}U=I\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch19/SameNumberSamePicture.py}, which checks it for random
turns.

Here the pictures win outright: three slides through the cap against a
sum over three indices. And the picture shows \emph{why} the turns
cancel. Each spider meets its own conjugate through the cap and the two
turns add to nothing, from the inside out, as in the mirror Euler of
§19.2.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{one-answer-out}{%
\section{§19.4 One Answer Out}\label{one-answer-out}}

So far the pictures have had open wires: processes with inputs and
outputs. A whole computation is different. It starts from states nobody
chose freshly each time, runs a process, reads \emph{one} answer, and
lets everything else go. From the outside it is a closed box with one
wire coming out. What can such a box tell anyone?

\hypertarget{a-run-and-a-class-of-problems}{%
\subsection{A run, and a class of
problems}\label{a-run-and-a-class-of-problems}}

\textbf{On the blackboard.} A \textbf{run} of a quantum computer on
\(n\) wires starts each wire at \(\ket0\), applies a unitary \(U\),
reads the first wire, and ignores the rest. The answer is \(1\) with
probability
\[p_1\;=\;\bra{0\cdots0}U^{\dagger}\bigl(\ket1\bra1\otimes I\otimes\cdots\otimes I\bigr)U\ket{0\cdots0},\]
and \(0\) with probability \(p_0=1-p_1\). A single run gives one bit,
and it may be the wrong bit. So the useful notion is a machine that is
right \emph{often enough}.

A yes-or-no problem is in the class called \textbf{BQP} if there is a
family of circuits, one for each size of input, with these three
properties. The circuit for inputs of size \(n\) has a number of gates
bounded by a polynomial in \(n\). The circuits can be written down, one
for each \(n\), by an ordinary computer. And on every input, one run of
its circuit answers correctly with probability at least \(\tfrac23\): on
an input whose answer is ``yes'' it reads \(1\) with probability at
least \(\tfrac23\), and on one whose answer is ``no'' it reads \(1\)
with probability at most \(\tfrac13\). For the class and its place among
the others, see Nielsen and Chuang's textbook. We use the class only to
fix words; this book proves nothing about how BQP compares with any
other class.

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} A run is a closed box with one wire out.
Draw it doubled, as in Chapter 9: each quantum wire with its mirror copy
below it, the copy carrying the conjugate process \(\bar U\). Every wire
and copy starts at a red point at rest, \(\sqrt2\ket0\), so four such
points need the number \(\tfrac14\) in front. The wire that is not read
is let go: it is capped to its own copy (row 67). The wire that is read
goes, with its copy, into the read-spider (row 68), a green spider at
rest that takes a wire and its copy and gives out one classical wire,
drawn doubled-stroke:

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, x=1.1em, y=1.1em,
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
  \node[sdlabel] at (-1.6,0) {$\tfrac14$};
  \draw[wire] (0,3) -- (6.5,3) -- (8.5,0);
  \draw[wire] (0,-3) -- (6.5,-3) -- (8.5,0);
  \draw[wire] (0,1.5) -- (5,1.5);
  \draw[wire] (0,-1.5) -- (5,-1.5);
  \sdcap{5}{1.5}{-1.5}
  \node[sdbox, minimum height=3.6em, minimum width=2.2em] at (2.6,2.25) {$U$};
  \node[sdbox, minimum height=3.6em, minimum width=2.2em] at (2.6,-2.25) {$\bar U$};
  \draw[cwire] (8.5,0) -- (10.8,0);
  \node[xsp] at (0,3) {}; \node[xsp] at (0,1.5) {};
  \node[xsp] at (0,-1.5) {}; \node[xsp] at (0,-3) {};

The copies are drawn in reflected order, the first wire's copy lowest,
so that every cap is nested and no two lines cross; the box \(\bar U\)
takes its legs in that reflected order. The value of the whole picture
is a classical vector, \((p_0,p_1)\): the odds of the answer. That is
all a closed box gives out: one answer, with odds.

\textbf{\emph{Why this definition.}} Why a probability of \(\tfrac23\),
and not certainty? Because a quantum computer's answer comes with odds,
and demanding certainty would throw away most of what it can do. Why
\(\tfrac23\) exactly? It is a convention: any fixed chance above one
half can be pushed up by running the machine several times and taking a
vote, and here is the smallest case of that, done exactly.

\hypertarget{three-runs-and-a-vote}{%
\subsection{Three runs and a vote}\label{three-runs-and-a-vote}}

Suppose one run is right two times in three. Run it three times,
independently, and take the majority. The majority is right when all
three runs are right, with probability \((\tfrac23)^3=\tfrac8{27}\), or
when exactly two are, in three ways, each with probability
\((\tfrac23)^2\cdot\tfrac13=\tfrac4{27}\). In all,
\(\tfrac8{27}+\tfrac{12}{27}=\tfrac{20}{27}\), which is more than
\(\tfrac23=\tfrac{18}{27}\). Is that a lucky number, or does a vote
always help?

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 19.10 (a majority of three).} If each of three
independent runs is right with probability \(p\), the majority is right
with probability \[f(p)\;=\;3p^2-2p^3 .\] If \(p\ge\tfrac23\), then
\(f(p)\ge\tfrac{20}{27}\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} The majority is right when all three runs are, probability
\(p^3\), or exactly two are, three ways of probability \(p^2(1-p)\)
each: \(p^3+3p^2(1-p)=3p^2-2p^3\). Then \(f'(p)=6p-6p^2=6p(1-p)\ge0\) on
\([0,1]\), so \(f\) does not decrease there, and \(p\ge\tfrac23\) gives
\(f(p)\ge f(\tfrac23)=\tfrac{20}{27}\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch19/OneAnswerOut.py}, which checks
\(f(\tfrac23)=\tfrac{20}{27}\) exactly and \(f(p)\ge\tfrac{20}{27}\) on
a grid of \(p\) from \(\tfrac23\) to \(1\).

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Dirac's Blackboard.}\nopagebreak

\emph{The same polynomial, read the other way.} Chapter 18 counted the
failure of a vote of three, each copy flipped with probability \(p\):
\(F(p)=3p^2-2p^3\). Here \(p\) is the chance a run is \emph{right}, and
the majority's success is the same polynomial. That is no accident. The
majority of three is right exactly when the majority of their failures
is not, so \(f(p)=1-F(1-p)\), and
\[1-F(1-p)=1-3(1-2p+p^2)+2(1-3p+3p^2-p^3)=3p^2-2p^3 .\] So
\(F(p)+F(1-p)=1\): the curve is symmetric about the point
\((\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\). And \(f(p)-p=p(1-p)(2p-1)\), which is positive
for \(\tfrac12<p<1\). Votes can be stacked. Three groups of three runs,
a majority taken in each group and then a majority of the three results,
are right with probability
\[f(\tfrac{20}{27})=3\cdot\tfrac{400}{729}-2\cdot\tfrac{8000}{19683}=\tfrac{32400-16000}{19683}=\tfrac{16400}{19683},\]
about \(0.833\). Each level raises a chance above one half, and the only
resting points of \(f\) in \([0,1]\) are \(0\), \(\tfrac12\) and \(1\),
so stacked votes climb towards \(1\), as Chapter 18's toy showed.
\end{quote}

\textbf{In the sketchbook,} three runs are three closed boxes side by
side, three classical wires out, and the vote is a classical process on
those three wires. The pictures could evaluate it, but the count of
ways, and the inequality, are the blackboard's.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{what-pictures-cannot-do}{%
\section{§19.5 What Pictures Cannot Do}\label{what-pictures-cannot-do}}

A book that has drawn pictures for many chapters owes its reader a list
of their limits. Each item below is either sourced or said in the form
``this book has derived no such chain''. Nothing on the list is proved
here, except one number.

\textbf{Not every deck is complete.} Van de Wetering: ``The ruleset we
presented in Figure 1 is not complete'' (§7.3). His example opens his
§9: an equation that, he writes, ``is not provable using the rules of
Figure 1 for any \(\alpha\) that is not a multiple of \(\frac\pi2\)'',
citing Perdrix and Wang's paper of 2016 on why ``supplementarity is
necessary''. He adds: ``this equation only holds up to a global
scalar''. Here it is with its number worked out. Two green points,
turned \(\alpha\) and \(\alpha+\pi\), feed a red spider with two legs in
and one out:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 19.11 (an eighth-turn instance).} For every \(\alpha\),
exactly:
\end{quote}

\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1.6) (0,1.6);
  \draw[wire] (0,1) -- (2,0);
  \draw[wire] (0,-1) -- (2,0);
  \draw[wire] (2,0) -- (3.4,0);
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]left:{$\alpha$}}] at (0,1) {};
  \node[zsp,label={[ph]left:{$\alpha+\pi$}}] at (0,-1) {};
  \node[xsp] at (2,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;=\;\frac{1-e^{2i\alpha}}{2}\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
  \path (0,-1.6) (0,1.6);
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (1.4,0);
  \node[xsp] at (0,0) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\]

\emph{Proof.} On the blackboard. The points are
\(\ket0+e^{i\alpha}\ket1\) and \(\ket0-e^{i\alpha}\ket1\). The red
spider sends \(\ket{ab}\) to
\(\ket+\braket{+|a}\braket{+|b}+\ket-\braket{-|a}\braket{-|b}\). Here
\(\braket{+|a}\braket{+|b}=\tfrac12(1+e^{i\alpha})(1-e^{i\alpha})=\tfrac12(1-e^{2i\alpha})\),
and \(\braket{-|a}\braket{-|b}=\tfrac12(1-e^{i\alpha})(1+e^{i\alpha})\)
is the same. So the output is \(\tfrac12(1-e^{2i\alpha})(\ket++\ket-)\),
and \(\ket++\ket-=\sqrt2\ket0\) is the red point at rest.
\(\;\blacksquare\) See \texttt{Code/Ch19/SameNumberSamePicture.py},
which checks the instance at \(\alpha=\tfrac\pi4\), where the number is
\(\tfrac{1-i}2\).

At \(\alpha=\tfrac\pi4\), the eighth turn, the number is
\(\tfrac{1-i}2\), which is not zero, so the equation says something. The
blackboard proves it for every \(\alpha\) in two lines. Whether this
book's deck, with the Euler card, can prove it at \(\alpha=\tfrac\pi4\)
we do not know: the book has derived no such chain, and we have not
compared the deck with van de Wetering's Figure 1, so his statement
about Figure 1 is quoted as his and not claimed for the deck.

\textbf{One rule was not enough for every turn.} Ng and Wang, citing
Schröder de Witt and Zamdzhiev: ``the original version of the
ZX-calculus plus the Euler decomposition of Hadamard gate is incomplete
for the overall pure qubit quantum mechanics''. The Euler card of §19.2
was what the Clifford pictures lacked; it is far from all that every
turn needs.

\textbf{A finite deck for all turns may be out of reach, or may not.}
Van de Wetering's §9.5 presents a complete rule set for any turns that
needs one extra rule, and says that its ``complicated side condition''
betrays the benefits of graphical reasoning ``a bit''; he adds, citing
others, that ``it however seems unlikely that all the relations between
phases that are not rational multiples of \(\pi\) can be captured by a
finite set of rules''. That is a judgement, not a theorem, and we quote
it as one.

\textbf{Some processes have no known single picture.} Van de Wetering
(§10.1, 2020): ``there is currently no known representation of partial
decoherence in the ZX-calculus''. Chapter 18's noise (row 136) was drawn
as a weighted \emph{sum} of two pictures, which is consistent with this:
a sum is not one picture.

\textbf{For one kind, completeness with letting go was left open.}
Carette, Jeandel, Perdrix and Vilmart (2019, §4.3), for turns by
multiples of \(\tfrac\pi4\) with discard: ``we leave open the complete
axiomatisation of quantum operations for this fragment.'' We report what
the paper says; we do not claim to know whether the question is still
open.

\textbf{A rewrite proves an equality of processes, and nothing else.}
This is the book's own rule, and it is the most important item on the
list. A chain of cards proves that two pictures have the same matrix. It
does not prove that a circuit is short, that an algorithm is fast, that
a code is good, or that a problem is in any class. Completeness says
that a chain \emph{exists}; it says nothing about how long the chain is
or how to find it, and the book makes no claim about either. And no
rewrite decides a question about \emph{all} pictures of a kind at once:
§19.9 meets a theorem that says, for one such question, that no
procedure of any kind can.

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} Row 152 of the Rosetta Table is the only row
of the book whose right-hand column is empty on purpose. Its entry is:
no picture. The equation of Result 19.11 has a picture on each side, and
so does every equation a deck can prove; the claims on this list are
claims \emph{about} decks, and a claim about all pictures of a kind is
not itself a picture.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-theorem-twice-19}{%
\section{§19.7 The Theorem, Twice}\label{the-theorem-twice-19}}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 19.6 (the hinge), restated.} Let \(\mathrm{Hub}\) be two
wires, each carrying a green spider turned \(-\tfrac\pi2\), the two tied
to one red spider at rest, from which hangs a green point turned
\(\tfrac\pi2\). Let \(\mathrm{Tie}\) be two wires, each carrying a green
spider at rest, the two joined by a wire with a yellow box on it. Then,
exactly, with the number \(1\),
\[\mathrm{Hub}\;=\;\mathrm{Tie}\;=\;\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\,\mathrm{CZ}.\]
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{diracs-blackboard-19}{%
\subsection{Dirac's Blackboard}\label{diracs-blackboard-19}}

Write a basis word on the two wires as \(\ket{x_1x_2}\), top wire first.

\textbf{Step 1: the feet.} Each foot is a green spider with one leg in
and two out (one along the wire, one to the hub), turned
\(-\tfrac\pi2\): \(\ket{00}\bra0+e^{-i\pi/2}\ket{11}\bra1\). So on
\(\ket{x_1x_2}\) the two feet give
\[e^{-i\frac\pi2x_1}\,e^{-i\frac\pi2x_2}\;\ket{x_1x_2}\otimes\ket{x_1x_2}_{\text{ties}} .\]

\textbf{Step 2: the hub.} The red spider at rest, with the two ties as
inputs and one output, is \(\ket+\bra{++}+\ket-\bra{--}\). On
\(\ket{y_1y_2}\) it gives
\(\tfrac12\bigl(\ket++(-1)^{y_1+y_2}\ket-\bigr)=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\ket{y_1\oplus y_2}\).
The hanging green point, as an effect, is \(\bra0+e^{i\pi/2}\bra1\), so
it closes the output with \(e^{i\frac\pi2(y_1\oplus y_2)}\). Hub and
point together send the ties \(\ket{x_1x_2}\) to the number
\(2^{-1/2}\,e^{i\frac\pi2(x_1\oplus x_2)}\).

\textbf{Step 3: the product.}
\[\mathrm{Hub}\ket{x_1x_2}\;=\;2^{-1/2}\,e^{\,i\frac\pi2\left(x_1\oplus x_2-x_1-x_2\right)}\ket{x_1x_2}.\]
Since \(x_1+x_2-(x_1\oplus x_2)=2x_1x_2\) for bits, the exponent is
\(-i\pi x_1x_2\), and \(e^{-i\pi x_1x_2}=(-1)^{x_1x_2}\). Word by word:
\(\ket{00}\), \(\ket{01}\), \(\ket{10}\) get \(2^{-1/2}\), and
\(\ket{11}\) gets \(2^{-1/2}e^{-i\pi}e^{0}=-2^{-1/2}\). So
\(\mathrm{Hub}=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\,\mathrm{diag}(1,1,1,-1)=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\mathrm{CZ}\).

\textbf{Step 4: the tie.} Each green spider at rest copies its wire's
bit onto the joining wire, \(\ket{x_k}\mapsto\ket{x_k}\ket{x_k}\). The
joining wire carries \(x_1\) from the top, through \(H\), into the
bottom spider's leg, where it must meet \(x_2\): the amplitude is
\(\bra{x_2}H\ket{x_1}=2^{-1/2}(-1)^{x_1x_2}\). So
\(\mathrm{Tie}=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\mathrm{CZ}\) as well. \(\;\blacksquare\)

\hypertarget{coeckes-sketchbook-13}{%
\subsection{Coecke's Sketchbook}\label{coeckes-sketchbook-13}}

Start from \(\mathrm{Hub}\). Every step names its card, and every number
is written.

\textbf{Step (i): the hanging point changes colour} (Result 19.5, Lemma
A). The green point turned a quarter round is \(e^{i\pi/4}\) times a red
point turned a quarter back.

\textbf{Step (ii): the point joins the hub} (row 57). The red point and
the red hub at rest are joined by a plain wire, so they fuse. The hub
now has two legs, the two ties, and is turned \(-\tfrac\pi2\).

\textbf{Step (iii): each foot slides apart along its own tie} (row 57
backwards). The upper foot becomes a green spider at rest on the wire
and a green spider turned \(-\tfrac\pi2\) on the tie; the same for the
lower foot. Number \(1\). The tie now runs, from top to bottom: a green
quarter back, a red quarter back, a green quarter back. By row 63 it may
be read as one wire, straight down.

\textbf{Step (iv): three quarters back are a yellow box} (Result 19.3,
the mirror Euler). They are replaced by a yellow box and the number
\(e^{-i\pi/4}\).

\textbf{Step (v): the numbers.} \(e^{i\pi/4}\cdot e^{-i\pi/4}=1\). What
is left is two green spiders at rest joined by a wire with a yellow box
on it: \(\mathrm{Tie}\).

\hypertarget{the-verdict-19}{%
\subsection{The verdict}\label{the-verdict-19}}

The blackboard wins, and the chapter says so. Its proof is two lines and
one identity about bits, \(x_1+x_2-(x_1\oplus x_2)=2x_1x_2\). The
sketchbook needs five moves, and before it could make them it needed a
new card, the Euler card, and three cards derived from it. By any count
of ink the algebra is shorter.

But the point of the sketchbook here is not that it is shorter. It is
that it \emph{exists}. Chapter 17 reached this step and could only check
it; now the step is a chain of cards, and a skeptic of pictures has one
fewer place to point. What the picture shows, and the algebra hides, is
where the quarter turns go. The hub's hanging quarter changes colour and
slides into the tie, the feet give up their quarters to the tie, and the
three quarters on the tie are one yellow box: a controlled half-turn
\emph{is} a Hadamard edge because an Euler decomposition was hiding
inside the gadget. What the algebra shows, and the picture hides, is why
the number is \(-1\) on exactly one word: the carry of a one-bit sum.
Elsewhere in the chapter the pictures win outright: letting go after any
turn (Result 19.9) is three slides through a cap, and in \emph{The
Closed Box} the watchers slide away by fusion alone, where the
blackboard needs a partial trace of a three-system state. The numbers of
§19.4 and §19.9, \(\tfrac{20}{27}\) and \(\tfrac1{12}\), are the
blackboard's alone.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-closed-box}{%
\section{§19.8 The Closed Box}\label{the-closed-box}}

Here is the chapter's master diagram. It is the watching scene of the
dialogue, drawn: a Cat asleep in a closed box, Achilles watching the
box, the Tortoise watching Achilles, the answer read from the Cat, and
both watchers' pages let go. It is also the shape of every run of §19.4:
points in, a process, one read wire out, the rest let go.

There are three systems, each started by a point. \textbf{The Cat's
wire} starts at a green point at rest, \(\ket0+\ket1\): its two basis
states stand for asleep and awake, in even measure. \textbf{Achilles's
page} starts at a red point at rest, \(\sqrt2\ket0\): blank. \textbf{The
Tortoise's page} starts the same way. There are two looks, each a joiner
(row 64): \textbf{Achilles's look} is a green spider on the Cat's wire
tied to a red spider on his page, and \textbf{the Tortoise's look} is a
green spider on Achilles's page tied to a red spider on hers. At the
end, the Cat's wire is read by the read-spider (row 68), which gives out
one classical wire, the answer, and both pages are let go (row 67).

The picture is drawn doubled and unfolded, as in Chapter 9: each quantum
line has its mirror copy below, in reflected order, so that the
Tortoise's copy lies nearest the middle and the Cat's lowest. Every
spider is at rest, so each mirror copy is drawn the same as its
original. Walk it by its lines. On the Cat's wire: from its point to
Achilles's look, and from the look to the read-spider; and the same two
on the copy. On Achilles's page: from its point to his look's red
spider, from there to the Tortoise's look's green spider, and from there
to the cap that lets the page go; the same three on the copy, the last
of them being the cap's other leg. On the Tortoise's page: from its
point to her look's red spider, and from there to the cap; and the same
two on the copy. The two looks' ties, and their copies. And, alone, the
classical answer, drawn with a double stroke. No two lines cross, and
every cap is the unnormalized one, \(\bra{00}+\bra{11}\).

We call the picture \textbf{The Closed Box}. Before evaluating it,
guess: does it matter that anyone watched? Achilles's page, after his
look, records the Cat; the Tortoise's page records Achilles's page. The
Cat's odds were even before anyone looked. Are they still?

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 19.12 (The Closed Box).} The Closed Box equals the Cat's
own green point at rest, on the answer wire, with the number \(1\): as a
classical vector, \((1,1)\). Normalized, the answer is asleep or awake
with odds \(\tfrac12\) and \(\tfrac12\), the Cat's own.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} \textbf{On the blackboard.} Undoubled, the three points
give \((\ket0+\ket1)\otimes\sqrt2\ket0\otimes\sqrt2\ket0\), top wire
first. Each look is \(\mathrm{CNOT}/\sqrt2\) (row 64): Achilles's look
gives \(\sqrt2\,(\ket{00}+\ket{11})\otimes\ket0\), and the Tortoise's
look gives \(\ket{000}+\ket{111}\), so all three records agree. Doubled,
the state is \(\ket\Psi\otimes\ket{\bar\Psi}\) with
\(\ket\Psi=\ket{000}+\ket{111}\). Letting go of both pages is the
partial trace over them: the Cat is left with \(\ket0\bra0+\ket1\bra1\).
The read-spider, \(\sum_i\ket i\bra{ii}\), takes the diagonal:
\((1,1)\).

\textbf{In the sketchbook,} by fusion and one loop. Each red point at
rest is joined by a plain wire to a red spider, so it fuses into it (row
57); each of those red spiders is left at rest with two legs, which is
bare wire (the identity card). So each look becomes a plain wire from
the green spider above it:

Now the Cat's point, the green spider of Achilles's look and the green
spider of the Tortoise's look are joined by plain wires, and all three
are green at rest: they fuse into one green spider (row 57), with three
legs, one to the read-spider and one to each cap; the same on the mirror
copy. The caps are plain wires between the two green spiders (only the
connectivity counts, row 63). Fuse the two along one cap (row 57); the
other cap becomes a loop. The read-spider is green at rest, so it fuses
in along one of its two legs, and its other leg becomes a loop too. Both
loops come off, with the number \(1\) each (row 90). What is left is one
green spider at rest with one leg, the classical wire: a green point at
rest, the Cat's own. \[=\;
