See \texttt{Code/Ch19/OneAnswerOut.py}. It builds \emph{The Closed Box}
line by line as drawn, checks its value, and lets PyZX's simplifier
reduce it to one green point at rest with the number \(1\).

A warning about that number. The Cat's point is unnormalized,
\(\ket0+\ket1\). The picture's value is the vector \((1,1)\), and if the
answer wire were closed as well, summing over both answers, the number
would be \(2\), not \(1\). Normalized, the odds are \(\tfrac12\) and
\(\tfrac12\).

The pictures made the watchers vanish, but only these watchers. Would
any watching do the same? Not any: a look that copied the Cat in another
basis could change its odds. If the Cat were surely asleep, \(\ket0\),
and a look copied its \(\ket\pm\) instead, the joint state would be
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket+\ket0+\ket-\ket1)\), and the Cat alone would be
left with \(\tfrac12(\ket+\bra++\ket-\bra-)=\tfrac12I\): asleep or awake
at even odds. But the looks in \emph{The Closed Box} are of two harmless
kinds.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 19.13 (whoever watched).} Let the Cat's wire, together
with any watchers' pages, be in any state. Apply any sequence of looks
of two kinds: (a) a look that copies the Cat's asleep-or-awake,
\(\sum_{c}\ket c\bra c\otimes U_c\), with \(\ket c\bra c\) on the Cat's
wire and any unitaries \(U_c\) on the pages; (b) any unitary on the
pages alone, which includes a look by one watcher at another. Then the
Cat's odds of asleep and awake are unchanged.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} Let \(\rho\) be the state and
\(\rho_{\mathrm{C}}=\operatorname{tr}_{\text{pages}}\rho\) the Cat's
part. Its odds are the diagonal entries
\(\bra c\rho_{\mathrm{C}}\ket c\). For (b),
\(\operatorname{tr}_{\text{pages}}\bigl((I\otimes V)\rho(I\otimes V^{\dagger})\bigr)=\rho_{\mathrm{C}}\),
since the trace does not change under \(V\). For (a), write
\(W=\sum_c\ket c\bra c\otimes U_c\). Then
\(\bra c\operatorname{tr}_{\text{pages}}(W\rho W^{\dagger})\ket c=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(U_c\,\bra c\rho\ket c\,U_c^{\dagger}\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bra c\rho\ket c=\bra c\rho_{\mathrm{C}}\ket c\),
where \(\bra c\rho\ket c\) is the block of \(\rho\) on the pages for the
Cat's value \(c\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch19/OneAnswerOut.py}, which checks it with random non-real
states for the Cat and both pages and random unitaries in both looks.

In \emph{The Closed Box} Achilles's look is of kind (a) and the
Tortoise's of kind (b). So the answer's odds are the box's own, whoever
watched, by a look of these kinds. That is all a closed box gives out,
and nobody who only takes note of it changes it.

In the dialogue the same picture is the Crab's lute. Each paired course,
a string and its unison twin, stands for a line and its mirror copy; the
single top string stands for the answer, which has no twin, as a record
has none. It is an analogy and no more: a mirror copy carries the
conjugate of its line, and a unison twin carries nothing of the kind.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{watchers-watched}{%
\section{§19.9 Watchers Watched}\label{watchers-watched}}

Take stock. The pictures we have drawn since Chapter 1 form a theory of
processes, a dagger compact closed category, in which the mirror is the
dagger (Result 19.1). Every card of the deck balances, number and all,
in any surroundings (Result 19.2). One card was missing, the Euler card;
with it, three more cards follow (Results 19.3 to 19.5), and the hinge
that Chapter 17 could only check is a rewrite (Result 19.6, proved
twice). A dare was won with the cards alone (Result 19.7). For each of
four kinds of picture a complete deck is known, quoted with its source
and its scope (Result 19.8), and letting go after any turn is letting go
(Result 19.9). A vote of three runs turns two in three into twenty in
twenty-seven (Result 19.10). One equation with an eighth turn shows that
a deck can be sound and still not enough (Result 19.11). And a closed
box gives out one answer, with the odds of what is inside it, whoever
watched, by a look that copies the Cat's asleep-or-awake or watches only
the watchers (Results 19.12 and 19.13).

The last result had a condition, and the condition matters. Its watchers
only took note. What if a watcher could do more: undo a whole room,
watcher and all, and ask it a question? And what if the question is not
about one box but about every box of a kind? Two recent results answer
these, and we report them at the level of a survey: stated, quoted, and
not proved.

\hypertarget{watchers-who-can-undo-a-room}{%
\subsection{Watchers who can undo a
room}\label{watchers-who-can-undo-a-room}}

Frauchiger and Renner begin from Wigner. In their words: ``In 1967,
Wigner proposed an argument, known as the Wigner's friend paradox, which
should show that `quantum mechanics cannot have unlimited validity'.'' A
friend \(F\) in a sealed laboratory \(L\) measures a spin and sees one
result. A watcher \(W\) outside, who has not seen it, may treat the
whole laboratory, friend and all, as one quantum system in a
superposition. Frauchiger and Renner then build a thought experiment
with two sealed laboratories and two outside watchers.

In laboratory \(\bar L\), agent \(\bar F\) runs a random generator that
gives \(r=\) heads with probability \(\tfrac13\) and tails with
\(\tfrac23\). On heads she prepares a spin in the state
\(\ket\downarrow\); on tails, in
\(\ket\to=\sqrt{1/2}\,(\ket\downarrow+\ket\uparrow)\); and she sends it
to agent \(F\) in laboratory \(L\), who measures it and records
\(z=-\tfrac12\) for \(\ket\downarrow\) or \(z=+\tfrac12\) for
\(\ket\uparrow\). Then watcher \(\bar W\) measures the whole of
\(\bar L\), and watcher \(W\) the whole of \(L\), each in a basis that
contains a state called \(\ket{\mathrm{ok}}\), and each announces ``ok''
or ``fail''. The rounds are repeated until both announce ``ok''.
Frauchiger and Renner credit the preparation and the choice of
measurements to ``a construction due to Hardy''.

\textbf{On the blackboard.} Write heads as \(0\) and tails as \(1\), and
\(z=-\tfrac12\) as \(0\) and \(z=+\tfrac12\) as \(1\), and let each
laboratory's state stand for its record. Before the watchers act, the
two laboratories are in
\[\psi\;=\;\tfrac1{\sqrt3}\bigl(\ket{00}+\ket{10}+\ket{11}\bigr),\]
laboratory \(\bar L\) first: heads with \(\ket\downarrow\), or tails
with \(\ket\to\) spread over both records. For both laboratories
\(\ket{\mathrm{ok}}=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket0-\ket1)\): Frauchiger and
Renner's \(\sqrt{1/2}(\ket{\bar h}-\ket{\bar t})\) for \(\bar L\) and
\(\sqrt{1/2}(\ket{-\tfrac12}-\ket{+\tfrac12})\) for \(L\).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 19.14 (the numbers of the sealed rooms).} Exactly,
\[(\bra1\otimes\bra{\mathrm{ok}})\,\psi=0,\qquad(\bra0\otimes\bra1)\,\psi=0,\qquad(\bra{\mathrm{ok}}\otimes\bra0)\,\psi=0,\]
and
\((\bra{\mathrm{ok}}\otimes\bra{\mathrm{ok}})\,\psi=\tfrac1{2\sqrt3}\),
so both watchers announce ``ok'' with probability \(\tfrac1{12}\).
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof.} The first: the tails part of \(\psi\) is
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt3}\ket1(\ket0+\ket1)\), and
\(\bra{\mathrm{ok}}(\ket0+\ket1)=0\). The second: the heads part is
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt3}\ket0\ket0\), which has no \(\ket1\) in \(L\). The
third: the part with \(L\) at \(0\) is
\(\tfrac1{\sqrt3}(\ket0+\ket1)\ket0\), and again
\(\bra{\mathrm{ok}}(\ket0+\ket1)=0\). The last:
\(\bra{\mathrm{ok}}\otimes\bra{\mathrm{ok}}=\tfrac12(\bra{00}-\bra{01}-\bra{10}+\bra{11})\),
which meets \(\psi\) in \(\tfrac1{2\sqrt3}(1-1+1)\); squared,
\(\tfrac1{12}\). \(\;\blacksquare\) See
\texttt{Code/Ch19/WatchersWatched.py}.

Each zero is a certainty held by an agent, in Frauchiger and Renner's
analysis. \(\bar F\), having seen tails, is certain that \(W\) will
announce ``fail'' (the first zero). \(F\), having seen \(z=+\tfrac12\),
is certain that \(r\) was not heads (the second). \(\bar W\), having
announced ``ok'', is certain that \(F\) saw \(z=+\tfrac12\) (the third).
Chained, the certainties say: if \(\bar W\) announces ``ok'', then \(F\)
saw \(z=+\tfrac12\), so \(r\) was tails, so \(W\) will announce
``fail''. Yet one round in twelve, both announce ``ok'', and the
experiment halts on exactly that round.

Frauchiger and Renner name three assumptions that together give the
contradiction: quantum theory everywhere (Q), that an agent ``can be
certain that a given proposition holds whenever the quantum-mechanical
Born rule assigns probability 1 to it''; consistency (C), that ``the
different agents' predictions are not contradictory''; and single
outcomes (S), that ``from the viewpoint of an agent who carries out a
particular measurement, this measurement has one single outcome''.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 19.15 (Frauchiger and Renner's theorem; quoted, not
proved).} ``Any theory that satisfies assumptions (Q), (C), and (S)
yields contradictory statements when applied to the Gedankenexperiment
described in Section 2.1.''
\end{quote}

And, in their introduction: ``The theorem itself is neutral in the sense
that it does not tell us which of these three assumptions is wrong.''
This book takes no side either. The numbers of Result 19.14 are all we
have checked.

\textbf{In the sketchbook.} The state \(\psi\) is a sum of two pictures:
\[\sqrt3\,\psi\;=\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  zsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=green!55,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt}]
  \path (0,-1.3) (0,1.3);
  \draw[wire] (0,0.7) -- (1.6,0.7);
  \draw[wire] (0,-0.7) -- (1.6,-0.7);
  \node[zsp] at (0,0.7) {};
  \node[zsp] at (0,-0.7) {};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;-\;\tfrac12\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd, baseline=-0.25em, x=1.2em, y=1.2em,
  xsp/.style={circle,draw,line width=0.9pt,fill=red!75,minimum size=1.0em,inner sep=0pt},
  ph/.style={font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt}]
  \path (0,-1.3) (0,1.3);
  \draw[wire] (0,0.7) -- (1.6,0.7);
  \draw[wire] (0,-0.7) -- (1.6,-0.7);
  \node[xsp] at (0,0.7) {};
  \node[xsp,label={[ph]left:{$\pi$}}] at (0,-0.7) {};
\end{tikzpicture}\] Two green points at rest make
\(\ket{00}+\ket{01}+\ket{10}+\ket{11}\); a red point at rest beside a
red point at a half makes \(2\ket{01}\); half of that, taken away,
removes the one corner, \(\ket{01}\), that \(\psi\) lacks.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Coecke's Sketchbook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{Four closed pictures and a sum.} Every number of Result 19.14 is a
closed picture, or rather a sum of two. The effect \(\bra{\mathrm{ok}}\)
is \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) times a green spider turned \(\pi\) with one leg;
the effects \(\bra0\) and \(\bra1\) are \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) times red
effects at rest and at a half. Close each of the two pictures above with
a pair of these, and each closed picture reduces, by copy and fusion, to
a number; subtract, as the sum says. Take the first zero. In the first
term, \(\bra{\mathrm{ok}}\) on the lower wire meets a green point at
rest; the two fuse into a green spider with no legs, turned \(\pi\),
whose number is \(1+e^{i\pi}=0\). In the second term, the effect
\(\bra1\) on the upper wire meets a red point at rest, and they fuse the
same way, to \(0\). The zeros are exact cancellations, and the
\(\tfrac1{12}\) is one term surviving. What the pictures do \emph{not}
do is add: a sum of pictures is not one picture, so the subtraction is
the blackboard's, and so is the paradox. The pictures agree with every
number and settle nothing about which assumption to drop.
\end{quote}

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Feynman's Notebook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{From Wigner's friend to Frauchiger and Renner.} Frauchiger and
Renner's paper, ``Quantum theory cannot consistently describe the use of
itself'', was posted in 2016. Their first figure shows two older
arguments. In Wigner's, as they tell it, the outside watcher, ``having
no access to'' the friend's result, would assign a superposition to the
whole laboratory; Frauchiger and Renner point out that this is no
contradiction, since the friend and the watcher simply know different
things. Deutsch ``later noted that agent W could in principle test this
state assignment by applying a carefully designed measurement'' to the
laboratory. Frauchiger and Renner's step was to let agents use quantum
theory to reason about other agents who also use quantum theory: ``such
a self-referential use of the theory yields contradictory claims''. They
are careful about the laboratory itself: ``we do not claim that the
experiment is technologically feasible''. A watcher who can undo a room
is a thought experiment, and its purpose, they write, is ``to scrutinise
the consistency of our currently best available theories''.
\end{quote}

The Closed Box is consistent with all of this. Nobody in it undoes
anybody: the Tortoise watches Achilles, and never unmixes him. Result
19.13 needs exactly that, and it is exactly what Frauchiger and Renner's
watchers do not do.

\hypertarget{a-question-about-all-games}{%
\subsection{A question about all
games}\label{a-question-about-all-games}}

The second result is about questions of a different size. A
\textbf{nonlocal game} is played by two or more players in separate
rooms. A referee sends each a question; each answers without hearing the
others; the referee declares a win or a loss by a fixed rule. The
players may agree on a strategy beforehand and may share an entangled
state. The best winning probability over all such quantum strategies is
the game's \emph{entangled value}, written \(\mathrm{val}^*\). Chapter 7
played two such games: the CHSH game, whose best quantum strategy wins
with probability \(\cos^2(\pi/8)\) (Tsirelson's bound, stated there),
and a game for three players who, sharing one three-legged state, win
every time.

Ji, Natarajan, Vidick, Wright and Yuen (posted January 2020) proved
``that the class \(\mathrm{MIP}^*\) of languages that can be decided by
a classical verifier interacting with multiple all-powerful quantum
provers sharing entanglement is equal to the class RE of recursively
enumerable languages''. RE contains problems no computer can decide,
among them ``the Halting problem, which is to decide whether a given
Turing machine eventually halts''. The inclusion
\(\mathrm{MIP}^*\subseteq\mathrm{RE}\) is the easy direction, which they
note first; their main result is the reverse,
\(\mathrm{RE}\subseteq\mathrm{MIP}^*\), and they obtain it by building,
for every Turing machine \(M\), a nonlocal game \(G_M\) such that
\(\mathrm{val}^*(G_M)=1\) if \(M\) halts and
\(\mathrm{val}^*(G_M)\le\tfrac12\) if it does not.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Result 19.16 (\(\mathrm{MIP}^*=\mathrm{RE}\); Ji, Natarajan,
Vidick, Wright and Yuen; quoted, not proved).}
\(\mathrm{MIP}^*=\mathrm{RE}\). ``In particular for any
\(0<\varepsilon<1\), it is an undecidable problem to determine whether a
given nonlocal game has entangled value 1 or at most \(1-\varepsilon\)
(promised that one is the case).''
\end{quote}

``Using a known connection'', they add, the result gives a negative
answer to Tsirelson's problem and a refutation of Connes' embedding
conjecture, one a question about quantum correlations, the other a
conjecture ``from the theory of von Neumann algebras''. We name them and
do not explain them.

The games of the proof refer to themselves. The authors describe a
procedure that compresses games, and write: ``Intuitively, one would
expect that iterating this procedure and `taking the limit' gives'' the
family of games they need. ``Formally, we do not take such a limit but
instead define directly the family of games \ldots{} as a fixed point of
the Turing machine that implements the compression procedure.'' A
footnote names the tool: ``Kleene's recursion theorem''. The dialogue's
Genie, whose answer to a question about all questions goes up an endless
chain of Meta-Genies and comes back at once, is the intuitive picture,
the iteration and its limit. The paper's proof is not a limit but a
fixed point.

\vskip 0pt plus 4\baselineskip\penalty-100\vskip 0pt plus
-4\baselineskip

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Coecke's Sketchbook.}\nopagebreak

\emph{A strategy is a picture; the question is not.} Draw a strategy for
a nonlocal game: a state on two wires, a cup if you like, then on each
side a box chosen by that side's question, then a read on each side.
Each winning probability is a closed doubled picture, and the pictures
of this book evaluate it exactly. Chapter 7 drew one such strategy and
read off its value. So for any one strategy the sketchbook can say, with
the right cards, everything the blackboard can. What Result 19.16 is
about is different: whether the \emph{best} of all strategies, over
boxes of every size and states on wires of every number, wins every time
or loses at least some fixed fraction of the time. That is a question
about all pictures of a kind at once. No rewrite of one picture into
another can answer it, and the theorem says that no procedure of any
kind, drawn or computed, answers it for every game.
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{the-books-rule-honestly}{%
\subsection{The book's rule, honestly}\label{the-books-rule-honestly}}

This book has proved each chapter's headline twice, and the chapter's
question asked whether that is always possible. Here is the honest
answer.

Where a complete deck is known, yes. For pictures whose turns are
multiples of \(\tfrac\pi2\), or of \(\tfrac\pi4\), or anything at all,
and for the doubled pictures of the \(\tfrac\pi2\) kind with letting go,
every equation the blackboard proves between two such pictures has a
chain of rewrites by that kind's deck, with the scope its authors give
it, Backens's up to non-zero numbers (Result 19.8). Whatever the numbers
say, the pictures can say, \emph{with the right cards}. The book's
second proof is licensed there.

But the book's own deck is not shown to be any of those decks, and the
book's own chapters did not always reach a chain. The hinge closes one
recorded gap: Chapter 17's step (iv) is now a rewrite, from the Euler
card, the rule the sources say cannot be derived from the others of
Backens's calculus. Other gaps stay open, and we say so. In Chapter 14
the sketchbook borrowed the kickback of a general box from the
blackboard; a box that stands for an unknown unitary is not a picture of
any of the kinds above, and no completeness theorem speaks of it. In
Chapter 15 a drawing was checked by its matrix. In Chapter 16 re-tying
and the pivot were stated, not derived; the Euler card is now in the
deck, but the derivation is not given here. The rule ``proved twice'' is
a rule of this book's writing, and completeness does not make it a
theorem about this book.

And some questions were never the pictures' to answer: the number of
steps a chain needs, the class a problem belongs to, the value of the
best strategy in every game, and which of three natural assumptions the
watchers of the sealed rooms must give up.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

The chapter's question has an answer. If two pictures always give the
same numbers, the rules can turn one into the other, \emph{if the rules
are the right ones for the kind of picture}: for quarter turns, for
eighth turns, for any turns, and for quarter turns with letting go, such
rules are known, and for eighth turns with letting go they were left
open in 2019. This book's own deck lacked one card, the Euler card, and
with it the step Chapter 17 could only check became a rewrite. Every
card balances, so every rewrite is true; a closed box gives out one
answer, with odds that no watcher who only takes note can change; and no
procedure, drawn or computed, decides every question of the Genie's
kind.

The chapters are done, but there is one more rewrite. In the Epilogue,
\emph{The Empty Diagram}, the last rewrite removes the last wire, and
what is left is the empty diagram: the number \(1\), where the Prelude
began.

\hypertarget{postlude-on-the-same-sheet}{%
\chapter{Postlude on the Same Sheet}\label{postlude-on-the-same-sheet}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\emph{冬晴に}\\
\emph{見ず仕舞ひけり}\\
\emph{白き紙}

\emph{fuyubare ni}\\
\emph{mizu shimaikeri}\\
\emph{shiroki kami}

\emph{In the clear winter}\\
\emph{put away, and never seen ---}\\
\emph{the white sheet is left.}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\emph{{[}Achilles's table, a clear morning after a storm. Achilles and
the Tortoise come in together; he carries a stone bottle.{]}}

\emph{{[}Outside, the storm has left the sky washed clear and the wet
roofs shining; drops still fall quick from the eaves into the brimming
water-butt in the yard. The sun is up, low and pale, and lies on the
floor by the window, not yet on the table. The grate is swept and cold,
no fire laid, and the wall above the hearth is bare. The table is bare
too, with nothing on it to write with; Achilles's shawl hangs over the
back of his chair.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Home at last. The lane is all puddles from the Crab's
door to mine.

\textbf{Tortoise:} The storm blew itself out before dawn, and the Crab
sent us off with his cocoa, still warm.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}He sets the bottle on the table, fetches two
cups to stand beside it, and sits down.{]}} A whole night and not a
wink. I asked the Cat my one question, and it said awake; this morning I
mean to ask nothing.

\textbf{Tortoise:} \emph{{[}She takes the chair beside him.{]}} Good.
Did you keep what I gave you in the autumn?

\emph{{[}He opens the drawer on his side of the table, takes out a sheet
of plain paper, blank on both sides, and lays it flat before them,
leaving the drawer open.{]}}

\textbf{Achilles:} Your picture from the autumn. You told me to keep it,
and I kept it, in there beside my old coin.

\textbf{Tortoise:} May I have the coin too? The one I kept under my foot
from the middle of one evening to the end of the next, and you never saw
how it lay. One toss, and this time neither of us will see.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}He takes the coin from the drawer, puts it
in her hand, and rests his hands on his cup.{]}} Toss away.

\emph{{[}The coin lies in the Tortoise's fingers; the sheet lies blank;
the drawer stands open. She tosses the coin, it turns in the air, and
she claps it flat under her palm on the sheet. Now her palm lies on the
sheet over the coin, one face up, and neither of them has seen which.
What has changed: the coin is down, its face unknown. What has held
still: the sheet, blank round her hand; Achilles's hands on his cup.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} What is it worth, the whole of it, if we never look?

\textbf{Achilles:} A half. Heads, a half.

\emph{{[}The Tortoise lets the answer stand. Her palm lies flat over the
coin; the drawer is open below the table's edge. Without lifting it she
slides her palm, and the coin beneath, off the sheet and over the edge;
the coin drops into the open drawer with one small sound, and with her
other hand she pushes the drawer shut at once, neither of them looking
down. What has changed: her palm is empty; the coin is in the drawer,
its face never seen by anyone. What has held still: the sheet, exactly
as it lay before the coin came down on it.{]}}

\emph{{[}In the yard a last drop gathers at the eaves, lets go, and
falls into the brimming butt. It is one with the water at once, and the
surface holds the washed sky just as it held it before. Achilles looks
from the window to his cup, and says nothing yet.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} I didn't ask about heads.

\textbf{Achilles:} Heads a half, tails a half, and it lies one way or
the other for certain. A half and a half: once. Had it been loaded five
to one, five sixths and one sixth: once still. Whatever way it was set,
once.

\textbf{Tortoise:} And what is left on the table?

\textbf{Achilles:} Your sheet, as it was. Worth once, as we found it in
the autumn: the very picture you showed me then. \ldots Oh.

\emph{{[}For a while neither of them says anything. The eaves have gone
quiet, and the sun has come round onto the table and lies there, pale
and warm. Achilles sits back and rubs his eyes; the Tortoise rests her
hands against the stone bottle, still warm.{]}}

\textbf{Tortoise:} In the autumn you asked me why a picture of nothing
should come to one, and not to nothing.

\textbf{Achilles:} Because it is what is left when a thing is let go
unseen. Whatever the thing was, let go with all its chances together, it
comes to once, not to nothing. So your sheet is a picture after all: the
picture of what is left when the last thing is let go.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Then the question kept, as I said it would.
\emph{{[}She pours the cocoa.{]}} Drink it while it's warm; the sun is
on the table.

\textbf{Achilles:} \emph{{[}He puts his shawl round his shoulders.{]}}
Awake all night, and only now awake. I shan't open the drawer to see how
the coin lies.

\textbf{Tortoise:} Then leave it where it lies, and the sheet where you
laid it. The question has its answer, and what is left is what was here
in the autumn: my sheet, as blank as it came.

\emph{{[}Achilles drinks his cocoa in his shawl, and the Tortoise stays
where she is. Outside, the butt stands full and still under the dry
eaves, holding the whole of the sky, and the puddles in the lane are
going down. Indoors the sun lies on the table, on the cups and the stone
bottle and the sheet where he laid it, and nobody opens the drawer.
Neither of them moves; there is nothing left to do, and no hurry.{]}}

\hypertarget{epilogue-the-empty-diagram}{%
\chapter{Epilogue: The Empty Diagram}\label{epilogue-the-empty-diagram}}

\emph{--- Postlude on the Same Sheet ---}

What is left when the last wire goes?

Every picture since the Prelude has had something on it, and wires have
come and gone. This last page follows one wire to its end, and asks what
remains, and what that is worth.

\hypertarget{the-last-wire}{%
\section{The Last Wire}\label{the-last-wire}}

A wire can leave a picture in three ways. It can be \textbf{yanked}: an
S-bend pulled straight into one plain wire (Theorem 6.2, row 42). It can
be \textbf{fused} away: two spiders of one colour slide together along
the wire between them (row 57), and a plain wire from a spider back to
itself comes off with the number \(1\) (Chapter 19's card \emph{A loop
comes off}). And it can be \textbf{let go} into the discard, the ground
symbol of Chapter 9, which asks it no question at all (row 67). Earlier
chapters closed pictures into numbers (Theorem 2.1's \(1\), §9.3's
\(2\)) and wrote the number down; the last rewrite ends on the blank
itself.

Here is the picture this page undoes: a state \(\psi\) of one wire, let
go.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd]
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2,0);
  \node[sdstate, text height=1.5ex, text depth=0.5ex] at (0,0) {$\psi$};
  \sdground{2}{0}
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

The one line stands for two: the wire of a state is doubled, the system
and its conjugate copy (row 66), and the ground symbol is a cap joining
the copies (row 67). On the blackboard the discard, written \(\top\), is
the trace: \(\top\colon\rho\mapsto\operatorname{tr}\rho\).

An example first. Take \(\ket+=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket0+\ket1)\), whose
matrix Chapter 9 computed in §9.2:
\(\ket+\bra+=\tfrac12\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\).
Let it go and the trace adds the diagonal:
\(\operatorname{tr}\ket+\bra+=\tfrac12+\tfrac12=1\).

\textbf{Letting go is not looking.} A look closes the wire with an
effect (Chapter 2), which picks one answer and weighs it: the effect
\(0\) on the doubled \(\ket+\), a \(\bra0\) on each copy, gives
\(|\braket{0|+}|^2=\tfrac12\), the square of the amplitude \(1/\sqrt2\).
Letting go asks nothing, and weighs every answer at once. Reading an
answer and then forgetting it is letting go (Result 9.5).

\textbf{A wire does not always go for nothing.} A bare loop, a cup
closed by a cap, is \(2\): the doubled bare cup, discarded, is
\(\operatorname{tr}I=2\) (§9.3). An unnormalized point let go is \(2\)
as well, since \(\ket0+\ket1\) meets itself in \(1+1\). With
\(\tfrac12\) beside it the cup is the maximally mixed state (row 69), a
system cupped to its own mirror copy; let go, it closes into the loop,
and \(\tfrac12\times2=1\). That is the dialogue's covered fair coin: a
half and a half. So the last wire goes with the number \(1\) only
because what it carried was a state, with \(\braket{\psi|\psi}=1\).

\hypertarget{the-rosetta-table-18}{%
\section{The Rosetta Table}\label{the-rosetta-table-18}}

Two rows, following Chapter 19's row 152. Row 153 gives the Prelude's
picture the row it was left without; its right-hand column is a picture,
the empty diagram, not row 152's ``no picture''. Neither adds a new
picture element.

\begingroup\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.5}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1250}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4375}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4375}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\#
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
153 & the number \(1\): a process from no wire to no wire, the
\(1\times1\) matrix \((1)\) & \textbf{the empty diagram}: nothing drawn,
no wire in and none out; a picture, not row 152's ``no picture''; the
Prelude's page, given its row \\
154 & \(\operatorname{tr}\ket\psi\bra\psi=\braket{\psi\vert\psi}=1\) for
every state \(\ket\psi\) (row 72 with no wire in) & \textbf{a state let
go is the empty diagram}: a state box, a wire and the discard \(=\)

\end{longtable}

\endgroup

\hypertarget{the-theorem-twice-20}{%
\section{The Theorem, Twice}\label{the-theorem-twice-20}}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Theorem (the last rewrite).} For every state \(\psi\) of one
wire, the picture ``\(\psi\), then let go'' is the empty diagram:
\(\operatorname{tr}\ket\psi\bra\psi=1\), exactly, scalar included.
\end{quote}

\emph{Proof idea.} To let a state go is to meet it with its own mirror
image, and that meeting is the number \(1\).

\hypertarget{diracs-blackboard-20}{%
\subsection{Dirac's Blackboard}\label{diracs-blackboard-20}}

Letting go is taking the trace (row 67). Write
\(\ket\psi=\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1\). Then

\[\operatorname{tr}\ket\psi\bra\psi\;=\;\operatorname{tr}\begin{pmatrix}\alpha\bar\alpha&\alpha\bar\beta\\ \beta\bar\alpha&\beta\bar\beta\end{pmatrix}\;=\;\alpha\bar\alpha+\beta\bar\beta\;=\;\braket{\psi|\psi}\;=\;1\]

by Theorem 2.1. The answer is the \(1\times1\) matrix \((1)\), a process
from no wire to no wire: the number \(1\), which is the empty diagram
(Theorem 0.1). \(\;\blacksquare\)

\hypertarget{coeckes-sketchbook-14}{%
\subsection{Coecke's Sketchbook}\label{coeckes-sketchbook-14}}

Three moves:

\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd]
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (2,0);
  \node[sdstate, text height=1.5ex, text depth=0.5ex] at (0,0) {$\psi$};
  \sdground{2}{0}
\end{tikzpicture}
\;\;\overset{\text{unfold}\vphantom{g}}{=}\;\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd]
  \draw[wire] (0,1.2) -- (2.4,1.2);
  \draw[wire] (0,-1.2) -- (2.4,-1.2);
  \node[sdstate, text height=1.5ex, text depth=0.5ex] at (0,1.2) {$\psi$};
  \node[sdstate, text height=1.5ex, text depth=0.5ex] at (0,-1.2) {$\psi^{*}$};
  \sdcap{2.4}{1.2}{-1.2}
\end{tikzpicture}
\;\;\overset{\text{bend}\vphantom{g}}{=}\;\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd]
  \draw[wire] (0,0) -- (3.6,0);
  \node[sdstate, text height=1.5ex, text depth=0.5ex] at (0,0) {$\psi$};
  \node[sdeffect, text height=1.5ex, text depth=0.5ex] at (3.6,0) {$\psi$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\;\;\overset{\text{remove}\vphantom{g}}{=}\;\;
\begin{tikzpicture}[sd]\path (0,0) rectangle (5,3);\end{tikzpicture}\]

\textbf{Unfold the discard.} The ground symbol is shorthand for the cap
on a system's two copies (§9.3; rows 66, 67), and a state is its two
copies side by side, \(\psi\) above and its conjugate copy \(\psi^{*}\)
below (§9.2). The cap is the unnormalized \(\bra{00}+\bra{11}\) of
Chapter 6, and its scalar is carried, not dropped. One line has become
two.

\textbf{Carry the copy round the bend.} A box slid round a bend arrives
transposed (Theorem 6.4 in its cap form, rows 43--44), as Chapter 9 slid
the conjugate copy of its isometry round a cap to prove causality
(§9.6). A state is a box with no wire in, and states slide too: neither
proof of Theorem 6.4 needs the box to have a wire in (Chapter 6, §6.4).
So \(\psi^{*}\) arrives on the upper line as
\((\psi^{*})^{T}=\psi^{\dagger}\): the effect \(\psi\), the state's
mirror image, because the mirror conjugates (rows 10, 16). Two lines
have become one.

\textbf{Remove the closed picture.} A state meets its own mirror image
in the number \(1\) (Theorem 2.1, row 14); a closed picture is its
number (row 11); and the number \(1\) is the empty diagram (Theorem
0.1). The last term is the empty diagram: nothing is drawn there. The
last wire has gone. \(\;\blacksquare\)

The theorem is Result 9.4, causality, with nothing going in. There, a
doubled isometry capped by a discard left a bare discard, because its
mirror image undid it. Here the isometry takes no wire in, so it is a
state; its mirror undoes it, \(\braket{\psi|\psi}=1\); and no discard is
left over, because no wire is. Chapter 9 already let its fresh pointer
go this way (proof of Result 9.6). Nothing new is proved; what is new is
where it lands.

A mixed state is a weighted list of pure ones whose weights sum to \(1\)
(§9.2), so it too lets go to \(1\); that weighted sum belongs to the
blackboard, since a sum of pictures is not one picture.

\hypertarget{the-verdict-20}{%
\subsection{The verdict}\label{the-verdict-20}}

The blackboard wins on length, honestly. Its proof is one line: the
trace of \(\ket\psi\bra\psi\) is \(\braket{\psi|\psi}\), which is \(1\).
The sketchbook needs three moves, and its last move \emph{is} the
blackboard's fact, Theorem 2.1, read as a picture.

What the sketchbook shows, and the blackboard cannot, is a wire going:
one line drawn, two unfolded, one bent, then none. The blackboard's
answer was a \(1\times1\) matrix from the start, and it never had a wire
to lose. The rewrite proves an equality of processes and nothing more;
here, that was all there was to prove.

\hypertarget{the-empty-diagram-1}{%
\section{The Empty Diagram}\label{the-empty-diagram-1}}

The Prelude would not say what a diagram is; now it can be said. A
diagram is pieces joined and read from left to right. One with no wire
coming in and none going out is closed, and a closed diagram is a number
(Chapter 2). The last term of the chain is the closed diagram with
nothing in it: what the last rewrite leaves. Its number is \(1\), and it
is the Prelude's picture, drawn again as it was drawn there:

\[\begin{tikzpicture}[sd]\path (0,0) rectangle (12,6);\end{tikzpicture}\;=\;1\]

\begin{center}
\emph{The Empty Diagram.}
\end{center}

The Prelude showed this page before anything had been drawn, and said
the book would come back to such a page only at its end. Here it is,
reached from the other side: a state, let go unseen, leaves exactly
this. It is worth what it was worth then, one, and nothing is drawn
after it.
